Śrī.
The *Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*, composed by the venerable Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra.
(The third section: the Kriyāpāda).
Now begins the first chapter.
Having first prostrated before Śiva, Śakti, the Lord of the Command (Sādeśa), Gaṇeśvara, Śuddhavidyā, as well as Vāṇī and the Primordial Dharma, we shall now expound [this work]. 1.1.
Indeed, the general [types of] mantras pertaining to dharma, artha, and kāma have been shown in the first half by means of two verses; the remaining [particular types] are now being described. (1–2)
Through the primary dharma, consciousness attains enjoyments and liberation from the arising of both seen and unseen fruits; the Supreme Lord is the object of that dharma. (1.3)
Now, therefore, from the Vaiśeṣika sūtra beginning with "Dharma," it is stated that the purpose of dharma is liberation (mokṣa) and great worldly prosperity (abhyudaya). (1.4)
Various kinds of dharmas are proclaimed as impelled by their respective scriptures;
however, those are not the primary dharmas, for the primary dharmas are those declared by Śiva. (1.5)
Indeed, the primary scripture was taught in every respect by Śiva, who is free from the transformations of *māyā*, pure, of stainless nature, and the creator of all. (1.6)

For he, Śiva, is the cause of the manifold effects extending from Māyā up to the level of Bhūmi; he is both the creator and the transformer, and he is the object of the three means of valid cognition. 1.7
For this world is possessed of parts and is traditionally held to have an intelligent creator, because it is an effect—whatever is such [an effect] is like a jar, a cloth, or the like. (1.8)
And thus it has been said: "Therefore, that which was stated as the probandum is beyond doubt;
there exists that one Śiva, the creator, who is indeed distinct from all others. (1.9)
Established through yogic perception as well as through inference and scripture, how could its distinction from all other [means of knowledge] not exist? (1.10)
Śiva is distinct from all others because he is beginningless and stainless;
for while all [others] are possessed of impurity, whatever is inherently stainless [is Śiva]. (1.11)
Just as gold is distinct from copper and other such [metals], so too is that [Reality] distinct from those;
this is well-known and has been stated here, and it is also said in the Kiraṇatantra: || 1-12 ||
Due to its connection with beginningless impurity, the state of being stained resides in the gem;
due to its freedom from beginningless impurity, the state of being stainless resides in Śiva. (1.13)
Thus it is said. Rāmakaṇṭha also says:

"That which is the omniscient and omnipotent, pure Śiva, and likewise that which is the limited-knower and impure Self—belonging to these two, Śiva and the Self, are their respective pure and impure natures, characterized by stainlessness and the presence of impurity. And in the venerable *Lambita* [Tantra] as well:
"There was one Śiva, a Person, distinct from all others."
Thus it is said:
"Therefore, the selves (ātman) are traditionally held to be atomic (aṇu) and inherently impure due to beginningless [taints]."
The Great Lord is beginningless, stainless, pure, and indeed one;
if Śiva is stainless and one, he is distinct from all others. (1-14)
How can there be stainless Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras) who are abodes of Śiva? Yet, you yourself have stated that liberation from impurity occurs through initiation into Śiva. (1-15)
When the state of being Śiva is established for those who have been initiated according to the Śaiva Āgama,
even these [initiates] are still subordinate to this [supreme] Śiva, because they possess the nature of Śiva only through Him.
Therefore, it is indeed improper to claim that Śiva is distinct from all [others], because they were previously impure prior to their initiation into nirvāṇa. (1.17)
For after initiation, there is indeed stainlessness and the manifestation of Śiva-nature;
yet their Śiva-nature is traditionally held to have a beginning, owing to the grace of Śiva. (1.18)
Śiva, bestowing grace upon other atoms by means of his beginninglessly established Śiva-nature, is autonomous and distinct even from them. (1-19)
Here, the great elephants at the end of the three Vedas proclaim the non-duality of selves:
"Brahman alone is one without a second; how then can there be other selves? (1.20)
(3) From what could there be any distinctness for that in which difference is not established?
If there is no village, from where is the boundary, and for whom is Śiva the benefactor? (1-21)
When these [scriptures] which speak thus should be considered a valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa), then the consequence of duality follows; otherwise, they would indeed be non-authoritative. (1.22)
In this regard, by means of their respective statements, an answer is given to each subsequent [objection];
thus, what is established as dualism is, in brief, sublated by non-duality. (1.23)
Only when Brāhmaṇas and others exist do non-Brāhmaṇas and others come into being;
therefore, the acceptance of bondage and liberation would be contrary to that doctrine. (1.24)

When everything is indeed the one Brahman and no bound souls exist at all, then everyone is already liberated; therefore, what is the fruit of hearing [the scriptures] and other such practices? (1.25)
If [the Self] were truly manifest, approaching a teacher would be useless; why then should it be saluted separately?
Furthermore, the distinction between knower and known, as well as knowledge itself, would be rendered meaningless. (1.26)
The acceptance of such distinctions is also seen in the Vedānta texts, because duality is indeed well-known, as is the possession of qualities by the Self. (1.27)

What is the use of saying much more in this regard? Whether it be ignorance (*avidyā*), or darkness (*tamas*), or illusion (*māyā*), that which is other than the means of liberation must certainly be abandoned by one who seeks liberation.

Because it is seen in scripture that "the knower of Brahman attains the Supreme," it follows that one who does not know Brahman does not attain it; thus, a distinction is established by valid means of knowledge. (1.29)

Likewise, because there is no reason for a single self, the Buddhists who advocate a doctrine of a void self have been refuted here, even though they wander about due to a delusion of the intellect. (1.30)
Since action performed by an intelligent being yields its fruit, knowledge is therefore not without a cause for those who maintain that the fruit arises from activity. (1.31)
That karma would either be momentary or dependent and insentient;
it could not lead to the accomplishment of such a fruit without an intelligent cause. (1.32)
Since the attainment of the fruit of action occurs through their insentient mantras and such [insentient] ritual acts, the wise agent must surely be known as Śiva. (1.33)
The unmanifest, whose nature consists of the gunas, is also the material cause of the universe;
however, like a lump of clay [is insufficient for the production of a jar], it is not by itself a sufficient cause. (1.34)
Also by such passages as, "For the one unborn [Self], rejoicing, lies along [with the many]," and so forth:
"He who is beyond that which is merged in primordial nature (prakṛti) is Maheśvara. (1.35)
From such statements as these, even the Sāṅkhyas must seek Maheśvara, because the elements, as well as the collection of bodies and sense organs, are insentient. (1.36)
Indeed, the Cārvākas, having abandoned pride, must accept the non-selfhood [of the body];
for the elements and the sense organs certainly exist even in a dead body, and therefore [the self] is something other than these.
The self would be something to be sought after, and likewise the self would lack independence;
furthermore, the existence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa) would be established from the observation of eclipses of the planets and so forth. (1.38)
Because that cause exists, the Wise One seeks Maheśvara;
for he regards the self as being the size of the body, due to the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal. (1.39)
For even such a great sage among those speaking Jaina monks would possess non-violence (*ahantva*) in his doctrine due to his application of asceticism, such as non-injury and the like. (1.40)

Even he who possesses the power of "Siddham" and other such mantras is dependent upon austerity; therefore, casting aside all jealousy here, [one should know] that there is another who is the bestower of the fruits of that austerity.

By those who propound doctrines other than [the Buddhist]—as indicated by such statements as "Maheśvara is independent, beginningless, a creator, and one to be petitioned"—[the following is refuted]. (1.42)
Śiva is to be sought for the sake of the highest good by casting aside the distractions of one's own [limited] positions.
This is the chapter on the true nature of Śiva.
That Śiva, through the scriptures (āgamas) of both the supreme and the non-supreme which have issued from his own mouth— || 1.43 ||
For he favors the world for the sake of the attainment of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
In this regard, the *Svāyambhuva* states: "Now, for the sake of removing the state of being a bound soul (*paśutva*)— which is the continuity of the impurity of the self—
and for the manifestation of the nature of Śiva, knowledge proceeds from Śiva."
Although that [knowledge] is one, it becomes manifold due to its arising from the lotus-like mouth of Śiva;
through the distinction between the supreme (parā) and the non-supreme (aparā), it proceeds toward the attainment of its respective objects.
Thus, by means of the divine scriptures of others, such as the Śaivas and so forth, which bring liberation from the bonds. || 1-44 ||
(5) By means of other scriptures as well—such as the Vedas and so forth—which have issued from his own mouth and bestow the fruits of distinguished enjoyments, power, and the state of Śiva. (1.45)

For the sake of accomplishing fruits such as heaven, [the means are] by the higher Śiva-knowledge, consisting of the *Kāmika* and other scriptures that reveal the knowledge of the bound soul (*paśu*), and by the lower Vedic knowledge, which reveals the knowledge of the bound soul—so says Sadyojyotis. Among these, first, the Tantra called Śaiva emerged from the mouth of Śiva. (1.46)
It is known as Śuddhaśaiva because it rests upon the pure principles (tattva).
For how could Śiva, being partless (niṣkala), speak through the characteristics of sentences and the like? (1.47)
To this objection regarding the scriptures, it is replied: "Space is seen to be characterized by sound;
for this mantra-self is partless, yet it abides in a body of knowledge. (1.48)
In the act of creation, he emits through his own mouth the scriptures that have himself as their object;
herein, in the *Kiraṇa*:
"For the sake of favoring human beings, even the Supreme has assumed the state of the Non-Supreme."
Having made his body consist of mantra, he speaks the tantras in manifold ways.
Thus, the divisions of the Śaiva Āgama are first [the scriptures] beginning with the Kāmika. (1.49)
From that, there would be eighteen types of divisions, beginning with Vijaya and so forth.
Regarding this, in the *Svāyambhuva*: "The single knowledge of Śiva is further divided tenfold."
Likewise, it is further expanded through eighteen distinct divisions.
Thus it is said:
"Just as the desired [state] is produced by yoga, so too is the unconquered [reality] produced by inconceivable causes."
Dīpta, Sukṣma, Sahasra, Āpya, Aṃśumān, Suprabhedaka,
and the others known as the Śivabhedas— thus are the ten Tantras in their proper sequence.
Vijaya, Niḥśvāsa, Prodgīta, Pārameśvara,
Āgneya, Mukhabimba, and thereafter Svāyambhuva.
Raurava, Mākuṭa, Kiraṇa, and likewise Lambita;
Candrajñāna, Vīrabhadra, Siddha, and then Sāntānika.
Śarvodgīta, Vimala, and Vātūla— in this sequence,
these eighteen tantras indeed arise from the divisions of Rudra.
Their various divisions and subdivisions, as well as their respective specific treatises,
are so numerous that they are not enumerated here by name.
Due to its various subdivisions, there is no limit to the number of its distinctions;
all other distinctions, whether they be great or not great, are likewise included within it.
Thus, in the *Svāyambhuva*,
it is said: "Furthermore, during his voluntary incarnations,
the Supreme Lord proclaimed the Pāśupata Tantra, as well as the Vākula and the Soma Tantras."
Among those, the Śaiva [tantra] is indeed primary, as it was first spoken by Śiva;
[these are established] by means of these tantras, beginning with the Śaiva, which are distinguished by four divisions.
Through initiation and other virtuous rites, through conduct, knowledge, and yoga, Maheśvara delivers the stainless souls from the mire of suffering within the ocean of worldly existence.
The first division, consisting of the non-attachment to others, is recorded as being tenfold:
the Rigveda, the Yajurveda, the Samaveda, and the Atharvaveda.
The Śikṣā, Kalpa, Nirukta, Chandas, and Jyotiṣa,
as well as Vyākaraṇa— these are the ten limbs of the Vedas.
Mīmāṃsā, the science of logic (nyāya), the Purāṇas, and the Smṛtis—these are indeed the fourfold branches of knowledge; thus, all of them together constitute fourteen.
Of these very sciences, such as the Vedas and others, there are numerous distinct branches,
various divisions of the Saṃhitās, and manifold differences among the treatises.
They are generally impossible to enumerate, having been set in motion by the will of Śiva;
they are to be accomplished through rites such as the Agniṣṭoma, which have that [will] as their sole basis.
Through various rites— daily, occasional, and optional— as well as through sacrifices and works of public utility,
one may obtain animal-like enjoyments pertaining to heaven and other realms, both here and in the hereafter.
In this regard, some, out of ignorance, do not accept the emergence of the Vedas from the mouth of Śiva; however, that [objection] does not serve the welfare of the Vedas.
The Veda, consisting of words, whose internal structure comprises the meanings of words and sentences, is uttered by an intelligent person; it is not observed to be otherwise.
For in that case, the fact that it was composed by a reliable authority is certain due to its acceptance by the learned;
moreover, the fact that it was authored by an unreliable person is nowhere heard of in the case of the Veda.
Therefore, because all the Vedas were composed by Śiva,
who is the absolute authority and the creator of all, they become a source of valid knowledge for the wise.

Moreover, in this world, the human authorship of the Vedas along with their six auxiliary sciences, such as phonetics (śikṣā) and the rest, is established throughout the three realms; and even according to their own doctrine, the same applies to the Sūtras.
For the relationship of part and whole, involving a single genus and a single body, is well-recognized in the world even by women, children, and cowherds. (1.51)
A goat cannot be established by means of the limbs of an elephant, nor can an elephant exist by means of the limbs of a goat;
such relations of part and whole occur everywhere in this way, and not otherwise. (1.52)

The Vedas are authoritative, as declared by the wise [sages] who are like their own sons; for they possess limbs (auxiliary sciences) composed by those same [sages], and they likewise possess sūtras and other such works. (1.53)

Whichever [treatise] is seen here to be endowed with its own constituent parts as taught by the wise and authoritative, in that same way, its objectives are proven to be achievable through those very means, just like Āyurveda and other such works. (1.54)
Moreover, regarding this, there is a Smṛti: "The Vedas are four, along with Mīmāṃsā, Nyāyavistara, Purāṇa, and Dharmaśāstra; these indeed are the fourteen branches of knowledge (vidyās)."
Thus,
the Nyāya-vistara, Mīmāṃsā, Purāṇas, and Smṛtis are studied equally by the Vaidikas as being of the same class (sapakṣa), due to their similarity with the Vedas.
Furthermore, since Manu and others— who were skillful, authoritative, and the foremost among those who know the Vedas—
have established it, the authorship of the Śruti by an intelligent being who is a perfected lord of yogis is proven.
In this regard, the Veda itself declares the very birth of all the Vedas from the Primordial Person who desired to create; that is stated clearly as follows.
From that sacrifice in which everything was offered, the Ṛg-verses and the Sāman-chants were born;
from it the meters were born, and from it the Yajus-formulas were produced.
Thus,
regarding this matter, there are statements concerning the creation of Prajāpati even in the Purāṇas such as the Brāhma and Kūrma, as well as in the Vaiṣṇava and other texts. (1.55)
Namely:
from his first mouth, he fashioned the Gāyatrī, the Ṛc, the Trivṛt-stoma, the Rathantara, and the Agniṣṭoma among sacrifices.
From his right side, he created the Yajus formulas, the Triṣṭubh meter, the fifteen-fold Stoma, the Bṛhat Sāman, and likewise the Ukthya sacrifice.
From his western mouth, he created the Sāman chants, the Jāgata meter, the Saptadaśa stoma, the Vairūpa, and the Atirātra sacrifice.
From his northern mouth, he created the twenty-first [Sāman], the Āptoryāma, as well as the Ātharvaṇa, the Anuṣṭubh, and the Svarāja.
Thus: "For the authority of the Purāṇas has indeed been accepted by the Vaidikas through their single recitation among the fourteen branches of knowledge, beginning with the Vedas. (1.56)
Through these ancient statements, the Yajurvedic Śruti is also augmented by the meaning inferred therefrom; it is the ancient and primordial source of the Ṛgvedic verses. (1.57)
The scriptural injunction regarding the restriction of directions arises because [the Vedas] originated from the faces in the east and so forth;
indeed, such a restriction of directions is observed in the Vedas—otherwise, whence could there be any such restriction? (1.58)
The body of even Brahmā was formed from the principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth;
Māyā is the cause of those principles, and Maheśvara is the cause of Māyā.
"One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and Maheśvara as the wielder of Māyā"—from such statements, Maheśvara is the agent even of Brahman. (1.60)
The Siddha is also seen in the *Skanda Purāṇa*, in the *Devala-stava*, as follows:
"Having become Brahmā, [he created] the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans."
Salutation to Him who, abiding in the midst of the waters, creates [the universe] through His nature as Brahman.
Thus, for this reason as well, Maheśvara is to be known as the speaker of the Vedas. (1.61)
And so it is stated in the Nyāya:
"The author of the Veda is certainly not just any ordinary person;
rather, he is the Supreme Lord, skilled in the creation of the three worlds."
Thus: "If it is so, then since the origin of the scriptures is established as being from Maheśvara, some [object] that because of having a beginning, the Śruti would be non-eternal. (1.62)
If they say this, it is not correct, because Maheśvara is beginningless;
he is eternally pure, stainless, wise, and his very body is composed of mantra and vidyā.
His body of knowledge is likewise beginningless and imperishable;
and thus says the Śruti:
"O Rudra, that auspicious body of yours which is non-terrible and free from the appearance of evil..."
With that most peaceful body of yours, O Lord of the Mountain, [protect us].
Thus, its subdivisions—lava, kāṣṭhā, kalā, and so forth—are non-different from it. (1.64)

Precisely through the increase or decrease of his powers of will, action, and knowledge, and by means of the transformation of the *bimba* and so forth, there occurs the subtle internal gathering of the phonemes (*varṇa*). (1.65)
Having attained manifestation from the mouth of Śiva through the stages beginning with *vaikharī*, this speech, consisting of the Vedas and Āgamas, issues forth eternally from Him. (1.66)
Regarding that origin of speech, something more is said here as well:
all beings subsist upon that speech uttered by the Lord of All. (1.67)
Desiring to create, he emits this [nature], and he swallows it again during dissolution;
out of compassion, he effects creation for the sake of the experience and liberation of persons.
And for the sake of providing rest to those weary in this saṃsāra, there is the withdrawal [of the universe];
that Śiva is the primary one, beginningless, and distinct from all others. (1.69)
Likewise, the words uttered from his mouth are distinct from others;
both the Śiva-āgamas and the Vedas are indeed eternal by virtue of their authority.
The Śiva-āgamas are eternal, for they were originally non-different from the Vedas by Śiva; they remain eternally established, yet they are manifested within him, since they are beginningless. (1.71)
Whatever is eternally established and perpetually manifest from that [Supreme] source is indeed eternal, just as the divisions of time such as *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and *nāḍī* are. (1.72)
And thus, the subject under discussion is established; therefore, there is no doubt regarding the stated probandum.
This is the section establishing the authority of the two kinds of scriptures by virtue of their being composed by the Lord.
That pervasive Great Lord, desiring to emit the universe and the scriptures— (1.73)
He manifested his own power, just as the full moon manifests its own radiance;
for here,
there was the primordial unfolding of this [Lord] who desired to create, for the sake of bestowing grace upon both the conscious and the unconscious.
That reality of power is said to have attained non-differentiation from this very [consciousness].

Thus it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*: "That Śakti is non-different from Śiva; she is eternal, powerful, and constant. Though one, she is manifested in many ways for the manifestation of manifold effects."
Thus,
even regarding the Three Jewels:
"Even when one performs an act of desire while lacking the desire [for it], that is declared to be desire."
Though her nature is unknowable, she is knowledge; though she is action, she is yet non-action.
Thus, that power which is called Will (icchā) is also the power of Action (kriyā). || 1.74 ||
And the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) is to be understood [as distinct] because it initiates various specific effects;
for the Lord (īśa), impelled by will, performs everything through action (kriyā). (1.75)
One perceives through the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti), and that is considered to be Kuṇḍalinī;
it is the expansion of the nature of Śiva which arises from the equilibrium of the powers of knowledge and action (jñāna-kriyā-śakti).
That reality, known as Sadāśiva, whose body is knowledge and whose essence is Śiva, is said to be the object of worship beyond [the lower levels] as the very form of reality. (1.77)
When the power of knowledge is slight and the power of action is likewise predominant, there exists the principle called Īśvara, characterized by the majesty of universal agency. (1.78)
The instrumental cause of creation, known as Īśvara, is predominant in action;
just as the potter is the activator of jars, pots, and other such objects. (1.79)

When the power of action (kriyāśakti) is very slight and the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) is predominant, that is the principle (tattva) called Śuddhavidyā, which consists of the illumination of the nature of knowledge. (1.80)
As it is stated in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:

"That reality in which the power of agency becomes subordinate and the power called knowledge attains its fullness is the principle known as Vidyā; for it is illuminating by virtue of its nature as knowledge."
Thus:
"When the Bindu and Nāda are moist and take refuge in Sadāśiva, the Vidyeśvaras—Śrīkaṇṭha, Ananta, and Pūraka—are born therein. (1.81)
Wherein lies the reality called Vidyā, which rests upon Bindu, Nāda, and Śiva;
there, the Vidyās and Mantras flash forth like waves in the ocean. (1.82)
In this *Tattvaprakāśa*:
"Having favored the first eight, Śiva appoints them to the status of Vidyeśvaras;
he also creates the Mantras, which are said to be seven crores in number."
Thus it is said. Regarding the Three Jewels as well:
"In that regard, the mantras and vidyās of the eastern Vidyābhujas are known by name;
commanded by the Vidyēśvaras, they are reckoned at seventy million."
Thus: "In this way, there are indeed five pure principles (śuddhatattva), beginning with Śiva and ending with Vidyā, from the intermixture of which arise the Vidyeśvaras, Vidyā, and the rest. (1.83)
By the power of the mantras of the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras, and through the will of Īśvara, the impure principle called Māyā manifested like a magical illusion. (1.84)

(12) In this context, the principle of *māyā* is the seed of the magician’s trick (*indrajāla*). The Lord Śiva, who is the knower of that [seed] and the root of the stalk of *māyā*, manifests it himself by tearing asunder the impurity (*mala*). For she is not real in herself; for if she were real, she would not be *māyā* at all—thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasiddhi*. To explain: "Without the magician there is no *māyā*, and without *māyā* there is no embodied one;
just as in this world, in the case of a magician’s trick and the like, an agent is observed. (1.85)
Likewise, it is held that Māyā is the material cause of the principles beginning with Kalā;
though insentient, it appears as if sentient and manifold. (1.86)

Just as a magical illusion (māyā) is non-existent in itself yet always appears as real, so too the Supreme Lord, having agitated that Māyā by means of His own powers (śaktis), [manifests the world]. (1.87)
The treasury of compassion creates the universe in accordance with the karma of individual beings;
within that creation, the five principles beginning with time (kāla) and the divisions of time (kalā) arise in succession.
Just as impure things arise from that which illuminates reality,
so from Māyā, for the sake of the soul’s being a knower and an agent, there arises a pentad of principles:
Time (kāla), Necessity (niyati), Limited Agency (kalā), Impure Knowledge (aśuddhavidyā), and Attachment (rāga).
Thus it is said: "In that regard, the principle called Time (kāla) is threefold, consisting of what has previously occurred. (1.89)
The waking state clearly perceives both the present and the future;
likewise, it perceives the principle of necessity (niyatitattva), which consists of the nature of regulation. || 1.90 ||

Thus, having brought forth the principle of *kalā* from the impurity (*mala*) of the individual souls (*aṇu*), it manifests the power of agency (*kartṛśakti*) by means of its partiality; therefore it is called *kalā*.

In the *Tattvaprakāśa*, it is stated that impurity (*mala*) alone, when taken as the sole factor, manifests the power of agency (*kartṛśakti*). That impure knowledge (*aśuddhavidyā*) is the activator of the power of agency whose capacity has been strengthened by *kalā*; it is the indicator of objects for human beings. (1.92)
Furthermore, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*, it is stated that the principle of *vidyā* (knowledge) is born as the illuminator for the purpose of showing objects to the person (*puruṣa*).
From *vidyā*, that which is called the principle of *rāga* (attachment) arises; due to this, the person, through intense longing, engages with objects that are pleasing. (1.93)
Bound by these principles (tattvas), this [Self] has attained the state of being an atomic enjoyer;
that principle known as Puruṣa is augmented by the power of agency. (1.94)
For instance:
"When the bound soul (paśu), conjoined with these principles (tattvas), is brought to the state of being an enjoyer,
it then attains the designation 'puruṣa' and its reckoning among the principles."

Thus: "For the sake of the experience of the Spirit (puruṣa), the principle known as Nature (prakṛti) arises through the equilibrium of the three qualities; that very thing is designated as the Unmanifest (avyakta). (1.95)
Because it is the primal nature (prakṛti) of the transformations of the principles beginning with intellect (buddhi), it is likewise so remembered;
due to the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas), that unmanifested state is called "unmanifest" (avyakta). (1.96)

That nature (prakṛti), characterized by the capacity to be known and augmented by power (śakti), becomes the manifest principle of intellect (buddhitattva), which relies upon the quality of sattva. || 1.97 ||
That very intellect (buddhi) is called by the Sāṃkhyas the principle named Mahat;
it is indeed the unmanifest (avyakta), yet [it appears] as the manifest through the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. (1.98)
The principle of ego (ahaṅkāra-tattva) is characterized by delusion and the sense of "I.
That ego is of three types, distinguished respectively by the qualities of sattva and the others. (1.99)
The *sāttvika* [ego] is known as *taijasa*, while the *vaikārika* is recorded as being *rājasa*;
the *bhūtādi* is *tāmasa*. These too separately brought forth the principles (*tattvas*).
From the Taijasa [ego] arises the mind there, and from the Vaikārika [ego] arise the senses;
from the Bhūtādi [ego] arise the subtle elements (tanmātras)—from these, this creation proceeds.
Thus, in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:

"The principle of mind (*manastattva*), whose nature is will and which possesses conceptualization and discursive thought, is born from Taijasa alone; it is insentient and devoid of any [independent] continuity. (1.101)
But from the vaikārika [sattva] were born the ear, the skin, the eyes, as well as the tongue and the nose; these five are indeed the organs of perception (buddhīndriya). 1-102.
Likewise, speech, the feet, the hands, and also the organs of excretion and generation—
these five organs of action likewise arise from that which is called vaikārika.

Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth—these subtle elements (tanmātras) alone became the objects [of the senses] from the principle of the "origin of the elements" (bhūtādi) in successive order. (1.104)
From the subtle elements (tanmātras), however, arise ether, air, fire, water, and earth in sequence;
the wise declare these to be the five gross elements (bhūtas), each possessing one additional quality.

The five sense organs, beginning with the ear, serve respectively as the substrata for sound and the other [objects], and thus they are indeed the manifestors of the subtle elements (tanmātra). (1.106)
Speech, movement, grasping, procreation, and pleasure—these are the respective fixed functions of the organs of action. (1.107)
The entire visible world, which is an effect, is produced by the four kinds of great elements that have mutually penetrated one another and pervade space. (1.108)
On this point, the Sāṃkhyas and others might say: "The principles (tattvas) are either twenty-five in number, or there are twenty-four; there is no principle beyond these. (1-109)
"Since the world is established by this much alone, why rely on other principles?"—this and similar babble of theirs will not establish their intended meaning. (1.110)
To the question "How so?", we shall state the necessity for other principles (tattvas) as follows:
The Person (puruṣa) is not [identical with] the elements, the sense organs, the subtle elements (tanmātras), nor indeed with the internal organs.
Indeed, the principle of passion (rāga-tattva) is that which causes attachment, as it is colored by the objects of the senses.
"Passion" (rāga) and "desire" (kāma) are not different in meaning.
For it is from passion that one desires objects, and activity arises from desire;
therefore, let it be understood that there exists a reality called passion.
In the same way, regarding the principles (tattva) beginning with passion (rāga) and ending with the earth (bhūmi),
there can be no manifestation [of them] through objects and so forth by means of the power of external perception.
That which possesses the power to perceive another is declared to be a manifestor;
for the reality of knowledge (vidyātattva) is like the eye and other senses in the cognition of form and so forth.
Thus it is stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*.
Therefore, one should ascertain that there exists a reality called "knowledge" (*vidyā*). (1.111)

15) Likewise, in order to pierce the impurity (*mala*) that obscures the reality (*tattva*) beginning from *vidyā* and ending with *bhūmi*—which is beginningless and pervades the universe—it is otherwise impossible without the *kalā*-tattva. (1-112)

In the *Tattvasiddhi*, it is stated that for this Lord Prajāpati—who, out of compassion, desires to lift the individual soul (puṃs) out of the mire of delusion, that soul being obscured by impurities established from time immemorial—there arises, through the material cause of *māyā-prakṛti*, the principle of *kalā* (limited agency), which is capable of piercing through those impurities.

For indeed, it is only through the principles beginning with *kalā* and ending with *earth* (*kṣiti*) that any restriction regarding direction, location, substance, genus, and so forth, can ever be established. Otherwise, no such determination would ever be possible.
Their restriction is indeed something else, for it is Niyati (the principle of necessity) that acts as their restrainer;
therefore, it is understood that the reality known as Niyati exists.
Since time is not established by the principles beginning with necessity (niyati) and ending with earth,
investigators must accept that time exists as something distinct from them.

Likewise, it is impossible for the world-activity to proceed without a substratum, by means of factors beginning with time and ending with the earth, each having its own material cause as its sphere of operation.
Therefore, that illusion which serves as its substratum certainly exists, though it is difficult to trace,
just as a wall must serve as the support for various and diverse appearances.
Thus, on the impure path, the world— composed of elements from Māyā down to Earth, which are not significantly different from one another— is like a magical illusion.
Because the magical display of an illusionist's net is insentient, it cannot possess agency;
for the creator of the painted scene on a wall is indeed someone else entirely.
Likewise, Śiva—who possesses the principles of *vidyā* and so forth due to his manifestation through *māyā* and the rest—is the agent;
he is indeed distinct [from the individual soul], consisting of mantra, and is the cause of sounds, phonemes, and the like.
In that pure and stainless path of purification, beginning with Śiva and ending with Vidyā,
the sciences of sound (śabdavidyās) together with the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) are seen, moving within the sphere of space.
From the proximity of Śiva and Śakti, the Bindu came into being as the essence of Nāda,
just as the quality of delight arises from the union of the moon and its moonlight.
That which is the pure path from which it arises, wherein it exists, and into which it dissolves—
that is the Bindu known as Paranāda, the creator of Nāda, Bindu, and Aṇu.
Thus, in the *Ratnatraya*:
"That supreme seed known as Nāda, which resides within all beings,
is the divine bestower of liberation and the granter of all accomplishments."
It is peaceful, all-pervading, and empty, abiding in twelve measures;
O Six-faced One, the short vowels are declared to be Brahmā, while the long vowels are indeed the limbs.
Thus it is said in the Kālottara: "First, there was the sound (śabda) arising from the cause; from that, the Imperishable (akṣara);
and from the Imperishable, O Brahman, the knowers of Brahman know Brahman, which bestows liberation."
Thus it is stated in the *Svāyambhuva*. Regarding the Three Jewels (*ratnatraya*) as well:
"That sound, which arises from the agitation of the *bindu* for the sake of accomplishing the infinite goal, is fourfold through the distinctions of *vāk*, *vaikharī*, and so forth."
And the Vedic revelation states: "Speech has four measured quarters.
It is fourfold: Śakti, Nāda, Mahāmāyā, and Vyoman.
Furthermore, its four functions are said to be the Bindu itself. (1.113)
Vaikharī, Madhyamā, Paśyantī, and Sūkṣmā—
these arise in reverse order from Kuṇḍalinī as the starting point, proceeding sequentially.

The subtle Kuṇḍalinī, consisting of pure light and more minute than the smallest atom, is situated in the center; because it is beyond the range of hearing, she rises upward from there, moving upwards. (1.115)
Self-luminous, she becomes Paśyantī when resting upon the Suṣumṇā;
reaching the heart-lotus, she herself becomes Madhyamā in the form of sound. (1.116)
Merely consisting of internal discourse, it is undivided and moves upward; remaining in the chest, throat, and palate, it reaches the head, the nose, and the teeth. (1.117)

Vaikharī speech originates from the root of the tongue and the lips, assumes the grasp of articulated phonemes, generates the manifold expansion of sound, and is perceived by the sense of hearing. (1.118)
Then the letter *ha*, together with its vowel *ā*, was joined with the letter *ra*. || 1.119 ||
Therefore, he took on the vowel *ī*, adorned with the *bindu* and *nāda*.
But that seed-syllable of power (śakti-bīja), through its conjunction with that [Supreme], is the cause of the arising of all things.
And because of taking away and because of carrying away, let there be [the state] of Śiva and Śakti joined together. (1-122)
The verbal form of those two [syllables] uttered in union is said to be their seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The letter *ha* is Brahmā, while the letter *ī* is held to be Viṣṇu. (1.123)
The letter *ra* is Rudra, who is indeed Agni; the *bindu* is said to be Īśvara;
*nāda* is to be known as Sadāśiva, while the end of *nāda* (*nādānta*) is Śiva himself. (1.124)
The letter *ha*, having attained manifestation, is devoid of the resonance of the heart;
it has reached the state of the letter *a*, for its differentiation is indeed the sequence of syllables. (1.125)
The six letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ū' are its modifications;
however, there is a specific modification of the letter 'r', namely: ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ.
Due to the differentiation of the vowel *ī*, however, there are six syllables beginning with *ā* that are close [to it].
Thus, sixteen vowels known as *śaktis* have arisen from the seed-syllable (*bīja*). (1.127)
Others have declared that those [vowels] excluding ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ are twelve;
for the short vowels joined with the bindu are masculine and possess the form of the sun. (1.128)
Vowels with long sounds and those ending in the visarga are feminine and have the nature of Soma;
however, the group of four—ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ—is neuter and possesses the nature of both Soma and Agni.

The letter *ha*, possessing the quality of sound (*śabda*), first created space (*ākāśa*). From space arose wind (*vāyu*), which has the quality of touch (*sparśa*); from that [quality] arose the consonants beginning with *ka*. (1.130)
Those five groups of five syllables are indeed devoid of the letter *A*.
However, the four letters beginning with *Ya* are the bodies of air, fire, earth, and water.

Touch, form, smell, and that which is called taste are their qualities respectively; the remaining elements, beginning with space (śa), are all-pervasive, joined with fire and moon, and possess vowels as their touches. (1.132)
Thus, fifty phonemes have arisen through the differentiation of Śakti:
the twenty-five letters beginning with *ka*, as well as those beginning with *ya* and *śa*. (1.133)
They arise according to their specific forms through differences in place and effort, and also through the mutual conjunction of consonants combined with vowels such as 'a' and others. (1.134)
Every manifold proliferation of sound clearly arises from this;
for this is known as Mātṛkā, the collection of fifty phonemes. (1.135)
The universe, which is the entire collection of sounds, is clearly its transformation.
This very goddess of speech, whose form consists of her own phonemes, is the auspicious Vidyā whose essence is Śiva. (1.136)

The section on the *Tattvamātṛkā* has already been presented in detail within the *Sāmānyapāda*. From that *bindu*, which consists of *nāda*, [the letters] were set in motion by the will of Śiva. (1.137)
The five kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are those in which the universe is established;
the phoneme Kṣa and the earth-element (kṣiti-tattva) abide pervading Nivṛtti.
Thus, there are twenty-three syllables beginning with 'A' and ending with 'ṢṬakāra'. These exist up to the level of Prakṛti within Pratiṣṭhā, which is itself established within Kalā.
The seven letters beginning with *ña* and ending with *gha*, as well as those ending with *māyā* (the letter *ha*),
are indeed the seven principles (*tattvas*) situated within the kalā known as Vidyā.
The three castes, as well as the Śuddhavidyā and Īśvara [tattvas], constitute the Sadāśiva-tattva, which is established within that which is called Śānti. (1.141)
The sixteen vowels, from *a* to *aḥ*, in reverse order,
correspond to the Śakti-tattva and Śiva, who abide in the Kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta).
Thus has been stated in brief the pervasion of the *kalās* by the principles of the phonemes (*varṇatattva*).
Now the mutual pervasion of the principles and of the deities is being described.
Power (śakti) exists pervading the entire universe from Śiva down to the Earth;
Sadāśiva and Īśvara as well have as their domain [the phonemes] beginning with Bindu and ending with Kṣa.
The principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is established from Sadāśiva down to the level of Bhūmi;
the all-pervading principle of limited agency (kalātattva), however, extends from Māyā down to the earth (pṛthvī).
Beyond this follows the sequential arrangement of the principles (tattvas): Rudra presides over everything from Māyā down to Earth (kṣmā), while Viṣṇu extends from Māyā down to the Earth. (1.146)
Brahmā, pervading from the level of Puruṣa down to the Earth, is established within the [lower] principles (tattvas).
The Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras), beginning with Ananta, are established within the Vidya-tattva.
Vighneśvara and Sarasvatī reside in the principle of Sadāśiva; Nandī and the others are in Vidyā, and Caṇḍikā is situated in Prakṛti. (1.148)
Lakṣmī resides in the principle of Īśvara, while the other Śaktis reside in the intellect (buddhi);
Soma and Arka reside in the principle of sound (śabda), and the sacrificer (yajamāna) resides in the Puruṣa.
For the elements and the senses abide within their own causes; and the eightfold divine womb is likewise known to be contained within the city of eight (puryaṣṭaka).
All beings without exception— whether born from a womb, from an egg, from sweat, or from sprouting—
exist solely within the element of earth by the power of the portions of Śiva’s and Śakti’s energy.
Thus, the pervasion of reality has been demonstrated here in brief;
this very same [pervasion] is to be understood in detail further on in the "Determination of the Paths" (adhvanirṇaya).
By what is it restricted that there are exactly thirty-six principles? Their state of being is known as a "principle" (tattva), and that is observed even in the case of a jar and so forth. (1.153)

If someone were to speak thus, the reality therein is defined as follows: the word "that" (tat) refers to the subject matter at hand, while the word "thou" (tvam) pertains to its state of being. (1-154)
That which is continuous and pervasive remains as reality even until the final dissolution;
as it is stated in the *Tattvasiddhi*:
"Because they are pervasive (*tata*) and because they are continuous (*santata*), the wise know them therefore as *tattvas*."
Continuity is pervasion in terms of space, and constancy is [pervasion] in terms of time.
Thus it is said. Moreover, the lakṣa and so forth, as well as space, are all-pervading realities that endure until the dissolution of the world;
otherwise, even pillars, jars, and the like would follow as being ultimate realities.
Thus it is said in the *Tattvaprakāśa*:

"That which remains until the dissolution [of the universe], bestowing enjoyment upon all worlds—that is what is designated by the name 'tattva' (reality-principle); a body, a jar, or the like is not a tattva."
Thus, the thirty-six principles (tattvas) should be known according to their specific divisions. (1.155)
For that knowledge is indeed the knowledge of reality; otherwise, it is not the knowledge of reality.
There are exactly thirty-six principles (tattvas) according to their true nature for the sake of establishing the universe. (1.156)

Since there is no other reality apart from the supreme reality, the intended effect is accomplished by the cause to whatever extent is necessary, without depending on anything beyond that supreme reality. (1.157)

There is no other cause for this; indeed, that much alone is sufficient. For instance, the potter’s wheel, staff, water, lump of clay, and so forth, [are all required] for the arising of a jar. (1.158)
Just as there is nothing else that is both a cause and something to be depended upon, so too, this alone is declared here by the wise to be the object of proof. (1-159)
"This very path is thus to be known as real, as well as that which follows beyond it";
such is the exposition of reality set forth in this Tantra. (1.160)
For the sake of achieving the fruitfulness of ritual initiation, consecration, and other rites,
[one should seek] the Supreme Good which bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. The wise Creator of the universe,
who ferries across the stream of individual souls by means of His own mouth— the supreme knowledge arising from the higher and lower scriptures— [is the refuge].

He who is beginningless, pure, independent from others due to His distinct nature, all-pervasive, and composed of the principles (tattvas) such as the phonemes and kalās—He is Śiva, the perfected one, to be known by the wise. (1.161½)

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Indication of Subjects," in the section on Ritual Practice (Kriyāpāda) of the latter part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 1.
Now begins the second chapter.
Having first bowed with devotion to Gaṇeśvara, to Gira (Sarasvatī) who is the source of the universe, and to Śiva and Śivā,
I shall hereafter proclaim the initiation (*dīkṣā*) for the bound soul (*paśu*), which brings about the severance of the fetters and awakens the realization of one's own auspicious nature.
In this regard, the Mataṅga states: "The bound soul (paśu), the binder (pāśayitṛ), and the bond (pāśa)—these three are established;
they become manifest through the description of the relationship between the goal to be accomplished (sādhya) and the means of accomplishment (sādhaka)."

Thus: "He who is constant within the body, yet distinct from the body-bearer and characterized by bodilessness—he is called the living self (jīvātman) and the bound soul (paśu); he is remembered as the individual person (puruṣa), the subtle atom (aṇu) existing in the state of transmigratory existence. (2-2)
The categories (padārtha) are fivefold: the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), the Lord (pati), power (śakti), and discernment (vicāra);
action (kriyā) and conduct (caryā) are declared as the sixth in the Śaiva Āgamas.
"The bound soul (paśu), the Lord (īśvara) who is the source of knowledge (vidyā), and liberation (mukti) as the final [category] here"— thus it is stated in the venerable Parākhyatantra.
This concludes the determination of the true nature of each of the six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha).
Having understood this correctly, the initiate attains both enjoyment and liberation.
An animal is not considered to possess a body by its name alone;
for how could there be a self in this body that is distinct from the body?
Thus it is stated in the Mataṅga-tantra. For instance:

"The Buddhists, by means of reasoning, declare this [self] to be momentary and consisting of a stream of consciousness; whereas the foremost among the knowers of the three Vedas (Upaniṣads) desire that very same [self] to be eternal, one, and the innermost Self. (2-3)
The hosts of the Cārvāka-demons, who are naked and arrogant, declare that self to be independent and limited to the body;
they maintain that, according to their sole authority, the self here consists merely of the collection of elements, the body, and the senses. (2.4)
The Sāṃkhyas, who maintain the doctrine of primordial nature (prakṛti), declare this [Self] to be the supreme object of calculation;
they say it is a non-agent in its bound state, and a knower when it has attained the state of liberation.
According to the doctrines of Jaimini, the knower becomes the agent and attains a state of manifold selves;
or, upon liberation, he becomes like a stone, since dharma and knowledge are his sole means. (2.6)
Distinct from the Naiyāyikas and others, [the self] is endowed with cognition, pain, and pleasure, as well as with desire, aversion, and effort, and is also possessed of merit and demerit. (2.7)
For they maintain that the self, possessing dispositions and endowed with nine qualities, is distinct for each body;
thus, by treating word and meaning as non-different, they assert the eternity of the nature of the word. (2.8)
Bound and liberated—those who are the objects of such predictions arise from knowledge of that [Self].
Thus, due to mutual contradictions, the Self has been described differently by various schools of thought. (2.9)
That animal is bound by fetters; the Lord Śiva is the binder. (2.9½)
The individual soul (paśu) is indeed formless, eternally devoid of qualities, inactive, and its sphere of experience is the body of the Lord of Consciousness.
Though impure due to its impurities, it has attained the state of an enjoyer, being enveloped by the Māyā of the Lord through its own karma. (2.10)
But he himself, due to his limited knowledge and because he is colored by passion, is likewise affected by the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas;
nevertheless, through the intellect and other faculties, he perceives as a thinker, driven by a thirst for the arrangement of enjoyments. (2.11)
And thus it is said in the *Kiraṇatantra*:
"The bound soul (*paśu*), though eternal, formless, ignorant, inactive, and devoid of qualities, is yet a lord;
he is all-pervasive, situated within the belly of Māyā, and intent upon seeking the means for experience."
Thus Varuṇa also said: "The limited knower, who is impure, divided, the agent and enjoyer of his own actions,
distinct from the body, all-pervasive, eternal, capable of being refined, and possessed of a Lord— he is the bound soul (paśu)."
And thus it is stated in the Svāyambhuva [Tantra]: "The individual soul (paśu) is insentient, all-pervasive, eternal, devoid of qualities, inactive, powerless,
subject to obstruction, capable of experience, to be purified, to be awakened, partless, and [yet] a master."
Thus it is said; and in the *Parākhyatantra*:
"The embodied soul is perishable, pervasive, distinct, impure, insentient, the enjoyer of the fruits of its own karma, possessing limited knowledge, and dependent upon the Lord."

Thus it is said. What need is there for more?—When the helpless soul, like a bound beast (paśu), is constrained by necessity in an action that is otherwise neutral due to the influence of time, he may then be liberated through the appropriate initiation, having been purified by the descent of power (śaktinipāta) through the will of Śiva. (2.12)
In this regard—
when an equalized karma has arisen, then, by the force of time and through the descent of an intense power (śakti)—
Because it has been stated in the *Kiraṇatantra* with these and other words that the liberation from bonds for one who is initiated is established, therefore one who is uninitiated remains bound.
As it says in the *Svāyambhuva*: "The self is impure and bound, yet it is liberated again through initiation. Here—
The embodied being is bound by fetters due to the cause of imperfect knowledge. (2-13)
Whatever is thus [characterized] by being an enjoyer, like a cow and so forth, is exactly so. This is the section on the investigation of the bound soul (paśu).
(p. 23) Likewise, the fetters (pāśa) of embodied beings are threefold: impurity (mala), Māyā, and the accumulated karma.
That impurity called *āṇava* is co-emergent (*sahaja*), while that which is termed *māyīya* and *kārmaṇa* is likewise [co-emergent].
The fetters (pāśas) are also to be known as threefold: impurity (mala), illusion (māyā), and action (karman).
Thus says Varuṇa.
The fetter of those bound souls (paśus) is threefold, consisting of impurity, action, and illusion.
Thus it is stated in the *Rāmakaṇṭha*, and in the *Svāyambhuva* as well: "Now, the beginningless impurity of persons is proclaimed as their state of bondage (*paśutva*).
It should be understood as being like the husk and the chaff of the sprout of sin that is *māyā*."
The principle of Māyā is the seed of the universe, indestructible, and of the nature of Śiva. Karma is of two kinds, namely that which is to be experienced (bhogya).
In this body which is not the self, when there arises the notion of "self" and "mine" toward objects, and the perception of reality in what is unreal—
this triad here is clearly known as the impurity called ignorance.
"For the innate impurity is Māyā, while the future impurity is its effect," so it is said in the *Kiraṇa*. Likewise, in the *Mataṅga*:
"The impurity called delusion (*moha*) is considered to be innate to persons and beginningless."
For he, O best of the twice-born, is the foremost among the six [qualities] beginning with joy.
Thus [it is said]: "Impurity (mala) is impurity, which is ignorance (ajñāna)," says Varuṇa.

"Delusion (moha), intoxication (mada), envy (mātsarya), passion and aversion (rāga-dveṣa), and thirst (tṛṣṇā), as well as greed (lobha)—this sevenfold impurity of ignorance is innate to the bound soul (paśu)."
Thus it is said in the *Bṛhatkālottara*:
"Māyā" refers here to the aggregate of principles (tattvas) beginning with Kalā and ending with Earth,
within which this entire cosmic manifestation, together with the elements, comes within the scope of cognition.
Its effects, beginning with *kalā* and extending from the subtle to the gross down to the earth,
are inferred to be bound to this body through its own karma.
Since all effects are contained within it, it is therefore known as the principle of illusion (māyātattva).
Thus it is said in the Parākhya: "The [categories] are Kalā, followed by Niyati, Vidyā, Rāga, Puruṣa, Prakṛti,
Buddhi, Ahaṃkāra, the mind, the ten sense organs, and the five subtle elements."
In this world, the body of the enjoyer—the transmigrating soul—is established through these principles beginning with space, air, fire, water, earth, and ending with the ego;
for, under the influence of karma, it appears like a magical illusion or a sorcerer’s trick.
Since it is insentient yet appears as if sentient, manifold, all-pervading, eternal, and exceedingly subtle,
it is therefore impossible to describe the principle of *māyā* here even in its gross form exactly as it is.
Action, moreover, is of two kinds: that previously performed which is meritorious in nature and that which is sinful.
And these are indeed threefold, in sequence: mental, born of speech, and physical.

Furthermore, actions are of three kinds: those previously accumulated, those gathered here in this life, and those pertaining to the future; for the experiencer, their fruits consist of pairs [of opposites] in this world.
Indeed, the impurity of this minute, impure embodied soul is like the blackness of copper;
born together with it, it vanishes through the descent of Śiva’s power, just as [blackness] disappears from mercury through the process of alchemical transmutation.
But through the yoga of Śiva’s grace, immediately following the descent of power (śaktipāta),
once initiation has been performed, he is liberated from the state of being a bound soul (paśutva).
By the will of Śiva, that primordial power— supreme, infinite, belonging to Śiva, and bestowing the goal of Śiva—
descends upon a person in their final birth.
"From that union, his impurity—the cause of saṃsāra—is discharged.
Thus it is said in the *Svāyambhuva*.
And its signs are devotion and detachment from the ocean of existence.
For right knowledge and the manifestation of the state of Śiva indeed constitute [the means]. (2-14)

"Therefore, knowledge, devotion, and detachment—these are the true signs of the self for one who has been initiated; they do not belong directly to the rabbit-marked moon. (2.15) Thus ends the section on the investigation of Varuṇa’s noose.
The Lord is indeed pure, Śiva himself, eternal, ever-satisfied, omniscient in quality, and independent;
he is beginningless consciousness, possessed of undiminished power, endowed with infinite energy, and the protector of the entire path. (2-16)

On this point, Rāmakaṇṭha says: "The Lord is the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), who will be described according to the distinctions of the principles (tattva) such as Śiva and Sadāśiva, and according to the distinctions of the five worlds (bhuvana).
Having transcended the principles, he shines forth; having pervaded the entire void, he is indeed formless.
He is the Lord whose light is the void, immeasurable, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) who is without beginning, middle, or end. (2.17)
Playing, that one of supreme power descended from Vindu by means of his own Śakti, and being embraced by her,
desiring to emit the entire activity of all the paths, he became enveloped by the net of his own powers.

That Lord of Mantras, through the application of ritual metaphor (*upacāra-yoga*), assumed a body consisting of five aspects of his own mantra, together with the eightfold divisions of the powers of Viśveśvara, beginning with Ananta and Sūkṣma. (2.19)

[I salute] the one whose head is Īśāna, whose face is called Puruṣa, whose heart is Aghora, whose secret part is Vāmadeva, and whose form is Sadyojāta; likewise, [I salute] the captivating one, the progenitor, and the destroyer. (2-20)
In this regard, the Mataṅga states:
"The auspicious Śivā, whose body consists of the five mantras through ritual application,
has Īśāna as her head, Puruṣa as her face, and the Lord Aghora as her heart."
It is said that through the teaching on the secret left [path], there is the immediate form upon the seat;
the powers (śaktis) are the captivating one, the mother, and the obstructing one.

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, by such statements as "Ananta, whose nature is infinite vigor, the Subtle One," and so forth, the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśvaras) are well-known. In this way, the Lord (pati), who is of the nature of Sadāśiva, has been indicated in brief.
The Section on the Investigation of the Consort: Śiva’s power is his ultimate, subtle consciousness, autonomous and the cause of all accomplishments;
like light from a lamp, it is non-different from Śiva, yet it is capable of awakening and unfolding the manifestation of the world. (2.21)
And so it is stated in the Mataṅga:
"The Lord's power is supreme, subtle, and capable of unfolding the universe;
by means of that, the Lord Sadāśiva is awakened in soul and eternally autonomous."
The one of great splendor, whose foundation is established in the power of knowledge, is awakened.
Thus:
"In reality, she who is designated as Īśvarī is endowed with the four worlds in their entirety;
she is the power consisting of will, action, and knowledge, divided into three aspects, and further divided sixteenfold. (2.22)
And likewise in the Mataṅga:
"By the power of that Ananta,
that supreme splendor of the Lord is divided sixteenfold, consisting of will, knowledge, and action."
Thus:
she should be the Agitator (Saṃkṣobhaṇī), then the Progenitor (Jananī), and likewise the Provoker (Krodhayitrī) and the Protector (Goptrī);
she is declared next as the Leader (Netrī) and the Binder (Yoktrī), followed by the one called the Savior (Trāṇā) and the Restrainer of Vāma (Vāmaniyāmikā). (2.23)
From Raudrī comes Plāvikā; after that, Śraddhā; then Bhāsanī should follow.
Then Jvālinī, then Āhlādanikā is sung; there is also Stambhinī and the power (śakti) Vikirā. (2-24)

These sixteen varieties of Śakti have been described in succession; by means of them, Śiva, whose power is fully aroused, being partless (niṣkala) yet through the metaphorical attribution of parts (sakalopacāra), sports as the unborn agent among the worlds. (2.25)
The one of great splendor, who has made his abode in the power of knowledge, is awakened;
for it is through the differentiation of locations that his agency is ever proclaimed.

Thus it is said in the *Pārameśvara*: "Just as the body of the Lord and the enjoyments are established for the sake of the activity of the worlds, so too do those powers abide upon the path of the principles (*tattva*), enriched by activities corresponding to their own names. (2.26)

And thus Rāmakaṇṭha says: "In this context, the category of Śakti is designated as the fourth, accompanied by the four worlds that will be described under the principle of Īśvara; for without its presiding presence, knowledge cannot arise in souls.
And in the Mataṅga:
"Furthermore, it is the sport of [His] own nature, and that is remembered as 'agitation' (kṣobha)."
In ancient times, through agitation and extreme velocity, the body of the creator came into being.
Having descended from that reality known as Īśvara,
Ananta brought forth the great world-system for the sake of establishing its functional activity.
In this way, the Lord is known as the agitator, and the bound souls (paśus) are known as those to be agitated.
From this [state],

agitating the worlds with the *kṣobhaṇī* (the agitator), he performs the creation of enjoyment through the *jananī* (the mother); then, obstructing the individual souls (*aṇu*) with the *rodhayitrī* (the obstructor), he establishes them each in their respective fruits of karma.
By means of her as a protector she guards the world, and by means of her as a leader she guides the universe;
she is the mass of light and nooses, capable of dissolving whatever belongs to the enjoyer.
Thus it is said in the Mataṅga: "Having wiped away the succession of suffering for bound souls (paśu), she is called Plāvikā. (2.27)
She floods [the individual souls] with the nectar of enjoyments and unites them with objects through faith;
and by means of the states of existence, non-existence, and being, she brings the atoms (individual souls) to realization through her creative power.
Having withdrawn the universe with the Jvālinī [power], he also sets it ablaze during the withdrawal;
with the Hlādinī [power], he causes delight through enjoyments and liberation by taking refuge in Śiva.
By means of the power of immobilization (stambhinī), that Great Lord establishes the universe within his own command;
he scatters atoms into birth across thousands of diverse wombs.
Through Vikiraṇī, Śiva exists manifoldly within moving and stationary beings, as well as those that crawl; and in the Mataṅga [Tantra]:
"Through Vikiraṇī, within the range of the limbs and members of the body as they are acquired."
It manifests the bodies of the world in a thousand ways.

Thus, Śiva, possessing infinite power, having known the universe through the sixteenfold divisions of his powers and through the networks of his own complete manifestations born from those divisions, creates the world incessantly. (2.31)
Three and a half crores of powers (śaktis) have been appointed by formal decree for the ritual procedure of the Vidyā-tattva; they are indeed the manifestations of those [powers].
Moreover, they have emerged with the unfailing power of the Creator, and they have spread throughout the manifold world;
by them, each one's own noble conduct has been revealed through the nature of cause and effect. (2.33)

By means of the method of dividing the bonds, all the bound souls (paśus) have been opened up and made prosperous; through skillful means, the fruit of their karma has been distributed exactly as it was due to those who have arrived at the opportunity for enjoyment. (2–34)
These great powers, which are the lamps of the entire universe, abide under the control of the Lord. || 2-35 ||
Thus ends the section on the investigation of power (*śakti*).
By the word "investigation" (*vicāra*), however, [is meant] that of the person (*puruṣa*) according to his karma, and likewise that of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*).
And even though it was created by a common [cause], the world is sung of as being unique. (2.36)

(28) They say that the investigation (*mīmāṃsana*) here refers to the analysis of those twenty-six divisions of the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*), which are joined with the principles (*tattva*) of *vidyā*, *sadvidyā*, and *īśvara*, as well as the [investigation] of those previously mentioned starting with the "subsequent" (*paścāt*). (2-37)
The Section on the Subjects of Deliberation:
Here, "action" (kriyā) refers to the entire cycle of ritual duties (*kṛtyacakra*) joined with the specific techniques of purificatory rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*).
Constant, occasional, and optional ritual acts—this pair is called "conduct" (*caryā*); these constitute the subject matter. (2–38)

The sixth [category] is well-known in the Śaiva scriptures such as the *Kiraṇa*. Now, regarding these categories (*padārtha*), that which serves as their exposition here is the *tantra*, derived from the verbal root *tan* in the sense of "sustaining" (*dhāraṇa*). (2.39)
The Section on the Categories of Ritual Practice (*Kriyācaryāpadārthādhikāra*).

Furthermore, because it was stated in the first verse of this chapter—following the context of describing the pervasion of Śiva-nature through initiation—that "I shall now explain what follows," the wheel of ritual action (*kriyācakra*), such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, which is included within the category of ritual practice, will be demonstrated below.

Thus has been declared the seed of the Śaiva Tantra, which, through the investigation of the bound soul (paśu), the fetter (pāśa), the Lord of the bound (pati), and the Sovereign Goddess (īśvarī), bears fruit here in this world— when sown with virtuous practice— as a grove of celestial wish-fulfilling trees that grants all desired objects.

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Examination of the Six Categories," in the section on Ritual (Kriyāpāda) of the latter part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the third chapter.
Next, the daily ritual (*naityaka-karma*) which generally brings about accomplishment is described here according to the rule.
That which is the single necessary duty to be performed by all those who possess the marks of caste and stage of life.
For when the stars are still radiant, but before the appearance of the rising sun, the sages declare that it is the dawn twilight; during that time, one who is awake should abandon his bed. (3.2)
Remembering the supreme Śiva-light situated within the hollow of the heart-lotus and established within the self,
one should rise and proceed toward that pure direction in which abundant and easily accessible water is found.

At a distance from roads, water reservoirs, and the like, on a ground surface covered with grass, having wrapped his lower garment around him, facing north during the day or south at night, and having discarded his excrement, he should then grasp his penis. (3-4)

(p. 29) With the sacred thread suspended over his ear—that is to say, with his head covered—and having reached a body of water, he should take pure clay obtained from a pit eight finger-breadths deep; placing it to his right, he should perform the ritual purification according to rule with the water held in his hands. (3–5)
One application of clay should be made on the penis, three on the two hands, and five on the anus;
twelve applications of clay should be made on the left hand, and the same number on both hands—this is indeed the primary rule for purification. (3–6)
Having risen and properly donned his garment, he should thoroughly wash his feet and hands up to the knees with pure clay and water, and cleanse his face with water used for rinsing the mouth.
For one desiring food, a tooth-stick made from the Plakṣa, Āmra, Jambū, Kakubha, Aśvakarṇa, Mālūra, Kāśoka, Lavaṅga, Jāti, Vaikaṅkata, Udumbara, or Campaka is indeed recommended. (3.8)
Measuring twelve of one's own fingers, it should be equal in girth to the little finger and covered with bark;
sitting facing east and observing silence, one should eat from left to right, beginning first with the lower left tooth.
For those seeking liberation, thorny trees—such as the *śirīṣa*, *arjuna*, and *naktamāla*—are like thorns;
however, the *apāmārga* is praised here for the cleansing of the teeth, with a length of eight finger-breadths. (3.10)
One who stands, talks, lies down, or even eats while anointed with oil, or while holding nimba, dhātrī, dhava, selu, śigru, vānīra, eraṇḍa, grass, or kuśa grass, shall not use a tooth-stick. (3.11)

One who has not fasted should not clean his teeth with fingers or nails before breaking the fast, nor on his birth asterism, nor on a festival day, nor on the new moon day, nor on the days of the eighth lunar tithi or śrāddha ceremonies. (3.12)

In this regard, the *Kālottara* states: "O Guha! On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the festival days, on the sixth, or even on the ninth, it is declared that there is a great fault in using a wooden tooth-stick."
In the same manner, having cleansed the tongue and discarded that tooth-stick and so forth at a distance,
one should afterwards perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with twelve mouthfuls of water and then commence the bath.

In the rivers such as the Gaṅgā and other principal holy fords (tīrthas), as well as in other major rivers, bathing is of the highest order; it is of middling quality in lakes, ponds, and the like; whereas in wells and at home, it is considered inferior. (3.14)
One should bathe in wells and similar sources with water collected by twice-born men who have themselves bathed using pure vessels.
However, one should not bathe in hot water, for that is not considered suitable for ritual acts, as it is intended only for those who are ill. (3.15)
Having dug the ground eight finger-breadths deep and having removed the earth from below with the Astra-mantra,
one should take that excavated earth and completely fill the pit once more.
Having again established it upon the head on the washed bank of the milk-ocean,
and having purified it with the *śikhā*, one should divide it into three parts with the *varman*.

Having smeared one portion [of the body] with [the substance] that has the luster of the navel, and having washed [the hands] and sipped water while remaining silent, one should smear the limbs with the second [portion], which is joined with the weapon-mantra and is radiant. (3-18)

Having restrained his breath and submerged himself in the water while recollecting the weapon-mantra—which resembles the fire of cosmic destruction—he likewise [performed this] in the water near the riverbank. (3.19)

Having sat down and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), and having performed the binding of the directions with the weapon-mantra (astramantra), one should take the remaining portion of the clay previously set aside and place it in the water reaching to the navel.
Having stood [there], one should then divide that [substance] held in the left hand into three parts:
the southern portion with the weapon-mantra (astra), and the northern portion first with the root-mantra (mūla).

Having anointed [the disciple] with the limb-mantras and having taken hold of his right [hand] with the weapon-mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ*, the wise one should cast it toward the ten directions for protection.
Having first taken water with the right hand while the root-mantra is not yet recited,
one should pour it out and swirl the water while recollecting the Śiva-tīrtha.
Having smeared the entire body with the remaining portion ignited by the heat of the charcoal, one should invoke that sacred site (tīrtha) by its own name and worship it.
With perfumes and flowers as they may be obtained, or with a concentrated mind even in thought, he should bathe at principal rivers, oceans, and sacred fords; he should not praise other fords.
If one recites [the name] in vain, it shall be fruitless; therefore, one should not recite it while being angry.
The recitation of the names of holy places such as the Gaṅgā is prescribed only when there is pure water. (3.26)
Therefore, one should proclaim those various sacred fords (tīrthas), each of which bestows its specific fruit;
then, having restrained the vital breaths, one should immerse oneself three times with a concentrated mind.
Immersed [in the water], one should recite with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and with power the root-mantra along with its limbs;
being capable, one should recite the eighty-one-word mantra for the removal of sin (aghamarṣaṇa).
If he is a twice-born, he should mutter the Vedic hymn for the purpose of rubbing,
beginning with "hiraṇyaśṛṅgam" and so forth, as described in the previous manual.

Just as even a vast accumulation of salt is instantly dissolved when thrown into a flood of water, so too it is certain that even a great heap of sins goes to destruction through the *aghamarṣaṇa* rite. (3.30)

Then, standing in the water, one should contemplate the left and right hands as being of the nature of the moon and sun, and the two Śivas; then, with the root mantra and the *kumbha-mudrā*, one should perform the consecration upon the head, and likewise with the limbs [of the mantra]. || 3.31 ||
Then, having come to the water's edge, he should change his loincloth and girdle, or otherwise cause him to put on two white garments. (3.32)
As Brahmaśambhu states:
"The loincloth of the celibate students (brahmacārins) should be a second [layer], spread across the hands;
it should have thirteen knots for the contraction of the senses, and its girdle should consist of the threads of the sacred cord."
The mention of the *brahmacārin* is illustrative; the meaning is that this applies to ascetics (*yatins*) and those wearing sectarian marks (*liṅgins*) as well.
Having bathed, he should not rub his limbs with his hand or with a wet garment.
Likewise, he should not look upon heretics, outcasts, those of the lowest castes, or the impure. (3.33)
If, through negligence, he should look upon a funeral pyre, a Caṇḍāla, a sacrificial post, a cemetery, wood from a cremation ground, or a donkey, he becomes pure again by bathing. (3.34)

Boars, cocks, women in their courses, jackals, owls, crows, those who have recently given birth, young children, those in a state of ritual impurity, great sinners, and the unclean—[one should avoid these]. (3.35)
If one touches a *devalaka* (a temple-priest who lives off temple offerings), one should enter the water with one's clothes on;
likewise during occasional rites (*naimittika-kṛtya*), such as eclipses, the waning of the moon, and so forth.
One should bathe with one's clothes on at the two solstices, at sacred fords (tīrtha), and so forth;
likewise after the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā), after shaving, and after contact with those who have voided urine or feces, those defiled by food remnants, or those afflicted with leprosy. (3.37)
Upon contact during sexual intercourse or vomiting, upon touching the ocean on a non-parvan day,
and even upon touching a Śūdra or those born of inverse unions (pratiloma), as well as a cat— 3-38.
After performing the rite of shaving, one should perform the Vāruṇa rite;
likewise before giving gifts, bathing, reciting prayers, offering libations, or performing fire-sacrifices. (3.39)
In all cases, one should be accompanied by the *pavitra*; otherwise, it would be demonic (*āsura*).
Or [it is demonic] if one has disheveled hair, is naked, is talking nonsense, or has one's head covered. (3.40)
One should know that all rites such as those for the gods and others which one performs at that time are demonic;
therefore, one should perform the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) before the sun has risen.
Therein, having first washed both hands and feet with earth and water, one should sip water twice according to the ritual rule, as enjoined by one's own tradition and the Smṛtis. (3.42)
p. 32) For example:

the divine *tīrtha* is at the tip of the index finger (*aṅgulyagra*), the brahmic at the base of the thumb (*aṅguṣṭhamūla*), that of the sages (*ārṣa*) at the joints of the fingers (*parvasandhi*), the progenitor’s (*prājāpatya*) below the little finger (*kaniṣṭhāmadhas*), and for the twice-born, the ancestral (*pitrya*) at the base of the forefinger (*tarjanīmūladeśa*). (3–43)
It is said that on the right side of the hand is the sacred site (tīrtha) called Āgneya, while on the other side is the Saumya;
another is the Daiva. One should perform ritual actions from one's own [appropriate] tīrtha, but one should sip water (ācamana) with the waters using the Brahma-tīrtha.
On the tip of the thumb is Agni; on the tip of the index finger is Vāyu; on the tip of the middle finger is Arka (the Sun); on the tip of the ring finger is Surendra (Indra);
and on the little finger is Prājāpatya—thus the fingers in the right hand of the Brahmin are presided over by these deities. (3–45)
Here, the mention of the word "vipra" (brahmin) is an elliptical expression meaning "initiated twice-born men.
Facing either east or north, wearing the sacred thread over the left shoulder, having tied his topknot, and with his arms placed between his knees—
Then, desiring water, he should sit down comfortably, remain silent, and with a one-pointed mind, remain humble while intending to consume [the food]. (3.46)

One should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) with pure water that is not hot, which is free from foul tastes, smells, and the like, and which is devoid of insects, foam, or bubbles, after having gazed upon it.
Having looked upon it, one should drink water three times, joined separately with the principles of Self-knowledge and Śiva, ending with "to Īśvara" and preceded by the *praṇava*.
Having formed the hand like a cow’s ear, one should drink water that reaches the depth of a barley grain,
three times as prescribed, through the *brahmatīrtha* without making a sound.
Having wiped the lips with a cloth, one should touch all the apertures with one’s whole being.
As stated in the *Kālottara-ṭīkā*:
"Water, when applied according to the prescribed rule, purifies the twice-born in succession as it reaches the heart, the throat, and the mouth."
By sipping water three times, even those who have drunk from the vessels of a *vṛṣala* woman, or from *kuṇḍa*, *anuloma*, and other such [low-caste] women,
as well as the gods and the ancestors, are gratified; and when one wipes [the mouth] twice,
the Ṛgveda, the six Vedāṅgas, the Sacrificial Person (*yajñapuruṣa*), and the sacred fires are likewise pleased.
The ring finger, when joined with the thumb, gratifies the Sun through contact with the eyes;
likewise, the index finger joined with the thumb, held level against the two nostrils, [controls] the winds;
the little finger with the thumb [placed on] the ears [gratifies] the quarters; and [the middle finger] from the navel [gratifies] the Vasus.
One should not touch oneself with the heart or the shoulders, nor the sky or the sages with the head, using all the fingers together.
