Thus, having sipped water twice correctly, one becomes pure; likewise after eating, when washing the feet, upon unfastening a girdle, upon loosening the topknot, or after spitting, yawning, or sneezing. (3.50)
The Section on Bathing and Sipping Water (p.
33): Having thus performed the sipping of water, one should then perform the Sandhyā-vandana. 3.51.
In that regard, prior to the Vedic [initiation], there is the Tantric twilight rite (sandhyā) called mantra;
thereafter, both Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas likewise perform it, while others perform only the purely Tantric one.
Īśāna, Puruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta, as previously described—these five, each followed by the fourth [syllable] and ending with "namaḥ," are distinct. (3.53)
The heart, head, crest, armor, eye, and weapon—these six limbs, together with their respective seed-syllables, follow in sequence; the root mantra is known as the Prāsāda.
And the weapon known as the Pāśupata—this is the collection of mantras.
Regarding this, in the *Kālottara*: "The Brahma-mantras, Śiva with his limbs, the Netra, and the Pāśupata."
This entire auspicious extraction of mantras has been told by you in brief.
Thus, the limbs of Śiva are written here for the sake of attaining the ritual action that is about to be described. (3.55)

Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the heart of Śiva. Oṃ hīṃ, svāhā to the head of Śiva. Oṃ hūṃ, vaṣaṭ to the crest-lock of Śiva. Oṃ haiṃ, huṃ to the armor of Śiva. Oṃ hauṃ, vauṣaṭ to the three eyes of Śiva. Oṃ haṃ, phaṭ to the weapon of Śiva. The second letter of the sixth group (ṣa), adorned with the fourth of the first group (a);
and the first syllable of the second group (ka), joined with the fifth of the first group (u). (3–56)
This is the Pāśupata weapon, together with its instruction, according to the proper sequence;
indeed, when joined with the Śiva-weapon, this very [mantra] destroys all obstacles. (3.57)
Having rubbed the two hands, which are smeared with fragrance, against each other, one should ward off the host of obstacles with the sound of three claps and the Astra-mantra;
then, one should sequentially assign the mantras beginning with Īśāna to the fingers starting from the thumb (jyeṣṭhā) down to the pair of little fingers (kaniṣṭhikā). || 3-58 ||
Just as the syllable of space (ha) is joined with the short vowels ending in the bindu,
so too should one assign [the letters] beginning with o and ending with a, starting from Īśāna and the other [faces].
Then, one should again perform the placement [of mantras] on the fingers beginning with the little finger using the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra),
and place the weapon-mantra (astramantra) on both palms, ending with the thumb.
With the thumb lost and the fist closed, facing downwards, it is the gesture of Īśāna;
the remaining fingers of Puruṣa and the others should be held as the Jyeṣṭhikā grasp. (3.61)
The mudrās proclaimed by the five Brahmās are thus set forth in sequence for the ritual placements (nyāsa).
With them, one should [place] from the head, mouth, heart, secret place, and feet, up to the top of the body. (3.62)
One should place Īśāna and the other deities with their respective mantras upon the head—starting from the front of the skull, then on the right, the north, and the rear parts of the head. (3.63)
One should place one's own limbs, beginning with the heart, in their respective locations;
[one should realize] Sadāśiva as the body of knowledge (vidyādeha), whose faces are the five Brahmans, and who is identical with oneself.
In the twilight worship, ritual adoration, and so forth, one should contemplate "I am Śiva.
This is the section on the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa (the rite of making [the self] complete).
On this point, in the Kālottara:
Having perfected the body through the sciences and meditated upon the twilight according to the sequence of time,
one should contemplate it respectively as having the appearances of red, white, and dark-blue.
The power of Śambhu, which manifests as distinct through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of causes such as Brahmā and others, and which is the witness of all actions, is celebrated as Sandhyā.
"One should make one's own body enter the expanse of that circle of light.
For example:

One should meditate upon the morning twilight, the mother of the three worlds, who is worthy of worship; she is mounted upon a swan, adorned with garments and unguents of jewels from her own radiance, lotus-eyed, and holding in her four arms a rosary, a flowing water-pot, and a staff.
She is the Sāvitrī verse, the Savitṛ herself, possessing fresh youth within the orb of the fierce-rayed sun.

Mounted upon Garuḍa, lotus-eyed, possessing the luster of Indra’s sapphire, holding the conch and discus with her four arms, she who is the very foundation of the worlds and who utters the Yajurvedic mantras—
Vaiṣṇavī, radiant and beautiful with the glow of many swaying necklaces, shines at midday.
Sāvitrī, whose form is that which is to be meditated upon, shines within the orb of the sun, clad in yellow garments.
One should meditate on her who has five faces and a circle of matted locks beautiful with streaks of tawny lightning; who bears the moon upon her crest;
whose body is smeared with ashes resplendent with the rays from the jewels of the hoods of the dancing serpents that serve as her ornaments;
who holds a skull-topped staff, a trident, and displays the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons; and who is clothed in a tiger skin.
Sāvitrī, who possesses three eyes, whose age is mature, and who follows the path of the Sāman chants at the end of the day; || 3.67 ||
Having meditated upon each twilight separately, in succession, at every junction of day and night.

Having again meditated upon one's own right and left hands as being of the nature of Agni and Soma, and further as being of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, one should take water in the right [hand]. (3.69)
Recalling Śivatīrtha, which is accompanied by the Gaṅgā and other rivers,
and having recited the Saṃhitā, one should apply it to the head with the water-pot mudrā.
Then, having taken water with the right hand from the Astra-mantra and having placed it in his left hand, he should meditate upon it as divine nectar (*sudhāmṛta*).
Then, taking with his right hand— equipped with the pavitra— the drops of water that have flowed out, while reciting the mantras of the Saṃhitā.

Sprinkling [the water], one should join it to the crown of the head; then, placing the remainder in the right hand, one should meditate on it as consisting of blazing light through its connection with the right nostril.
The sin residing within the body, consisting entirely of darkness,
was cast out by the radiance of that light and emerged through the left nostril.
One should further contemplate [the body] being burned by the weapon-mantra (astra) and cast it upon the ground;
for this is indeed the Aghamarṣaṇa rite that effects the destruction of all sins.
"Oṃ hauṃ, salutation to the Sun, whose nature is Śiva.

Having taken water in his joined palms with this mantra and having sprinkled it three times upward toward the Sun, he should again perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) while facing the Sun. (3.76)
Having recited the Śivagāyatrī, complete with its introductory and concluding phrases,
one hundred and eight times according to one's capacity, or even ten times.
Having meditated upon the Sun as the self of Śiva, having performed three circumambulations,
and having offered salutations and obtained permission, one should then begin the libation (tarpaṇa).

With his upper garment anointed with ghee and holding purifiers in his hands, he [should recite] the Brahma-mantras and the Aṅga-mantras, as well as the four-faced [Brahmā], Viṣṇu and Rudra, and likewise Īśvara and Sadāśiva. (3.79)

Having gratified [the deities] with cool, pure water, using their own names ending in "svāhā" and "namaḥ," one should subsequently utter the syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and the pair of feet [of the mantra], followed by the words "vāgvādini" joined with "svāhā" at the end.

Having gratified the directions of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra, by joining their respective names with the dative case and ending with "namaḥ," as well as the zenith reaching to the vault of heaven and likewise the earth enjoyed by the nāgas; (3.81)
Thus concludes the libation to the ten directions.

One should satisfy those ten—Indra, Agni, Vaivasvata, the Lord of Rākṣasas, the Lord of Waters, Vāyu, Arthapati, Soma, the one called Īśa, Vedhas, and Ananta—with their respective names as before. (3.82)

In that regard, the instruction is that one should know Soma to be in the direction of the Giver of Wealth (the North), Brahmā—the lord of the upward direction—between Indra and Īśāna, and Ananta—the lord of the downward direction—between Nirṛti and Varuṇa.
Thus ends the libation to the lords of the directions.
[The sages] Atri, likewise the one named Kauśika, Pulastya, Bhāradvāja, Aṅgiras, and Vasiṣṭha.
Then another Dakṣa, as well as Bhṛgu and Marīci—having gratified these as before, he should perform the sacrifice. || 3.83 ||

"I satisfy Sanaka, Sanātana, Sananda, the one named Bhṛgu, Sanatkumāra, and Paila, together with Pañcaśikha"—with these words, the ritual from the beginning up to the end of the day should be performed separately for each. (3.84)
Thus [he should satisfy] the yogis and human beings; and he should likewise gratify Śiva, Rudra, Śrī, Umā, Brahmā, Agni, Viṣṇu, Vāyu, Sūrya, as well as Dharma, Soma, and Īśāna. (3.85)
Thus [he worships] the Siddhas;
and likewise the Sun, the Moon, Mars, Mercury,
Jupiter, Venus, Saturn, Rāhu, and Ketu— these nine planets.

One should offer libations with one's own names in the dative case, ending with "namaḥ. Having satisfied all the spirits (bhūtas) with the mantra: "Oṃ, vaṣaṭ, obeisance to all beings," one should then, with the sacred thread over the right shoulder (apasavya), satisfy the ancestors (pitṛs) using sesame seeds, darbha grass, and water through one's own tīrtha, [reciting]:
"Soma accompanied by the Pitṛs, Yama, Aṅgirasvat, Agni Kavyavāhana, and the other ancestors—to those ancestors, I offer svadhā and obeisance; may they be satisfied."
One should satisfy the wives of the ancestors, the groups of ancestors, and the wives of the group of ancestors;
thereafter, one should also satisfy one's own ancestors by means of their respective names and lineages.
At the end [of each name], one should employ the formula "svadhā namaḥ tarpayāmi" together with the [specific] name:
for the fathers, the grandfathers, and likewise the great-grandfathers. (3.88)
One should likewise satisfy the mothers, the paternal grandmothers, and the paternal great-grandmothers; as well as the maternal grandfathers and the maternal grandfathers' fathers.
[He should offer for] the great-grandmothers of his mother, as well as the maternal grandmothers of his mother, the grandmothers of his mother, and the great-grandmothers of his mother. (3.90)
Furthermore, [he should honor] his kinsmen and the wives of his kinsmen, as well as his teachers,
his friends and their wives, and others born of his own lineage.

Having offered libations as before and bowed, saying "Obeisance to the Waters," one should contemplate [the dissolution] for the sake of pacifying the defects caused by disturbances such as the shifting of the feet.
Having withdrawn the sacred site from the small palace, one should join it within the heart.
Thus, through rising, the necessary purification, and the cleansing of the teeth— (3.93)
"Following the ritual of the bath and the twilight prayers, the Āgneya bath is prescribed;
or, having first performed the Vāruṇa bath, one should subsequently perform the Āgneya bath," according to this scriptural statement.
And so it is stated in the Mataṅga:
"In this way, O best of sages, a wise man who has bathed in the water even once according to his capacity becomes entitled to the ash-bath; not otherwise."
Thus, when one is unable to bathe due to the affliction of disease, [one may perform it] during the Vāruṇa [period]. (3.94)
For him, the fire-related rite alone is desired, for it pacifies disease;
bathing with fire-related ashes destroys all sins. (3.95)

By means of that very [mantra] born of his own splendor, Śiva himself bathed at the three junctions of the day, at the beginning of the recitation of prayers, and at the commencement and conclusion of his ritual observances.
Having eaten, slept, drunk water, or performed necessary duties such as voiding,
or having touched a woman, or those of low caste, or mice, or impure things— (3.97)
One should perform the fire-purification bath (āgneyasnāna) exactly as prescribed in the Atharvaveda when in the vicinity of a deity, fire, a guru, or sacred knowledge, or upon seeing an outcaste.

A wise person standing on an impure ground or on a path should not shake [the ritual items]; likewise, one should not shake that which is "without time" (akalpaka), due to its divisions into Kalpa, Anukalpa, and Upakalpa. (3.99)
The fourfold ash described by Śiva is such that each preceding one possesses superior qualities:
[the first is] that which has fallen on the ground from a healthy cow accompanied by her calf. (3.100)
Having taken cow dung with either a lotus leaf, a Palāśa leaf, or another such vessel, the pure-souled one [should do so] with the Gāyatrī mantra known as Śiva. (3-101)

One should fetch from afar, away from villages and the like, purified cow-dung from the forest, which has been consecrated with the *saṃhitā* mantras in the fire of Śiva and is designated as "kalpa. (3.102)
That which has been burnt by the Śiva-fire as previously described constitutes the secondary (anukalpa) form;
and that ash is of four kinds, free from any mixture of castes.
Then, having taken ashes from forests consumed by fire and forming them into balls bound with cow urine, one should dry them in the fire of Śiva.
That which has been burnt should be prepared as ash; or else, it is said that [the ash] should be obtained from a distinguished Brahmin, a cow-pen, or a temple of the deity. (3-105)
Having taken it and processed it as before, that ash shall be free from conceptual construction (*akalpaka*).
And that ash is of four kinds, devoid of any confusion of caste (*jātisaṅkara*).
The white ash, which others have not claimed as their own, which is untainted by contact with [impure] actions and the like, smooth, pure, and free from disease, should be placed in a vessel. (3.107)
The ash suitable for the Āgneya bath is as described by Brahmaśambhu: it should have been obtained according to one's capacity through the mantras of the Saṃhitās and must be well-protected. (3.108)
Having taken [the water] from the vessel with the right hand and having consecrated it with mantras,
one should purify it by means of the *dhāraṇī* mantras according to the procedure for the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).

Having first consecrated [the water] with the six-limbed mantra, and then again with the *astra* mantra, one should perform the impurity-bath starting from the head and proceeding in sequence with the left hand.
Then, with the [mantras] of Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāma, and Sadyojāta,
one should [worship] the entire body in sequence, from the head, face, heart, and private parts down to the shanks.

A twice-born man should smear [the ashes] over his entire body, while others should wear the triple marks (tripuṇḍra) on the forehead, shoulders, heart, and other parts; likewise, Brāhmaṇas and the other castes should do so.
One should maintain the *triyāyuṣa* [mantra], because the authority of the Veda is observed therein;
for there is the scriptural testimony beginning with, "The *triyāyuṣa* of Jamadagni, the *triyāyuṣa* of Kāśyapa," and so forth.
This concludes the section on the *Āgneyasnāna*.
(39) Even the *aindra* and other ablutions are seen, according to the teachings of the Āgamas. (3.113)
By bathing in these, one finds the destruction of evil, merit, and prosperity;
and when the sun shines in a cloudless sky, one sees rain by raising one's arms.
The Māhendra bath should be performed by Īśāna, extending for seven steps,
with dust raised from the hollows of cows' hooves and carried by the wind.
A twice-born man standing in the midst of cows should recite the *Tatpuruṣa* [mantra] or the *Gomati-sūkta*;
another, however, should utter the praise of cows or the words "Salutation to the cows. (3.116)
One should perform the Vāyavya bath, which destroys all sins;
among all baths here, the Vāruṇa is both the root and the most excellent.
Therefore, having first performed the rite dedicated to Varuṇa, one should thereafter engage in the subsequent bath;
having washed one's hands and feet and sipped water (ācamana), one should then remain restrained in speech.
Having become endowed with the body of knowledge, one should perform the mantra-bath;
a Brahmin [should do so] with the five Brahma-mantras and with the Gāyatrī known as Śiva. (3-119)
Recalling the Śiva-tīrtha with the root mantra and the six limbs,
one should sprinkle one's own head using a bunch of *darbha* grass or from the roots of *kuśa* grass.
In that [initiation], the twice-born initiate, having practiced the mantras beginning with Īśāna as well as the root-mantra and its limbs, should sprinkle his own head. (3.121)
The Vedic ritual bath is indeed performed with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā";
by that as well, a Brahmin should perform the purification, and he shall attain supreme purity. (3.122)

Then, while going to the sacrificial hall, one should withdraw the sacred site (*tīrtha*) by means of the short [measure], that is to say, by the short temple (*hrasvaprāsāda*). Having fastened the bathing garments and other items upon the staff, one should take leave of that water. (3-123)
Having remembered the Guru and Gaṇeśa and having worshipped them within the heart,
one should purify the path with the Astra-mantra while remaining in the midst of the five astras.

One should proceed toward the sacrificial hall while mentally constructing the levels of reality (tattvas) below, meditating upon the abode of the Vidyā-tattva, the sanctuary of all knowledge. (3.125)
Having placed the ritual vessels for bathing and so forth upon some such thing as a peg, in a clean and secluded place, the practitioner, observing silence, should then commence the worship. (3-126)

In connection with the twilight worship (*sandhyopāsti*), this cycle of daily obligatory rites (*naityaka-karmacakra*) prescribed by injunction has been briefly described here according to the Śaiva Tantra for those bearing the sectarian marks (*liṅgin*) and those belonging to the [four] stages of life (*varṇin*).
It bestows the attainment of desired results, both seen and unseen, and is practiced here by the sages; thus say the virtuous.
May they accept their own wealth as if it were their own, leading their friends onto the path of the virtuous.
Thus ends the third chapter, on the daily bath and related rites, in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Having prostrated before Śambhu, who is crowned with the crescent moon, Bhava, the destroyer of worldly existence, [I shall describe] in brief...
The purification of the self through the sequence of the natural purity is proclaimed for the sake of attaining success in yoga, recitation, and so forth. (4.1)
Having bathed according to rule and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), he went to the sacrificial hall and purified his feet;
having sipped water (ācamana) and entered within according to the injunctions, he sat down upon an auspicious seat, restraining his speech. || 4.2 ||
Meditating upon his own body from head to both feet as containing a very subtle cavity within it,
he should then project that pure power, which has the luster of the sky, externally and then [re-absorb it] into the middle of the body.
Having visualized the radiant seed-syllable *huṃ*, and having restrained the breath while fixing the mind upon it,
one should gradually effect the piercing of the knots with the weapon-mantra ending in *phaṭ*, as prescribed at the conclusion of the exhalation (*recaka*).
By the word "astra" (missile), it is meant the *pāśupatāstra*.

Those five knots, well-known as being located in the heart, throat, palate, between the eyebrows, and in the head, and which are extremely defiled by darkness (*tamas*),—through their piercing, however, the path of the channels (*nāḍī*) becomes established. (4–5)

Having restrained the vital air within oneself, from the half-measure of inhalation (pūraka), one should contemplate—by means of the word "sāntātmaka," which refers to the *haṃsa* mantra—the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) consisting of pure consciousness as the *bindu*.
Having visualized that [soul] as the *bindu*, free from all affliction, within one's own heart-lotus through the practice of retention (*kumbhaka*), [one should meditate]. (4–6)

There, by the upward movement of the breath, one should lead the individual soul (jīva), which has been placed at the crown of the head via the path of Suṣumṇā, to Śiva who resides within the "End of the Twelve" (dvādaśānta) by means of the mere upward thrust (udghāta) through the function of the seed-syllable (bījavṛtti). || 4-7 ||

A *udghāta* (upward stroke) is said to consist of twelve *mātrās*. Regarding this in the *Yogānuśāsana*: "The wise know that a *mātrā* is the duration of a finger-snap performed by circumambulating the knee, neither too fast nor too slow."
A duration of twelve mātrās is called an *uddhāta*.
Thus:
"In this [space] of twelve finger-breadths, one should conceive a white, auspicious thousand-petaled lotus;
it is filled with the nectar of the sky, faces downward, and its center is to be understood as occupied by Śiva. (4.8)
Absorbed in Śiva, with his self protected by his limbs, he visualizes the tree of the body with its face turned downward;
then, having led the thirty-six principles (tattvas) in reverse order into dissolution within their respective causes, [he attains absorption].
Namely:
from earth, water, fire, air, and ether, there arise smell, taste, and form;
likewise, that which is called touch and sound are declared, as well as the generative organ, speech, hands, feet, and the anus.

The nose, tongue, eye, as well as skin, ear, mind, ego, and intellect; the constituents (guṇas), primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), attachment, impure knowledge (aśuddhavidyā), limited agency (kalā), and necessity (niyati). (4.11)
In the same way, Kāla, Māyā, Viśuddhavidyā, and likewise Īśvara;
Sadāśiva, Śakti, and then Śiva—these are declared to be the principles (tattvas) beginning with Śiva. (4.12)

Then, the five elements beginning with space (khādīni) are to be purified within one another in reverse order, because they are presided over by Viriñca and the others, along with their respective digits (kalā), forms (bimba), qualities (guṇa), senses (akṣa), and deities. || 4-13 ||

The terrestrial sphere, which is square, devoid [of impurities], marked with thunderbolts, endowed with the quality of fragrance, and ever-present—that is the olfactory faculty, joined with its partial manifestation (*nivṛtti*) and presided over by the four-faced deity. (4.14)
From the seed-syllable *hrāṃ*, through inhalation (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*), one should contemplate that [the body] is pervaded from the two feet up to the knees;
then, one should meditate on it being purified until the end of the five upward-expulsions (*uddhātaka*), as it enters into the wind.

The reflection [of the deity] is white as the half-moon, with the symbol of a white lotus enriched by the essence (rasa); it is the sense organ of taste, situated on the left, accompanied by Viṣṇu, and joined with the kalā of Pratiṣṭhā—it is to be purified. 4-16.
The seed-syllable *hrīṃ*, purified by the fourfold extraction, then enters the navel region of the fire;
it becomes the triangular, ruddy orb of fire, possessing the digit of knowledge (*vidyākala*) and marked with the auspicious sign (*svastika*).
The visual organ, which has form as its quality, together with Rudra and the seed-syllable *hrūṃ*, conjoined with Aghora, is to be purified.
Having contemplated it as pervading up to the throat, one should cause it to enter the water through three *uddhātas*. || 4-18 ||
Then, the wind-element is marked with six dots; it is black, hexagonal, and situated within the Puruṣa.
Endowed with the qualities of touch and tranquility, it is to be purified by the Lord through the seed-syllable *Hraiṃ* and the two types of upward expulsion (*udghāta*). (4.19)
That [space] is pervaded up to the limit of the pair of eyebrows; it has entered the earth by means of its gross portion alone.
It is the circular orb of the sky, white as crystal, together with the ear and sound, and endowed with the power of the Bindu. (4.20)
That which is conjoined with the seat of Īśāna, extending beyond and pervading everything from the root-mantra and the weapon-mantra up to the crown of the head,
is entirely saturated by the streams of nectar-water from the moon arising from the root-mantra situated at the *dvādaśānta*.
Having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*) by immersion and having established the principles (*tattvas*) in their proper sequence,
one should, by the will of Śiva— who is the substratum of his own power— accomplish a body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*) consisting of the principles from Śiva down to Earth.
Having produced a pure body by the will of Śiva, one should then offer a seat in the heart with the syllable *praṇava*.
Having placed the pervasive Śakti of Śiva, in which the individual soul (jīva) residing in its own seed-syllable is established,
one should then, by means of inhalation, bring that [soul] from the *dvādaśānta* through the channel into the center of the heart-lotus.

Having established [the deity] and flooded it with the full streams of the root nectar-water, one should begin the worship and other rites. This concludes the section on the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Herein, another clear purification of the self is described, which proceeds through the sequence of drying and so forth within the upper body. (4.24)
By bestowing purity through the complete destruction of all defects, it destroys diseases, old age, and even death;
as before, one should contemplate a cavity within one's own body and the internal-external power pervading it. (4.25)
With the life-force of the mind situated in the syllable *huṃ*, having restrained the breath through inhalation (*pūraka*), one should pierce the knots;
then, at the end of the exhalation (*recaka*), having turned back the wind from the expulsion by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*), one should perform the inhalation again.

Having drawn forth consciousness together with the tranquil life-force from the heart-cavity— that light known as "the Untainted"— one should draw that beloved [light] upward by means of the path of Suṣumnā through the force of the expulsion at the end of breath-retention (kumbhaka).
Having brought the principles (tattvas) to dissolution in reverse order, one should unite them with Śiva residing at the end of the twelve;

and having brought the phonemes, as declared in the sequence beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*, to dissolution in reverse order, one should likewise dissolve the stream of sound into the Power (Śakti).

Having contemplated the body as empty, consisting of nothing but impurity and sin, one should then visualize at the navel-center the syllable *yaṃ*, which is black and has the color of thick smoke; this is the fierce wind (*caṇḍavāyu*) within the sphere of air.
"One should meditate upon the body as the nature of the tree of transmigratory existence— having its branches below and its roots above.
"The tree of worldly existence, whose essence is the body, should be meditated upon there with the self as its downward-facing trunk," so says Brahmaśambhu.
One should dry that evil impurity with the fierce wind emerging from the navel, while the evil impurity itself is being dried.

p. 43) Having first mastered its drying up by means of the five *uddhātaka* breath-retentions through the restraint of the vital air, one should thereafter [meditate upon] the final syllable in the heart-lotus, conjoined with fire, accompanied by the *anugraha* vowel, joined with the half-moon, and endowed with resonance (*nāda*). (4.31)
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable, which is like fire, one should place it within the fiery image as red in color;
then, by means of the spreading thousands of flames from the six-cornered trident of blazing fire, [one should burn away] the multitude of sins.
One should contemplate that which is called the body as being completely reduced to ashes while it is being rightly burned;
for it is stated in the *Parākhyatantra* and the *Pauruṣatantra* that "one should burn [it] with the *pāśupatāstra*," or else one should burn it with the *pāśupatāstra*.
And having driven away all those ashes by scattering them in every direction with the seed-syllable of the fierce wind (*caṇḍānilavāyu*), [one should proceed]. (4-33)

Having contemplated the body as empty and equal to space, yet pure and consisting solely of the remainder of merit, [it arises] from the power of the will, action, and knowledge of Śiva’s Śakti, who resides within the lotus of the sky and desires to create. (4.34)
Having produced the principles (*tattvas*) by means of the groups of letters (*lipivarṇa*) according to their respective potencies (*śakti*), and having fashioned from them a body,
he then brings into being the entire world in the form of the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*), conceiving it as pure and free from the bonds of fetters (*pāśabandha*).
Having drawn up that life-force (jīva), which has its seed-syllable placed at the *dvādaśānta* and is mixed with the *pūraka* breath,
one should lead it through the path of the *brahmarandhra* and place it in the center of the heart-lotus as Śiva in the form of the Self.
Enriched by the vowels located in the digit of the moon in the center of the sky-lotus, one should bring [the breath] through the Suṣumṇā by means of the nectar-drops of the sixteen-petaled support,
filling it individually and correctly with the vowels in reverse order.
Sāmṛtāmāninī, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, as well as Prīti, Rati, Śrī, Śānti, Sudhā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Haimavatī, Prabhā, Pūraṇī, and Amā with Vāmā constitute the sixteenth [digit]. (4.38)

From the right big toe, following the sequence of the ankle, knee, hip, abdomen, wrist, and arm, one reaches the head; this is the sequence for the right side. Half [of the sequence] is likewise on the left side. The locations have thus been described; one should place the *kalās* in the reverse order.

"AḤ, salutation to Amā; AṂ, salutation to Vāmā; OṂ, salutation to Pūraṇī"—having thus deposited the sixteen digits (kalās) from the thumb to the top of the head, one should fill [the body] with their nectars in sequence; such is the instruction.
One should contemplate the water in the sky-lotus as having the luster of the half-moon and the full moon, possessing the vowel-sounds derived from those digits.
Then, filling one's own body through the path of the Brahma-nāḍī with nectars as white as a conch, a jasmine flower, the moon, or cow's milk. (4.40)

He who even once meditates with his intellect upon the pure one—whose form is like that of a sixteen-year-old, whose body is composed of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā), and whose form is being bathed by the overflowing flood of its nectar, and who is acquired through a multitude of merits—he shall become a yogi. (4.41)
Thus, through such practice, one whose being is purified attains the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) by the grace of the Lord.
Through recitation, worship, and other rites, one achieves mastery over activity; likewise, the Goddess of Speech, being well-pleased, shall issue forth from his mouth. (4.43)
For the purification of this most defiled body cannot be achieved by mere washing with specific waters alone; thus,
the virtuous have declared that inner spiritual purification is of two kinds.
One should also constantly practice that which has been taught along with its ritual procedure.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, beginning with the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 4.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Now, the worship of this Śiva, the Supreme Self whose body is the Vidyā, should be known as that which brings about accomplishment and bestows both visible and invisible fruits. (5.1)
For that worship is divided into three types according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior:

that which is performed with sixteen modes of service (*upacāra*) is the supreme worship; that which arises here from ten modes of service is the middling; and the inferior service is by the rule of five modes of service—one should undertake the worship of these according to one's available means. (5.2)
The seat, the invitation, the arghya, the water for the feet, and the water for sipping; || 5-3 ||
Likewise, the ritual bath with its primary and secondary components, as well as garments, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, and the offering of sacrificial rice (caru).
The fire-ritual, prostration, recitation, worship, and dedication—thus, in brief, sixteen services have been specified. (5.5)

Water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), water for sipping (ācamana), bathing water, fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings (naivedya), and prostration—these are your ten [articles of worship]. 5–6.
In the middling worship, however, the ritual services (upacāras) are proclaimed as follows:
perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings—these five shall be the services in the lowest [worship].
Furthermore, the subdivisions of these characteristics are being inscribed for the benefit of practitioners. (5–7)
On this point, Brahmaśambhu states:
"Having invoked the form of the seat [of the deity] upon the path of Meru,
and having understood it through the relationship of the pervaded and the pervader, one should begin the sacrifice."
The seat consists of Śuddhavidyā; the form is within it, extending as far as Śakti. Having invoked that Śivā, he stands above, possessing the form of a fist.
Moreover,
the infinite seat is the form of Śakti, and Śiva is its possessor;
yet others of perfected intellect say that the seat is Śakti alone.
Thus:
"Or rather, the support is the seat; the deity, seated upon it, is worshipped as the desired divinity.
Since the root *ās* signifies 'sitting' (upaveśa), its accomplishment is established; therefore, the seat is praised first. (5-8)
One should install the foundational power (ādhāraśakti), radiant as moonlight, which has reached the tortoise-stone (kūrmaśilā).
One should place Ananta, who has become the infinite seat, upon the Brahma-stone;
for "Ananta" is indeed Viṣṇu, the power that is the cause of protecting all.
Then, one should worship the four lion-shaped legs of the pedestal located in the directions of Agni, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and Īśāna.

In sequence, [one should worship] the letters *i*, *u*, *ka*, *śma*, *ī*, *ra*, *ta*, *ā*, *li*, and *va*, together with the *tāra* (oṃ), the heart-mantra (*hṛd*), the names, the sounds, and the *mon* mantras. || 5-10 ||
In the same manner, one should likewise assign Adharma, Ignorance, Non-detachment,
and Lack of Sovereignty to the directions of Indra and the others, as well as to the seat (pīṭha), respectively.
In this *Kiraṇa*:
"The great root of the four ages, with the earth-principle as its bulb,
the principle of *kalā* as its stalk, and the fifty states of being as its thorns."
The great knot of the principle of Māyā is adorned with the lotus of Śuddhavidyā,
covered by the petals of the Vidyeśvaras, and endowed with the filaments of Śakti.

One should thus conceive of the pedestal as originating from the seed-syllables of the Mātṛkās, adorned with the seed-syllables at its pericarp, which are produced from the two powers of Śiva and Śakti.
Thus it is said.
Also in the *Kālottara*:
"The lotus has eight petals and is white; its pericarp has the luster of gold."
The wheel of power (śakticakra), resembling the rising rays of the sun, is Manonmanī.
One should meditate upon the circle of the army as having the luster of moonlight in its own form;
the solar disc pervades the petals, and Brahmā shall be its presiding lord.
Likewise, the lunar disc is at the filaments, with Viṣṇu as its protector;
and the fiery mandala pervading the pericarp has Rudra as its presiding deity.
The powers beginning with Vāmā belong respectively to the eight forms [of Śiva] beginning with Earth;
by their means, through the command of Śiva, the growth and perfection of the world are accomplished.
The ninth, however, is the goddess Manonmanī, the very power (śakti) of Śiva;
thus [the powers are] Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālā, and Kalavikaraṇī. (5.12)
Balavikaraṇī, then Balapramathinī, the one named Sarvabhūtadamanī, and the ninth shall be Manonmanī. (5.13)

White, red, black, yellow, dark-green, black like collyrium, and luster like the *japā* flower or moonlight— these beautiful forms are said to be Vāmā and the others, their limbs adorned on all sides.
"They should be visualized as having one face and two arms, with palms joined in *añjali* and facing toward the deity," according to the *Kālottara-ṭīkā*.

"Having first [uttered] the seed-syllable of the Heart preceded by *Tāra*, and [the deity's] own name ending in *namaḥ*, and having mentally constructed (*saṅkalpya*) the throne of Śiva and performed meditation, one should worship that which traverses the path of the principles (*tattvādhvan*). (5.15)
Others say it is "constructed throughout all times without exception. This concludes the section on the seat.
Regarding the reality that is inherently complete, here [in the context] of worship and so forth—
The manifestation [of the deity] before one with reverence is intended as its invocation. || 5-16 ||
Then, having filled his joined palms with flowers while recollecting the form of Śiva,
he should deposit them upon the liṅga or other receptacle, using the mantra beginning with the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) and ending with "namaḥ."
Just as the form [of the deity] is constituted by the principles beginning with Earth and ending with Śakti:
she is seated in the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), possessing the luster of the pure moon, resembling a sixteen-year-old girl, with a divine appearance as described;
she has five faces through the five Brahmans, and three eyes representing the triad of the powers of Action, Will, and Knowledge. (5.18)

She holds in her ten arms—numbering five on each side—the *śakti*, the trident (*śūla*), and the *khaṭvāṅga* along with the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) that grants desired boons; on the other [left] side, she holds a serpent, a rosary (*akṣasraj*), a *ḍamaru*, a blue lotus (*utpala*), and likewise a citron (*bījapūra*).
"Having five streams for heads, tranquil, with ten directions as arms, the Lord"— thus says Brahmaśambhu.
Having thus meditated upon the form, one should cast a handful of flowers onto the *liṅga*.
Then, with a full handful of flowers, one should meditate upon Śiva as the body of knowledge (vidyādeha).
Moreover, for the sake of the accomplishment of the stainless Self, which possesses a body with parts... || 5-21 ||
With the crown of her head being the kalā beyond peace (śāntyatīta), with peaceful lotus-faces,
with broad shoulders that are knowledge (vidyā), and with the secret maṇḍala of establishment (pratiṣṭhā).

Her calves and feet are born from the path of cessation (nivṛtti); she has the paths of the worlds as her body hair; she possesses the paths of the castes and mantras as her blood, and is endowed with the paths of the states (pada) as her flesh and veins.
"This auspicious body consists of the elements of marrow, semen, bone, and earth.
Having thus meditated upon the body of Vidyā, joined with the Tāra, the Heart, and the Root-mantra at the heart; (5.24)
Having uttered "obeisance" to the Vidyā-body, one should apply it to the form;
here, one should install the thirty-eight kalās within the Vidyā-body.
Just as previously stated, that ritual placement (nyāsa) is intended for the object of worship;
thereafter, one should invoke the omnipresent Lord Śiva into the body of the Vidyā.
On this point, Brahmaśambhu says: "In this [system], the Supreme Lord is the ultimate cause, entirely free from all limiting adjuncts (upādhi),
endowed with qualities such as omniscience, and beginningless."
One should honor the partless [deity] within the embodied self through ritual arrangements,
with devotion, while reciting the mantra of the temple-self (*prāsādātman*) beginning with the invocation (*āvāhana*).
Having filled his joined palms with flowers, he should recite [the mantra] directed toward Śiva, who resides at the forefront of the heart,
until the state of the partless (niṣkala) is attained.
For the purpose of the rite of invocation, one should meditate upon [the deity] arisen within the drop (bindu), pervaded by the cultivation of that state, amidst a shimmering circle of rays.
Therefore, having taken hold of it with confidence, one of steady intellect, while the body stands before him as the object of focus, should fix and stabilize that [consciousness] within the heart.
Thus:

"The acts consisting of installation (sthāpana), bringing into proximity (sannidhāpana), confinement (sannirodha), the nectarization (amṛtīkāra), and the veiling (avakuṇṭhana) are ancillary to the invocation (āvāhana). (5.27)
In this worship performed with devotion, "sthāpana" (establishment) is defined as the continuous stabilization of Śiva, who has been invoked here within the body of knowledge (vidyādeha). 5-28.
Therefore, in relation to the connection between property and its owner, that which is his presence—even though he is omnipresent—is proclaimed here as the manifestation of his own power. (5.29)
That presence of Śiva which persists until the completion of the worship is designated as *sannirodha* (complete absorption), even for the Lord himself, through devotion. (5.30)
The reality is the abode of bliss, whose form is existence, consciousness, and bliss;
that which pervades all this here should be meditated upon as the covering. (5.31)
Even for those things that possess distinct natures, that which is their non-distinct purpose constitutes the "immortalization" of the parts together with the whole. (5.32)
Like a veil, it increases the brilliance of the radiant limbs;
that should be performed with the Great Seal (Mahāmudrā), for it is indeed an incitement [to practice]. (5.33)
The Section on Invocation.
That *arghya* is of three kinds, distinguished as Śaiva—with six or eight limbs—and Śākta; the Śākta *arghya* consists of eight limbs, as it has been explained.
Fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice grains, kuśa grass, the tips of dūrvā grass, and likewise water—
this is declared as the sixfold arghya (offering water) spoken by Bhoja, Indra, Brahmā, and Śambhu.

Kuśa grass, unbroken rice grains, sesame seeds, dūrvā grass, fragrance, flowers, and likewise barley, as well as milk—this eightfold water for the arghya offering is declared by Vijaya to belong to Śiva. (5.36)
O Mataṅga, water, bilva fruit, dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, flowers, rice grains,
cow’s curd, and the tips of darbha grass are declared to be the eightfold arghya.
Fragrance, flowers, unbroken rice grains, barley, tips of *kuśa* grass, tips of *dūrvā* grass,
mustard seeds, and water— by means of these eight substances, they declare the *arghya* offering for the Śakti.
The vessel for the *arghya* offering should be made of gold, silver, or copper; in their absence, it may be made of wood. It should be filled with three *kuḍuba*s, or it may be a conch shell.

Having sprinkled that [vessel], which rests upon the support of the mechanical device and has been cleansed with weapons-mantras, with its mouth turned downward, one should turn it upward and place therein the *kūrca* and the *śakti*.
While reciting the *saṃhitā*, one should [meditate on] Śiva as being joined with the nectars dripping from the full moon;
then, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using either the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*) or the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).
Having touched it with the *mantrasaṃhitā* and the *prarocī-amṛtamudrā*,
and having worshipped it with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and incense, one should protect it well with the *astra-mantra*.
That [mantra], well-guarded by the armor [mantra], wards off all obstacles;
then, one should sprinkle one's own head with water using a bunch of *kuśa* grass.
One should sprinkle the materials for each individual worship and the ground in sequence;
that which is offered during the worship is the special *arghya*, kept well-concealed.
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water alone, along with fragrant flowers and unbroken rice grains (akṣata),
it should be known as the "General Arghya" (sāmānyārghya) consecrated by the recitation of the Śiva-weapon mantra (śivāstra) for the worship of Śiva.
The procedure for the *arghya* offering:
The *pādya* (water for the feet) should generally be understood as consisting of *dūrvā* grass, *śyāmāka* grain, and lotuses.
Having filled the vessel as before with water, one should offer the *pādya* at the [deity's] feet. (5.45)
Water that is cool, mixed with nutmeg, mace, cloves, camphor, and sandalwood, should be known as *ācamanīyaka*. (5.46)
Furthermore, regarding the waters for sipping (ācamanīya), fragrant water is recommended;
[it should be offered] with the heart-mantra joined by the six classes of vocatives: *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*. (5.47)
One should thus offer the fourfold set beginning with the *arghya* in due order;
there should be three vessels for the *arghya* and likewise three for the *pādya*.

There should be six vessels for sipping water, or even just one if [more] are unavailable; water for the guest-offering (arghya) is likewise offered at the beginning, during the bath, and at the conclusion of the worship. (5-49)
At the beginning, at the end of the bath, and at the end of the ornaments—at these three times—one offers water for the feet (pādya).
Also after the water for the feet, after the honey-mixture (madhuparka), and at the beginning and end of the bath, as well as with the garments and other items. (5.50)
At the conclusion of the offering, one should give water for sipping (ācamanīya) to those six;
having offered each substance separately, such as perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Having offered the general sipping of water (ācamana), the subsequent rite should be performed.
This is the section on the water for the feet (pādya) and the sipping of water (ācamana).
Having performed the purification of the self, the locus, the substances, and the mantras in their proper sequence—5.52.
Just as here in this chapter on worship,
it is correctly taught that one should worship the Sun, Vighneśvara, the Guru, and oneself.
Having worshipped with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, having made the formal resolve (saṅkalpa), and having offered sacrifice to the seat of Śiva,
one should invoke the manifest Śiva into the liṅga according to the prescribed path.
Having placed *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice on the head and having offered the special *arghya*,
one should indeed wash the water-pitchers, the cloth, and oneself once with the *astra-mantra*.
One should fill the water-jars and the vessel for increasing the weapons with dripping water;
then, using either the Hṛdaya-mantra or the Gāyatrī, one should separately cast in perfume and flowers. (5.56)
Then, having placed the root mantra upon those [flowers], he should cast a drop of the *arghya* water upon them;
with that water, he should bathe the deity who has been worshipped and perfumed once again.
Regarding this, Brahmaśambhu says:
"Having placed water-pots with lingas on their tops upon the palm of the left hand,
one should remove the previously deposited flower by means of that arghya."
Having washed his hands with his own mantra, he should bathe the head of the Lord with water that is not moving, poured from a conch-mudrā.
One should not wave the hand above, nor should one form a mudrā below;
furthermore, one should not sprinkle the ritual substances with water that has been drawn up [from a source].
Thus: having anointed [the area] with fragrant oil, having dried it with powders of barley, black gram, and so forth, and having washed it with lukewarm water. (5.58)
Having worshipped and offered incense with extensive offerings such as flour-lamps and the like,
one should perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana) accompanied by songs, instrumental music, hymns of praise, and auspicious rites.
With milk, curd, clarified butter, honey, and sugarcane juice,
each [substance] being successively interspersed with water, flowers, and incense.
Having consecrated it with the five products of the cow, either collectively or individually,
one should then rub it dry and wash it with substances perfumed by fragrant flowers.
Having especially consecrated the non-empty top of the *liṅga* with water-pots as prescribed, or with conch shells, or even with jars (*gaḍḍuka*).
If the twice-born should consecrate him with the *saṃhitā* mantras together with those dedicated to Rudra and Pavamāna, the other [the officiant] should recite the *saṃhitā*.
When it has reached full capacity, having performed the ritual bath with fragrant water according to the Vedic rites,
one should wipe it with a white cloth so that it reaches a state of being free from moisture.
This procedure is prescribed for a fixed liṅga and is likewise approved for a mobile liṅga;
having carefully placed the mobile one upon its pedestal on the bathing altar (snānavedī).
Having bathed [the image] according to the prescribed rite and having placed it upon the altar of worship,
one should duly perform sacrifice to the manifest [deities], as well as to the Śaileya [deities] and the jewels.
Others do not recognize the necessity of daily bathing for images made of metal;
others maintain that there is no such bathing for paintings, nor for other types of *liṅgas*. (5–67)
When the sacrificial ground and the fire are momentary, bathing is considered to be mental.
[This concludes] the section on bathing.
(p. 52) Then, [one should wear] garments that are pure, fine, and new. 5-68.
For those cloths such as dukūla, paṭṭa, cotton, and devāṅga, which have not been used elsewhere, are free from hair, and are unwashed; 5-69.
With devotion, one should clothe the God with whatever garments are available,
as well as golden ornaments resplendent with various gems.
One should adorn him with those things suitable for his feet up to his hair;
or, if these are unavailable, one may do so mentally or by showing him a mirror. (5.71)
The Section on Garments and Ornaments.
As for fragrance, it is of two kinds: that of Śiva, which is fivefold or eightfold. [It consists of] sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, and saffron, mixed with cold water. (5.72)
These finely ground fragrances are declared to be the "five-fold limb" (pañcāṅga):
sandalwood, saffron, costus, clove, and agallochum.
Camphor and *hirivera* are proclaimed as the eightfold fragrance (*gandhāṣṭāṅga*).
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, saffron, ushira,
gorochana, costus, and snow-water constitute the eightfold fragrance beloved by Śiva.
Thus it is said in the Vātula:
"Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, spikenard, saffron, gorocana, musk, and civet—
this eight-ingredient incense is declared to belong to the Śakti."
And thus:
"In this world, those flowers which are indeed white in color are of the nature of sattva. (5.74)
Those that are red are characterized by rajas, while those that are black are characterized by tamas;
that which is dark grey is a mixture of tamas and rajas, and that which is yellow is characterized by rajas and sattva.
From flowers that are *sāttvika* and so forth, the fruit shall be *sāttvika* and so forth.
[One should offer] white *arka*, *karavīra*, lotus, *dhurdhūra*, *āragvadha*, royal *arka*, white lotus, *tulasī*, along with *aśoka* and excellent *campaka*.
With *kalhāra*, *baka*, *pāṭala*, *vakulaka*, the two types of *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *pālāśa*, *sthalapadma*, *darbha*, *damana*, *apāmārga*, and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass. || 5.76 ||
p. 53) Likewise, [the ground is auspicious] with granthi, śamī, bṛhanmaruvaka, punnāga, nāgāsana, nandyāvarta, tamāla, kubja, vijayā, mandāra, and kāśmīraka;
as well as with excellent utpala, karṇikāra flowers, and those of the kādamba and bilva trees.
And the blue lotus—these flowers are said to belong entirely to Śiva. (5.77)
With lotuses, blue water-lilies, bandhujīva, vijayā, punnāga, and nāga;
likewise with jasmine, kunda, karaṇḍa, campaka, japā, yūthī, and ramā-pāṭala;
with bilva, aśoka, hayāri, kubja, damana, mandāra, and dūrvā leaves—
The flowers known as *rnandī*, *āhvā*, and *aparājitā* are fully declared to be suitable for the Śaktis. (5.78)
Those that are odorless, or possess a pungent and bitter smell, those that are untouchable or defiled, or those damaged by improper means; those cut by worms or nails, or broken;
those defiled by wool, thread, hair, and the like, or those that are withered and ancient.
Furthermore, one should likewise avoid flowers that have passed their season or are out of bloom. (5.79)
The two auspicious *tulasī* plants, white lotus, red lotus, *pālāśa*, jasmine, *kubjaka*, *mādhavī*, *damana*, *punnāga*, *nāgāsana*,
*nandyāvarta*, *śamī*, wild lotus, *vijayā*, *asan*, *mallikā*, and *campaka*—
And *arbuda*, *bilva*, blue lotus, *ketaka*, fresh *kunda*, as well as *pāṭala*. || 5-80 ||
Lakṣmī, Devīsaha, Bhṛṅga, Musalī, Bhītendravalī, Sadābhadrā, Śrīpatilaṅghitā as the tenth, Dūrvā, Jambū leaves,
Kalhāra, Karavīra, Ekadalaka, Padma, Kuśa grass, and Kairava— these are [the herbs].
And if it is red, by way of reverse order, the flower shall indeed yield superior fruit for a Vaiṣṇava.

Among the varieties of flowers mentioned in three ways, those not explicitly stated therein are to be excluded; furthermore, there may be cases where even the mutual prohibition [of certain flowers] is indicated despite the absence of an explicit statement. Likewise, those flowers intended for another purpose are to be excluded according to that same reasoning.
Whatever is specifically prescribed for each person here, one should satisfy that particular deity.

For the Sun and Agni, three kinds of flowers are desired; likewise for the Lord of Obstacles (Vighneśvara), there are those belonging to Śakti as well as those belonging to Śambhu. For Skanda, Ārya, Caṇḍa, and others, only those belonging to Śakti are preferred—namely, those dear to Manojavā, Girisutā, Durgā, and the Eight Mothers.
Likewise, the lotus-throne of Viṣṇu, the king of gods, and Lakṣmī are to be worshipped by the Vaiṣṇavas. || 5.83 ||

One should worship with *nandyāvarta* flowers in the morning, or with *mālatī* and *mallikā* in the afternoon or at night; with lotuses during the day, or with blue water-lilies (*utpala*) at all times; or with golden flowers in the morning, and with *kesara* flowers during the early part of the night.
A lotus remains fit for worship for three nights until its filaments change color; a leaf from the *bilva* tree and a wreath likewise.
The *karṇikāra* flower is fit for worship for a fortnight, while the one called *vaka* remains so for six months, provided it does not wither.
The Chapter on Flowers:
Among all substances for incense, black agallochum (kṛṣṇāguru) is the most excellent. (5.86)
Camphor is the most excellent, as is agallochum (agaru);
likewise, the resin known as mahiṣākṣa-guggulu is indeed supreme and dear to Śiva.
Sandalwood and uśīra are proclaimed as being of medium quality;
śrīvāsa and sarja are the lowest, followed by lac, ghee, and honey.
With all these ingredients combined with sugar, the ten-fold incense (daśāṅga) is described;
it should be offered upon smokeless, glowing embers that are flameless and devoid of fuel.
One should offer incense while sounding a bell slightly with the left hand;
the wicks should be made of auspicious cotton and wound with a pure white thread.
Cow’s ghee is the primary substance for a lamp; oil from a buffalo is secondary and tertiary.
A lamp with camphor as the tenth ingredient bestows a fruit exceeding a hundredfold.
A lamp made of pure camphor alone is said to be a thousandfold more effective than ten, nine, or eight lamps filled with abundant oil. (5.92)
The *ārātrika* ceremony should be performed with fresh lamps flickering nearby;
one should not, however, rekindle the lamp using a wick that has been partially burnt.
The ritual for incense, lamps, and the *ārātrika* offering should not be performed with leftover food, impure oil, and the like, nor with oils or ghee other than those [specified]. (p.
55) Five hundred grains of rice make one *tala*; two of those [talas] doubled make one *prakubja*.
Two of those [māṣas] are a *prasṛta*, and likewise two *prasṛtas* are a *kuḍuba*; two of those are a half-*prastha*.
A *prastha* is a *pātra*, then an *āḍhaka*, a *śiva*, then a *droṇa*, and a *khārī* in sequence.
Indeed, three *khārīs* are declared to be a *bhāra*; such is the measurement according to the scriptures.
The food offering (naivedya) is considered to be of two kinds: the regular (nitya) and the occasional (naimittika).

That [rite], which is the most excellent of the excellent and so forth, will be described according to its nine divisions. Among those, for the daily rite (nityavidhi), one should use eight *droṇas* of husked rice grains.
One should offer it during the worship performed at the four times of day, including midnight;
that food is of four kinds: milk-rice, rice-and-pulse porridge, and beef. (5.97)

Accompanied by appropriate side-dishes, clarified butter, curd, and excellent rice-pudding, it was further enriched with song, dance, and instrumental music, along with offerings and auspicious rites performed for the spirits.
In that regard, five hundred lamps would constitute the most excellent of the excellent;
having worshipped with six *droṇas* [of offerings] at the four times of the day, one should present them. (5.99)
Likewise, there should be two hundred lamps; one should perform [the rite] with song, offerings, and dance according to the previous method—that shall be the superior or middling [type]. (5.100)
Five *droṇas* [of offerings] should be presented four times a day for the ritual offering and worship;
likewise, there shall be one hundred and eight lamps, as well as the performance of song, instrumental music, and the offering of oblations (*bali*).

And one should perform the fire-ritual; in this way, there shall indeed be the highest and lowest [levels of practice], including the food offering of four *droṇas* and worship appropriate for the four periods of the day. (5.102)
With song and the like, as well as offerings (bali) and oblations (homa), there should be seventy lamps;
thus it would be the middle-high [grade]. Now, the middle-middle is described. (5.103)
The food offering, accompanied by worship, should consist of half a bhāra of rice;
the fire sacrifice (homa) should take place at midday alone, while dancing and other such performances should occur twice a day.

There should be forty lamps in the very center, as well as an offering (bali); the food offering (naivedya) consists of four khārīs of rice, and there is the bali for worship at the four times of the day.
There should be twelve lamps for a human [sacrifice]; song and so forth are for the middle and lowest [grades]. (p.

56) At evening and morning, with two *āḍhaka* measures [of offerings], there is Śiva; at midday, during the day, there are Vedic lamps. At night, there should be eight; that which consists of worship at the three times of day with five musical instruments is called the "lowest-best" (*kaniṣṭhottama*). || 5.106 ||
In the morning there should be one vessel, and likewise in the evening; at midday, however, there should be one āḍhaka of oil for the lamps during the day.
There should indeed be four lamps for the night. This worship performed at the three times of day is said to be the middling [form]; in the lowest [form], it is as follows.
In the evening and in the morning, there is the offering of two sets of sacrificial food and worship by the Pratiprasthātṛ.
To say "there is a lamp by day and lamps by night" would be the lowest of the low. [This concludes] the section on the daily food offering (*nityanaivedya*).
Beginning with eight *droṇas* up to twelve *bhāras*— 5.109.
The offering of food (naivedya) should be occasional and of nine kinds, as before; one should likewise assemble the worship, beginning with the most excellent of the excellent.
The food offering may be optional, lasting as long as desired;
there is no restriction regarding the time for it, though worship with all its constituent parts is recommended. (5.111)
The procedure for occasional and optional rites:
For milk-porridge (pāyasa), there should be three parts of milk and one part of rice;
the rice should be equal in measure to split green gram (mudga); the clarified butter (ghṛta) should be half of that [rice], and the jaggery (guḷa) should be half of the butter.
From the rice grains, cow's milk should be six times that amount; and from that, guḷānna (rice cooked with jaggery) is prepared together with the fruit of the rambhā plantain.
The twice-born, having cleansed their teeth and bathed in white garments, should silently wash the rice grains with water filtered through a cloth;
likewise, they should kindle the fire seven times while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, using a fan or similar implement.

Having meditated upon the hearth, the Śakti, and Agni, and having worshipped Rudra with the seed-syllable of fire or the *tāraka*, they should prepare the oblation in that fire; having consecrated it with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning, they should bring it forth.
Large plantains, as well as *kraṇḍahālya*, along with *kūśmāṇḍa*, *urvāruka*, and *karkaṭī*;
likewise *kāravallī*, *āmra*, *śṛṅgavera*, large mung beans, mung beans, and coconut. (5.115)
Likewise, black gram, pigeon pea, *āḍhakī*, citron, and lentils are recommended as side-dishes for wines.
A soup made from the cooked fruits of the plantain tree and others, combined with sugar, the three pungents (*tryūṣaṇa*), salt, and a decoction of cumin and curd, should also be prepared. (5.116)
Likewise, one should prepare sweetmeats and side dishes with ghee, the three pungents (vyoṣa), salt, and ground yavānī and iṣṭa;
then, having cleansed the collection of vessels outside, one should raise them up accompanied by the sound of conchs and an umbrella. || 5.117 ||

p. 57) Having sprinkled water over the mantra for the gold and other items while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*, or having sprinkled water over leaves such as those of the plantain tree (*kadali*), one should place the sacrificial offering (*havis*) there, accompanied by side dishes and the like, along with ripe fruits such as plantains and sweetmeats (*modaka*). || 5-118 ||
There, upon sugar, honey, and the cream of curd, one should offer fresh cow’s ghee in sixteen pairs of portions;
having offered it into this [liṅga] which has been worshipped with flowers, one should then sprinkle it with the nectar from the *dhenumudrā*.
Having sprinkled [it] with the root mantra, one should offer water, fire, and the beloved of Agni (the oblation). || 5-120 ||
With his right hand holding a flower, he should touch the oblation and offer it;
he should mentally contemplate that divine food, which is the cause of satisfaction. (5.121)
Having offered him pleasant, cool, and fragrant water for drinking,
and having gone outside, he should also offer the remainder of that food into the fire.

Having offered the bali-oblation prescribed therein with the respective mantras according to the rules for the root-mantra, the limbs, and so forth, the practitioner should dismiss the fire with devotion. (5.123)
One should propitiate him with circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise;
having thoroughly washed one's feet and sipped water for purification, one should then enter within. (5.124)
Having recollected Śaṅkara as being fully satisfied, one should offer water for sipping (ācamanīya),
followed by cloves, camphor, black pepper, and betel nut.
Then one should offer betel leaf honored with perfumes and flowers;
having worshipped and paid obeisance, one should recite the root mantra according to one's ability.
Alternatively, having placed the food intended for the oblation in a vessel and kept it protected,
one should employ it in the fire-rite once the Lord of Gods has been fully satisfied.
The Section on the Food Offering (Naivedya):
One should worship the limbs and the retinues of attendants according to the rite of the five offerings, as far as possible;
however, whatever is unavailable here in this worship, one who is composed in mind should mentally provide that.

In this regard, others speak of different types of worship according to the distinctions in ritual practice; we shall describe those as well, based on slight variations from what was previously stated. (5.129)
Ten services (upacāras) are prescribed at the end of the food offering during worship; however, sixteen services are prescribed at the conclusion of the fire sacrifice (homa). (5-130)
Furthermore, they are known as being twenty-five in number when including the offerings (bali);
or else, thirty-six modes of service (upacāra) are proclaimed when including the end of the dance.
In the case of the highest-of-the-high worship, or indeed in the highest [worship],
there are the seat, the invocation, the water for honor (arghya), the water for the feet (pādya), and the water for sipping (ācamanīyaka).
The complete ritual bath, as well as garments, a sacred thread, ornaments, scents, flowers, garlands, incense, a lamp, and a mirror. (5.133)
The waving of lights (nīrājana), the food offering (naivedya), the fire ritual (agnikārya), circumambulation (pradakṣiṇa),
prostration (namaskāra), hymns, instrumental music, song, and likewise the daily oblation (nityabali).
And the offering of worship—these twenty-five are prescribed.
Then follow the five beginning with the seat, and the consecration with the five products of the cow. (5.135)

There is the consecration with the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) and the bathing according to royal protocol; [the offering of] garments, the sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, flowers, garlands, and unbroken grains (akṣata). (5.136)
Then follow incense and lamps, a mirror, and the rite of lustration (nīrājana);
then the food offering (naivedya), betel, and thereafter the worship of the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
The fire-ritual according to rule, as well as the sandals,
the fly-whisks, the parasol, the daily procession, the offering of oblations, and the sacred thread.
Circumambulation, prostration, hymns of praise, as well as instrumental music, song, dance, and thereafter the offering of worship and so forth. (5.139)
Thus, the thirty-six modes of service (upacāra) are proclaimed in sequence in the Tantra.
Thus, these ritual procedures, whose paths have been laid out, are taught here individually according to their sequence as seen in the Śaiva tantras;
they are to be understood exactly as they are in the sacrificial rites of Śambhu.
The attainment of one's desired fruit shall come to pass, just as it does for those who possess devotion.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on the Ritual Offerings (*upacāra*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*. 5.
Now begins the sixth chapter.

The accomplishment of ritual action is achieved through six components: mantras, mudrās, maṇḍalas (as with the sacrificial pits), the procurement of materials, and the practitioners; these, as proclaimed in this tantra, will be explained here correctly. (6.1)
In this regard, [it is said] in the Mataṅga:
"The mudrās, maṇḍalas, and mantras, as well as the sacred sites, ritual substances, and practitioners— learn from the Guru exactly how these are to be employed."

Thus it is said: "In that regard—for example—the nature of reflecting and protecting belongs to the deity within the expressive word; where [these qualities reside] through the characteristics of short, long, and other vowels, that is designated as 'mantra'. (6.2)

Because it protects all beings from the ocean of saṃsāra through the act of contemplating, the power of that [mantra] is indeed of the nature of mantra, possessing the characteristics of both contemplation (manana) and protection (trāṇa). || 6-3 ||
Regarding the Three Jewels:
Brahman, whose nature is free from conceptual construction, is the essence of Śiva; it is indeed eternal, stainless, all-pervasive, and a mass of consciousness, possessing a form of perpetual bliss.
That power is non-different from Śiva; it is eternal and, like Him, perfectly pure.
Consciousness, being autonomous, is indeed considered the cause of the manifestation of the universe.
The activity of that Śiva, the ocean of compassion, is fivefold:
creation, maintenance, dissolution, concealment, and grace.
That power, which is divided into the categories of will, action, and knowledge, becomes established through its own will;
that power attains the state of the *bindu* through the distinction between the supreme (*parā*) and the non-supreme (*aparā*).
And from that, indeed, arose the primordial seed-syllable (mūlabīja) whose essence is Śiva. For it is said: "That supreme seed known as Nāda is established within all beings."
It bestows liberation, supreme and divine, the granter of all perfections;
it is peaceful, omnipresent, void, and established within the twelve measures.
O Six-faced One! The short vowel is declared to be Brahmā, while the long vowels are indeed the limbs (aṅgas).
The anusvāra becomes the eye, situated above all of them.
One should apply the sixth [vowel] up to the end of the thirteenth [consonant] within the fifth [group];
one should know that to be Śiva, Sadāśiva, whose form is the mantra.
Thus it is said in the *Kālottara*: "The root mantra is prescribed by the Brahmins as being joined with its own limbs;
it consists of the letter 'A', the letter 'U', and the letter 'M', together with the Bindu and Nāda."
This Praṇava, known as Tārā, is indeed considered to be the essence of Śabdabrahman;
it is declared to be the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, enriched with the vowels A, ĪM, and the Bindu and Nāda.
That which bestows the prosperity of all speech shall indeed become the body of Vāgīśvarī;
likewise, there is the seed-syllable of Śakti, the Tāra (Oṃ), and thereafter the Vāgbhava (Aiṃ).
The Supreme Goddess Mātṛkā consists of the fifty phonemes;
the letter *a* is her face along with its limbs, and the *ka* and *ca* groups are her two arms.
The *ṭa* and *ta* groups are likewise the two feet; *pa*, *pha*, *ba*, and *bha* are the two sides;
the syllable *ba* is the back, *bha* is the navel, and *ma* is the heart.
Skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen are the seven constituent elements (dhātus) beginning with *ya*; the letter *ha* is held to be the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The letter *kṣa* is the manifestation (*sphūrti*), full of wrath, with a body composed of the entire universe;
here, the limbs of the script, beginning with the heart, are written down in their proper sequence.
The heart-mantra consists of the last letter of the sixth group, accompanied by a bindu and repeated;
the first of the first group, likewise joined with a bindu, is known as the head.
The second [syllable] of the first [mantra], together with the anusvāra, is likewise the Śikhā;
the word *kaca* repeated is similarly remembered as the Kavaca.
The third and the fourth [letters] of the first [group], the three-eyed one (the letter *ra*),
and the final letter of the group (*kṣa*) with the visarga— when repeated, this is called the weapon-mantra (*astra*).

One should sequentially join at the beginning of the six limbs of the Mātṛkās the syllable 'A', endowed with the *tāra* (the syllable Om) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and adorned with the white vowel-sound 'O'.
*Namas*, *svāhā*, *vaṣaṭ*, *huṃ*, *vauṣaṭ*, and *phaṭ* are the [six] classes [of utterances];
they should be joined in due order at the end of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantra) ending in the dative case.
Holding a *mudrākṣa* (or *rudrākṣa*) rosary, a crystal rosary, and water-pots in her right and front hands, she also carries a book; she has three eyes, is adorned with white garlands and unguents,
possesses a body and speech as bright as jasmine, bears the crescent moon upon her crest, and has a serene countenance.
The deity of the syllable should be meditated upon as seated upon a lotus, adorned with [pearl-like] ornaments.
Having thus meditated upon that very form consisting of fifty phonemes within one's own body,
and having sequentially deposited those phonemes, he shall accomplish his goals by reciting the mantras.
One should place the vowels at the hairline, the circumference of the face, the two eyes, the two ears, the two nostrils,
the two cheeks, the two lips, the two rows of teeth, the head, and the mouth.
One should place the *ka*-group on the right hand, the *ca*-group on the other arm,
the *ṭa*- and *ta*-groups on the two feet, and the *pa* and *pha* letters on the two sides of the body.
One should place those designated as *ba*, *bha*, and *ma* on the back, the navel, and the heart;
[and] skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and breath in the lotuses [of the hands].
One should place the eight syllables beginning with *ya* that reside on the petals within the heart, which is situated in the self;
however, one should place the letter *kṣa* in the pericarp, contemplating it as all-pervading.
The Mātṛkānyāsa:
The deposition of the essential forms of the five Brahmans is also prescribed;
the Brahmans beginning with Sadyojāta are to be used for extraction and recitation. (6.4)
These very [faces], beginning with Īśāna, are indeed employed in the rites of ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth.
Sadyojāta is white as cow’s milk; Vāmadeva is red as a hibiscus flower.
The face of the All-pervading Lord known as Aghora has the luster of blue collyrium; the face called Puruṣa has the radiance of saffron;
and the face named Īśāna resembles pure crystal.
The faces, the phonemes, their mantras, the digits (kalās), and their forms (mūrtis) should indeed be understood as both non-distinct and distinct in their respective contexts. (6–7)
Sadyojāta is in the west, Vāmadeva likewise in the north,
Aghora with its face to the south, and the one called Tatpuruṣa in the east.
Īśāna is the upward-facing face; these five indeed belong to Brahmāṇī.
One should [place] the short vowels joined with the bindu, preceded by the syllable Om (tāra), for the Brahmās in their respective order.
Having first joined [the name] ending in the dative case and ending in "namaḥ" separately for each, these five Brahmāṇīs shall be used for general purposes such as worship and so forth. (6-10)
For all those who have been initiated, however, the subjects to be studied are without distinction;
namely, the five Brahmans as declared in the Vedas and Agamas. (6.11)
These are to be studied by the twice-born and never by women, Śūdras, or others;
they are extracted as the Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, approved by the Śaivas.
In the same way, there is the Pāśupata weapon and the king of mantras that pervades the sky;
it consists of the *tāra* (Om), the white syllable *ya*, followed by the sixth vowel (*ū*), and joined with fire (*ra*). (6.13)
From the mantra beginning with "ṣaṣṭhādyaṃ dyāmicet," one should extract nine syllables;
[the first is] Sadyojāta in the dative case, followed by the twelfth vowel, which is water (ja). (6.14)
Having uttered "bhava" twice for the sake of non-destruction,
and having said "bhaja" followed by "mām," [he spoke] the word "bhavodbhavam" ending in the dative case.
The *namaḥ* mantra consists of thirty-nine syllables;
it is the *praṇava* and the *vāmadeva* mantra, ending in the dative case and accompanied by *namaḥ*. (6.16)
Jyeṣṭha, Rudra, and Kāla—these three end with "namaḥ.
At the conclusion of the power of time (kālabala), there should be a word for the sake of dissolution. (6.17)
Then there should be *balapramathanāya*, followed by the word *sarvabhūta*; then *damana* ending in the dative case, and likewise *manonmana* with that same case-ending. (6.18)
Salutation to him who is praised by nine Tārās and seventy-five syllables;
this is the mantra of Vāmadeva, augmented by the nine Śaktis.
Having uttered the syllable *tāram* (om) and the first letter of the [respective] class, one should extract the words "ghorebhyaḥ" and "atha".
Then, this word "muktam" is spoken again, followed by the two words "ghora". (6.20)
After *tārebhyaḥ* and above the three syllables, [one should utter] the word *sarvataḥpadaṃ*;
having said *śarvasarvebhyaḥ*, one should then say the two words *naḥ* and *teta*.
At the end of the word *rudra*, one should utter the word *rūpebhyaḥ*;
this is said to be the Aghora mantra, consisting of thirty-six syllables.
Having extracted "Tāraṃ tat" (Oṃ tat), then the word "puruṣāya," then the two syllables "vidmahe," and then one should extract "he mahādevāya. (6.23)
The fourth [syllable] of the fifth [group], adorned with the fourth vowel, is "mahitannaḥ" consisting of four syllables; then "rudraḥ" followed by the three syllables "pretya. (6.24)
This mantra beginning with "codayāt" consists of twenty-five syllables;
it belongs to Tatpuruṣa, and now Īśāna is described.
Having extracted the fourth vowel *tāra* (the letter *i*), and from the seventh [vowel] (*u*) as well as the fifth (*e*),
and having taken four syllables ending with the long *sarga* (*ḥ*) in the fifth [position], [one forms the mantra].
He is the Lord of all sounds and of the sciences, and the six imperishable syllables;
he is the foremost of all castes and of all beings, and is also known as the Sovereign of Brahman.
The word "brahma" ending in the genitive case is pronounced, followed by "adhipatiḥ tu";
then the three syllables "brahmā śivaś caturvarṇān me astu" [are recited]. (6.28)
With Sadāśiva at the beginning and Tārā at the end, this mantra of Hīśāna consists of forty syllables; these indeed are the five Brahmāṇīs.
Eight, thirteen, eight, four, and five;
these are the digits (kalās) of Sadyojāta and the others, totaling thirty-eight in due order.
One should perform the placement [of mantras] upon the body with devotion to Brahman, and one should place them upon the five faces with devotion to the faces;
one should perform the placement of the kalās in their respective locations in due order with devotion to the faces.
One should likewise place the five digits (kalās) of Īśāna— Śaśinī, Aṅgadā, iṣṭā, Marīcī, and Jvālinī— with their five respective words.
One should assign these four— peace (śānti), knowledge (vidyā), establishment (pratiṣṭhā), and cessation (nivṛtti)— to the [mantra] Tatpuruṣa, along with their respective words, in due order.
And likewise, from Aghora were born the kalās: Tāmasī, Mohā, Niṣṭhā (also called Kṣapā), Mṛtyu, Māyā, Bhayā, and Jarā. (6.34)
