Likewise, [he should worship] Rājasī, Rakṣā, Rati, and Pālinī; then Sajjanyā, Kriyā, and also the one called Buddhi and Chāyā.
One should place Dhātrī, Bhrāmaṇī, Mohinī, and Abhayā with their own respective feet of Vāmadeva; these indeed are the thirteen kalās.
One should install these digits of Sadyojāta— namely Siddhi, Ṛddhi, Dyuti, Lakṣmī, Medhā, Kānti, Svadhā, and Sthitī— in their proper order according to their respective words.

A wise person should sequentially assign the five kalās of the Īśāna mantra using nine, eight, and so forth, up to sixteen syllables, or even using five, four, and so forth, up to twenty-five syllables.
The digits (kalās) of Tatpuruṣa are formed by nine, eight, four, four, and five syllables; and by five, five, two, twenty-four, five, three, five, and five [syllables].
The wise one should arrange the eight digits (kalās) of Aghora with their respective syllables upon the head and the directions—
namely, the zenith, the east, the south, the north, and the west.
One should separately assign the five digits (kalā) of Īśāna, ending with the word "namaḥ. One should assign the digit called Śāntyatītā to the upper face with the syllable Om (praṇava).
Then, one should place the [mantras] of Aghora; that is to say, one should assign them to the heart, the throat, and the two shoulders of Aghora, in due order. (6.42)
One should place the *kalā* on the navel, the abdomen, the back, and likewise on the chest;
then above the secret organ, on the secret organ itself, and also on the two thighs, the two knees, and the two shanks.
One should place the portion of Vāmadeva on the buttocks, the waist, and the sides;
likewise, on the feet, the hands, the nose, and the head.
One should place the eight kalās of Sadyojāta on the two arms in sequence;
one should first place them on the pair [of shoulders] starting from the right shoulder.
(65) This sequence [of placement] on the left side shall be the same everywhere, each with its own respective mudrā.
Generally, the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) of the Brahmās will now be described in order. (6-46)
As it is stated in the *Prayogamañjarī* and in the *Pauṣkara* commentary:
"The word 'Sarvajña' (the All-Knowing One), preceded by 'Śaratārā' and so forth, should be accompanied by the fourth case ending. (6.47)
The heart-mantra is said to end with *namaḥ*. Next, one should extract the first letter of the [first] group;
it is joined with the sixth vowel, followed by the seventh, and then the first letter of the fifth group joined with the tenth vowel.

The word *tejomālinī*, joined with the word *brahma* for the sake of satisfaction, followed by the dative case ending for the head (*śiras*), and ending with *svāhā*, is declared to be the Śiva-mantra. (6.49)
Then, from the third [group], the third syllable, accompanied by water (the vowel *i*), and from the seventh [group],
the third [syllable] joined with its own vowel (*u*), followed by the letter *ta* conjoined with the word "fire" (*śikhi*).
One should extract "Śikhe," "anādibodho 'yam," "jātiyuktaṃ śikhāṃ tathā," "vajriṇe," and "vajraśabdaṃ dharāya. (6.51)
The independent [seed-syllable] ending in the dative case, joined with the [mantra] "kavacāya" and the [mudrā] of its class;
the first of the eighth, the first of the third, and the fourth of the eighth.

One should extract [the syllables] ending with the thirteenth [vowel], followed by the bindu, in due order; likewise, the word "īśa" for the one whose power is undiminished, and the term "netratraya. (6.53)
Having extracted the word ending in the fourth case, "netram" (the eye) should be joined with its respective seed-syllable;
then one should extract the five-syllabled Pāśupata weapon-mantra.
Having uttered "anantaśaktaye," that weapon-mantra (astra) should be joined with its own respective seed-syllable;
Śiva himself, ending with the visarga, is proclaimed as the Śivāstra.
The second [syllable] of the sixth group, however, is joined with the first half-mora of the fourfold [vowel];
by joining the first two from the fifth [group], it becomes a two-syllable [unit]. (6.56)
This is the Pāśupata weapon, which removes all misfortunes;
at the beginning of this, one should employ the Śiva-weapon within the seed-syllable of the crest (śikhā).

This divine mantra, which removes all obstacles and bestows liberation through recitation and other practices, consists of the eighth vowel (Ṣa) joined with the letter 'Bhū' (Bha), followed by the third vowel (I) and the nasal bindu (Ṃ). (6.58)
The first seed-syllable is indicated; the second shall be the first of the sixth [group].
The third, however, is the first of the eighth [group] conjoined with the fifth vowel. (6.59)
With "varmāstre" [as the fifth], this five-syllable weapon is known as the Pāśupata;
thus is the Pāśupata weapon, and now the Aghora weapon is described.
Having extracted the first [letter] from the sixth [group], together with the letter *agni* (the third), and the word *sphura* repeated;
and the fourth [letter] of the second [group], conjoined with the vowel at the end of the twelve. (6.61)
Having spoken "Agni" again and those two [syllables], then the first of the fifth [group] and the fire-syllable (*anala*),
and having spoken the word "tanu-rūpa," one should extract the pair of *caṭa* syllables.

Having uttered twice "pracaṭa," followed by two pairs of "kaha" and two "vams," one should repeat the word "ghātaya," as well as the armor-mantra (varma), the weapon-mantra (astra), and the beloved of Agni (svāhā).
The Aghora weapon-mantra, beginning with Tārā and consisting of forty-two syllables,
is composed of groups measured by six, six, four, ten, eight, and eight [syllables].
Those six limbs ending with the weapon-mantras are joined with syllables associated with the [six] classes;
the third letter of the third [class], however, is joined with the staff of the fifth vowel.
One should utter the two syllables beginning with "Śukla" and ending with the Visarga;
this [mantra], which begins with the star Tārā and ends with a protracted vowel (pluta), is known as Mṛtyuñjaya.
Having meditated upon [the deity] situated within a moon-maṇḍala enclosed by white lotuses, which distills the essence of mindfulness and destroys death and disease— 6.67.

One should meditate upon the vital breath (prāṇa), conjoined with the bindu and nāda, white and pale-yellow, situated within the heart-lotus; this mantra of consciousness has Śiva as its essence. (6.68)
The syllable *praṇava* (Om) and the word *tat*, followed by the word *maheśāya*;
then the word *vidma* at the end of *he*, and *dhīmahi* for *vāgviśuddhāya*. (6.69)
"Rudra shall be at the end of its *pada*, but one should place *codayāt* at the end of the syllable *pra*.
Having thus been declared, this is the Śiva-gāyatrī; now the Śaiva Sāvitrī is being stated.
One should extract the syllable enriched with the thirteenth vowel, conjoined with water (va) and wind (ya),
ending with the sixth [vowel], as the first constituent of this word.
One should know the word *vyoma* ending in the dative case, and the word *vidma* joined with the letter *ha*.
[The next syllable is] *śukla*, joined with the sixth vowel, and the final [syllable] joined with the end of the sixth [vowel]. (6.72)
Having likewise extracted the subtle sound ending in the dative case, along with "dhīmahi" and so forth as before, it becomes the Sāvitrī known by the name Śiva.

The third [syllable] of the second [group], however, conjoined with the *bindu* and the *nāda*, is to be known as the seed-syllable of Gaṇeśa; the assignment of its limbs is performed by means of its own long vowels.

The syllable *tāra* (oṃ) and so forth for the second [name], the third [syllable] joined with the ear-dot (*bindu*), followed by "to the gurus" (*gurubhyaḥ*) and at the end "obeisance" (*namaḥ*); this is the mantra recited for the worship of the gurus.
At the end of *tārā* there should be the word *vacat*, and at the end of *bhuvaḥ* there should be *natir*.
This seven-syllable mantra of Skanda accomplishes all aims. (6-76)

Having extracted the seed-syllable of Śakti—consisting of the letter preceding *ra* (i.e., *pa*), followed by the ether (*ha*), the long fire (*ra*), and surmounted by a dot (*bindu*)—and joined it with the white [vowel *u*], one should utter "Salutation to Sūrya"; thus the nine-syllabled root mantra of the Sun is formed.

Oṃṃ *brahmatejo jvala jvala* (blaze, blaze, O splendor of Brahmā), *namaḥ* to the heart. Oṃ *am viṣṇutejaḥ prajvala prajvala* (blaze forth, blaze forth, O splendor of Viṣṇu), *svāhā* to the head, O Sun. Oṃ *aṃ rudratejo jvala bhūrbhuvaḥ svaroṃ jvālini* (blaze, O radiant one of the three worlds, O splendor of Rudra), *vaṣaṭ* to the crest-lock (*śikhā*). Oṃ *aṃ maheśvaratejaḥ śūlini* (O wielder of the trident, O splendor of Maheśvara), *hum* to the armor (*kavaca*). Oṃ *aṃ satyasadāśivatejaḥ kapardini kapardini* (O wearer of matted hair, O splendor of Satyasadāśiva), *phaṭ* to the weapon (*astra*). Oṃ *aṃ haṃ śivatejaḥ śakte* (O power, O splendor of Śiva), *vauṣaṭ* to the three eyes. These are the limbs of the Sun, purified by his own weapons in both hands.
Having assigned [the mantras] to the fingers starting with the thumb in sequence, one should assign the weapon-mantra (astra) to both palms.
Having sequentially placed those very limbs upon the head, face, heart, genitals, feet, and the directions, one should likewise place them in sequence upon the heart and the other [limbs].
One should perform worship, recitation, and other rites; one attains the desired accomplishment. [The mantra is:
the *tāra* (OM) ending with *sa* (s), joined with the *bindu* (m), and the beautiful *kānta* (ka), likewise endowed with the *bindu*. (6.80)
One should extract the second syllable of the second [word] as "ṣotkāya";
this mantra, known as the *prayojanatilaka*, is prescribed for Bhāskara.
Even by the Śaivas, the Sun should be worshipped daily with this [mantra] for the attainment of desired goals.
Now I shall declare the mantra known as Vyomavyāpin, which consists of eighty-one distinct words;
its syllables number three hundred and sixty-eight.
The first word is the high-pitched *tāra*, while the last [word] of the seventh [section] is conjoined with the skin (*tvak*). (6.83)
Having thus extracted [the syllable] endowed with the thirteenth vowel, and likewise again,
the second five-syllabled [mantra] is "vyāpinyai," which is the last letter of the sixth [vowel].
The word *vyoma* is for form (*rūpa*), and *sarvavyāpine* (the all-pervading) is also [for that];
when the five-syllabled phrase has been uttered, *śivāya* consists of three syllables.
With the words *anantānātha* in the fourth case, there is a four-syllable pada;
then, with the five syllables *anāśritāya*, the eighth pada is formed.
In the third and fourth syllables of the four-syllable mantra, [one should recite] "the eternal and the constant" (dhruvaśāśvatau),
as well as "to him who is established on the seat of yoga" (yogapīṭhasaṃsthitāya) and "to the ever-united one" (nityayogine).

In the five-arrow-syllable [mantra], the syllables "śara" (five) and "varṇa" (color) are for the purpose of meditative nourishment; however, the six-syllable phrase beginning with "tārā" is the primary one. (6.88)
Then, with five syllables, there is the word *sarvaprabhave*;
thereafter, *śivāya* consists of three syllables; then follows the pentad beginning with Īśāna. (6.89)
Having spoken [the mantras] for the head, the face, and the heart,
and further for the secret part and the form— thus according to the number of six and seven sages (thirteen).

The five words should consist of syllables numbering the oceans and the four oceans respectively; the first word is *tāraṃ* (the syllable Om), followed by *namaḥ* repeated, which constitutes the five-syllabled word.
With six syllables, [one worships] the protector who is more secret than the secret; with two syllables, the word [is offered] to the one who has no end;
and with five syllables, [one worships] the Lord of all Vidyās.
The eight-syllable mantra is: *saptārṇaiḥ sarvayogādhigatāya*, and with five syllables: *jyotīrūpāya parameśvaraparāya*. (6.93)
The phrase "the state of the Supreme Self" consists of eight syllables and is composed of Vedic letters;
the phrase "the insentient and the sentient" is recorded as having seven syllables.
In the sky [of consciousness], there is a pair consisting of four syllables; likewise, there is a pair of the Pervasive One (Vyāpinī).
Formless and repeated six times, the first two are likewise [to be applied].
The pair of splendors, the four colors, and likewise the pair of lights—
formless, without fire, and smokeless— [are described] by these three [terms] each.
"Abhasma," "ca," "api," and "anāde"—these four words of the Lord consist of three syllables each. (6.97)
The first [syllable] is *tārā* (om), followed by *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svaḥ*, which consist of two, three, and two syllables respectively;
the *padāni* (padas) consist of four syllables beginning with *anidhana*, and the *nidhana* consists of three syllables.
The five-syllable mantra beginning with *nidhana* and *udbhava*, and the two syllables *śiva*—these two together should be understood here by the teachers as the word *śarva*. (6.99)
The five-syllable mantra *maheśvara*, likewise the four-syllable *mahādeva-pāda*,
the five-syllable *sadbhāveśvara*, and the four-syllable *mahātejas*.
O Lord of Yoga, the five-syllable mantra releases four pairs;
the first two [pairs] are formed by six [syllables], and the four pairs of Śarva are formed by four [syllables].
The pair of existences (bhava-dvandva) consists of four, and there are four origins of existence (bhavodbhava).
Now, this eight-syllabled phrase bestows happiness upon all beings. (6.102)
The seven-syllable [mantra] is the foremost of all, and it is also known as "the one who brings presence.
The eight-syllable [mantra] consists of the words for Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. (6-103)
"Unhonored," "honored," likewise "unfamiliar," and "repeated"—these four preceding terms are to be known as the eight-syllable pada. (6.104)
*Sākṣidvandvam* consists of four syllables; *vedārṇam* is a pair of four [syllables];
*pataṅga* consists of three syllables; and *piṅgayugmam* is a group of four. (6.105)
The two cognitions, the pair of sounds, the subtle pair, the three words, the individual syllables of the Vedas, and the pair Śiva-Śarva—each of these is a dyad. (6.106)

The phrase "sarvada" consists of three syllables; "oṃ namo namaḥ śivāya" consists of five syllables; and the three-syllable word [for Śiva] should be understood by the best of teachers as consisting of three syllables. || 6.107 ||
The five-syllable word preceded by *tāra* (oṃ) and followed by a pair of salutations (*namaḥ*) is thus remembered;
in this manner, exactly eighty-one words are to be understood in their proper sequence.
The syllable *tāra* (om), accompanied by the light of the universal self (*sarvātman*), is known as the heart;
having uttered the second word, it is joined with the words *saśiva* and *brahma*.
The head-mantra is said to be joined with its own seed-syllable;
having uttered the third word, one should practice the word "jvālinī" twice. (6.110)
Then one should extract the fourth word as taught for the *śikhā*, joined with the *jāti*;
having uttered the word "piṅgala," it shall be the *varma* (armor) joined with the *jāti*.
Having uttered the fifth word, and likewise [the words] Śiva, Aghora, and Astra, that Astra-mantra should be joined with its [respective] gender; for these indeed are the five limbs (aṅgas).
The six limbs of this Vyomavyāpin mantra, as seen according to the path taught in the *Candrajñāna*, are now written down in their proper sequence. (6.113)

Oṃ Vyomavyāpin Śiva, Oṃ, salutations to the Self of All, to the Supreme, to the Supreme Lord, to Yoga, to the Source of Yoga, Karakara Kurukuru Satyasatya Bhavodbhava Vāmadeva, O Great God who pacifies all undertakings, O Sadāśiva, be gracious; salutations be unto You, Svāhā! Salutations to the Heart, Oṃ! To the Head of Śiva-Brahman, Svāhā! Oṃ! To the Blazing One of Śiva’s Heart, Svāhā! Vaṣaṭ to the Flaming Crest! I invoke the Great God, whose nature is Śiva, the Omniscient, the Imperishable Lord—the auspicious, tawny-hued, and most formidable Armor (Kavaca). 6–114.

Come, Piṅgala! O Great Armor! By the command of Śiva, bind, bind the heart; blaze, blaze; whirl, whirl! O Wielder of the Śakti-vajra, having entered the Vajra-noose, paralyze, paralyze all evil ones! Huṃ Phaṭ! To Piṅgala, the Armor: Huṃ! Oṃ Juṃ Saṃ, to the three eyes of the nature of light: Vauṣaṭ! As before, the Aghora-weapon is indeed the weapon. All are performers of every rite; all accomplish every purpose.
All assume every form; all possess unfailing power.
"All [deities] arising from Śiva’s activity are in no way to be subjected to critical analysis," as stated in the Mataṅga.
Thus, for this mantra, separate deities are not traditionally taught.
For Śiva is its deity, Śakti its seer, and that which is known as Gāyatrī its meter. (6.115)
Furthermore, another [seed-syllable] is known as Chanda; it should not be questioned in any way.
It is situated on the sixth earth-seed and is joined with the bindu of the fifth vowel.

The word for water is *toya*, or else *sargi* and *jala*; likewise, *vāyu* joined with the end of the twelfth [vowel]; the sixth and the final [consonants] form *vyāpini*; and the word for the Lord (*īśa*) is joined with the beloved of the fire-god (*hutabhuj*). (6.117)
This ten-syllabled mantra begins with *tāra* (Om), pervades the sky, and is of the nature of Śiva.
*Tāra* (Om) is followed by [the letter] *ra*, then the second vowel, and two vowels equal in number to the Vedas and the seasons (four and six).
This ten-syllable mantra consists of "vyomavyāpin" ending in the dative case, followed by the syllable "tāra.
It comprises the syllable "tāra," the seed-syllable of the Prāsāda mantra, and the three syllables "śivāya. (6.119)
The obeisance consists of seven syllables, and there is also the mantra of Śiva;
at the end of the seed-syllables of the limbs mentioned for Prāsāda, however, are the letters beginning with Śi.
Indeed, by joining them with the appropriate case endings, they become the limbs of Śiva;
the word "Śiva" is in the dative case, while the sequence beginning with "Nati" consists of five syllables.
This Śiva-mantra, which bestows dharma, kāma, artha, and mokṣa, has been extracted;
for the twice-born, it should begin with "Tāra" (Om), and so forth.
...the six-syllabled [mantra]. There is no other mantra equal to this for accomplishing all aims. (6.123)

This six-syllabled mantra, beginning with the seed-syllable of Śakti and preceded by the *satāra* (the five *praṇavas*), is indeed known as the eight-syllabled Śaiva mantra; it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. || 6-124 ||
When one joins pure consciousness (cinmātra) at the end of this very eight-syllabled mantra,
it is declared to be a ten-syllabled mantra that grants all desires like a wish-fulfilling tree.
The meters of the five mantras are stated in sequence as follows: the Paṅkti, the Gāyatrī, the Bṛhatī, and again the Paṅkti. (6.126)
Vāmadeva, Dadhīca, the great sage Śilāda, and Sanatkumāra—these sages have been mentioned in their proper order. (6.127)
Śiva himself is directly the deity of the first two mantras;
however, for the remaining three, the deity is Śiva together with Śakti.
The individual rituals for these have been written in the previous manual;
they are those in which the mantras are extracted within the section on mantras (mantrapāda). (6.129)
All possess immeasurable power, and all bestow the accomplishment of every purpose.

Thus, here the mantras have been correctly described according to their primary importance as established in the Śiva-tantras. By means of these, all ritual actions are accomplished, as well as prosperity preceded by the state of Śiva and liberation. (6.131)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, on the Extraction of Mantras, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 6.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

I shall describe the mudrās well-known in the Śaiva tantras, by which the accomplishment of the ritual of worship is ordained. First, there are six specific mudrās for the Sun, and afterwards, ten other principal mudrās of Śambhu are to be known.

With the hands facing each other in the shape of a lotus, the two thumbs are placed together in the middle like the pericarp; this is called the *padma* (lotus) mudrā. When the same [mudrā] has the middle fingers joined and the thumbs extended, it is known as the *bimba* mudrā. (7.2)
As before, when the hands are joined, the Niṣṭhurā mudrā is formed by moving the thumbs at the tips of the fingers.
Having formed a fist with the right hand, the Govṛṣa mudrā consists of releasing the index and middle fingers while they are vibrating.
When the hands have their fingers interlaced and the tips of the middle fingers joined at their two ends,
while the ring fingers and little fingers are likewise joined at their tips with the palms turned away from each other, this indeed constitutes the mudrā known as the *dhenu*.
Having formed a fist with the right hand and extended the index finger,
one becomes a terrifier by striking the palm of the left hand with that index finger.
Thus ends the sixfold mudrā of the Sun. With both hands extended and facing downwards, one should touch the body starting from the feet up to the head; this is proclaimed as the Mahāmudrā.

Having joined the palms with the hands turned upward and having separately bent the tips of the two index fingers, one should touch the base of the two ring fingers; this shall be the mudrā known as āvāhana (invocation).

This [mudrā] is to be placed facing downwards on the very day of invocation (āvahani). When the two hands are held with fists joined and the pair of jyeṣṭhās (thumbs) positioned upwards with their tips raised, that is the Sānnidhāpanī;
furthermore, if in this same position the thumbs are inserted into the palms, it is called Niṣṭhurā.
Having joined the palms in the shape of a lotus bud, with the right thumb pressing upon the left thumb,
this mudrā, which is worthy of salutation, is to be employed in the rite of prostration.
When the two hands have their fists clenched and the thumbs joined facing each other, it becomes the Śaiva Kālakarṇī; the others are recorded as [the following]. (7-10)
The right fist is turned downward, and the left *jyeṣṭhā* finger is placed within that fist;
then, from the middle of the left hand, the other *jyeṣṭhā* finger extends across the right side and encircles [the thumb]—this is the *liṅga-mudrā*. (7.11)
The dhenu-mudrā is exactly as previously described:
when the tips of the two little fingers are crossed and the two thumbs are placed upon them, one should join the index and middle fingers while the two ring fingers are raised. (7.12)
Having joined them at the tips, the mudrā becomes five-faced.
This concludes the section on the ten mudrās.
Then, having contracted the tip of the little finger and pressed it between the thumb and middle finger... [7-13]
The remaining fingers should be straight and extended; this is known as the *śakti* [mudrā].
Indeed, this same mudrā is called *śakti* when the three fingers are spread apart and pointing upward. (7.14)
If it has the form of three prongs, it is called the trident mudrā (śūlamudrā). Having joined the palms with both hands, one should grasp the two ring fingers. (7.15)
With the remaining fingers extended, this is proclaimed as the *dravyamudrā*.
Having extended the right hand, with all the fingers starting from the little finger [extended]... (7.16)
One should quickly contract [the fingers] in succession; this is considered the *saṃhāriṇī* mudrā.
The hands are placed back-to-back with their fingers interlaced with one another. (7.17)
Having performed [the gesture], having bound [it], having turned [it] away, and having bowed, that shall be the mudrā for seeking forgiveness. Thus are the five mudrās.
In this way, the mantras and the principal mudrās have been proclaimed, through which the accomplishment of ritual actions is ordained.
Through knowledge of these, through their retention, and through their recitation and practice, they obtain their desired objects. || 7-18 ||
Thus ends the seventh chapter, on Mudrās, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, which is the Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati. || 7 ||
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Whether in a temple, a pavilion, or a house— wherever that rite is performed—
it should be done on a purified spot smeared with cow dung.
Having placed and stretched a long thread from Varuṇa to Indra (west to east) here in the center, and having marked a point in its middle,
one should then mark the other two directions (south and north) equally according to that thread.
Furthermore, having divided that thread-segment into equal parts, one should mark it as well; then,
by means of a thread measured by the marks for the east, west, and center of the central point, and laid down accordingly,
one should draw a pair of fish-marks from the central point toward the south and north, following the equal marks.
Having placed the cord between those two, it should extend from south to north.
In this manner, one should establish the thread called Brahma and the north-south thread.
Then, using a measurement equal to half the area of the field, one should mark points in the four directions according to the threads as desired.
Having thus established the marks, from each pair of those marks, two corner-fish (koṇamatsya) will indeed be formed by means of two threads. (8–5)
Those fish were caught on all sides in every direction by means of threads cast down.
The site should be square, divided into four equal sections, level, and auspicious; it is the basis for the construction of all mandalas, sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), and other structures.
The construction of the square [fire-pit]:
A square pit is recommended at the outset, as well as one shaped like an aśvattha leaf, a half-moon, and likewise a triangle; there may also be a circle, a hexagon, a lotus, or an octagon. (8–8)
For fifty oblations, it should be one *ratni* in measure; for a hundred oblations, however, it should be one *aratni*.
For a thousand, it should be the measure of a *hasta*, and for ten thousand, it should be two *hastas*.
For one hundred thousand oblations, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) should be four cubits; for one million, six cubits;
and for ten million oblations, it should be eight cubits, as stated in the *Bhojendrapaddhati*.
All the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) should be equal in length and width according to the measurements prescribed;
the excavation should also be made equal to the width, and there should be three girdles (mekhalās) above in succession.
The excavation should be level on all sides; above the excavation, one should construct three girdles (mekhalās), leaving a space of one finger-breadth on each of the four directions.
The first girdle should indeed be one *ratni* in measure; the next by two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), and another by one finger-breadth.
Furthermore, on a *ratni*, they should be made with measures of three, two, and one finger-breadths respectively.

Regarding this, King Bhoja states: "In a *hasta*-sized sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), the first girdle (*mekhalā*) should be two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) wide; the second, one *aṅgula*; and the third, half an *aṅgula*. For a pit measuring one *aratni*, the [girdles] are three, two, and one *aṅgula* respectively. In a *hasta*-sized pit, the girdles should be four, three, and two *aṅgulas* in sequence."
One should construct [the altar] with six, four, and three finger-breadths respectively, even when it is two cubits in size.

In a fire-pit of four cubits, these [lines] are made with eight, six, and four finger-breadths; likewise in one of six cubits, with ten, eight, and six; and in an eight-cubit pit, they are sixteen, twelve, and eight in number.
All [the altars] in all the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are equal in width and height;
they are surrounded by a perimeter equal to their own dimensions and are free from depressions or elevations.
Regarding this, King Bhoja states:
"In all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), three girdles (mekhalās) should be constructed in sequence, strictly according to the dimensions of the pit."
One should fashion the *yoni* either to the west or to the south of the *kuṇḍa*,
situated above all the *mekhalās* in the middle.
In the *ratnikuṇḍa*, the yoni measures twelve *aṅgulas* in length from its base to its tip;
it is equal in width to eight, four, and two *aṅgulas* respectively, rising gradually in height by one *aṅgula*, and its tip emerges sharply outward.
In sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) measuring one cubit (aratni) and so forth, the yoni is prescribed by increasing the length and width by two finger-breadths (aṅgula) each in successive order.
In this *Bhojarājendrapaddhati*:
"Thus [is the rule] for the first fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*); for the remaining ones, the vulva (*yoni*) should be fashioned with an increase of two finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) each. And in the *Mañjarī*:
In the direction of the Lord of Waters (the west), there should be a pit one cubit in measure and one span in length; it should be shaped like an *aśvattha* leaf, gradually sloping downward,
with a navel ten or six finger-breadths wide, and its tip being a sphere four finger-breadths in diameter.
Thus:
"The sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may be either square or circular for daily rites and for rites of pacification (śāntika);
others say it is square for all purposes, while [some say] it is circular. (8-20)
Having marked a single portion of the cord outside the boundary lines in front of the Lord of Waters (the northeast),
and having fixed a thread from that measurement between the two corners,
one should then extend it from the center to the end of the other diagonal, reaching the previous mark at the corners.
But according to the Sūtra, having struck [the ground], the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) may also be shaped like a vulva or like a leaf of the Aśvattha tree.
Having divided the square into parts consisting of four *yāma*-units, one should worship at the final [point] in the north;
then, by means of this same [measurement], having placed two external marks from east to west, [one proceeds].
In the same way, by rotating the thread situated in the middle toward the south for both [sides], there arises a beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shaped like a half-moon. || 8-23 ||
In a square divided into four parts at the corners of the Vedas (the cardinal points), having cast a line-measure outward from the eastern division toward the north,
and having drawn two lines in two directions upon the cord fixed between the central and western marks,
two fish-figures shall be formed; then, in front of those two, three cords [should be drawn] according to the marks.
Having cast [the fire] toward the direction of Nairṛta, that pit becomes known as triangular. || 8-24 ||
Having taken the sixth part previously deposited and situated at the southwest (nairṛta), one should cast two threads ending at the northwest (vāyavya); thus there may be a triangle. 8-25.
Having placed the thread situated at the central point so as to mark the eastern arm, and having rotated it, there shall be a circular pit, which is most beautiful. (8-26)
Because of the intended meaning of the word *bhuja* (arm), since the word *prāk* (eastward) is seen before the *bhuja*, it means "having placed the fingers" (*aṅgulān*).
Having established the sixth external part, which was placed by Indra and Varuṇa, in the middle of the Vedic corner, one should then rotate the thread equally between those two on the outside.

There are four fish-shaped figures there; subsequently, when [the cords] fall exactly upon the marks situated on the cord located to the south of the direction of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada), there shall indeed be a hexagonal sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa).

In a circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*), one should draw eight lotus petals on the outside above its rim; having made them extend for half the length of the pit, it shall be known as a "lotus" (*padma*) pit.
From the solar portion (ādityāṅga), both internally and externally, one should draw lines with haste in all directions;

from those two [lines], two fish-figures (matsya) shall arise in every direction. By means of the threads extended through those [fish-figures] according to rule, there shall be a beautiful eight-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or else by means of the corners formed by the half-diagonal threads.
Or [the time] is obtained by adding half of the remainder to the eight fish produced from two pairs of fifty-five *śaphara* [units]. || 8-29 ||
Having divided the square into nine parts, one should project a portion outward and inward at the cardinal and corner directions; then, by means of threads placed accordingly within those divisions,
two squares of equal measure shall be formed, and from their intersection, an octagon is produced.
Or it may be in the northeast, being perfectly level and very beautiful, just like the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 8-30 ||
The Chapter on the Kuṇḍa: Having prepared a square, one should then divide it into eighteen parts;
there will indeed be two hundred and fifty-six squares here.
One should draw a lotus with six petals using six squares in the center; outside of this, a pedestal in a single row; and outside the pedestal, a pathway (vīthī) on all sides with two rows.
Outside that, in two rows, one should likewise mark the doors, their thresholds, and the adjacent areas in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
And one should draw the gallas and upagallas in the corners of Agni, Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Īśa. || 8-32 ||
Some say [the sequence is] *kaṇṭha-upakaṇṭha*, *galla-upagalla*, *kapola-upakapola*, and *śobhā-upaśobhā*.
Having established the directional lines within the lotus-field and having smoothed out the other [lines], one should discard the outer twelfth part and rotate the rest. (8.33)
One should divide the field into four parts by means of cords, in an equal and orderly sequence;
these divisions constitute the pericarp, the filaments, the lotus, the joints, and the tips of the petals. (8.34)
One should rotate outward that which was previously omitted as the twelfth part;
this shall be the fifth field, known as Vyoman (the Sky), and it constitutes the tips of the petals.
Having extended two diagonal threads from corner to corner through the center of the directions,
and having struck out four threads [thereby], there shall be sixteen threads.
To achieve the perfection of the petal-tips, one should place a thread at the midpoint of the junction between petals, measuring up to the tip of the petal;
then, by means of crescent-moon shapes arising from the rotation of the space between two petals, the petal is perfected. (8.37)
Having divided the center of the sixteen lotus-lines by means of threads, there shall be thirty-two segment-lines equal to the circumference at the tips of the petals. (8.38)

Then, taking the thread situated at the tip of the thread on both sides of the petal-tip thread, one should lead it from the base of that tip to the end of the petal-tip thread while drawing; in this way, the petal-tip will become beautiful. (8.39)
Powdered rice flour is said to be white; turmeric mixed with a little sugar is pale yellow;
safflower, vermilion, and jasmine are red; and powder made from burnt barley and the like is blue.
The dark-colored [mandalas] are prescribed by those learned in sacrifice to be made with the leaves of the Śamī, lotus, Bilva, and other such trees;
one should indeed fill the mandalas with grains and other materials of their respective colors.
A yellow powder made from realgar and yellow orpiment is highly recommended.
For the five-colored powders, the five forms beginning with Brahmā are assigned. (8-42)
The deities become their [forms], as do the kalās beginning with nivṛtti;
likewise, the ages—Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and the Kaliyuga—become time.

One should contemplate and join [the mantras] with the discs (bimba) that consist of cool, red, dark, yellow, and black, as well as white, red, and likewise black— corresponding respectively to the three principles (tattva), the three Vedas, the three fires, the three worlds, the three powers, the three twilights, and the three qualities (guṇa). || 8.44 ||
For the purpose of enjoyment one should circumambulate counter-clockwise (apasavya), but for the purpose of nourishment, clockwise (pradakṣiṇa).
The discerning practitioner should apply the falling of colored powders within the mandalas;
he should drop them with his fist for the sake of nourishment, if liberation is desired. (8.46)

In rites for pacification (*śāntika*), one should use the middle finger, the thumb, and the index finger, or indeed all the fingers; if one desires the supreme accomplishment (*siddhi*), one should construct mandalas here with gems of those respective colors— namely, pearls, topaz, rubies, sapphires, and emeralds.
Regarding such powders, King Bhoja states that one desiring success should prepare them with pearls, coral, and other such materials;
furthermore, all the lines everywhere should be white and measured by the middle finger.
In a [mandala] of two cubits, the lines should be the size of a thumb; or in a [mandala] of one cubit, they should be equal to the ring finger.

Regarding this, King Bhoja states: "These lines should be the measure of the first finger (one *aṅgula*); the others should be less by a barley-corn (*yava*) and have intervals of a barley-corn. All should be made equal for one desiring liberation, and for one desiring enjoyment. (p.
79) The pericarp should be yellow in color, and all the lines should be white and equal. (8.49)
"In a [mandala] of two cubits, the lines should be the size of a thumb; in one of one cubit, they should be measured by the middle finger," so say others.
In the center, there should indeed be a very yellow pericarp (*karṇikā*), and within it, nine dark-colored seed-syllables (*bīja*).
Two filaments each, slightly curved at their tips, are to be drawn separately in the middle of the petals. (8.50)
At the base they are thin and yellowish-green; in the middle, they are thick and reddish-brown. || 8.51 ||
At the base they are quickly yellowish-green, and at their tips they are indeed slightly white;
King Bhoja states that the mass of filaments is white, red, and yellow at the root, middle, and tip respectively.
One should make those eight petals white, equal in size, with raised tips that are beautiful to behold.
Likewise, those with palms joined together are for enjoyment, while those with sharp tips are for liberation during the sacrifices to Smara and other deities.
One should cause even the four tips of the petals to be red in color;
thus it is said in the Ajita.
The petals for Gaurī, Sarasvatī, and the others should be like the leaves of the holy fig tree (aśvattha). 8.53.
One should cause the ears (or corners) of the lords of the sciences and the planets to be shaped like those of a cow;
the pedestal, moreover, should have feet that are white, reddish, yellow, and black, and be adorned with a blue peg;
one should fashion it with four limbs of various colors, or otherwise according to one's preference.

In this *Tattvasāgara*: "Two squares should be erased in the cardinal directions at the pedestal (*pīṭha*); likewise, one should erase three [squares] each in the corners. One should adorn the pathway with creepers, canopies, and so forth, as well as with leaves.
Outside of that, in the cardinal directions, one should fill in the four gates with white [pigment]. (8.55)

In both cases, for the sake of the doors, two squares each situated in the inner row of the lines of the directions should be used; one should then erase those six squares in the cardinal directions located in the outer row.
There are three chambers on each of the two sides of the inner doors. || 8-57 ||
One should rub each [of the teeth] externally for the sake of achieving the success of the throat and its vicinity.
In this way, there arise eight [areas], including the four quadrants of the individual sockets, as well as the throat and its vicinity.
On their sides, there should likewise be the cheeks and the vicinity of the cheeks, facing in the opposite direction. (8.58)
Then, in the corners, the remaining six squares are [to be marked] individually.

One should release [the syllables] for the sake of accomplishing the corners, or one should write them upon the bull-figures; with red [pigment], one should write the *kaṇṭha* and *upakaṇṭha*, as well as the *kapola* and *upakapola*. (8.60)
One should cover the eight [squares] with yellow so that the ground is no longer visible;
then, one should draw the external qualities all around in the order prescribed: namely, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.
These should be colored red, white, and black respectively, measuring one thumb in width, with intervals between them equal to a barley grain.
The Bhadraka is the supreme [mandala]:
when the square is divided eightfold and thus formed into sixty-four squares. || 8-62 ||
In the center, one should draw a lotus pedestal using four squares;

indeed, the pathway (vīthikā) shall be in the row immediately outside that, and the doors in the four directions using four squares in the two outer rows. Having smoothed them out, one should make them white and equal in size. || 8-63 ||
On both sides of the doors, in the outer row, there is one square each.
Having joined [the lines] at the door, one should erase them; thus there should be the *kaṇṭha* (throat) and *upakaṇṭha* (sub-throat).

Then, having established [lines] in the corners, one remaining square [is formed]; by means of the five remaining individual squares joined together, those *vedakapola* (face-cheeks) and an equal number of *upakapola* (sub-face-cheeks) are produced. (8.65)
Among those, the cheek (kapola) should have its lines extending from east to west,
and the sub-cheek (upakapola) should extend from south to north.
Thus, O Ajita: having filled the pericarp and so forth, as well as the walkway, with the colors previously mentioned according to the stated method;
the doors should be white, while the pilasters (kapola) may be red or yellow. (8.66)
Here, in the Ajita [mandala],
one should visualize red, yellow, dark blue, and white respectively on the cheeks and temples in the southeast and other corners.
Thus: the squares in the corners starting from the southeast (vahni) should be colored yellow, dark green, black, and red. (8.67)
Or else, others have declared that one should fill all [the squares] with the color black;
having drawn the three qualities (guṇatraya) on the exterior with white, reddish-brown, and black colors as before,
this shall be the Sarvatobhadra, which is auspicious due to the unification of the six squares in each corner.
In all mandalas as well, the lotus petals are white;
the doors and the walkways (vīthī) are likewise, being undistinguished by [the addition of] creepers and so forth. (8-73)
The Chapter on the Sarvatobhadra:
In this square divided into thirty-two parts, there are one thousand and sixty-four cells;
one should draw a lotus in its center using cells equal in number to the principles (tattvas), as previously described.
The pedestal (pīṭha) should be formed by the outer row; outside of that, one should draw eight liṅgas with seven rows on both sides of the lines marking the cardinal directions.

The auspicious pedestal, together with its neck, extending from Brahmā to the water-band (jalapaṭṭa), should be formed by squares of six, four, two, and six [units], arranged both crosswise and lengthwise.

Indeed, above the pedestal, by means of the four squares situated in pairs within the middle rows, there shall be a *liṅga*; its head is aligned with the central line passing through it, or it may have its top tapered toward the center. (8.77)
One should draw inward-facing signs for those desiring enjoyment;
for those desiring liberation, one should make them the opposite, with the seats directed inward.
The two auspicious [pillars] situated on both sides of the pedestal of its neck should be formed by means of four compartments;
furthermore, within the intervals between the liṅgas, creepers should be fashioned in the corners using twenty-five compartments.
Just as the lines intersecting like cow’s urine (gomūtrikā) occupy those squares,
so too, by the removal of other lines, there arise creepers extending toward the intermediate directions.
Alternatively, one may draw the leaves of creepers within the spaces between the spokes;
these should have their roots attached at the beginning of the creeper and possess curved tips and so forth. (8.81)
Outside of that, one should clear out a pathway with two rows as before;
likewise, having adorned the pathway with various *kalpalatā* creepers, one should also [clear] the three outer enclosures.
Here, for the sake of the doors, one should omit squares numbering four, six, and eight, starting from the interior.
The primary ornament (śobhā) and the secondary ornament (upaśobhā) may also occur through the omission of two, four, or six [elements]. || 8.83 ||
One should erase three times seven squares separately in each corner;
one should then adorn everything, beginning with the lotus, like the *bhadraka* diagram, using five kinds of colored powders,
or one may fill it according to one's desire with the colors prescribed for the eight-faced *liṅga*.
Thus has this Prāsāda-maṇḍala been described by the beloved of Pārvatī;
it is adorned with eight liṅgas, creepers, lotuses, walkways, and enclosures. (8.85)
The Section on the Temple of the Beloved of Pārvatī:
A square field measuring four cubits should be divided into twenty parts, resulting in four hundred squares;
in its center, a lotus is formed by twenty-five squares.
The pedestal (pīṭha) shall be made with one row [of cells], and the path (vīthī) with another;
then, with four rows, there shall be the doors and liṅgas, surrounded by creepers, and the outer path (bāhyavīthī) shall also be formed by the outermost row.
One should construct the lotus seats and the pathways according to the rules, like those of Bhadraka; likewise, one should fashion doors in all directions using two or eight squares per row.
From the interior of the street, there are three cells connected by a door; then the floor-base (bhūpīṭha) consists of a single cell.
Next, the neck-base (kaṇṭhapīṭha) is formed, followed by the water-band (toyapaṭṭa) with three cells, and then the liṅga with one cell.
Below and above that, one should draw lines from the corners toward the interior of the four square compartments of the pedestal,
using a measurement equal to half the length of the compartment's side-line.
Having rotated it, one should discard the outer four broken corners;
thus the pedestal (pīṭha) becomes beautiful, adorned with twelve points.
Having filled the entire mandala, from the lotus to the edge of the path, with colored powders as previously described,
that mandala is known as the "Emergence of the Lata-liṅga," which is beloved by Śaṅkara.
The Chapter on the Emergence from the Embrace of the Creeper:
On a square field divided sixteenfold in the four directions, one should fashion four liṅgas using the compartments, like [the faces] of the Beloved of Pārvatī. (8–93)

In the center, by means of the remaining Vedic squares, and likewise within the intervals between the liṅgas by those same counts, a four-petalled lotus shall arise of its own accord; it is thus formed upon the liṅgas whose tops have been joined together.
There should be eight auspicious syllables (*bhadrāṣṭaka*) at the necks and creepers in the corners as before;
having written this, it shall be the mandala designated as the Five Brahmans.
In the center of the lotus, there should be a circular pericarp that is yellow; here, the row of filaments is red and thin.
Īśa is in the middle, while Puruṣa and the others also have lingas of gold in the directions. (8–96)
But having drawn svastikas in the positions where the creepers would normally be,
the omission of squares is prescribed in sequence as one, three, and then five.
Indeed, this Svastika-maṇḍala-lotus is [drawn] within these fields, or else in this [area] divided into twelve parts;
in the center, there should be a lotus formed by sixteen squares, and likewise, there should be svastikas in the eight directions.
Having filled the svastikas and the lotus as before with powders, the svastika is recommended for the sake of well-being and is praised by all the gods. (8–99)
The section on the double-svastika lotus:
In this field divided into eighteen parts, having first conceived the center of the svastika in its middle, one should erase the five squares on all sides that resemble a crossroads. (8–100)
Lines extending across the entire area, curved in the form of a svastika and mutually supporting one another, should be established by omitting the remaining [lines]. (8–101)
In this [mandala], there shall indeed be fifty *svastikas* together with seven *sūryabhadrakas*;
and in the centers, there shall be fifty-two *sarvatobhadras* and crossroads.
One should decorate each of the remaining single squares in the corners with white;
likewise, one should decorate the auspicious crossroads with blue, yellow, red, and dark colors.
This indeed is the mandala named Sarvatobhadrasvastika;
some call it Sarvasvastika, for it is dear to the two Śivas.
Alternatively, when the site is divided into sixteen parts— whether by the numbers fourteen, twelve, ten, eight, or seven— the mandalas,
complete with svastikas and auspicious signs, shall be formed everywhere according to the previous method of elimination.
The svastika and sarvatobhadra designs [are described].
In a square measuring two cubits, there should be a wheel and lotus, devoid of a pedestal;
it should have a single nave, and its characteristics should follow the sequence of measurement in finger-breadths (aṅgula).

Having placed the thread upon the lotus-bindu, then by measuring nine finger-breadths for half a lotus and three [further] measures of eight and four [finger-breadths], through rotation, the navel, the spokes, and the rim of the lotus shall be formed.
Having drawn a lotus as before, one should fill the navel with yellow [pigment].
Then, having extended the lines of the petals in a wheel whose spokes are equal to the petals, [one proceeds]. (8.108)

Then one should correctly draw the spokes within them; likewise, on the two spokes adjacent to each petal, the spokes here shall be formed by extending the lines from the tips of the petals and the lines from the joints of the petals. (8–109)
Having divided the ground into three parts, one should mark two [sections] with lines in between;
then, having struck out those [lines] like fish-tails, one should draw the spokes using threads.

They may resemble the petals of a blue lotus or an aśvattha tree, or they may have the shape of a mātuluṅga fruit; they may have the luster of a lotus leaf, or be shaped like a grain of barley, or thin in the middle like an ant. (8.111)

The Arakas are red, the Arunas are dark-blue, and they should be of alternating colors in sequence; at the end, they should have the luster of yellow orpiment (gorocanā), and the joints of the spokes (arasandhis) should be pale-yellow.
Having divided the rim into three parts, one should fill the middle with white and the exterior with black;
having filled the interior corners with yellow, they should be made beautiful with the svastika mark in black.
Standing within the interval between two spokes, one should revolve outside the rim;
standing in the middle of the space between two spokes, one should rotate the base of a spoke.
Standing in the middle of the spokes, one should rotate the center of the spokes;
in this way, the spokes are successively perfected, having the shape of citron fruits.
From the junction at the base of the spokes, a thread should likewise be placed on both sides of each spoke;
having struck them out individually, the spokes shall become like the petals of a wide-open lotus.

Situated in the middle of the spokes, having left a small portion at the tip like a lotus petal, the spokes of the lotus petals arise from the rotation of the hub and the rotation of the tips. (8.117)
The roots should be slender and the middles broad; they should be made with a thickness of one-third at the joint of the *ārā*.
Those which enter within, known as "barley-belly" (*yavodara*), are successful; they should gradually become sharp at the tip. (8–118)
Having divided the protective field into three parts,
one should stand in the middle of the second and first portions, rotate [the instrument], and [mark] the third portion like the tip of a petal.
One should draw the tips of the petals with two half-moon-shaped lines;
in this way, the spokes indeed come to resemble the leaves of the *aśvattha* tree.

Then, having moved four finger-breadths from the junction, at the middle division, by rotating transversely half a division on both sides, there should be *kāra* syllables with thin middles between two lines; these are the spokes called *pipīlikā* and *kroḍa*. (8-121)

Having adorned the interior of the mandala with various flowers, one should then decorate even the exterior of the bimba with rows of flowers, provided it has not been smeared [with ointment]. || 8.122 ||
And it has been said: "The lotus-wheel with a single nave is dear to Śiva, Āryā, Ravi, and Keśava;
other lotus-wheel mandalas should be understood as being beautiful with nine naves. (8.123)
The section on the wheel and lotus:

By means of a measurement equal to half the pericarp, and through the process of rotating the previously established thread, twelve fish-diagrams (matsya) shall arise by joining its two sides. (8.124)
By means of the sūtras that fall upon those [lines] along with the connecting sūtras, there arises from the division of the eight-petaled lotus an equal lotus, beautiful with sixteen petals. (8.125)
From the thread at the end of the sky-line of the filaments to the tip of those filaments, one should mark it like a fish; thus there shall be a five-petaled lotus.
From the junctions of the pericarp and the petals, as before, for the sake of accomplishing the six-petaled [lotus];
from the space-line and the pericarp, the tips of the petals are established by means of the seven [lines]. (8.127)

By means of the petals, the junctions, and the pericarp, with a fish-mark placed at each petal-junction, there shall be a nine-petaled lotus; by stretching five lines, it shall become a row of petals.
Having placed [the center] in the sky between the filaments and the space, one should mark it;
thus, by the casting of the threads, there shall be a lotus with eleven petals.

Having placed [the cord] at the tip of the petal and at the joint of the petal, and having marked the tip of the petal, one should strike the cords across them; thus there shall be the petals of the lotus.

If, beyond this, one should desire an increase in petals, one should draw the lotuses according to one's wish by means of lines, following this same method and sequence, inferring [the proportions] by way of the "fish" [formed by the intersecting lines].

The characteristics for the division of the [mandala] sections: (p. 86) By means of the measurement and the laying of the lines for the half-moon and other types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*), one should fashion the forms of the half-moon and so forth in accordance with their proportions. || 8.132 ||
Thus, the procedure for the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and the mandala has been primarily described, which grants success in the specific rites of Śiva;
having extensively examined various Śiva Āgamas here, it brings satisfaction to the foremost of teachers. (8.133)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on the Fire-pit and the Mandala, in the upper section of the Kriyāpāda of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 8.

Now begins the ninth chapter. I shall describe the characteristics of the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*) and the offering spoon (*sruva*). Furthermore, the ladle should be one cubit (*hasta*) in length; it may be made of *pālāśa* wood, or likewise from *khadira* or *śamī* wood, and should be beautiful.
The mouth, which is four-cornered, should be measured by six finger-breadths for the best, five for the middling, and four for the lowest;
it should be slightly depressed, and its interior should be covered with three parts [of that measurement].

The excavation should indeed be equal in width [to the base], and it should be circular on the outside; there should be three external rims (mekhalā), and likewise, there should be a lotus in the center of them.
The neck (kaṇṭha) should have a width of one *aṅgula* like a sphere, and its height should be one *aṅgula*.
The tip should be nine finger-breadths long, and its width should be equal to that.

At the neck there should then be a hollow in the middle; that indeed is triangular and filled with oil, through which [the liquid] flows out as far as the cavity, just as the little finger would enter.
Its back is marked with a lotus, and its entire face is like an elephant's trunk.
The remainder [of the staff] shall be a rounded handle, and its tip should be marked with a lotus. || 9-3 ||

The tip of the staff, measured in circumference, should be as thick as eight finger-breadths at its base—just like a lotus—and it should gradually taper toward the forearm; its root should likewise be eight finger-breadths.
Therein should be a bull, or else a lotus, smooth in form on all sides.
Having cut down trees grown in auspicious places that are free from defects, one should have the sacrificial ladle (sruk) fashioned.
The *sruva* ladle should be made of *śrīparṇī* wood, well-constructed, and two *tāla* units in length;
its mouth should be one finger-width in diameter, and its cavity (*avaṭa*) half a finger-width deep.
The middle wall between the two smooth cavities is said to be one *yava* in thickness.
It is the size of a *karṣa* of clarified butter, shaped like a cow’s hoofprint, and on its back, the two buttocks are marked by two barleycorns.

A line measured by the size of a barley grain is drawn through the middle of the buttocks; below the face is the neck, marked with the characteristics of a lotus, and below that is the shaft (*daṇḍa*), which is well-rounded and even.
The tip of the shaft is one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) in circumference, while its base is one and a half [fingers] greater than that.
It may resemble a cow's tail from the neck downwards, for its base is indeed thick, like [the root of] that [tail]. (9.5)
Some say that the *sruva* ladles should be one cubit (*bāhu*) or one forearm (*aratni*) in length;
this is the support for the *sruk* and *sruva*.
Having cut a branch of the *pippala* tree, as well as [branches] from within a *śamī* tree and from an *aśvattha* tree...
Having cut a piece of wood free from defects, six finger-breadths in length and equal [in width], one should have it fashioned into an *araṇi*.
Its circumference should be six finger-breadths; its head is said to be at the base and its foot at the tip.
The *yoni* is situated in the middle, measured by four finger-breadths, and it should be suitable for the churning stick. || 9-7 ||

Likewise, the upper fire-drill (uttarāraṇi) should also be made of *aśvattha* wood; one should fashion its rotating pin (*bhrāmaka*) from *khadira* wood, six finger-breadths in length, straight, and with a cord (*netra*).
One should produce fire there using fuel that is pithy and stripped of its bark.
It is also taught that [the fire] produced from excellent wood, once divided, should be fanned with a whisk or similar implement.
The procedure for the fire-drills (*araṇi*):

those that are crooked, with withered leaves, thin, infested by worms, split, brought from an inauspicious place, short, with bark missing from large sections, damaged, long, burnt by fire, and so forth, are unfavorable.

Fuel sticks originating from pure ground should be avoided; the remaining ones should be cut evenly with the middle and ring fingers, those equal in length to the middle finger are praised, while those equal to the little finger are inferior. || 9-9 ||

The sacrificial fuel (idhma) is declared to consist of eighteen kindling sticks (samidh), being one span (prādeśa) long, or in some cases measured by a cubit (ratni). There should be three enclosing sticks (paridhi) of one cubit in length;
the southern one is long, while the western one is thick and the northern one is thin and short.
In the north, those born in Kauśika and Bālakakuśa are indeed the best types of darbha grass, respectively.

Those that are torn, those plucked by hand or nails, those killed by insects, those engaged in other tasks, those belonging to Yama, those damaged by leaping over tigers and the like, those that are smoky-colored, upright, or dried out, as well as those that are dark, tender, fresh, cut, or moist while dry—these should be avoided. (p. 88)
If *darbha* grasses are to be used here, they are mentioned in the chapter on fire-rituals (*agnikārya*), as well as the braided hair (*veṇī*) and other such matters. || 9-11 ||

In that regard, there is a braid made of thirty blades of *darbha* grass; or else, the *darbha* blades for the surrounding strewn grass (*paristaraṇa*) should number eight, sixteen, twenty-four, or thirty-two, starting from the east. A bundle (*kūrca*) tied with blades of *darbha* numbering according to the principles (*tattva*, i.e., twenty-five) is the "sword of knowledge" (*jñānakhaḍga*); some say it consists of thirty-two *darbha* blades. A general bundle is made with two *darbha* blades, while a special bundle (*viśeṣakūrca*) is made with five *darbha* blades, according to the *Saṃhitā*.

This is the rule for the fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and the sacrificial grass (*barhis*). The vessel for the clarified butter (*ājya*) should be like a shallow cup (*śarāva*), measuring eight finger-breadths in width.
The stem should be half the width in height and four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) wide;
the vessel for the *praṇītā* water should be six finger-breadths high and equal in width;
and the *prokṣaṇī* vessel should be eight finger-breadths in both width and height, provided with a stem.
In this regard, the Pauṣkara states: "In all cases, vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or clay yield results that are superior, middling, or inferior respectively.

A sacrificial pot (*caru*) filled with eight *kuḍuba* measures is considered the lowest; one made of copper, measured by twelve [the number of the sun] *svaras*, is middling; and the highest is [that which is] measured by sixteen.
The best [ladle] is three times seven finger-breadths in length; the inferior one is measured at twenty-one finger-breadths in length.
Here, the head should be circular with seven arrow-finger-breadths (five fingers), and the tail with two.
Śāli rice, white ṣaṣṭika rice, kalama rice, and grains produced from wild nīvāra—these husked, pure, and free from grit or sand, being white, are recommended for the caru.
Fresh ghee from one's own animal is the best; that which is purchased is middling.
Clarified butter that is not fresh, having been purchased, is inferior; it should be cow's butter that has been strained. || 9.14 ||

Honey that is not corrupted by smell or taste, even if purchased, should be accepted after being strained again; likewise, fresh white sugar-candy, jaggery, and sugarcane products, when purchased, are acceptable.
Among these, each preceding one is more highly recommended than the next, provided it is entirely pure and obtained through honest means.
And for the sake of the oblation and other rites, all grains such as sesame seeds and the like should be thoroughly washed and purified.

Furthermore, whatever other delicious, pure, and fresh fruits such as roots and tubers may be taken, for those an oblation measured by the size of the thumb is prescribed; however, in the case of rice and similar grains, it is said to be five finger-breadths. For liquid substances such as clarified butter, the oblation is declared to be the full capacity of the *sruva* ladle.
Indeed, there should be a mere handful of parched grains, and for flowers such as the lotus and others, only one each. || 9.16 ||

For creepers, it should be four finger-breadths; for sesame seeds and groats, it should be the "deer" (mṛgī) measure, which indeed consists of the middle finger together with the thumb and is known by the name "deer.
For fragrant substances, it is the size of a chickpea (*caṇakī*), while for *guggulu*, it is like the seed of a jujube fruit (*badarī*).
And for edible foods such as large fruits and the like, the oblation should be the measure of an akṣa. || 9-17 ||

In the rite of oblation involving various mixed foods, one should offer individually each of the fruits of the date-palm, the *iṅguda*, the *goṣṭhanī*, the jujube, and the rose-apple, as well as their leaves, and likewise a single joint of sugarcane; these are held with the five fingers.
Likewise, three tips of dūrvā grass, as well as each individual fuel-stick, constitute an oblation.
The measure of the oblation:
the *vardhanī* should be filled with a full *bhāra* of water; the *kumbha* holds a *khārī* of water;
the *kalaśa* is completely filled with a *droṇa* of water; and the *karkarī* is filled from the *pūrṇāśiva*.
A *pūrṇā* consists of one *ghaṭikā* and one *āḍhaka*; two *kuḍuba*s are known as a *śarāva*.
A conch-shell vessel and a lamp are considered full when they hold one *kuḍuba* or more.
The measure of the vessel:
I shall now describe here the purification regarding the vessel and the substances and so forth; one should wash it with water until the scent, ointment, and other such residues have disappeared.
One should also scrub with powders and then wash again with warm water;
this is the purification for vessels here, and now the specific purification is being described. 9-20.
A golden vessel is purified by water so that the coating may be removed;
one made of copper by acidic water;
one made of silver by cow-dung; bell-metal by ash and water; and likewise one made of gems by the rays of the sun or by water.
If a clay vessel is [purified] by fire, it becomes as new; likewise, a wooden one [is purified] instantly. || 9-21 ||
The purification of iron from burning has thus been declared by those who work with metals;
likewise, other metals are purified by contact or by approaching a horse's mouth, provided they have not been struck [by fire].
Regarding hides, ropes, and garments, purification occurs through washing with alkaline water.
And water and air may enter gourds and flutes through the rubbing of cow-hair. (9.22)

p. 90) Purification shall occur even for water-vessels by means of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*); likewise, for grains, fruits, *darbha*-grass roots, and sacrificial fuel-sticks, it occurs through sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*) and washing (*adhāvana*).
As for those garments made of silk (*kauśeya*), fine cotton (*dukūla*), or woven cloth (*paṭṭa*) which have been dyed—
The eyes, the ears, and the virāga [membrane] are purified by white mustard seeds mixed with water. || 9-23 ||
Furthermore, vessels made of wood, bamboo, or clay, as well as those defiled by phlegm, food remnants, filth, and the like, or corrupted by the remains of offerings (*nirmālya*), must be discarded.
Regarding oily substances as well, purification is possible if they are not spoiled; otherwise, they must be illuminated [with fire].
Then one may be purified by the sight of the crest of fire in reservoirs of water and other such places during the nights. || 9-24 ||
The ground—whether trampled by cattle, dug up to its base, ploughed, or excavated—is purified; likewise, houses and other structures are purified when smeared with water and cow-dung.
Furthermore, the earth is purified by the declaration of a "holy day" (*puṇyāha*), by feeding Brahmins, or by the act of scraping.
One who has committed a sin is purified by speaking with another; the purification of speech comes from conversing with the twice-born.

The body, together with the mind, is purified by breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) when one has touched things that should not be touched while immersed in water with one's clothes on; likewise after eating such things, or upon sneezing, belching, yawning, or seeing an outcaste, a dog, or an untouchable, one is purified by sipping water (ācamana) at the end. (9.26)
Water drawn from wells and other sources becomes pure here by contact with the rays of the sun when it has become a great body of water;
fire is purified by sprinkling with water accompanied by mantras; and a fire into which oblations have been offered is purified by expiatory rites and the sprinkling of water. (9.27)

The purification of perfumes and other such items is achieved by sprinkling them with water consecrated by mantras; likewise, for milk-rice and similar foods, one should sprinkle clarified butter (ājya) and then illuminate them with a blade of darbha grass. If there is only slight contamination, the purification of even the remnants should be inferred in this same manner. || 9-28 ||
In general, the cause even of the qualities of excellence is the purity of the mind with respect to action, substance, self, and [other] entities.
That purity belongs to one who is untainted by passion and the like; for such a person, all four aims of human life are as if held in the palm of the hand. (9.29)

Thus ends the ninth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles and other implements, in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*. 9.
Now begins the tenth chapter.

The first initiation, the *agamadīkṣā*, has been explained with detailed consideration in the chapter on the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*). I shall now describe that [initiation] along with its specific qualifications for the true guru and its various divisions. (10.1)

For by this initiation (dīkṣā), the state of Śiva is bestowed upon the bound soul (paśu); indeed, the root *dā* here signifies "giving. Simultaneously, his state of being a bound soul along with its fetters (*pāśa*) is destroyed; for the verbal root *kṣi* is established in the sense of "destruction" (*kṣaya*). || 10-2 ||

When the Sun is on its northward course, during the waxing moon, on an auspicious day of the week, and when it is conjoined with one's own natal asterism, ascendant, or lunar day, one should indeed perform initiation on a day favorable to oneself. (10.3)

On ground purified and endowed with auspicious characteristics—whether at a temple on the banks of the Sindhu river, or in a cow-pen, a monastery, or one's own home—one should construct a well-made, square pavilion as desired. (10.4)

In this beautiful and well-secluded house, either to the east or to the west of that [main hall], the sowing of auspicious sprouts is desired for the protection [of the site] and for the prosperity of the patron. (10.5)

In various festivals, such as initiations and the installation of deities, as well as in the rite of the sacred thread (pavitraka), that auspicious rite which is performed preceded by the sowing of auspicious sprouts becomes truly auspicious. || 10-6 ||
On the seventh day prior to the auspicious day of the sacrifice, or on the ninth,
or even on the fifth— a favorable day and an excellent moment— one should perform the rite for the auspicious sprouts (maṅgalāṅkura).
In this context, three types of vessels are prescribed: the *pālikā*, the *ghaṭikā*, and the *śarāva*.
These three, dedicated respectively to Viṣṇu, Padmabhava (Brahmā), and Śaṅkara, should be used individually in their proper order.
The *pālikā* is indeed twenty finger-breadths in height and likewise in the width of its mouth;
two [other measures] are described for the middle and inferior methods, corresponding to the count of eight and four *jagatī*s respectively.
The width at the base should be half of that [measurement], and the cavity of the neck should be one-third of it;
the remainder of the entire length should be like a staff, with a pleasing circumference equal to that of the neck. (10.10)
Equal in height and width, the vessel known as the *ghaṭikā* should be five finger-breadths (*tāla*) in measure;
it shall have four faces toward the cardinal directions and one face in the center, with its parts symmetrically arranged.
The mouth of the shallow bowl (śarāva) should be as wide as a palm tree and its height equal to that;
its handle should be half that measure, with a navel (nābhi) of four finger-breadths, and its neck should be elevated, excluding the cavity.
When available, they should be made of gold, silver, copper, or clay; otherwise, they may be newly fashioned.
Having been washed with water consecrated by the Śiva-weapon mantra, one should place them with their necks wrapped in thread. || 10-13 ||
In a charming house for auspicious sprouts, provided with a canopy, one should arrange vessels filled with pure clay, sand, and powdered cow dung, and equipped with bundles of *kuśa* grass. (10.14)
Having smeared the ground with cow-dung water and having sprinkled it with water consecrated by the root-mantra of one's own deity,
one should mark out a square area according to the prescribed characteristics using threads coated with flour.
Having worshipped Vighnarāja in front, on an auspicious day, one should have [the text] recited by those distinguished in the Vedas;
there would be more than eighty words in the four squares when it is thus described.
Then, in the center, one should draw a white lotus with nine squares, adorned with a pericarp, eight petals, and filaments; it should be well-fashioned with raised centers using rice-powder.
There, having placed upon the *kuśa* grass a jar wrapped with thread and fumigated,
one should fill it with the nectar-water dripping from the "twelfth" [cakra], along with *kuśa*, a bundle of grass (*kūrca*), and gold.

It was fragrant with the scent of fresh sprouts of *pippala* and mango trees; its face adorned with garlands, flower wreaths, and unbroken grains of rice; provided with an abundance of *śāli* rice and fruits; and made beautiful by pairs of garments and flowers.

Having visualized that [deity] situated within the lotus of the Mātṛkā, endowed with the sixteen digits (kalās) joined with the sixteen vowels, resembling the cool-rayed moon with its upward-shooting beams, like the Lord of Herbs accompanied by the circle of stars.
One should worship with special offerings and present milk-rice mixed with ghee;
then, one should place the vessels for the sprouts separately upon the auspicious squares marked out with colored powders.
In Āditya, in Samarīci, in Vivasvat, and likewise in Yama; in the Lord of Waters (Varuṇa), in Mitra, in Soma, and in the Supporter of the Earth (Bhūdhara). || 10-22 ||
One should place eight *ghaṭikās* in these positions in sequence:
in Agni, Pūṣan, the one called Pitṛ, Dauvārika, Roga, and Nāga. (10.23)
One should also place the earthen bowls in Aditi and Īśāna;
in the middle positions among these, eight [should be placed] according to the sequence of the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The locations for the pitchers have been described; one should place them within these.
Having first drawn the squares (padas) therein, one should fill them with white powder. || 10.25 ||

Having separately placed one *āḍhaka* measure of each type of rice on separate mats of *darbha* grass, and having set down the water-clocks (*ghaṭikā*) and other instruments, one should sow the seeds therein. (10.26)
Māṣa beans, mudga beans, kulattha, niṣpāva, sesame, śāli rice, mustard seeds, mārga, wheat, śyāmāka, vrīhi rice, and barley. (10.27)
Priyaṅgu, āḍhakyā, and veṇu—these seeds of the three and five groups are declared, in order, to be the best for sprouting. (10.28)
The two groups [of mantras] should be in the middle, and the five seed-syllables in the lowest;
having washed the seed-syllables with water, one should thereafter wash them with milk. (10.29)
Having tied it firmly in a piece of cloth and kept it in water for one day,
one should extract it and sow it once two watches (yāmas) have passed.
Soma is the deity of seeds, for he is radiant during the night;
therefore, one who desires to enjoy the harvest should sow the seeds only at night. (10.31)
Having first consecrated [the seed] with the heart-mantra, one should sow it with this mantra:
"Oṃ, to Tryambaka, to Śarva, to Śaṅkara, and to Śiva. (10.32)
"Homage, homage to the eternal one, the foremost of all the worlds!
With this very mantra, one should sprinkle [the image] with water mixed with turmeric. (10.33)
Having worshipped with the fivefold offerings and having clothed [the image] in white garments,
one should present the bali offering for seven nights according to the sequence that will be described.
The Brahmās, Bhūtas, Indras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Rakṣasas, and Piśācas—these seven classes of meat-eaters are designated respectively by those names. || 10.35 ||
In the first watch of the night, the *bali* offering consists of food, flowers, and *kuśa* grass;
it includes rice, curd, powdered *niśā*, parched grain (*lāja*), barley meal (*saktu*), and sesame seeds.
One should cause the offering known as Bhūtakrūra to be given at night among the spirits;
it consists of food mixed with Indravallī and garlic, along with groats, milk, and curd.
On the third night, dedicated to Indra, the preceptor should offer an oblation consisting of rice cooked with bamboo shoots mixed with milk; on the fourth night, it should be for Gāndharva.
In the fifth [night], called Yakṣarātra, the bali offering consists of flowers, cooked rice, clarified butter, and water;
but in the sixth, the Rākṣasa [night], it consists of red rice together with husks and fine earth.

(p. 94) Furthermore, in the seventh [birth], that of the Piśācas, one should cause to be offered black gram food, rice-and-pulse porridge (kṛsara), honey, turmeric powder mixed with plenty of oil, and meat. || 10.40 ||
Otherwise, some teachers have stated that there are seven groups;
these are here described as the Bhūtas, the Pitṛs, and the Guhyakas. (10.41)

For seven nights, one should cause the offering (bali) to be given to the Nāgas, Brahmā, Śiva, Viṣṇu, and the deities, using their respective names preceded by the syllable Om and ending with "namaḥ."
On the first night of the spirits, one should cause [the offering] to be given with the *bhūtakrūra* [mixture];
on the second night of the ancestors, with sesame seeds mixed with rice.
On the third night, one should offer coconut water and śāli rice to the Yakṣas;
on the fourth night, to the Nāgas, one should offer milk, flour, parched grain, and water.
In the fifth watch of Brahmā, one should offer food with lotus seeds, rice, and clarified butter;
in the sixth, which belongs to Śiva, one should cause [the offering] to be given with food including cakes and clarified butter.
On the seventh day, dedicated to Viṣṇu, the offering consists of jaggery and rice mixed with clarified butter;
when nine days have passed, milk-rice and kṛsara are offered in succession.
One should worship the designated group of deities with the designated offerings;
no one else whatsoever should ever look upon the sprouts.
