Either the preceptor himself or his disciple should enter by his command;
one should then indicate the auspiciousness or inauspiciousness for the patron based on the sprouts that have grown.
One should declare loss of wealth from dark or black sprouts, disease from those growing sideways, and blood-related ailments from red ones;
one should predict suffering from crooked sprouts, death from those that fail to grow, and the loss of one's position, country, or desired object from broken ones.

By means of sprouts that are white, yellow, well-developed, fully formed, quickly produced, beautiful, and long, the performer shall obtain fortune, nourishment, complete success in his desired aims, and auspiciousness. (10.50)
If the teacher perceives that the sprouts there are unfavorable, he should perform a rite for pacification (śāntika) in this case;
having offered oblations with the root mantra, the ancillary mantras, and the Brahma-mantras, ending with the vyāhṛtis, it will become auspicious, as will [the offering] with sesame seeds. (10.51)
Thus ends the tenth chapter, on the offering of seedlings (*aṅkurārpaṇa*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 10.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
Furthermore, regarding the initiation and consecrations, the preeminent teacher should observe the previously mentioned auspicious time desired for them,
as well as the place and time in which there may be prosperity for both the disciple and the guru.

Spring is considered the best season, winter is middling, and the summer is regarded here as the least favorable; the bright fortnight is auspicious, as are the days of Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter; however, the new moon day and the "empty" lunar days (Riktās) are to be avoided. (11-2)

The constellations Tiṣya, Prajeśa, Aditi, Soma, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Indra, Pūṣan, Anila, Nairṛta, and the Maitras (Anurādhā) are declared to be free from planetary obstacles during initiations and consecrations. (11.3)

Having ascertained the time—whatever else is desired by the astrologers, such as the auspicious lagna and so forth, which is free from unfavorable factors—the Guru should initiate those disciples here according to the method appropriate for their qualification. (11.4)
Born in a distinguished region and family, he shall be a Brahmin, learned in the scriptures, and of virtuous character;
pure, wise, with limbs possessing auspicious marks, and gentle—he is thus qualified for the office of a teacher. (11.5)
He who was devoted to truth, firmly established in the virtues of tranquility, self-control, and uprightness, intent upon the eightfold yoga, learned in the scriptures of Śiva,
and adorned with the eightfold devotion to Śiva;
A teacher should always be one who practices renunciation and is an abode of compassion. || 11-6 ||

The disciple should be steadfast, grateful, endowed with noble lineage and good character, devoted to Śiva as well as to the guru, humble, highly desirous of service, a giver of what is desired, and possessed of virtues such as freedom from greed. (11.7)
He who, through his preeminence in learning, conduct, and practice, as well as through his capability and devotion,
favors others as one more venerable than himself, is considered a guru.
He who is born in the places enjoined by the Tantras and practices with austerity shall become a teacher through his knowledge, showing the highest good to others as well. (11.9)
One who acts according to the [proper] instruction is a "guide" (deśika).
One who is refined by birth, lineage, and conduct, who relies upon a teacher, and who distinguishes himself by his qualities is called a "disciple" (śiṣya). (11.10)

The form [of the word] is derived from the verbal root *śās* with the suffix *kyap*, meaning "instructed by the teacher. The regions situated between the mountain of Agastya and the Himavat, excluding the eight regions beginning with the letter *ka*, are recognized as such by the teachers (*deśika*).
In the region of Māhendra,
on the island of Kumārī, between the Himavat mountains, in a place naturally inhabited by black antelopes—
any learned twice-born man born there is worthy of the office of an Ācārya.
Thus it is said regarding the Vīra [initiation]: "Whether born in Āryāvarta or elsewhere, provided he is devoid of the eight letters beginning with 'ka',
he should be of noble birth, skillful, dexterous, humble, and pleasing in appearance."
"One who knows the reality of the Śaivasiddhānta and has mastered the *Pratiṣṭhātantra*," as stated in the *Pratiṣṭhāsamuccaya*. Here, in the *Yogaśivapaddhati*:
"Those born in the Middle Country, Kurukṣetra, Lāṭa, and Ujjayinī..."
The Antarvedipratiṣṭhānas, the Āvantyas, the most excellent Gurus,
the Gauḍas, those born in Suhyā, the Tairas, the Māgadhas, and likewise the Keralas.
The Kosalas, the Daśārṇas, and the seven Guravas are the middle [castes],
as are those born in Karṇāṭaka, Mahārāṣṭra, Kaccha, and Nīra.
The Kaliṅgas, Lāmbākās, and Kāmbojas are considered the lowest;
as are those born in the regions of Kāñcī, Kaśmīra, Saurāṣṭra, Pāṇḍya, and Aṅga.

Those born in Kāverī and Koṅkaṇa are considered censurable; likewise, those from Gurava, Kuṇḍa, and so forth, as well as those afflicted by disease, are blameworthy even if they are natives of their own country.
The lowest of men who is born from one who has fallen from his vows or from an outcaste—
those two, known as Bhasma and Aṅkura, are to be shunned and censured in all ritual acts.
But one who belongs to another sect, having abandoned that [status] and been initiated again into the Śaiva tradition,
is also censurable for [performing] consecrations and the like, and does not deserve the status of a preceptor.
One who has not received Śaiva initiation and merely recites the scriptures,
though he may call himself "Self-born" (Svayambhū), is blameworthy and censured in all Śaiva rites.
Sannyāsins who are physically impaired or deformed, those who eat at monasteries,
and those residing in Karṇāṭaka, Kaliṅga, Kaccha, and Kashmir;
as well as those from Koṅkaṇa, Karahāṭa, Kamboja, and Kāmarūpa.
Those regions designated by the eight *kakāras* are devoid of true guides (*deśika*).
According to the *Vijaya*, some say these are the *Kīkaṭas*.
[Such a person] is cruel, of little learning, addicted to vices, ungrateful, hypocritical, a remarried woman, and lacking devotion to the Guru.

One who is possessed of stinginess, one who is addicted to sensual objects, one who is concerned with worldly activities, and a logician seeking status and the like—these should be avoided in matters of consecration and similar rites.

Thus it is stated in the *Mañjarī*: "A renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), an atheist (*nāstika*), an Ambaṣṭha," and so forth; by these verses, those unworthy of being a Guru according to the opinion of the Goddess are described.

Furthermore, in the *Svāyambhuva*, it says: "The Guru should be impartial, illustrious, a *agrajanmā*, and very handsome," and so on. A *agrajanmā* is indeed a Brāhmaṇa, because he was born first from Brahmā.

A teacher who is endowed with birth in the [proper] land, learning, proper conduct, and the qualities of ethical discipline; who is possessed of the power of spiritual essence, and who has been appointed as a teacher by a [senior] teacher.
Thus says Brahmaśambhu:
"In this manner, initiation is accomplished by the preceptor according to his specific qualification;
and he [the preceptor] must be born in a sacred land, possess an excellent form, and be endowed with learning and virtuous conduct."
Thus says Somaśambhu:
"One who has witnessed [the efficacy of] ritual action, who is pure, skillful, intent upon favoring disciples,
who knows the true nature of Śiva, who is a scholar, and a knower of the Self— he is the supreme teacher."

Thus it is stated in the *Mataṅga*. Initiation of this kind is performed by an Ācārya who has received [the requisite authority]. King Bhoja states that he should be born in a land such as Āryāvarta, endowed with learning, good character, virtues, and proper conduct, and possessed of a pure disposition. The *Prayogamañjarī* describes him as: "Excellent in terms of country, family, and disposition; modest; eloquent; of noble birth," and so forth.
"The Ācārya is one who knows the Śiva-śāstra, born in a praiseworthy land, whether a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) or a householder (*gṛhastha*), and solely devoted to devotion for Śiva."
"A preceptor is said to be one born under a constellation favorable to the patron," according to the *Devīmata*.
"A king initiated by a Guru endowed with all auspicious characteristics [attains success]."
One attains all desires and, in the hereafter, a blessed state.
Whether he has matted hair, a shaven head, or a topknot, he should be born in an auspicious region;
he should be a twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Śiva scriptures and is endowed with learning and virtuous conduct.
He who constantly takes refuge in Śiva alone through the actions of speech, mind, and body is designated here as the *ācārya* in rites such as the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śiva.
Thus, O Ajita: one who is learned in the Vedas, serene in soul, consecrated by the initiation of Śiva,
a knower of the Śiva-āgamas, wise, and devoted to the worship of Śiva.
Wearing a rosary of rudrākṣa beads, his body marked with the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra),
born of a pure region and lineage, and endowed with virtuous conduct and proper behavior.
"One who knows the true meaning of the Vedas and the Shastras is called a wise guru"— thus it is said regarding the *sāntānika* fire.
That place where a black-colored deer wanders by its very nature is [the site for the *vāstu* sacrifice].
One should know that region to be fit for sacrifice which is inhabited by Brahmins.

"But the teacher who has arisen in that place and time is one approved by the scriptures," as stated in the *Sarvajñānottara*. "He is born in an auspicious land, illustrious, and a knower of words, sentences, and the means of valid cognition."
Content with the meaning of the Śiva scriptures, a treasure-house of compassion toward all,
having fulfilled the vow of an ācārya, the mantra-practitioner is serene in heart and countenance.
One who is skilled in the knowledge of the characteristics of gender and so forth regarding the continuity of ritual action,
whose lineage is unimpaired, and who is likewise a celibate student or a householder;
The householder who belongs to a spiritual lineage is the best, as he observes the conduct of his tradition;
the material celibate is he who was formerly a student and later becomes a householder.
That householder who is devoted to the elements is called an *ācārya* by those who know the truth;
he is the most excellent, and his son shall be the *guru* who ensures the continuity of the lineage.
One who knows the reality of the pervasion of the deities, is proficient in the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan),
and understands the signs of auspiciousness and inauspiciousness— what need is there for further elaboration?
Right birth, thorough knowledge, and conduct—these are the first three qualities.
He who possesses these is the most excellent teacher, the bestower of the fruits of all desires.
Thus, in the *Pratiṣṭhāpaddhati*:
"A mantra-practitioner who has completed the vow of full knowledge (*vidyāvrata*), who is wise and well-composed,
a renowned ascetic established in the sacred ash (*bhasman*), or even one belonging to the *bhautika* [stage], shall be the Guru."
Thus it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"The Guru, who always follows the conduct of a Brahmin, must be constantly observed. O twice-born one, he who conducts himself in this manner is a knower of Brahman; such a Guru is to be revered."
Thus it is said in the Parākhyatantra:
"One who is of auspicious birth, established in good conduct, born in a holy land,
devoted to the ritual section [of the scriptures], tranquil, righteous, and affectionate toward his guru."
He brings joy to those who follow his path; he is endowed with purity and firm in his vows;
through his knowledge, he is a bestower of fearlessness, free from greed and fickleness.
"Having obtained such a Guru, who would not be liberated from bondage?
Thus it is said in the *Vātulottara*. "One who is righteous, truthful in speech, and so forth," as stated in the *Sarvajñānasamudra*.
"Even if devoid of all [external] characteristics, a Guru who possesses knowledge is desired."
And knowledge is the realization of reality, which rests upon the knowledge of the six paths.
Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who are purified are known as practitioners (sādhakas).
O Six-faced One! According to the sequence of their own respective castes, they may become teachers (ācāryas)."
Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhatkālottara*.
What is the point of saying much more, which would only cause heaviness to the book?
For, due to the abundance of such scriptural statements, it is indeed the Brahmin alone [who is qualified]. (11–11)
One who has been initiated, endowed with the prescribed qualities, gentle, and pleasant of speech, is fit to be a king’s preceptor and for others as well; of this there is no doubt. (11–12)
(100) One who is endowed with noble lineage, virtuous conduct, and proper behavior; who is devoted to his guru;
who has studied the tantras under his guru; and who is purified by the initiation of a practitioner (sādhaka). || 11-13 ||
He who accomplishes the mantras with firm devotion is a practitioner (sādhaka), having realized that cyclic existence is essence-less and that human birth is difficult to obtain. (11.14)
One should uplift oneself by means of oneself; one should not let oneself sink.
This is for the sake of attaining the enjoyments of this world and the next, and also for the sake of liberation. (11.15)
There is no other easy means for twice-born men who have not received initiation in their own duties, such as Vedic study and the like, except by taking refuge in Śiva. (11.16)

Just as there is no entitlement here [to Vedic rites] following the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), so too there is none for those who have not been initiated into the rituals of the *tantras*, mantras, worship, and so forth. (11.17)
Therefore, one has no authority [to perform rites]; thus, one should make oneself consecrated by Śiva.
For it is said:
"One who is not Rudra cannot remember Rudra; one who is not Rudra cannot worship Rudra. (11.18)
One who is not a devotee of Rudra should not recite the Rudra-mantra, and one who is not a devotee of Rudra shall not attain Rudra.
Having undertaken the vow of Śiva, the wise man should observe it every day.
For example: "Better indeed is the cutting off of my head, better indeed is my death,
than that I should eat without having first worshipped the Blessed Three-eyed One."
"There is no dharma equal to the worship of Śiva in these three worlds;
having realized this, Sadāśiva should be worshipped with diligent effort."
Thus, in the *Śivadharmottara*:
"Therefore, by those bound by the observances (*samayins*), by practitioners (*sādhakas*), and likewise by gurus, Sadāśiva should always be worshipped, applying diligent effort every day. (11.20)

Regarding this, Patañjali said: "O Lord of manifold forms! Even if one were to place a single flower, devoid of fragrance, at Your lotus feet by mere chance, that person surely enjoys many most delicious fruits in this world."
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Sādhaka and the Ācārya," in the Kriyāpāda of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 11.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.

Here we shall describe the forms of the deities appropriate for their retinues, as well as other details concerning the gods that must be known specifically for worship and other rites, by means of which complete success in the fruit [of one's efforts] may be attained. (12.1)

Having first worshipped the Sun for the pacification of obstacles, then the Lord of Obstacles (Gaṇeśa), and likewise the Guru, one should perform the worship of Śambhu after properly completing the fire-ritual (agnikārya); and the members of the retinue (parivāra) should also be worshipped.
Now, at the worship of the Sun, there is the gatekeeper Daṇḍin, holding a sword and standing on the right;
and on the left is Khaḍgin, tawny-colored and named Piṅgala. Both of them wear red ornaments and have fierce appearances. || 12-3 ||

Slaying obstacles, elephant-faced, with a reddish body, clad in red garments, moon-crested, and three-eyed—he who is two-armed, auspicious in appearance, and stands on the right—is to be worshipped constantly; he is one's own Guru situated in the southeast corner. (12.4)

One should visualize a golden, square pedestal named *Prabhūtāsana*, supported by four legs in the form of lions—white, red, yellow, and black—representing the four ages beginning with Kṛta, and bearing the names Vimalā and so forth. Upon a circular, reddish orb in its center, one should contemplate a solar lotus seat with eight expanded petals. One should worship the limbs beginning with the Heart in the petals at the corners starting from the southeast, the Weapon-mantra in the cardinal petals, and the Eye-mantra in front; these are red in color, dressed as women, and with palms joined in reverence. One should worship those nine Śaktis who are red in their ornaments, graceful-limbed, well-attired, and glowing like vermilion.
Next, in the ninth [position], the pericarp, are Dīptā and the others, who have two arms and hold salutation-gestures. || 12-5 ||

Having meditated upon the Blessed Lord Bhāskara, situated in the center of the pericarp of that lotus, accompanied by the two goddesses named Prabhā and Sandhyā standing at his two sides, one should worship him with the rites of invocation and so forth.
[He is] resembling the bandhūka flower, delicate, well-attired, of divine form, two-armed, with a lotus in his hand;
clad in red garments, with eyes as copper-red as a lotus, the soul of the Vedas, with a body of shining gold. (12.6)
One should meditate upon the God who is adorned with divine ornaments such as jeweled earrings, armlets, bracelets, and necklaces; whose face is serene and who wears a garland of light.

One should meditate upon the Moon, who is clad in white garments, holding a blooming lotus in his hand, possessing the radiance of the moon, two-armed, white as a pearl necklace, lovely in form, lotus-eyed, gracious, and mounted upon a white horse. (12.7)
In the northeast, one should meditate upon Tejaścaṇḍa, who is red in color, adorned with red garments and other ornaments, and holding a trident in his hand.
Alternatively:
he is white, dressed in white garments and ornaments, two-armed, and bearing a mace.
Candra, the bestower of boons, should be meditated upon as mounted upon a chariot drawn by ten horses.

Clad in red garments, bestowing boons, and holding a spear and a mace in his four arms, the Lord born of the Earth (Mars) should be depicted as mounted upon a ram, with graceful limbs, well-attired, and having the hue of the bandhūka flower. (12.9)

The son of the Moon (Budha) is yellow in color, possessing a divine form, wearing a crown, with his limbs adorned; he is mounted upon a lion and holds in his arms a yellow garment, the gesture of granting boons, a sword, a shield, and a mace.

Dhiṣaṇa, adorned with yellow garments and yellow in color, should be depicted standing upon a golden chariot; he holds a staff, a rosary, the gesture of granting boons, and a water-pot in his arms; he wears a turban and his limbs are adorned with jewels. || 12-11 ||

The Lord Bhṛguja (Saturn) should be white in appearance, as pale as a pearl necklace, wearing a crown, with his limbs adorned; he stands upon a silver chariot, holding in his hands a staff, a rosary, a garland, the gesture of granting boons, and a water-pot.
Clad in blue garments, bearing a trident, resembling collyrium in hue, holding a spear, a boon-granting gesture, an arrow, and a bow;
mounted upon a vulture on his own chariot, with his limbs adorned—the Lord Maṅgala is to be meditated upon at the beginning of worship and other rites.

Rahu, dark as crushed collyrium, resembling clear and split black antimony, bearing a trident and a sword, richly clad in a garment of skin, having the form of darkness with a face formidable with white fangs—let him be yoked to the chariot by the dark heroes of the monkeys. (12–14)
Smoky-colored, two-armed, with prominent fangs and a smoky luster, they hold maces and are richly adorned.
Indeed, having fierce forms and seated upon vultures, they are to be meditated upon as many chariot-borne banners. (12-15)

All the planets, adorned with ornaments such as crowns and the like, youthful, initiators of the course of worldly affairs, and bestowers of enjoyments, sovereignty, and boons, should be meditated upon; these are the forms for the worship of the Sun. The temple, which consists of the nature of Śiva and Śakti, should be composed of the principles beginning with the Earth and ending with Śakti.
Indeed, the form of Śiva known as the temple should first be meditated upon and worshipped. || 12-16 ||

The gate of Peace (Śānti) should be in the east as the first; Knowledge (Vidyā) in the south, and then Cessation (Nivṛti) in the west. That which is in the north should be Establishment (Pratiṣṭhā); indeed, the gate of Peace is recommended for perpetual rites.
An elephant-faced, white elephant with lotuses in its trunk, holding a goad, a noose, and a sugarcane in its hands, should be meditated upon at the gate;
he has a protruding belly, wears a crown, is adorned with red ornaments on the right, bears the moon upon his head, and possesses three eyes. (12-18)

In the same way, Vāṇī should be meditated upon as seated on a white lotus; she has the luster of crystal and the moon, holds a mudrā, a rosary, a water-pot, and a book in her hands, wears white ornaments, bears the moon on her crest, and possesses three eyes. (12.19)
Nandīśa and Mahākāla will be described as the two excellent gatekeepers in the enclosure.

To the south shall be Gaṅgā, a young woman of divine form, whose complexion is as clear as her lofty, surging waves; she is adorned with white ornaments, possesses two arms, holds a lotus in her hand, and her other left hand is clearly visible as she offers salutation. (12–20)

Kālindī should be a young woman of divine form, dark as her own surging waves, with tremulous side-glances; she holds a lotus in her left hand, while with the other she displays the *dhṛtavanadanyā* mudrā. (12.21)
The Nārāca weapon, shining like slender lightning and resembling fire and the sun, stands at the threshold;
the lord of the site (Vāstvīśa) is an asura with his face turned downward, his limbs scattered, lying with his head toward the northeast.
In that regard, the Vāstupuruṣa is an asura lying upon the ground with his face downward and his hands and feet outstretched;
beyond him, Brahmā is to be known as the lord of the site (vāstvadhipati).
The power (śakti) called Ādhārā is said to be white, resembling moonlight, having the luster of the sky, and beautiful in form.
She who, by the will of the Supreme Lord, eternally sustains all the worlds—therefore, she is to be worshipped first. (12.23)

Indeed, the splendor of Viṣṇu, honored by those thirty-two principles beginning with Earth and ending with Vidyā, is called the infinite seat; for that serpent Ananta is indeed the form of the pedestal. (12.24)

Dharma is red in the form of a bull, Jñāna is a lion and dark blue, Bhūta is yellow, Vairāgya has the form of an elephant with white limbs, and Aiśvarya is likewise; these are the legs of the pedestal in sequence. (12.25)
Others say that these are white, saffron, and the color of bees, and are shaped like lions.
These four, beginning with Adharma (Non-Virtue), which belong to the pedestal, are beautiful and golden in form.
Furthermore, in the *Mañjarī*, it is stated: "The beams are Adharma," and so forth.
The lotus should be white, with eight wide petals, beautiful with its filaments and rich with a pericarp.

On a yellow discus, Brahmā should be meditated upon as having four faces, wearing a crown, mounted on a swan, and holding a water-pot, a rosary of beads, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture known as fearlessness with his four hands; he has a white face. (12.27)
In the gentle form of Garuḍa, Viṣṇu is dark as a rain-cloud, holding a discus, a conch, a mace, and a lotus;
he wears necklaces, a garland, bracelets, and a beautiful crown, and is clad in yellow garments and adorned with the Kaustubha gem.

In the orb of fire, upon a bull, is Śvetarudra, who has the moon as his crest-jewel; he is white, ten-armed, and three-eyed, wielding an axe, a deer, fire, a trident, and a serpent, while his hands display the thunderbolt, an eye, a garland, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness.
These are to be meditated upon here as pervading the petals, the filaments, and the pericarp. As it is said in the Vātula:
"Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are the abodes of the orbs of the Sun, Moon, and Fire;
Īśvara pervades them there, and therefore Sadāśiva is to be worshipped."

Thus: one should worship Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra as pervading the mandala through its petals, filaments, and pericarp, and one should worship Īśvara as pervading that [mandala] as well. All four possess the authority [to perform this], since they serve as the seat for the deity Sadāśiva. Regarding this, Varuṇa says:
"The eternal Lord (Dhruva-Īśvara) is to be known as having eight arms, four faces, three eyes, the luster of crystal, and wearing a serpent as a sacred thread."
Thus:
white, red, black, yellow-colored, dark-brown, black, collyrium-colored, and having the luster of a *japā* flower;
or having the luster of moonlight—these are said to be the beautiful-formed goddesses, beginning with Vāmā, whose limbs are adorned on all sides. (12.30)
Seated in the bound lotus posture, with the luster of a pure moon, appearing like a youth of sixteen years and possessing a beautiful divine form;
having five faces with the five Brahmans, and eyes that are the sun, moon, and fire, characterized by the powers of action and knowledge.
With arms numbering ten, he holds the *śakti* and the trident while bestowing fearlessness and desired boons;
furthermore, in his right hands he holds the *khaṭvāṅga*, a serpent, and a rosary, while in his other [left] hands he holds a drum (*ḍamaru*), a blue lotus (*utpala*), and a citron (*bījapūra*).

With a most serene countenance, wearing divine garlands and garments, adorned with ornaments blazing with gold and jewels, and filling the quarters with the moon shimmering within his massed locks of matted hair—there, the Lord of Sādā should be meditated upon. (12.33)

Some describe him as having the luster of lightning, all-pervading, and possessing the form of Īśāna; others, however, say he has but one face, the brilliance of moonstone, is a bestower of boons, holds a trident in his hand, wears the moon as a crest, is elegantly attired, and is youthful.

One should meditate upon the yellow-hued Puruṣa, whose body is adorned, who has the luster of Kāśmīra saffron, who bears the crescent moon with matted locks upon his head, who holds a citron and a rosary of beads, who possesses a divine form, and whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (12.35)
With bitten lips and face, tawny beard and hair, of terrifying form, and adorned with red garments;
wearing a serpent as a turban, formidable with white fangs, his limbs decorated by fierce serpents and bees.

One should meditate upon Aghora, who is dark as a rain cloud, adorned with ornaments, and holding in his arms a trident, an axe, a sword, a staff, the one called khaṭvāṅga, a shield, and a noose; he holds weapons along with a skull-cup and many skulls. (12.37)

One should meditate upon the left [face], which has the luster of a bandhūka flower, is graceful, possesses the charm of a woman, and has a divine form; it bears a braided hair-tuft with a moon, and is adorned with red ornaments, garments, unguents, and garlands, while holding a shield and a sword in its hands.

One should remember Sadyojāta, who is as white as the moon, cow’s milk, or yogurt; who wears white ornaments, garments, and perfumes; who has three eyes; who bears seven serpents; whose hands display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; who is crowned with the moon; and who appears in the form of a child. (12.39)
The powers Vāmā and the others belong respectively to the eight forms beginning with Earth;
by their means, through the command of Śiva, the successful engagement of the world is accomplished.
Thus it is stated in the *Kālottara*. Therefore, the eight forms (*aṣṭamūrtayaḥ*) are also shown according to their essential nature:

The Earth-form has four faces and eight arms; she is mounted upon a tortoise, possesses a divine form, is yellow in color, and holds a stalk of rice and a blue lotus. Her body is encompassed by mountains, islands, oceans, and rivers. (12.40)
Mounted upon a ram, red in color, holding in his hands the gestures of granting boons (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhīti*), as well as a spear (*śakti*) and a *svastika*;
wearing a crown garlanded with flames, five-faced, adorned with golden ornaments, of pleasant countenance, and possessing seven tongues [of fire]—(12.41).

Wearing a white turban and his body anointed with fresh butter, holding a black antelope skin along with its limbs, accompanied by his wife and wearing a white sacred thread, the sacrificer standing at the sacrifice should hold a sacrificial ladle in his hand.
Seated upon a chariot drawn by horses of the seven meters, Bandhūkābha is fair-faced and of beautiful form;
he wears red ornaments, garments, garlands, and unguents; as Sūrya, he is clad in armor, wears a crown, and holds a lotus in his hand. (12.43)
Ambhomūrti is described as white in color, mounted upon a crocodile, and holding a boon-granting gesture and a noose;
her limbs are adorned with various nets of pearls, she wears bright ornaments, and her beautiful crown consists of two yugas.

Riding upon a deer, Pavana is smoke-colored, with stout shoulders, wearing a crown, with knitted eyebrows, dressed in black garments, four-faced, holding a goad, possessing a divine form, having four arms, and bearing a banner. (12.45)

The sky also shines with the light of the full moon; he should be meditated upon as standing upon a bull, wearing a matted lock and a crescent moon on his head, three-eyed, and holding in his arms a trident, a drum (ḍamaruka), a conch, and a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga). 12.46.

The moon, white as snow, cow’s milk, or curd, adorned with white ornaments and graceful limbs, wearing a crown, and standing upon a horse, should be worshipped as he holds a conch, a lotus, the so-called "boon-granting" gesture, and a mace in his hands. (12.47)

Śarva and the other seven—these eight shall be the guardians of the images (mūrtipās). They have bulls as their vehicles, possess three eyes, and have four faces; they wear matted hair and crescent moons; they hold a trident, a thunderbolt, an arrow, and a bow; and they are adorned with serpent ornaments. || 12.48 ||

Likewise, those who are the lords of the forms (mūrtīśas), beginning with Ananta, and those who are the lords of the Vidyās, are respectively white, yellow, red, and black; they possess coverings of lotus-yellow, red, white, and yellow, and are red and black. They are identical in color to their respective [presiding] letters. || 12-49 ||

Endowed with yoga, possessing pleasant faces and beautiful forms, with garlands fastened at the tips of their braided hair, all these lords of knowledge are said to be gentle, richly dressed in fine silken garments, and to have hands like serpents. (12.50)

The limbs [of the deity] may also take the form of women, appearing in colors resembling white, gold, ruddy, and black; they should be meditated upon as possessing three eyes, richly endowed with the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, and holding a trident and a ṭaṅka-axe.
In this *Mañjarī*:
"The heart and other limbs are female deities with two arms, having that same form;
they hold the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness in their hands, while the weapon is somewhat reddish-brown."
Thus: (p.
106) The one named Nandīśa, wearing a crown, golden-colored, with slightly protruding fangs and a handsome face, stands at the right [door].
At the door, there should be a trident-bearer stationed with a mace, having the form of a Daitya, radiant, and three-eyed. (12.52)
Dark as a cloud, of auspicious appearance, wearing a crown and red ornaments, holding a chisel, and three-eyed;
standing at the door with a mace in his left hand, possessing fangs, he is known as Mahākāla. (12.53)
With fleshless limbs, holding a trident, possessing three eyes, having the appearance of a preta, with a thin and long belly and mouth,
he who is known as Bhṛṅgīśa and is dear to the Supreme Lord shall stand at the western side of the southern gate.
Golden-hued, holding a chisel and a rosary, wearing red ornaments, elephant-faced, and three-eyed;
short-limbed and having a serpent as his sacred thread—this one indeed stands at the southern gate, positioned in front. (12.55)

Resembling Mount Kailāsa, white as the rays of the snowy moon, lofty, horned, with thick limbs and a hump—Dharma himself, manifest in the form of a bull, four-footed, stands at the rear gatekeeper position in the northern quarter. (12.56)

Six-faced and with twice as many eyes, endowed with arms, red in color, having a peacock for his vehicle, and wearing a crown; adorned with red ornaments, he bears weapons such as the peacock-feathered spear and the rosary, appearing in the guise of a youth. (12.57)

The goddess Kanyā, blue in color, riding a lion and adorned with red ornaments, holds in her hands a discus, a sword, arrows, a trident, a conch, a shield, a bow, and displays the gesture of granting boons; she is stationed at the eastern gate of Dhanada.
With limbs reddened, bearing an axe and a water-pot in his hands, as well as a trident and a rosary;
Caṇḍeśa should be depicted wearing a crown, possessing three eyes, with divine hands, and adorned with red garlands and garments. (12.59)
Indra, who has drunk [the nectar], wears a crown, has two arms, and is adorned with necklaces, breast-ornaments, bracelets, armlets, and other divine regalia;
holding the thunderbolt and lightning, he stands upon Airāvata in the east together with the gods.

The Fire-god has the luster of molten gold; he holds in his four arms the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a water-pot and a golden rosary; he is adorned with golden ornaments, has a pleasant face, and bears the appearance of an elder. (12.61)
Seated within his own mandala encircled by flames, accompanied by Svāhā stationed at his right side, and mounted upon a ram;

dark as a blue cloud, powerful, staff-in-hand, possessing a divine form, with four arms, wearing a crown, dressed in black garments, and mounted upon a buffalo—this indeed is Yama, the Lord of the Departed, who is Dharma personified. (12.62)
Surrounded by his own attendants such as Citragupta and others,
Nirṛti, the lord of the Rākṣasas, is dark-complexioned, fanged, and armed with a sword; though adorned with black garlands and garments,
he is of terrifying form yet beautiful appearance, and he stands in his own quarter mounted upon a man.
Surrounded by hosts of *rakṣasas*,

with a complexion as clear as the moon or crystal, wearing yellow garments, a crown, and adorned limbs, mounted upon a crocodile and holding a noose— Varuṇa, the beautiful and gracious deity, should be meditated upon. (12.64)

Surrounded by the Gaṅgā, Yamunā, and other rivers in divine forms, as well as by Nāgas, the god Vāyu— smoky-colored, with graceful limbs, youthful, wearing blue ornaments, with arms like the Yuga-staffs, seated upon a deer, bearing a banner and a goad— should be meditated upon together with the Maruts. (12.65)
Having a golden luster, with eyes tawny like honey and a gentle countenance, adorned with divine ornaments, riding a man, and bearing a mace;
he has a protruding belly, is somewhat stout, possesses short arms, is the lord of the yakṣas, and is surrounded by treasures. (12.66)

The Lord Īśāna is the master of knowledge, a portion of Śiva; he is pearl-colored, holds a trident, has three eyes, wears white ornaments, possesses matted hair and a crescent moon, has a gentle form, rides a bull, and is a partial incarnation of Śiva. (12.67)

Surrounded by the embodiments of the Vidyās, resembling molten gold, with a swan for a vehicle, endowed with four faces and four arms, Brahmā— wearing matted locks and possessing a beautiful form— bears a rosary, the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, a water-pot, and *kuśa* grass. (12.68)
To the left is Sāvitrī and to the right is Sarasvatī; Prajāpati is surrounded by the gods and all the worlds, as is Kuśadhvaja.

Being served by all the lords of the nāgas, possessing a gentle form with white and red radiance, adorned with divine ornaments, holding a lotus and a discus in his hands—Ananta, the crest-jewel of the earth, should thus be meditated upon. (12.69)
His head is illuminated by the rays of the jewels upon his thousand hoods;

he resembles a conch shell, rides upon a bull, possesses three eyes, and is adorned with serpent ornaments. Wearing matted hair and a crescent moon, though of terrifying form, he is exceedingly auspicious. Residing beneath a banyan tree, bearing a trident and an axe, he is Vīrabhadra. (12.70)

Mounted upon a swan, with a ruddy luster, holding a water-pot and a rosary with her four faces and arms, the goddess Brāhmī dwells in the Palāśa tree; adorned with divine ornaments, she grants boons and displays the gesture of fearlessness.

On a Plakṣa tree, Māheśvarī should indeed be white, adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon, three-eyed, and wearing serpent ornaments; she is mounted upon a bull and holds a battle-axe, a trident, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness. (12.72)

Kaumārī is clearly seated upon an udumbara tree; she has the luster of a bandhūka flower, is ruddy, beautiful in her attire, possesses hands displaying the śakti, rosary, boon-granting gesture, and the gesture of fearlessness, has a divine form, and bears a peacock on her banner. (12.73)
Dark as a rain cloud, adorned with yellow garments, seated upon a śrīvṛkṣa tree, and decorated with a crown and other ornaments;
holding a conch, a discus, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness, and mounted upon Garuḍa—she is indeed Vaiṣṇavī. (12.74)

Mounted upon a ram, holding a plow, a discus, and a lotus in her hands, dressed in blue garments and possessing the luster of clearly crushed collyrium, Vārāhī shall have the face and tusks of a boar; she is both terrible and beautiful, dwelling in the Karañja tree. (12.75)

Aindrī is dark-complexioned, adorned with excellent garlands and ointments, holding a vajra, a noose, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness; she wears golden ornaments, stands within the shade of a wish-fulfilling tree, and is mounted upon a four-tusked elephant.

Cāmuṇḍā is black and fierce, resembling a mountain, and stands beneath a banyan tree; she holds a trident, a sword, a ḍāmaru drum, and a skull-cup; she is dressed in red, rides upon a corpse, and wears a garland of the entrails from the heads of warriors. (12.77)
The Lord of Obstacles, elephant-faced and the color of collyrium, holding a chisel, rosary, garland, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness in his hands;
adorned with red ornaments, the Blessed One, whose vehicle is the rat, is pleased by offerings of food. (12.78)

All the various other mothers in the world, diverse in appearance and richly endowed with auspicious colors and weapons—having received worship, they should be meditated upon as being pleased and gracious when united with Śivā. (12.79)

Resembling gold, wearing a crown, and holding a vajra, a rosary, a lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her four arms; of divine form, adorned with white ornaments, and seated upon a lotus—this is Nivṛtti. (12.80)

Pratiṣṭhā should be meditated upon as seated upon a red lotus, dressed in red garments, with a complexion as clear as crystal, holding a noose, a rosary, a lotus, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands, and adorned with various jewels such as a crown and other ornaments. (12.81)

Red as a *guñjā* berry, with matted hair, three faces, and the moon as her crest-jewel; holding a spear and a rosary of beads; seated upon a lotus, with hands displaying the lotus and the gesture of fearlessness; adorned with divine ornaments—she is indeed the goddess Vidyā Kalā. (12.82)

Endowed with four arms and four faces, Kṛṣṇā is clothed in black garments and other such attire; she is adorned with ornaments of serpents, wears matted hair, and holds a banner, a rosary, and the gesture of fearlessness—she is described as the one named Śānti.

Śāntyatītā, seated upon a lotus, is white with ornaments, possessing five faces, adorned with matted hair and a crescent moon, and holding a lotus, a rosary of *padmākṣa* seeds, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness in her hands. (12.84)

Seated upon a lotus, four-faced, and brilliant yellow, with mind one-pointed in meditation, he holds the gesture of the lap with two arms; above him are a rosary, a garland, and a flask; he possesses a divine form and celestial ornaments, and has expounded the reality of the inner self.

Dark as a cloud, with eight lotus-like arms resting upon his city, he holds a water-pot, a lotus, a noble rosary, the support of knowledge, the gesture of fearlessness, and the mudrā of awakening; thus manifesting the principle of Vidyā, he possesses a divine form.

One should meditate in samādhi upon the Śiva-tattva as seated on a lotus, white as the moon, possessing four arms and faces, divine in form, holding an axe and a rosary, with matted hair, and resting upon the ocean. (12.87)
(109) Furthermore, there are other innumerable lords of the hosts (gaṇeśas), both gentle and fierce, possessing various forms and enriched with excellent attire and weapons;
they who abide in the ten directions should be remembered, as will be described hereafter in brief. (12.88)

One should know the weapons in their respective order as yellow, red, black, blue, resembling lightning, multiform, golden, and possessing the brilliance of fire-flames, the moon, and the sun— namely the thunderbolt (vajra) and the others.

Skilled in protection, stationed in the directions of their respective world-protectors, subduing obstacles, and beautiful in human form; adorned with red ornaments, two-armed, with their own heads upon their laps, and holding weapons with palms joined in reverence—this indeed is how each [deity] should be visualized. (12.90)
There, Gadā and Śakti were two women.
[He was] resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns,
with faces made terrifying by fangs and filled with vomiting flames of fire.
With infinite arms, each possessing many mouths and eyes and terrifying with various weapons, he discharged missiles at his adversaries.
He is enriched by a serpent used as a sacred thread, terrifying with his serpent ornaments,
wearing red perfumes and garments, and adorned with a garland of heads and entrails.
He was surrounded by many spirits with the faces of lions, pythons, snakes, vultures, dogs, tigers, boars, and elephants, who were terrifying with their loud, mocking laughter.
It is the protector of the devotees of Śiva, the destroyer of all calamities, the tormentor of rival deities, and the repeller of enemy armies. || 12-95 ||
This form of the Pāśupata weapon has been described in brief:
it resembles a mountain of crushed collyrium and is most terrifying with its red ornaments.
One should visualize a Vetāla with a face made terrifying by fangs, with blazing hair standing erect on its head,
holding the base of a trident and a sword in his right hands.
With eight arms, he holds a ḍamaruka drum, a skull-cup, a bell, and a trident; the all-pervading Lord is clothed in a tiger-skin garment.
A garland of the faces of excellent warriors from whom blood was still flowing as they were recently decapitated,
and a row of spiders and scorpions reaching from the neck down to the knees.
Ankle-bells, a waist-cord, a breast-band, as well as armlets, bracelets, a golden medallion, earrings, and crest-jewels. (12.100)
Wearing the sacred thread (*upavīta*) and treading upon jeweled sandals, with his left foot placed forward, he was terrifying at the onset of battle. (12.101)
One should meditate upon the Aghora weapon, which removes all calamities, which is remembered as the shatterer [of obstacles], and which is accompanied by its prescribed retinue.
Thus, the root seats and their constituent parts [are worshipped] along with the lords of the womb-gate and the world-regents;
those which are known as their forms are called the "armour" (astra) enclosures.
All of these have indeed been described here primarily for worship and other rites;
they should be recollected exactly as they are in these rituals, such as the daily ceremonies.

Thus ends the twelfth chapter, on the Coverings and the Iconographic Forms, in the section on Ritual Practice (Kriyāpāda) of the Upper Portion (Uparibhāga) of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*. 12.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Next, I shall describe the worship of the Sun, which grants the pacification of obstacles to the worship of Śiva.
Having bathed and performed the twilight rites (saṃdhyā), and having offered libations, one should proceed to the hall of worship.
Having gone there, washed his feet, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), he should worship the two gatekeepers by name:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Daṇḍin; Oṃ, obeisance to Piṅgala. Having entered within and sat down, he should perform the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma). (13–2)
One should perform the purification with the Astra-mantra and place the limbs, beginning with the heart, [on the body].
Meditating upon oneself as the Sun, one should then offer the arghya water as prescribed.
One should perform the placement of the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-vinyāsa*) there, and also worship the primary limbs (*mūlāṅga*).
Then, with water for sprinkling, oneself, the established [deity], the articles of worship, the circle (*cakra*), and *kuśa* grass—[one should proceed]. (13-4)

"Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati; Oṃ guṃ, obeisance to the Gurus. Thus one should worship Vighna to the south and the Guru to the north. Then [one should worship] the abundant seat and pedestal, preceded by the syllable Om (tāra) and the consonant classes (varga). || 13-5 ||
Having worshipped [the deity] with his own name, one should then worship the four feet and the four monkeys,
as well as Vimala, Sāra, Ārādhya, Sukha, and Paramapūrva.
(111) One should worship with names beginning with the respective groups of consonants ending in *tāra* (oṃ) and *bindu* (m), followed by *namaḥ*.
In the same manner, one should likewise [worship] the Supreme Self seated upon the solar lotus. (13-7)
One should worship Dīptā, Sūkṣmā, Jayā, Bhadrā, Vibhūti, Vimalā, Amoghā, and Vidyutā, in sequence, upon the petals of the eight directions.
The second [syllable] of the seventh [group], however, is differentiated by the long vowels; one should prefix it with a bindu for the Śaktis and append "namaḥ" at the end. (13.9)
Having worshipped Tārā and the others, who face in all directions, upon the ninth pericarp,
one should then display the throbbing mudrā and [worship] Bhāskara.
With a steady mind, one should meditate within the heart upon the God who bears the aforementioned form, situated upon a white lotus and established within the orb of his own luster.

Having filled the joined palms with flowers and having uttered the *khaṣolka* mantra together with the root mantra, one should [invite the deity] from the lotus at the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *āvāhana-mudrā*.
Having invoked [the deity], one who is well-composed should establish it upon the lotus with the *sthāpanī* [mudrā];
having brought it into close proximity with the *sannidhānī*, one should bind it with that called *niṣṭhurā*.
Then, having illuminated [the deity] with the *dhenu-mudrā* and offered the *arghya* and other honors,
and having worshipped with the root mantra together with its ancillaries (*sāṅga*), one should show the lotus and the image.
Having offered the bathing water, the garments, and the sacred thread, one should worship the limbs in sequence—
namely the heart and the others— on the petals of the southeast, northeast, southwest, and northwest.

In the center is the Eye (netra), and then the Weapon (astra) in the cardinal petals; one should display the Dhenu-mudrā for the Heart-mantra and the others, and the Go-vṛṣa-mudrā for the Dṛk-mantras.
One should again worship with perfumes and other offerings even the weapon that causes terror;
and in the directions starting from the east, one should worship Soma, Budha, and Bṛhaspati.
One should worship Bhārgava (Venus), as well as the planets situated in the directions of Agni, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and Īśa— namely Aṅgāraka (Mars), Śanaiścara (Saturn), Rāhu, and Ketu.

Then, having offered praise with their names preceded by the syllables "Tārā" and so forth, ending with the nasal bindu, one should worship these [deities] with perfumes and other offerings, and then [worship] Bhāskara.
Having offered the concluding oblation and worshipped the planets in their proper order, one should display the lotus-named *bimba-mudrā* and offer words of praise. (13–20)
Having recited the mantra according to one's capacity and offered the *arghya*, one should perform the dismissal (*visarjana*);
having withdrawn the mantras with the appropriate mudrā, as well as the deity along with his limbs and the planetary deities.
One should join [the deity] within the heart or at the end of the twelve [fingers] in the solar orb;
one should cause all that remains from his offerings and so forth, as well as the radiant energy, to be given to Caṇḍa.

In the sphere of one's own abode, preceded by the syllables of the Tāra-mantra and the consonant groups (varga), worship is performed everywhere with names in the dative case, ending with "namaḥ. (13–23)
The Chapter on the Worship of the Sun.
Now, having removed the *pavitra* and performed ritual sipping (*ācamana*), one should worship the door.
Having sprinkled the door with the general offering (*sāmānyārghya*) and with flowers, one should consecrate it with the Weapon-mantra of Śiva. (13–24)
Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ saṃ, obeisance to Sarasvatī.
(Thus) one should worship those situated on the right and left at the top of the udumbara post.
Oṃ, obeisance to Gaṅgā. Oṃ, obeisance to Yamunā.
One should worship the deity in this manner in the upper portion, as well as in the southern and northern portions.
Oṃ naṃ, obeisance to Nandīśa. Oṃ maṃ, obeisance to Mahākāla.
Thus, situated on the right and left, they rest upon the door-posts below.
[One should offer] a flower consisting of blazing weapons, which destroys the multitude of obstacles. (13–26)
One should cast the Śiva-weapon, like an iron arrow, into the interior of the house of worship;
[one should drive away] those on the ground with three strikes of the heel, and those moving in the sky with snaps of the fingers.
With the threatening gestures of the index fingers, one should gradually dispel the obstacles dwelling in the heavens;
thereafter, one should mentally establish Indra and the other gods in their respective directions.
In this *Mañjarī*:
"Having established Indra and the other world-protectors, along with their weapons, intent upon protection in the ten directions, one should oneself enter within the mandala."
Thus it is said:
one should enter without touching the threshold with the right foot;
having quickly taken hold of the northern doorpost, one should then turn back. (13.29)
p. 113) One should place a flower, consisting of blazing weapons, upon the threshold while recollecting [the deity], which wards off the multitude of obstacles; then:
*oṃ vāṃ vāstupuruṣāya namaḥ* (Oṃ vāṃ, obeisance to the Vāstu-puruṣa); *oṃ vāstvadhipataye brahmaṇe namaḥ* (Oṃ, obeisance to Brahmā, the lord of the Vāstu).
"One should offer it at the station of Brahmā," so [it is said]. (13.30)
Having circumambulated the sacrificial hall and inspected the ritual implements as well, he should worship his own seat with the mantra:
"Oṃ Aṃ, obeisance to Anantāsana.
Having thus worshipped, he sits there facing north.
One should perform the ritual procedures for drying and so forth, as well as the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi);
having fashioned the "Hand of Śiva" moist with fragrance according to the previously mentioned method.
One should again form the *liṅgamudrā* and the *karakacchavikā* mudrā,
having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the thirty-eight *kalās* within oneself as prescribed.
Having invoked [the deity] whose nature is Śiva by means of the root mantra into the lotus of the heart,
one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon oneself with the six limb-mantras beginning with the Heart.
Having performed the act of supreme transformation, one should contemplate, "I am Śiva.
Having joined with the Mahāmudrā, one should inspire oneself by means of the self. (13.35)
Having struck down the obstacles with three claps of the hands, gestures of sight, and the sound of the index finger,
and having cleared the directions, purified them, and then enclosed them [with a protective circle].
Having thus purified the basis, one should remember the Mantra upon the lion-throne, [visualizing] Sadāśiva within the light-liṅga in the hollow of the heart-lotus. (13.37)
With a steady mind, one should worship [the deity] who is the size of a thumb, using the perfected substances in their proper order, according to the ritual service of a universal monarch.
One should satisfy Śiva with the outpourings of supreme nectar in the fire of the navel-cavity, and within the cavern of the throbbing bindu between the eyebrows.
Having meditated upon Śiva, who is supreme and subtle, and having completed the internal sacrifice,
one should meditate on Sadāśiva as identical with oneself for the protection of the physical basis.
As Brahmaśambhu states:
"Then, with the Astra-mantra, one should fashion a raised enclosure wall three *tāla*s high,
and outside of that, a moat dug out, using the armor-mantra (*tanutrāṇa*)."
Thus, as the special arghya is described here in the chapter on ritual conduct (upacāra-paṭala):
having filled [the vessel] and worshipped it, one should sprinkle one's own head with those waters using kusha grass.
Having applied the triple marks (tripuṇḍra) according to the prescribed rule with fragrant ashes,
one whose self is thus purified should perform the purification of ritual materials.
Having inspected the aforementioned materials for worship according to one's capacity,
[one should purify them] with the root of *kuśa* grass or with a *kūrca*, using the water for the *arghya* offering while reciting the *varman* mantra.
Having sprinkled [the materials] and touched them, one should then recite the mantra with the *ajāta* or the *hṛdaya* [mantra].
Then, one should offer perfume with the left hand, and likewise the garments over the head.
Or with the name Kṛṣṇa, or with the word Śikhā, one should offer ornaments and garlands;
or with the word Puṃsā, or with Varma, one should likewise offer the food offering (naivedya) and fruits and so forth.
Furthermore, one should offer flowers and other items with the Īśa mantra or the Gāyatrī;
curd and milk with the Kaṅkaṭa mantra, and ghee again with the Śikhā mantra.

Then, one should sprinkle the sugar with the *hṛdaya* mantra, the honey and water with the *śikhā*, and the remaining [ingredients] with the *mūla* mantra; these are the droplets of *arghya* water to be cast upon them.
Having made a tilaka mark on the forehead with sandalwood paste using the root mantra,
one should place a flower upon it with the root mantra, and then sprinkle it upon one's own head.
Thus, the purification of the substance is accomplished; now the purification of the mantra is described.
As Brahmaśambhu says:
"One should slowly recite the mantra upwards through the sequence beginning with the three measures (trimātrā)."
Until the attainment of the ultimate state, that is his [practice].
"In this way, the purification of the mantra occurs by relying upon the pure reality (tattva).
Thereafter, one should perform the purification of the liṅga according to the sequence of the ritual services (upacāra) as taught. (13.49)

Having filled the *gaḍḍukas*, *vardhanīs*, and *kumbhas* with pure water, the practitioner, being pure and of serene mind, shall then open the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*) with the *astra-mantra*. (13.50)
Having first offered the general *arghya* with the *gāyatrī* mantra known as the "Śiva-mantra," having removed the *nirmālya*, and having repeated the five-fold *brahma-mantra*,
one should immediately place that flower upon the crest of the *liṅga*.
For a stable image, one should offer the *arghya* oblation first and then present it with a staff;
for a mobile object such as water and so forth, having cast [the offering] therein, one should sprinkle it with water consecrated by the Heart and Weapon mantras. (13.53)
One should first wash the pedestal (piṇḍikā) and immediately thereafter the liṅga.
As Brahmaśambhu has said:
"One should diligently wash the liṅga with the right hand alone."
First, one should purify the support along with the water-jar and the liṅga with the water of the weapon-mantra.
"Afterwards, one should perform the consecration with the general *arghya* waters while reciting the mantra.
Thus, during the consecration, worship, and other rites, the *liṅga* must have its head not empty [of water]. (13.54)
One should perform [the worship] with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, for that indeed brings about the presence [of the deity].
Thus [are described] the purification of the self, the substratum, the substance, the mantra, and the *liṅga*. (13.55)
The five [deities] must be worshipped by the followers of Śiva; worship in any other manner is not desired.
With "Oṃ Gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati," one should worship the Lord of the Gaṇas in the northwest corner. (13.56)
In the southwest (Nairṛta), one should meditate upon the elephant-faced [Ganesha] in the form of Varuṇa as previously described;
[reciting] "Oṃ Guṃ, obeisance to the Gurus.
Likewise, in the northeast (Īśāna), one should remember the Gurus with their previously described forms and other attributes.

With the general *arghya* and offerings beginning with *gandha* up to *naivedya*, according to one's capacity, one should worship the five gurus—namely, the Guru, the Paramaguru, the Parameṣṭhiguru, the Pūjyaguru, and the Mahāpūjyaguru—with the mantra "oṃ nitya" and so forth. Oṃ hām, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti.
This Śakti, who resides upon the Tortoise Stone (*kūrmaśilā*), is to be worshipped beneath the pedestal (*pīṭha*). (58)
Having the luster of a lotus fiber, seed, or sprout,
[one recites] "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Anantāsana," and [the deity] resides upon the Brahma-stone.
One should worship Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, and Aiśvarya in their proper sequence. (13.59)
One should place the feet of the pedestal as prescribed, starting from the southeast (Āgneya) and ending at the northeast (Īśa),
and likewise [place] Adharma, Ajñāna, and Avairāgya in the cardinal directions.
And one should worship lack of sovereignty (anaiśvarya) in the seats starting from the east and so forth in sequence,
using their names in the dative case combined with the seed-syllables of Tāra and Hṛdaya.

The other enclosures (āvaraṇas) should be worshipped in a general manner without specific distinction. Om Hām! Having thus worshipped below the girdle (mekhalā) in the presence of Knowledge (jñāna), || 13-62 ||
One should worship the upper covering, as well as that which stands above, situated in the direction of the power of sovereignty (*aiśvaryāśā*), with:
*oṃ hāṃ padmāya namaḥ* (Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the lotus); *oṃ hāṃ karṇikāyai namaḥ* (Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to the pericarp).
Having thus worshipped, one should worship the eight powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vāmā in sequence upon the filaments (*kesara*).
All those previously mentioned [deities] should be worshipped, well-seated in all directions as described before:
"Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Vāmā; Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Manonmanī. One should worship the ninth power, Manonmanī, in the pericarp (karṇikā). 13–64.

Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the solar disc (sūryamaṇḍala). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Brahmā, the lord of the solar disc. Thus, having meditated on the pervasion starting from the front petal of the lotus, one should worship. Oṃ hāṃ, homage to the lunar disc (somamaṇḍala). Oṃ hāṃ, homage to Viṣṇu, the lord of the lunar disc.
Having meditated on the pervasion [of the deity] from the tips of the filaments and so forth, one should worship the dyad.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Rudra, the lord of the fire-maṇḍala.
Thus, one should worship the image and the lord of the image in the center of its pericarp.
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the space-maṇḍala. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to the seat of Śiva.
Thus has the seat been described; it is to be worshipped here according to the Pauṣkara:
"When one prepares a seat for a stable, fixed liṅga..."
In the case of a movable liṅga, there may be a distinction: its pedestal may be either movable or immovable.
After the ritual bathing, having placed [the deity] either on a pedestal or within a mandala,
one should worship the Lord seated there in a firm posture, whether he resides in a stationary image or a mobile liṅga.
Thus, having filled his joined palms with flowers. || 13.66 ||
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Śiva.
With this [mantra], one should install the form characterized by the aforementioned features upon the liṅga.
Oṃ hāṃ hāṃ, salutation to the form of Īśvara, whose nature consists of knowledge and action.
And likewise, there are thirty-eight kalās in the five faces of Brahmā. || 13-67 ||
One should install [the deities] upon the image with their respective mudrās, according to the sequence prescribed for nyāsa;
then, having formed a handful of flowers (puṣpāñjali), one should [invite] the Lord Sadāśiva into that [image].
Then, having divided the *vidyādeha* and joined it with the *tāra*, the *hṛt*, and the *mūla-hṛt*,
one should utter "to the *vidyādeha*, [namas]" and install it upon the image.
Then, having raised a handful of flowers joined with the seed-syllables *tāra* (oṃ) and *hṛd* (namaḥ),
and having consecrated it with the root-mantra of Sadyojāta while reciting the mantra ending in a prolated vowel (*pluta*), || 13.70 ||
One should meditate on the supreme light, auspicious and identical to Nāda, from the lotus of the heart;
having led it upward to the lotus at the end of the twelve, one should unite it with the partless Śiva.
As Brahmaśambhu has said:
"One should utter [the mantra] until the sphere of the partless (niṣkala) is attained,
being permeated by the contemplation of that state within a throbbing circle of rays."
Meditating upon that which has arisen within the *bindu* according to the ritual of invocation,
one should, with a steady mind and full confidence, take [the deity] from there while it stands before him.
"Having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon the body made the object of focus,
one should thus invoke Śambhu with the invocation-mantra as prescribed."
One should establish the Lord with the Tāra, Hṛdaya, and Vāmadeva mantras, using the Sthāpanī mudrā.
Having uttered the heart-mantra of Tārā along with her face, one should cause [the deity] to be present by means of the mudrā;
having spoken the Praṇava and the Aghora-heart-mantra, one should address him by the name "Niṣṭhura. (13.73)
Furthermore, having filled and raised his joined palms with flowers,
he should utter "namaḥ," "svadhā," "svāhā," "vaṣaṭ," as well as the heart-mantra and the armor-mantra.
Having offered a handful of flowers, one should conceal them with both hands;
then, O Śivā, one should place the limbs upon their respective locations with their own mantras.

Recalling in due order those various purposes of the invocation and other rites that were demonstrated in the chapter titled "The Ritual Services" (Upacārākhye), [one should perform them here]. 13-76.
Just as fire is by its own flames and the sun by its rays, so too is Śiva capable and invincible through his own limbs. (13.77)
His heart is true being, his head is the sovereignty over all, and his qualities are mastery that is not dependent on another; that which stands above is the topknot. (13.78)
The energy (*tejas*) of others is protected by its own nature and is generally capable; because it shares the same characteristics as armor (*kavaca*), it is designated by that name. (13.79)
That prowess of his, which is irresistible by enemies,
he discharges as a weapon, whereby he swiftly casts those who create distance far away.

Thus, having performed the visualization of the limbs through recollection as spoken by Brahmaśambhu, one should likewise perform the nectarization (*amṛtīkaraṇa*) of this [body] with the root mantra. (13.81)
The invitation (prarocana) has also been declared; that should be performed with the Mahāmudrā. The special arghya, the pādya, and the ācamana [water] should be offered with the Hṛdaya mantra.
One should present [the offerings] ending with *namaḥ*, *svadhā*, and *svāhā*.
Some say that after first giving the water for the feet (*pādya*) and the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), one should subsequently give the respectful offering (*arghya*).
Having given the *arghya* upon the five heads with the heart-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, [one proceeds]. (83)
One should place a mass of *dūrvā* grass, flowers, and unbroken rice grains upon his head, having worshipped Sadāśiva with excellent perfumes, flowers, and incense. (13.84)
One should bathe the deity seated upon the bathing altar according to the prescribed method;
having wiped [the deity] with a cloth, one should then offer water for the feet at the feet and [water] for the head at the crown.

Having quickly offered the water for honor (*arghya*), the water for sipping (*ācamana*), garments, and ornaments, one should again worship the Lord through the sequence beginning with the seat and the image (*mūrti*). (13.86)
Having smeared it, along with its pedestal, with the paste of fragrant substances as described,
one should adorn it with golden bands, necklaces, garlands, flowers, and petals.
One should adorn it with *puṣpapratisarā* cords and *tamiṇḍa* cords;
likewise, one should recite the *praṇava*, the root mantra, and "namo śivāya. (13.88)
Having pronounced the name of each substance, one should offer it to Śiva;
one should worship the Brahmās in the five faces with the Brahma-mantras in their proper sequence.
One should worship with those limbs, namely Īśāna and the others, which belong to the limbs of Śambhu.
Then, having extracted those Brahmans from the faces of Śiva, one should proceed as follows.
Then, like a flame blazing forth from a lamp, one should project the limbs [of the deity] from the limbs of Śiva;
meditating on the forms and other attributes as previously described, one should place them within the centers of the petals.
One should place Īśāna upon its pericarp in the northeast,
and the others on the petals according to their respective directions, seated facing toward Śiva.

Having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the heart and the other limbs, ending with the armor (kavaca), upon the petals in the directions of Agni, Īśa, Rakṣas, and Vāyu, one should then place the weapon (astra) in the cardinal directions in due order.
And one should place the Eye in front of Śambhu with its specific mantra;
having meditated upon them in their described forms, one should worship them in sequence with water for the feet and the arghya offering.
Regarding this, Brahmaśambhu states:

"For these [mantras], there is no veiling (āvakuṇṭhana), nor the rite of making them immortal (amṛtīkaraṇa); there is no separate bathing, no preparation of lamps, and no distinct arrangement of limbs."
Thus, one should offer the aforementioned incense while ringing the bell with the left hand;
first for the deity, and thereafter for the limbs of Brahmā in their proper order. (13.95)
Rākṣasas, asuras, yakṣas, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas perish by the sound of the bell; incense brings about their presence.
Having displayed a lamp placed in a lamp-vessel within the range of vision of the Lord, and having brought it down as prescribed, one should likewise perform the *ārātrika* circumambulation. (13.97)
Since Śiva resides in the Śivaliṅga and the universe is established within Śiva,
the lighting of lamps and the application of collyrium to it are traditionally held to bring peace to the world.
In the case of incense, lamps, food offerings, bali-offerings, and likewise in homa, the word "svāhā" should be employed; for the remaining [rites], there should be a salutation (namaskṛti).
Whatever has been mentioned or not mentioned, all that is performed by means of the heart-seed syllable (hṛdbīja);
thereafter, one should present the offering as prescribed for the ritual services (upacāra).

The offering for the Lord should be made with the root mantra itself, while that for the limbs of Brahmā should be half of that; it is prescribed that the offerings for the secondary limbs may be in separate vessels, or otherwise, all together in one.
Having offered water for drinking to him, one should give water for washing the hands,
as well as powder for rubbing the hands, and water for sipping.
Betel, mouth-freshener, collyrium, and likewise a mirror; a parasol and chowries, as well as dance, song, and instrumental music. (13.103)
Having meditated upon Sadāśiva, who is accompanied by Prakṛti and the Goddess, and who is joyful, with praises consisting of the five auspicious great titles and with auspicious hymns; 13.104.
At that time, one should congratulate him with these and other such words;
here, at that moment, one should offer him congratulations. According to Brahmaśambhu, [the recipient] should be joyful and accompanied by his natural disposition.
[One should also present] a golden sacred thread (*upavīta*), tips of *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). (13.105)
One should install this daily *pavitra* upon Śivā with the root mantra.
Having recited the root mantra accompanied by the three principles (*tattva*) and ending with *svāhā*, one should place the *pavitra* upon the head of the Liṅga.
Whatever has been deficient or excessive, or whatever has been omitted or fallen away during the worship—[all that is rectified].
Because it purifies and protects, it is therefore called *pavitraka*;
immediately thereafter, for the sake of attaining the state of being beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*). (13.107)
Having uttered the supreme mantra of the Mantra-deity, one should install the Prāsāda-mantra as before,
having first gratified it according to rule with the mudrā previously employed.
Having worshipped again with flowers and incense, the *ārātrika* lamp should be circumambulated.
On the southern side of Śiva, [one should worship] the goddess seated upon a lotus with the root-mantra and its limbs. (13.109)
One should worship the rosary with offerings beginning with fragrance and ending with incense.
Herein,
that restraint which is produced regarding the senses (akṣa)— those things comparable to dice— is [the true rosary].
The rosary is said to be that which effects desired results, both visible and invisible.
One hundred and eight akṣas, together with Meru, were consecrated by all the Śambaras; then another half of that, and then a quarter.
Thus says Brahmaśambhu:
"One seeking liberation should recite twenty-five times; one seeking wealth should recite thirty times. (13.110)
One seeking nourishment [should worship] with twenty-seven [stems]; for prosperity, with fifty-four;
and for the attainment of the fruits of all desires, with one hundred and eight.
With a thread spun by a maiden, tripled and threefold, it is said that [the beads] should be strung facing forward, with a *meru* at the top.

One should perform recitation for the sake of liberation using a rosary obtained from one's guru, or, in his absence, one fashioned by oneself; for the sake of prosperity, one may use knots of *kuśa* grass, gems, or gold. (13.113)
A Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya [should wear beads] that are auspicious, pure, measured, and symmetrical;
while Vaiśyas and Śūdras [should wear] all types of Rudrākṣas, including those from the Putrajīva tree. (13.114)
The rudrākṣas were produced directly from Rudra; they are identical in essence to Śiva.
By muttering prayers with them and by wearing them, one attains the state of Rudra. (13.115)
"In this regard,
even animals, when joined with rudrākṣas, have attained the state of Śiva," so it is said in the Śivadharmottara.

Up to sixteen faces, according to the divisions beginning with one face—those with eight, eleven, and sixteen faces are likewise excellent; however, a single-faced rudrākṣa is indeed rare and is the most supreme of the supreme. (13.117)
Those with three, four, or five faces are the youngest and easily obtained;
the remaining ones are declared to be the middling, and all bestow the fruits as described.
Having first worshipped the rosary and consecrated it with the nectar-mantra (*amṛtīkṛta*), one should indeed perform the recitation;
while uttering the mantra, one should slowly pull through each individual bead. (13.119)
For liberation, one should use the thumb and forefinger; for the sake of enjoyment, it is joined with the middle finger;
and for nourishment, having abandoned the little finger, one uses the other fingers.
Japa is indeed threefold: it may be loud, whispered, or mental. The loud [japa] yields inferior fruit, while the mental one grants middling success. (13.121)

The whispered (*upāṃśu*) recitation yields the best fruit; therefore, the wise man should perform it with that method. Here, because mental recitation is accomplished only through extreme effort, and because external recitation results in inferior accomplishment, the whispered method should be employed as the standard form. All three types [of recitation] must not be performed too fast, nor too slow, nor with indistinct syllables, nor with a distracted mind. Bhoja states that in obligatory and occasional rites, one should perform them with a single-pointed mind, facing either east or north. Regarding this:
"Asuras and Rākṣasas seize that recitation and fire-oblation which is performed without the proper count."
If one is not silent and is impure, then the recitation belongs to the Piśācas.
Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhatkālottara*: "Having performed the recitation as prescribed in the *Kalpa*, as well as the worship and [the worship of] oneself... (13.122).
For the sake of attaining success in mantra, worship, and so forth, one should offer it to Śiva.

Regarding this, King Bhoja states: "Then, having enclosed the recitation with the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*), protected by the weapon-mantra (*astramantra*), and veiled by the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), the seeker of enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) should offer the recitation, the worship, and himself—mixed with *kuśa* grass, flowers, sandalwood, and fragrant water in three handfuls (*culuka*)—at the feet of the God with these three verses, saying: 'May this be the means for the attainment of my fruit.
However, if he is a seeker of liberation (*mumukṣu*), [he should say]: 'O God! May this rite not be a cause of bondage for me. (13.123)
Thus: Om!
You are the protector of the most secret of secrets; accept this recitation performed by us, so that through your grace success may be mine, [resting] in you. (13.124)
O Lord! Whatever I do, whether good or evil, may you, O Śaṅkara, who abide in the state of Śiva, destroy that for me—huṃ kṣaṃ! (13.125)
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, and Śiva is this entire world;
Śiva performs sacrifice everywhere, and he who is Śiva is indeed myself. (13.126)
Having thus offered himself, along with his recitation and worship, with devotion, he then bows to Śiva and receives permission from Śiva. (13.127)
As it has been said: "Having properly performed and completed the fire-rite (agnikārya), one should then unite Śiva, who resides in the fire, with the fire within the liṅga. (13.128)
Then, one should apply the single covering to the faces and limbs of the deity;
and the deity [should be installed] in the form of the *liṅga*, preceded once again by the offering of water (*arghya*).
Having worshipped with the eightfold offering of flowers (aṣṭapuṣpikā), one should dismiss him with due consideration.
The Yoga-pīṭha, the Mūrti, and Śiva constitute its five limbs (aṅgapañcaka).
Thus, one should worship the eight [deities] individually with eight mantras, honoring them with respect.
Emission (visarga) is traditionally held to be of two kinds: that which is dependent and that which is independent.
Once the *liṅga* has been installed, whether it be fixed or mobile,
its emission [of power] remains dependent [on the practitioner], for the sake of bringing about the presence of Śiva.
However, the removal of the general signs is traditionally taught to be independent [of external conditions];
for even these general signs are momentary, being made of clay. (13.133)
Sandy, made of flour, then fresh butter, cow dung, made of fruit, drawn, and food—thus the common [types of offerings] are eightfold. (13.134)
Having immediately fashioned these [liṅgas], having invoked Śaṅkara at that very moment,
and having worshipped him according to the rule, one should dismiss him without further expectation.
For these, there is no ritual soaking in water, nor any installation or laying to rest;
there is no lunar day (tithi), no asterism (nakṣatra), and indeed no marking of characteristics or wearing [of the marks].
Having worshipped it immediately along with its pedestal and then dismissed it, one should cast it into water;
this same procedure is identical for an altar, a fire, and a mirror.
It should always be performed in a water-pot, in water, during worship, or within oneself;
[it is performed] on a square area smeared with pure cow-dung and water.
Having mentally fashioned a seat and invoked [the deity] there according to the ritual rule, one should perform worship; however, the bathing here is mental, not external.
On a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), this procedure should be followed; the remainder one should perform as before.
Likewise, it applies to all lingas made of clay, cloth, and so forth. (13–140)
One should offer flowers without water before their variegated [images], as well as worship with those made of gold, silver, and jewels. (13–141)
One should perform everything for all [types of lingas] as one does for the *niṣkala-liṅga*.
The purification of copper, brass, and bell-metal is traditionally taught to be by means of acids and similar substances. (13–142)
One should perform the ritual bathing during occasional rites, but one should not perform it as a daily rite.
