In the case of offerings made without expectation, one should first worship with the eight flowers.
Having emitted the Praṇava and performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon it, one should worship Caṇḍeśa;
then, having dismissed him as well as the mantras, one should join them in sequence within the lotus of the heart.

This procedure applies specifically to the ordinary sacrificial mound (*sthāṇḍila*). The dismissal (*visarga*) of consecrated fixed and mobile icons (*liṅga*) is indeed dependent [on further ritual]. As Brahmaśambhu states:
"The independent dismissal is prescribed for a common icon;
however, the dependent dismissal in the case of a consecrated icon has been demonstrated previously."
"Even in the case of a mobile liṅga, [the rite] is dependent [on other factors], whereas for a fixed liṅga on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), it is always independent.
On this point, it is also stated in the Pauṣkara:
"Whether the accepted liṅga be fixed or mobile..."
But in the case of a gift made without regard [for the recipient's worthiness], a great fault is declared.
Moreover,

at an auspicious time, under a favorable lunar mansion, and during a propitious moment, the installation of the *liṅga* is performed according to the prescribed rites and the injunctions regarding the mantra-form.
From that time forth, Śiva himself dwells within that linga;
therefore, in its daily worship, there is neither invocation nor dismissal.
For the purpose of performing worship toward that which is accepted as metaphorical,
the engagement in all activities is seen as the body of the embodied one.
Just as in the waking state, so too are its invocation and other rites;
all external objective activity having ceased, it remains as pure consciousness alone.
Just as the state of abiding is observed for an embodied being during deep sleep,
so too, at the conclusion of worship, the ritual dismissal (udvāsana) is prescribed with due consideration.
Whether the *liṅga* be fixed or mobile, for Śiva who has been installed therein,
there must indeed be a periodic awakening of the fire within its sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
The ritual is performed at the beginning and at the end; therein, the concealment of that very [liṅga] takes place.
Likewise, when the liṅga has been installed, there is the procedure beginning with the invocation (āvāhana).
But when the dismissal (*visarga*) is dependent [on further rites], having offered the *arghya* to Śambhu while facing away,
and having displayed the supreme *mudrā*, one should raise the limbs [of the deity] by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having meditated upon Śiva by means of the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā], one should unite him with both the formed and the formless;
having worshipped him with the eightfold flower-offering, one should meditate upon him as being of the nature of the partless (niṣkala).

Then, having worshipped the mantras from the vessels containing the *arghya* offerings and so forth with the *saṃhṛti-mudrā*, he should exit the inner sanctum while reciting the *varman* (armor mantra).
Having left that place and gone outside, having washed both his feet and hands,
and then having sipped water (ācamana) and meditated upon Śiva for the purification of any drops or slips [of semen], he should proceed.
"Having recited the Saṃhitā mantras, one should offer a gift dedicated to Śiva.
Thus, this worship of Sadāśiva, which bestows the attainment of desired goals, has been declared as having a single enclosure (ekāvaraṇa).
Having examined various Śaiva Saṃhitās, [he composed] the Śivaśaṅkara, which brings joy to the devotees of Śiva.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the worship of the single enclosure, in the Kriyāpāda of the Uparibhāga of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 13.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
I shall now proclaim the five-fold worship (pañcāvaraṇa-pūjā), which is desired for the self whose nature consists of the five mantras;
it is equal in ritual procedure to that of Sadāśiva, who here possesses five faces, as well as to that of him who has but one face.
Everything previously mentioned here is likewise applicable, including the worship of the Sun and the Śivāsana;
however, there may be someone here who has assumed a form as Brahmā, and there is a specific detail proclaimed in the *Prayogamañjarī*.
In this system, the one known as Īśāna has five faces, while Tatpuruṣa and the others have four faces.
Furthermore, the Vidyeśvaras here also have four faces, and they hold arrows, tridents, thunderbolts, and nooses in their hands.
(126) And for all these [deities] arisen within the single enclosure, the remainder—including their colors and so forth—should be understood as being entirely as described previously;
and that which was stated in the chapter titled "Form" regarding those situated within the five enclosures is also to be known here. (14.4)
One should meditate upon Sadāśiva, who has five faces, is seated upon a lotus, possesses ten arms, and is as pure as crystal;
he wears his matted hair bound with the crescent moon, has three eyes, and appears sixteen years of age. (14.5)
With his own right hands, he holds a serpent, a bell, the gesture of fearlessness, and a goad;
likewise, with the others, he sequentially bears a trident, an axe, a sword, a thunderbolt, and fire. (14.6)

Wearing a sacred thread of serpents, his limbs beautifully adorned, clad in incomparable tiger-skin, with a throat as dark-blue as a peacock's, his body anointed with ashes, he was delightful through every excellence of beauty. (14.7)

Having reflected thus, one should worship [the deity] upon the pericarp of that lotus as before; or alternatively, one may worship the single-faced [deity], endowed with four arms, bearing the moon on his crest, possessing the three eyes of knowledge, action, and will, and appearing serene. (14.8)
One should worship him, who holds a rosary and a trident, and who successively carries a khaṭvāṅga staff, a skull-cup, and a fragment [of a skull];
who is adorned, resembles an autumnal cloud, has matted hair, and is seated upon a lotus. (14.9)
The first [enclosure] consists of the limbs, faces, and coverings; the second enclosure is that of the Lords of Knowledge (Vidyeśvaras);
the third is the enclosure of Umā and the others; and the fourth is by Indra and the other groups of Mothers.
The fifth enclosure should be formed properly with the ten weapons previously mentioned, beginning with the vajra;
one should worship these with their own names preceded by the heart-mantra (tāra), using the dative case and ending with "namaḥ. (14.11)
Namely:
outside the lotus, one should worship the Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) beginning with Ananta at the exterior of the gates;
on the path outside of that, one should worship the weapons of these [Lords] on the outer perimeter.
For Ananta is indeed worthy of worship, as well as he named Sūkṣma, Śivottama, and likewise Ekanetra;
they are seated individually upon lotuses situated on the pedestals at the eastern, southern, western, and northern tips of the crescent moon. (14.13)

Then Śikhaṇḍī, Śrīkaṇṭha, Ekanetra, and others [were placed] in the southeast and other directions; while Umā, Caṇḍa, Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Gaṇeśvara, Bhṛṅgin, Vṛṣabha, and Skanda were stationed at the northern gate and the other [directions]. (14–15)
These very same [deities] are to be worshipped in pairs at the four gates beginning with the northern direction,
as well as in the Pavitrā and other rites, and in the case of a fixed liṅga, in the Jayāvalī.
Indra, Agni, Yama, as well as Nirṛti, Varuṇa, Vāyu, Vaiśravaṇa, and likewise Īśāna—these are the world-protectors (lokapālas). (14–17)
Brahmā, the lord of the upper worlds, is situated between Īśāna and Indra;
Ananta, the lord of the lower worlds, is situated between Rakṣas and Varuṇa.
Likewise, [he is the source] of the gods, of the radiant ones, of the pretas, and also of the rākṣasas;
of the waters, of the life-force yakṣas, of the various forms of knowledge, and of those who enjoy worldly existence.
In sequence, these lords, together with their mounts and retinues—ending with the term "attendant of Rudra" (rudrapārṣada)—as well as their respective attendants, are to be worshipped. (14–20)

Near the Lord of Wealth (Dhanada), one should worship Soma with the mantra beginning "To Soma, the lord of the constellations," and so forth. With the mantras: "Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Indra, the lord of the gods, together with his weapons, vehicle, retinue, and the attendants of Rudra; obeisance to his attendants," and others, one should worship these [deities] in the ten directions starting from the east. Furthermore, these deities should be worshipped specifically within the enclosure of the world-protectors (lokapālas).
Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vṛṣabha.
Indra resides in the east in the place of the bull;
if there is a bull, it is a bull that should be worshipped at a fixed liṅga, for it is taught that the bull is not [to be worshipped] at a mobile one.
Thus it is stated in the Lalita:
"Afterwards, Vīrabhadra is to be worshipped facing west from Yama;
Vighneśa faces east, and between those two are the Mothers. (14.22)

Oṃ laṃ, obeisance to Vīrabhadra. Oṃ gaṃ, obeisance to Gaṇapati. Oṃ vyoṃ, obeisance to Brahmāṇī. Oṃ māṃ, obeisance to Māheśvarī. Oṃ kāṃ, obeisance to Kaumārī. Oṃ hāṃ, obeisance to Vaiṣṇavī. Oṃ heṃ, obeisance to Vārāhī. Oṃ hoṃ, obeisance to Indrāṇī. Oṃ hūṃ, obeisance to Mahākālī and Cāmuṇḍā. In front of these, one should again worship all the Mothers with: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Mothers" and "Oṃ, obeisance to the hosts of all the Mothers. (p.
128) One should worship Śāstṛ by his own name slightly to the southeast of Nirṛti.
Near Vāyu, slightly toward the northeast, one should worship Skanda.
One should worship Durgā with her own mantra slightly to the west of Kubera;
and one should worship Caṇḍeśa with his mantra slightly to the southwest of Īśāna.
Having extracted the last two syllables of the fifth [mantra] joined with the fourth, the fifth, and the fire-vowel (R),
preceded by the Praṇava, one should then take the word "Caṇḍa" and the armor (Hūṃ).
The weapon of Caṇḍeśvara shall be seven-colored, and the mantra is:
*oṃ caṇḍāya namaḥ* and *oṃ caṇḍeśāya namaḥ*; with these one should perform the worship.
These deities, beginning with Vṛṣabha and ending with Caṇḍa, have thus been described. (14–26)
However, they should be worshipped at a fixed liṅga, but not at a mobile one, nor even on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila).
As it is stated in the Lalita:
"Whether on a mobile or a fixed sacrificial mound, one should not worship Vṛṣabha during the daily rite."
Neither the Seven Mothers nor even the fierce Skanda are desired there.
In occasional rites such as the Pavitra ceremony and others, their worship is especially distinguished.
Thus:
outside the enclosure of the fence, the vajras and so forth [are placed] by their own names. (14.27)
Having recollected [the deities] according to their own essential forms, one should worship them in sequence in the ten directions;
one should worship those situated in the enclosures with perfumes and other offerings as they are available.
Whatever among these is not yet accomplished, one should mentally visualize it;
furthermore, festivals and the offering of oblations (bali) are prescribed for a fixed liṅga.
One should not perform these two—singing, dancing, instrumental music, and so forth—at a portable altar or a fixed platform, even when one has the means to do so. (14.30)
For the fire-ritual is generally commended whether performed among stationary or moving beings; thus one should perform it everywhere according to the prescribed rule.
p. 129) And likewise, one should perform occasional rites (*naimittika*) such as the *caitra* and *pavitra* ceremonies.

Thus has the worship of Śiva with five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*) been correctly described as enjoined in the Śiva-tantras, by which worldly and otherworldly enjoyments and liberations are attained by embodied beings without effort. (14.32½)

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, the procedure for the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇapūjāvidhi*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 14.
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.

Then, having entered the fire-sanctuary (*agniśaraṇa*) and circumambulating it clockwise while reciting the root mantra (*mūla*), he should inspect the sacrificial materials (*homadravya*). Sitting facing the womb of the pit (*kuṇḍayoni*), with his face turned northward, he should gaze at the pit while reciting the root mantra within his own vision. Then, having struck it with the *astra-mantra*, sprinkled it with the *varma-mantra*, dug it with the *astra-mantra*, and extracted [the earth] with the *astra-mantra*, he should descend into it with that [earth]. Having filled it with the *hṛdaya-mantra* and leveled it with that same [mantra], he should perform the sprinkling, pounding, sweeping, and smearing with the *astra-mantra*. Having meditated upon and worshipped the Kalās—Śāntyatītā, Śānti, Vidyā, Pratiṣṭhā, and Nivṛtti—located within the pit in the directions of the center, east, south, west, and north respectively, using their respective names preceded by *Tārā* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, he should then encircle the pit with a triple-thread (*trisūtrī*) while reciting the *kavaca-mantra*. Having thus conceptualized the pit as consisting of the Kalās, saying "Oṃ, salutation to the pit composed of Kalās," and having worshipped it, he should then draw three lines extending either eastward or northward using the tips of fuel-sticks (*samidh*) representing the three principles (*tattvatraya*), and one additional line drawn transversely with the *astra-mantra*.

Their presiding deities are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, and Śiva. Then, having consecrated the crossroads within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with three *kuśa* blades as a thunderbolt by means of the Astra-mantra, one should place a seat of *darbha* grass, saying: "Oṃ, obeisance to the seat of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara. There, one should meditate upon Vāgīśvarī—dark-complexioned, having bathed after her menses, adorned with fresh youth, possessing a divine form, clad in celestial attire, and full of passion—and having invoked her with the Tāra, Hṛdaya-bīja, and her name ending in "namaḥ," and having worshipped her, one should likewise worship Vāgīśvara, whose form and other attributes correspond to hers. Immediately thereafter, having brought fire produced by friction, or fire from a jewel, or fire from the house of a learned Brāhmaṇa (*śrotriya*), which is situated in a vessel of copper or similar metal, free of smoke, and consisting of glowing embers alone; having discarded the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (*kravyād*); having inspected it with the Mūla-mantra, sprinkled it with the Astra-mantra, veiled it with the Varma-mantra, and protected it with the Astra-mantra; and having meditated upon that elemental fire (*bhautika-agni*) as having the form of rising light; one should take the Bindu-fire from the eye on one's own forehead with the seed-syllable of fire "Oṃ Raum," encapsulated by the heart-mantra, and through inhalation (*pūraka*), unite it with the elemental fire. Then, by means of one's own names, one should draw the fire of the pit (*kuṇḍa-agni*) upward through the *piṅgalā* channel with exhalation (*recaka*), expel it through the right nostril, and join it to the fire in the vessel.

(p. 130) Having unified the three fires, one should project consciousness (*caitanya*) into the fire with its own seed-syllable (*svabīja*) while reciting "Obeisance to the Consciousness of Fire. That same seed-syllable, joined with the long vowels, constitutes the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), beginning with the heart. Having consecrated the fire with these, having turned it into nectar (*amṛtīkṛta*) by means of the root-mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, having worshipped it with the heart-mantra, and having protected it with the armor-mantra (*varman*), one should grasp it with both hands. One should contemplate the agitation of Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara, who are united upon a divine bed in the northeast corner of the fire-pit (*agninirambara*). Then, lifting the fire from the vessel up to the neck, circumambulating the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) three times, and kneeling on the ground, one should meditate on the fire as the seed of Śiva facing oneself. One should cast it [into the pit] through the channel (*nāḍī*) of the Power (*Śakti*) using the root-mantra. Having unified the scattered [fire] with the weapon-mantra (*astra*) and clothed it with a garment, one should mentally resolve upon its purification, sipping of water (*ācamana*), and so forth. Covering it with fuel sticks using the armor-mantra and kindling it with a fan, one should tie a *darbha* bracelet—consecrated by the recitation of the weapon-mantra—on the right hand of Vāgīśvarī for the protection of the embryo. Then, for the rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*), one should worship with the *Sadyojāta* mantra and offer five oblations of sesame seeds with the heart-mantra. Likewise, one should perform the rite of male-conception (*puṃsavana*) with the *Vāmadeva* and *Śiras* mantras, and the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*) with the *Aghora* and *Śikhā* mantras. Having mentally projected the body with the mantra "Oṃ Hāṃ, obeisance to the body consisting of the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*)," one should cast a drop of water—the very essence of life—with the tip of a *kuśa* blade using the *Śikhā* mantra. Having mentally projected the five faces of the fire, beginning with *Sadyojāta*, by means of five oblations of sesame seeds, and having likewise performed the assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpanā*), one should similarly accomplish the purification of the faces. Immediately thereafter, having meditated upon Vāgīśvarī as having given birth and the fire as the newborn child, one should worship with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra and offer oblations with the armor-mantra; this constitutes the rite of birth (*jātakarma*).

Then, having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with water for the arghya offering while reciting the Astra-mantra, and having discarded the surrounding darbha grass and the darbha-bracelet to terminate the period of ritual impurity (sūtaka), he sprinkles the goddess Vāgīśvarī and the god Kumāra with water from the Astra-mantra. Having mentally resolved upon [offering] a bath, garments, ornaments, and so forth, he spreads darbha grass around the rim of the pit and offers five palāśa wood sticks—complete with their tips, a span in length, and smeared with ghee—into the fire with the Astra-mantra to remove saliva.

Then, having encircled the pit with a triple-braided cord (*veṇī*) made of thirty blades of *darbha* grass pointing toward the northeast, and having placed the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) as prescribed, he should invoke Brahmā upon the eastern seat of the enclosing sticks, Śaṅkara on the south, Viṣṇu on the west, Ananta on the north, and Īśvara [on the southeast]. Having worshipped them with their respective names preceded by the heart-seed syllable (*hṛdbīja*), and having worshipped the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in their own directions along with their weapons, he should proclaim the command of Śiva: "O gods, Brahmā, Indra, Viṣṇu, and others, together with your weapons, protect this Śiva-fire by remaining stationed in your respective positions! Having thus established the protection, he should wash and take up the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles; having inspected them with the heart-mantra while accompanied by four *darbha* blades, heated them with the weapon-mantra, washed them with the head-mantra, heated them again, and rinsed them, he should place the *sruva* down, take up the *sruk*, and cleanse the tip of the *sruk* with the tips of the *darbha* blades saying "oṃ hāṃ, for the Śiva-principle"; then the middle with the middle of the *darbha* blades saying "for the Vidyā-principle"; and then the base with the base of the *darbha* blades saying "for the Ātman-principle. Then, once more at the base, middle, and tip...

Having recollected and drawn the presiding deities of the principles (tattvas) of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, and having washed them, one should place [the *darvī*] face-down upon the *prastara* grass to the south. Having likewise consecrated the *sruva* ladle, one should place it face-down upon the grass near the *sruc* ladle. Then, having worshipped Śakti in the *sruc* and Śiva in the *sruva* by their respective names, the two become fit for ritual action once their necks have been encircled with a triple thread (*trisūtrī*).

Again, having worshipped Brahmā upon a bundle of *kūrca* grass to the south of the fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), and having provided a seat of *darbha* grass in the north, one should fill the *praṇītā* vessel with water along with a *pavitra* strainer. Having lifted it up with both hands holding *kuśa* grass until it reaches the nose, and being authorized by Brahmā, one should place it on its seat with the mantra: *Oṃ hāṃ, you are Varuṇa*. Then, having worshipped Viṣṇu in the *praṇītā* waters with the mantra: *Oṃ hāṃ, salutation to Viṣṇu, the slayer of the enemies of sacrifice*, one should inspect the clarified butter (*ājya*)—which has been strained into the aforementioned vessel—with the *hṛdaya* mantra, sprinkle it with the *astra* mantra, and heat it over embers in the north. Having heated it in the upward-facing fire-corner of the pit, one who is himself the embodiment of Brahmā should offer a drop of *ājya* with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, saying: *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Brahmā*. Then, having heated it over *kuśa* grass in the northeast above the pit, one who is himself the embodiment of Viṣṇu should offer a drop of *ājya* with the tip of a *kuśa* blade, saying: *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Viṣṇu*. Having placed the *ājya* upon the *kuśa* grass in the *yoni* [of the pit] and consecrated it with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should light two *darbha* blades and illuminate the *ājya* three times with the *kavaca* mantra. Then, casting the *darbha*-wick into the fire and washing both hands, one should visualize the two wings as white and black. Grasping the tips and the bases of the *pavitra* strainers with the thumbs and ring fingers facing oneself, one should wave them three times toward oneself with the *kavaca* mantra. After washing the *pavitra*, one should wave it again toward the fire and wash it; then, waving it again toward both sides with the *hṛdaya* mantra, one should remove the *pavitra*, wash it, and cast it into the fire. This is the purification of the *pavitra*.

Then, having illuminated the *kuśa* grass and performed the *nīrājana* (waving) rite over the clarified butter (*ājya*), one should cast it into the fire. Then, having conceptualized the southern and northern portions of the clarified butter as the bright and dark fortnights joined with the *iḍā* and *piṅgalā* channels, and the middle portion as the *parvan* (node) and the *suṣumnā* channel, one takes the clarified butter from the southern and northern portions with the *sruva* ladle and offers it into the right and left eyes of the Fire, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ Agnaye svāhā" and "Oṃ hāṃ Somāya svāhā. Immediately thereafter, one offers into the forehead-eye, saying: "Oṃ hāṃ Agnīṣomābhyāṃ svāhā. Then, taking clarified butter and saying "Oṃ hāṃ Agnaye Sviṣṭakṛte svāhā," one should offer it into the mouth of the Fire; thus having performed the opening of the Fire's mouth, one should consecrate the clarified butter by making it nectar through the *dhenu-mudrā*, protecting it with the *astra-mantra*, and veiling it with the *kavaca-mantra*. This is the purification of the clarified butter (*ājya-saṃskāra*).

This is the procedure for the first fortnight (*pūrvapakṣa*). For the second fortnight (*aparapakṣa*), there is this distinction: one offers oblations into the eyes with the mantras "to Agni," "to Sūrya," and "to Agni and Sūrya"; the remainder is as before. Then, having prepared a drop of clarified butter and having cast it into ghee, milk, honey, and so forth, one should consecrate it with the Heart-mantra; thus they become consecrated. Then, one should meditate upon Śivāgni as having five faces like Sadāśiva, with matted locks and a crown, seven tongues, [an image] facing each direction, three eyes, four arms holding the gestures of granting fearlessness and boons, the Śakti, and the Svastika, wearing fragrant garlands and garments, adorned with divine ornaments, and with a serene countenance. [One should meditate on him] in his four faces.

(132) There are four tongues; three are in the middle. Among these, they are *sāttvika* in rites such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*); they are *tāmasa* in minor rites; and they are *rājasa* in rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*). As it is said: "Hiraṇyā, Gaganā, and Raktā—these seven tongues are *sāttvika*. (15-1)
Kālī, Karālī, Vilohitā, Manojavā, Dhūmravarṇā, Sphuliṅginī, and Viśvaruci—these are the seven tongues of fire characterized by the quality of tamas. (15.2)
Karālī, Dhūminī, Śvetā, Lohitā, Bhadralohitā, Suvarṇā, and Padmarāgā—these seven tongues are of the rājasa nature. (15.3)

Having thus meditated upon that Śiva-fire, one should then perform the "anointing of the faces" (*vaktrābhidhāraṇa*). *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the form of Sadyojāta.* *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the secret [aspect] of Vāmadeva.* *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the heart of Aghora.* *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the face of Tatpuruṣa.* *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the head of Īśāna.* Having thus anointed [the fire] according to the faces, one should immediately thereafter perform the "joining of the faces" (*vaktrasandhāna*). *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the form of Sadyojāta and the secret [aspect] of Vāmadeva.* *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the secret [aspect] of Vāmadeva and the heart of Aghora.* *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the heart of Aghora and the face of Tatpuruṣa.* *Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to the face of Tatpuruṣa and the head of Īśāna.* Having offered oblations in pairs (*dvandvaśas*) in this manner and joined the faces, one should then utter the five seed-syllables beginning with Īśāna, preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with Sadyojāta. Taking clarified butter with the *sruva* ladle, one should offer it in an unbroken stream of ghee from the southeast corner to the northwest, and from there to the northeast, while reciting: *svāhā to Īśāna, Tatpuruṣa, Aghora, Vāmadeva, and Sadyojāta*. By this, one effects the unification of the faces (*vaktraikīkaraṇa*). Furthermore, the "unification of the faces" consists of the entry of the other faces into the principal face. And in the case of daily rites (*nityakarman*), since Sadyojāta is the principal [face], the entry of the others into it should be understood. As it is said in the *Saṃhitā*:
In the case of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), the downward-facing [sacrifice] is understood to be primary;
elsewhere, however, the upward-facing is primary, while the other is secondary.
In both occasional (naimittika) and optional (kāmya) rites, whichever face holds primacy,
its unification with the others is prescribed in each respective case.
Likewise, for one seeking liberation, the face of Hīśa (Śiva) is traditionally held to be primary during initiation;
the eastern [face] is for the attainment of perceived supernatural powers (*dṛṣṭasiddhi*), and the southern [face] for minor rites (*kṣudrakarman*).
"The northern face is called Vāmadeva; likewise, it is for pacifying (śāntika) and nourishing (pauṣṭika) rites.

Thus, having remembered Sadyojāta as the primary face for the daily rite (nityakarman), and having worshipped it with "Oṃ, obeisance to Sadyojāta," one should offer five oblations with "Oṃ hāṃ, svāhā to Īśāna," and then assign the name [to the fire] with "Oṃ hāṃ, you are Śivāgni, the consumer of oblations."

Then, having worshipped Vāgīśvarī and Vāgīśvara by their own names and offered clarified butter (ājya) once for each, one should dismiss them at the *dvādaśānta*. Then, having taken a small portion from the fire that has been consecrated by these five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*), one should preserve it for the sake of the sacrificial offerings (*bali*) and so forth, such as for the cooked rice (*caru*), the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*), and incense. As it is stated in the *Saṃhitā*:
"The cooked rice and sacrificial cakes are [prepared] in a fire consecrated by the five purificatory rites;
however, the oblation (*homa*) should be performed in a fire in which the deity has been invoked."
Thus it is said.

Then, with the root mantra ending in *vauṣaṭ*, one should perform the eleven sacraments (*saṃskāra*) with three separate oblations of clarified butter (*ājya*). They are as follows: one should perform the *upaniṣkrāmaṇa*, *annaprāśana*, *caula*, *upayana*, *upākarma*, *vratasaṃgrahaṇa*, *vratotsarjana*, *godāna*, *samāvartana*, *vivāha*, and *ādhāna* using the root mantra alone. Regarding this, it is stated in the *Mañjarī*: "In the sacraments of the Śiva-fire, a difference in procedure is observed; one should perform all sixteen rites beginning with *garbhādhāna*," and so forth through these verses. As for what was said regarding the ten-syllable *Vyomavyāpin* mantra: having performed the *garbhādhāna*, *puṃsavana*, *sīmantonnayana*, *jātakarman*, and *nāmakaraṇa* individually by offering eight oblations each in sequence, and having completed them, one performs the *upaniṣkrāmaṇa* with the *Śivagāyatrī*, the *annaprāśana* with the *Īśāna* mantra, the *caula* with the *Tatpuruṣa* mantra, and again the *upayana* with the *Īśāna* mantra. Then, having performed the *upākarma*, *vratasaṃgrahaṇa*, *vratotsarga*, *godāna*, *samāvartana*, and so on, in order with the *Brahmas* beginning with *Sadyojāta*, and the *vivāha* with the ten-syllable *Vyomavyāpin* and the *agnyādhāna* with the *Prāsāda* mantra—one of these two paths being followed—then, by means of the fire thus consecrated, the daily, occasional, and optional rites of the Śaivas are accomplished, and not otherwise. Now, one offers the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, having filled the *sruc* with clarified butter using the *sruva*, and placing the *sruva* face-down upon the *sruc*, holding a flower at the tip of the *sruc* and grasping the two handles joined together with both hands in the *śaṅkha-mudrā*, one stands up with feet firmly together. With the gaze fixed on the tip of the *sruc*, uttering the root mantra joined with the *hṛdaya* and ending in *vauṣaṭ*, and having received permission, one pours a stream of clarified butter into the Śiva-fire. Having invoked Śiva into the heart-lotus of the fire along with the limbs, forms, and enclosures (*āvaraṇa*) according to the sequence of the Śiva-throne and so forth, and having performed the rite up to the *prarocanā*, one should worship with the *arghya* and other offerings up to the lamps as available. Then one should effect the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) of Śiva and Śivā. As it is said in the *Pauṣkara*: [The passage continues with the ritual details.]
Having established a connection with the light emerging from the tip of the nose of Śiva residing in the fire,
through the *piṅgalā* channel until the completion of the ritual act.
One should contemplate that oblation being offered as a flow of nectar,
which, through the path of the *suṣumṇā* in both [nostrils], is the cause of Śiva’s delight.
Thus [it is said]. (p.

134) Now, one should offer oblations with clarified butter, rice, *vrīhi* grain, fuel-sticks, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), using the prescribed oblation-materials and the root-mantra. In that regard, one offers a tenth part of the [root-mantra] for Śiva, and [the same portion] for the forms (*mūrti*) and the limbs (*aṅga*), even in the case of occasional rites (*naimittika*), offering the oblations as prescribed and according to the specific injunctions for each instance. On this point, Brahmaśambhu states:
"One should observe the colors, the fragrances, the flames, and the sounds of the fire."
When success or failure is manifested, it occurs through the inner self that has been cultivated.
A flame that is glossy, turning to the right, whose sound is muffled by the ears,
which always rises upward, and whose crest is compacted and free from soot, is auspicious.
One should not offer oblations into a fire that is not blazing, nor into one with smoke, nor into one lacking fuel;
oblations should be offered into a blazing, licking fire for the successful accomplishment of the rite.
Thus it is said; and likewise in the Lalita:
"The fire that is white, yellow, or reddish at its crest, or lightning-colored, or tawny, glossy, and curling to the right, brings success in one's undertakings."

Fire that is black, grey, or smoky in appearance, variegated, or non-pradakṣiṇa (counter-clockwise), or harsh, or abounding in sparks, is said to bring inauspiciousness. For its pacification, one should perform [oblations] with Saṃhitā mantras as well as the Śiva-vyāhṛtis.
Likewise, by offering oblations of sesame seeds and clarified butter, only an auspicious result shall come to pass.

Thus: one should offer oblations with the respective mudrās for each. On festival days (parvan), one should perform worship, recitation, and fire-offerings twice as much as the daily routine. Having separately sprinkled clarified butter over three portions of the sacrificial porridge (caru) in sequence, one should offer them into the fire with the ladle (sruk) while reciting the root mantra. Then, having once offered the limbs of the deity’s form (mūrti-aṅga) by hand, and having sprinkled [the area] with water from the *prokṣaṇī* vessel using the *astra* mantra, one should present betel-leaf. Having propitiated [the deity] with circumambulations, prostrations, and hymns of praise, and having touched the ashes, saying "Forgive me," one should release the connection of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*). Having offered oblations with the *praṇava*, the *hṛdaya* seed-syllables, and the *vyāhṛtis*, one should extract the limbs of the form with the *astra* mantra and join them to their respective places within Śiva who resides in the fire. Having firmly established the Lord within the heart of the fire, one should preserve the perpetual fire (*naityika-agni*) in that very sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).

Alternatively, having worshipped Agni and Śiva daily, one should withdraw the mantras of Agni by means of inhalation (*pūraka*) using the *saṃhāra-mudrā*. Having led both Śiva and Agni sequentially to the *dvādaśānta* (the limit of twelve finger-breadths) and then established them within one's own heart, one should dismiss Śiva and Agni to the place of one's own *bindu* or to the heart. Having thus generated Agni every day, one performs the oblation (*homa*). In cases such as when traveling on a journey where a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) is unavailable, one should smear a square mandala measuring a cow-hide with cow-dung, prepare an altar (*sthaṇḍila*) there with pure sand, consecrate it with the rites of inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*) and so forth, and then establish the fire.

One must offer oblations. In this regard, if the fire associated with Śiva should go out through negligence, one should fast for three nights and recite the Aghora mantra. One should offer oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds according to one's capacity. Even though it has been stated that when the fire associated with Śiva and the fire of Śiva have gone out, one should fast for a day and night, perform a thousand recitations and oblations of the Aghora mantra, re-establish the fire, and then offer oblations; nevertheless, in the case of daily rites (*nityakarman*) and the ritual of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles, purification is achieved by washing the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass mats (*veṇī*), and their suitability for use in the daily oblations is thus specified. In a fire associated with Śiva, ashes and the like do not constitute *nirmālya* (remnants of worship). However, that very same [substance] becomes *nirmālya* and untouchable when Śiva has been dismissed (*udvāsita*). Thus, having restrained the fire and Śiva, and having dismissed the deities of the enclosing sticks and the sacrificial grass mats, one should worship with perfumes and other offerings in front of or to the north of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and present the *bali* offering with the remainder of the *caru*.

Therein, having offered bali-oblations with their respective names followed by *svāhā*—to Rudra, the Mothers, and the Gaṇas of Yakṣas in the four directions starting from the east; to the Planets, Asuras, Rākṣasas, and Nāgas in the corners ending at the northeast and northwest; to the Nakṣatras in the center; again, outside the Nakṣatras, to the Rudras and others in the intermediate directions starting from the northeast; to the Rāśis, the Viśvedevas, Kṣetrapāla, and Durgā—one should offer in the second mandala in the ten directions starting from the east, in due order, to Indra and the others with their respective names followed by *namaḥ*. Then, scattering [the remains] everywhere outside the mandala, one should give [the offering] with "Oṃ, to the Crows and others, svāhā. Then, having withdrawn the bali-mantras, [one should place them] on the mandala made in the courtyard.
Those Rudras who perform fierce deeds and dwell in fierce abodes, as well as those who are gentle and dwell in gentle abodes— (15.4).
May the Mothers of fierce form and those who are the lords of the Gaṇas—all of them, with well-pleased minds, accept this bali offering. || 15-5 ||

"May they quickly grant me success and always protect me from fears! Oṃ chaṃ chaḥ huṃ phaṭ! Having offered the *bali* with this [mantra], having washed one's hands and feet and performed the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*), one should offer water for the feet (*arghya*) near the *liṅga* in reverse order. Then, having withdrawn the limbs of enjoyment as before and re-united them with the *liṅga*, one should dismiss the Blessed One according to the method previously described.

Now, if a householder who follows the Śiva-āśrama wishes to eat, he should perform the *cullyāhuti*, the domestic *bali*, the *vaiśvadeva*, and the ten *balis*, and then eat. In that regard, having placed the first portion of the cooked food into a vessel, kindled the fire on the hearth, smeared it with cow-dung, and sprinkled it with *arghya* water, he should worship the fire and the deities to be described hereafter with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*). He then offers the food mixed with clarified butter (*ājya*) as an oblation, worshipping with the syllable *Oṃ* at the beginning and *namaḥ* at the end, and offering with *svāhā* at the end, to Agni, Soma, Savitṛ, Bṛhaspati, Prajāpati, the Viśvedevas, all the gods, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Having sprinkled [the area] again with *arghya* water, he should present the *bali* to the household deities. Therein, on the right and left sides of the hearth, he offers to Dharma and Adharma; in the cooking pot, to Saṃsāraparivartana; and in the water-vessel—

At the main door of the house, one should offer to Jalāmṛta Varuṇa; at the door, to Vighnarāja and Dvāraśrī; on the grinding stone, to Subhaga; in the mortar, to Raudra Koṭṭaharika; on the pestle, to Balabhadrapriya Mahāpraharaṇa; on the broom, to Mṛtyu Devocita; at the head of the bed, to Kāma Kusumāyudha; beneath the central pillar, to Skanda Gṛhādhipati. Immediately thereafter, in the center of the site (vāstu), within a circular mandala, one should present the Vaiśvadeva offering. Therein, in the center, having offered the oblation in a clockwise direction to Brahmā, the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Sādhyas, the Nakṣatras, to the Earth, to the beings moving upon the Earth, to the Atmosphere, to the beings moving in the Atmosphere, to those moving below, to the Sky, to the beings moving in the Sky, to the Quarters, and to the beings moving in the Quarters—one should then cast the oblation into the middle of the mandala for Viṣṇu, Lord of All Beings, who is attainable through meditation, using their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*. Then, wearing the sacred thread over the right shoulder (*prācīnāvītī*), one should go outside the mandala to the south and, with the thread over the right shoulder (*apasavyena*), offer to the ancestors: "Soma Pitṛmān, Yama Aṅgirasvān, Agni Kavyavāhana, and the other ancestors—svadhā namas to these Pitṛs! Svadhā namas to the Agni-pitṛs! Svadhā namas to all Pitṛs! Having thus offered in due order, one should exit and present the oblation to the deities of the directions.

Therein, having offered [the oblation] with "Oṃ, accept this for Indra, obeisance; Oṃ, accept this for the eastern quarter, obeisance," and so forth, extending thus up to Īśāna for the eight world-protectors from the east to the intermediate directions, he should worship with scents and other offerings using "Oṃ, to Suparṇa and Sauparṇī" in the upward direction of Brahmā, and "To the Nāga and the Nāgas" in the downward direction of Ananta. Then, having offered [the remainder] accompanied by scents and flowers with "Oṃ, may the crows, worms, spirits, the fallen, dogs, dog-cookers, those who break their vows, and whoever else there may be, accept this offering, obeisance," and having cast the rest upon the ground, he should wash his hands and feet, perform the ritual rinsing (ācamana), and satisfy guests, visitors, dependents, children, the elderly, the joyful, the wretched, the helpless, and others who seek aid with food and drink according to his ability. Finally, he should eat according to the prescribed rules for dining.

Thus it has been stated that this sacrifice in the fire of Śiva (or the fire of the Śiva-path) is dear to the followers of Śiva; by means of this, there shall be daily worship of the Lord along with his attendants, as established in the Śaiva Tantras.
When complete, it bestows fruit and the welfare of the world. || 15-6½ ||

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, on the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*), in the section on ritual action (*kriyāpāda*) of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 15.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Now, for those whose defects have been destroyed through the yoga of meditating upon Śiva, the descent of power (śaktipāta) occurs; and from that, moreover, comes the clarity of the intellect.
Therefore, by approaching a Guru, one obtains Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā).
Impurity (mala), karma, and māyā are the causes of bondage by the fetters (pāśa). (16.2)
From a specific excellence of that [initiation], the knowledge of Śiva arises for the one who is to be graced.
That is initiation (*dīkṣā*), because from the verbal root *dīkṣ* comes the sense of the destruction of bonds (*pāśakṣaya*). (16-3)
Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is said to be for the living being who is to be graced, that is, for the *paśu*.
In this regard, those to be graced are of three kinds: the *vijñānakala*, the *pralayākala*, and the *sakala*.
The first is bound by the single bond of impurity (*mala*); the second possesses both impurity and karma. (16.4)
The third is known as the *sakala* (the conditioned), which is joined with the impurities of karma and *māyā*.
Knowledge (*vijñāna*) that consists of a perverted understanding of the self is indeed ignorance (*ajñāna*). (16.5)
Because of the meaning of the root *dhā* [to place] in the context of the bond of *kala*, he is called *vijñānakala*.
Because he is bound by karma due to ignorance (*ajñāna*), he is therefore called *pralayākala*. (16-6)
However, because his knowledge has reached the state of ultimate excellence (*prakarṣa*), he is said to have attained dissolution (*laya*);
likewise, by means of the threefold bonds known as *māyā*, *karman*, and *mala*. (16.7)
Because they exist together with him in the present, all of them are so described;
these three—superior, middling, and inferior—are the recipients of Śiva’s grace. (16.8)
The grace of Śiva, the ocean of compassion, is also twofold:
with support and without support; each is distinct, according to the fitness of those to be graced. (16.9)

In this context, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is of two kinds: that which is without a substratum (*nirādhāra*) and that which has a substratum (*sādhārā*), corresponding to the nature of the grace bestowed. Furthermore, initiation is twofold: without a locus (*niradhikaraṇā*) and with a locus (*sādhikaraṇā*). As King Bhoja stated: "That initiation which is performed by the Lord, independent of a teacher, through His own power in the form of grace by means of an extremely intense descent of power (*śaktipāta*), for those who are *vijñānākala* and *pralayākala*, is 'without a locus. That which is performed by the Lord residing in the form of the teacher, through a descent of power that is mild, milder, or intense, for those who are *sakala*, is 'with a locus. And that [initiation with a locus] is either 'with seed' (*sabījā*) or 'seedless' (*nirbījā*), depending on the degree of qualification."
(138) Possessing the seed-syllable, endowed with the *samaya*, and joined with the practice of the *samaya*;
combined with the severing of the bonds and so forth—that [initiation] is prescribed for the wise alone. (16.10)
Furthermore, initiation without seed (nirbījā-dīkṣā) is recommended for kings, as well as for children, women, the very elderly, the severely ill, and the simple-minded. (16.11)
In the daily rites, occasional rites, and so forth, for both the practitioner and the teacher,
the practice with seed (sabīja) alone is prescribed, because they possess the authority to accomplish the welfare of both themselves and others.
That [initiation] is traditionally held to be twofold: the first is characterized by ritual action, and the other by knowledge;
[the former] consisting of the construction of the pavilion, the preparation of the sacrificial pit, the cutting of the noose, and the purification of the paths. (16.13)
That initiation which is joined with material oblations and the like is called "action-based" (kriyāvatī);
[that which is performed] without the pavilion, sacrificial pit, and so forth, by means of mental activity alone, is the other.

Initiation characterized by knowledge (*jñānavatī*) is said to culminate in the realization of perfect knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). It is of four types: initiation by sight (*cākṣuṣī*), initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*), verbal initiation (*vācikī*), and mental initiation (*mānasī*). As follows:
having meditated upon himself as Śiva and gazed at the disciple, he restrains the entire series of paths within him by his very look.
Having severed the bonds, that which is indeed the power of vision (cākṣuṣī) should establish the state of Śiva within this [individual]. || 16-15 ||
When Rudra himself, whose body is the mantra, places upon his own hand a lotus endowed with the forms of the limbs and the root-mantra,
and touches [the disciple] here while recollecting Śiva, that is the initiation by touch (*sparśadīkṣā*), by which the bonds of the fetters (*pāśabandha*) are cast off.

Having placed all the mantras within his own mouth, he whose self is Sadāśiva, joined with all paths, should gradually sever the bonds of the mind by means of speech; for therein lies the vocal initiation (vācikī dīkṣā). || 16-17 ||
Being himself of the nature of Śiva and free from all afflictions, he should meditate upon Śiva along with the mantra within the lotus of his own heart;
then, through mental initiation and by the power of knowledge, he should unite this [disciple] with the state of Śiva. (16–18)

Initiation (*dīkṣā*) is of many kinds, including initiation with ritual action (*kriyāvatī*), initiation into the observance (*samaya-dīkṣā*), initiation for liberation (*nirvāṇa-dīkṣā*), and initiation for the practitioner (*sādhaka-dīkṣā*). Among these, that by which one purifies the disciple merely through the purification of impurity (*mala*) by means of ritual action, introduces him into the observance (*samaya*), and brings about his identity with Rudra (*rudrātmatā*) is initiation into the observance (*samaya-dīkṣā*).
In this [initiation], the six paths (*adhvan*) are purified and the attainment of ritual action (*kriyā*) is abundant. (16–19)
That, moreover, is the severing of the bonds and the crest-lock; it is likewise the yoga in the state of Śiva.
That is declared to be the initiation into liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā), specifically for those who possess the requisite qualification.

But in that [state] where, through the loosening of bonds, one is purified during the stages of withdrawal and so forth, there is the attainment of qualities such as *aṇimā* and yoga in the state of Īśvara. (16–21)
And therein, at the outset, is the qualification (*adhikāra*), which is initiation (*dīkṣā*) called that of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
Together with the previously mentioned qualities, through initiation leading to liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*), one's own consciousness becomes a boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.

Through the reversal of the bodily attributes such as the exhaustion of karma and so forth, one attains the state of Śiva, which is the excellence of having acquired qualities such as omniscience. (16–22)
Surrounded by his disciples, the Guru, having entered according to the prescribed rite and completed the ritual acts to be accomplished, remained with a concentrated mind.
He [entered] the initiation hall—which was nine, seven, or five cubits in size, constructed according to his means, square in shape, and exceedingly beautiful. (16–23)
It was adorned at the four gates with four *aśvattha* trees serving as archways, and at the four directions with full water-jars,
parched grain, unbroken rice, various fruits, and diverse flowers, as well as with rows of various sprouts.

Having approached [the pavilion] which has a pure canopy white as the rays of the moon, adorned with exquisite silk hangings draped along its perimeter, featuring hanging strings of pearls and flower garlands, and surrounded by new white curtains; 16–25.
Wearing fine white garments and scented with white garlands and perfumes, his limbs radiant with various ornaments of gems and gold;
having washed both his hands and feet with pure water and performed the ritual sipping (ācamana), he remains intent on silence with his hand purified.

Then, with the general *arghya* in hand, having sprinkled the doors with the *astra-mantra*, and having worshipped the door-keepers at the western gate as usual, having struck [the ground] with his heel and driven away the obstacles with three snaps of the fingers and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), and having cast the *nārāca-astra* and entered within, he turns back, places the *astra* with a flower upon the threshold, gazes at the pavilion with the vision of reality (*tattva-dṛṣṭi*), circumambulates it clockwise, casts a flower in the station of Brahmā, worships his own seat, sits facing north, and performs the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*).
Having first cast off the body born of Prakṛti and other material elements through his intellect, and having contemplated his own form as "I am Sadāśiva," he—
having placed the mantra upon the hand of Śiva which is anointed with fragrance, and having duly performed the ritual of *sakalīkaraṇa* upon himself according to the eternal sequence— [proceeds].
Having mentally worshipped Śiva within the hollow of the heart-lotus, and likewise Agni situated at the navel and Śambhu residing in the *bindu*,
one should establish protection externally by means of three claps of the hands (*tāla*), using the powers firmly stationed in the moat, the weapons, and the rampart.
Then, having prepared the special *arghya*, one should purify the materials for the ritual bath.

Having prepared five compartments by the application of equal lines, one should fill a vessel with milk in the central compartment called Supratiṣṭhita within the Śiva-tattva, using the Īśāna-mantra and the Mūla-mantra; and [one should place] curd in the eastern compartment called Svaśānta within the Sadāśiva-tattva, using the Tatpuruṣa-mantra and the Varman-mantra.

(p. 140) In the south, in the *vidyā-tattva* known as *tejorūpa*, one should pour ghee with the *aghora* mantra and the *śikhā* mantra; in the north, in the *puruṣa-tattva* within the *nivṛtti* section, one should pour cow’s urine mixed with jewel-water using the *vāmadeva* mantra and the *śiras* mantra; and in the west, in the *kāla-tattva* called *amṛta*, one should fill [the vessel] with cow dung using the *sadyojāta* mantra and the *hṛdaya* mantra. One should recite [these mantras] once, twice, thrice, four times, and five times over the substances starting from the center respectively. Having consecrated the *kuśa*-water six times with the *śivagāyatrī*, one should pour it into each of the five substances, beginning with milk, in due order. Thereafter, one should combine the curd and other ingredients with the milk in the central vessel called *supratiṣṭhita*. Having stirred them together into a single mixture and worshipped it as Sadāśiva, one should set it down. Then, having prepared a *jñānakhaḍga* (sword of knowledge) consisting of *kuśa*-grass tufts equal in number to the *tattvas*, one should arrange the *vikira* offerings.
Roasted grain, sandalwood, white mustard seeds, ashes, flowers, kusha grass, and unbroken rice— these seven weapons are to be prepared by mixing them together with the Astra-mantra.
Thus says Brahmaśambhu:
"Sesame seeds, parched grain, barley, dūrvā grass, white mustard, and flowers,
slightly mixed with a paste of sandalwood, are known as *vikira* offerings."
Thus it is said in the Mataṅga:
having consecrated grains with the Astra-mantra, one should scatter them around as if with the Astra-weapon;
by their falling, the hosts of obstacles flee from that place in great fear.

Thus it is stated in the *Parākhya*. In this manner, one should prepare the *vikira* offerings for these [deities]. Regarding the turban (*uṣṇīṣa*) of the image: the preceptor should always wear a white, fine turban, six finger-breadths in height, perfectly even, and wound in a clockwise direction.
Thus it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"The preceptor, having obtained a white turban through the *mantra-saṃhitā*,
should wear it on his head, six fingers in height, like a royal fillet."
Thus it is stated in the *Bṛhatkālottara*.

Likewise, one should wear a white upper garment like a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*). Having prepared a nine-fold cord spun by a twice-born girl for the purpose of binding the noose, and having touched it with the topknot, one should place it in the vessel.
The cord, made of nine strands, should be double the length of the mandala.
Just as that is called Karaṇī, so too is the Ghaṭikā exceedingly pale.

One should place both of those, having recited them with the *mūrti-mantras*. One should also place an iron scissor, having consecrated it with the *astra-mantra* for the purpose of cutting the tip of the thread.
One should prepare powders of five colors for the sake of the mandala.
Likewise, one should provide gems, gold, grains, a water-pot (*kumbha*), and a small vessel (*karaka*). (16–31)
The water-pots, the vessels for the sacrificial oblation, and whatever else such as perfumes and flowers;
and garments that are white, fresh, and free from loose threads. (16–32)
One should prepare the sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, sesame seeds, parched grain, and whatever materials are required for the bath,
each separately with the mantras of the Kalās beginning with Śāntyatītā.
One should recite the root mantra seven times over a white uṣṇīṣa;
then, having wrapped it around one's head, one should remain composed while wearing the upper garment.
Thinking, "I am capable of bestowing grace; I am the omniscient Sadāśiva; I am independent; I shall liberate these bound souls (paśus)," [he remains]. (16.35)

Then, having placed the scattered offerings (*vikirān*) contained in the vessel into his left hand and standing in the southwest direction of the pavilion facing northeast, he should recite [the mantra] seven times with either the Aghora-weapon or the Śiva-weapon. He should then scatter the offerings, which resemble blazing fire, from the center of the pavilion toward the northeast corner using his right hand with the palm turned upward, while reciting the words "Śarva, Śarva. Having gathered the scattered offerings with a handful of *kuśa* grass while reciting the word "Dhū," and having established them in the northeast corner, he should place there, upon a lotus-seat (*padmapīṭha*), a measure of rice (*śālyāḍhaka*) and a seat of *darbha* grass. Having placed the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*), which has been prepared according to the rules, made of gold or other materials, well-washed, fumigated, and turned face down; and having meditated upon the pitcher as consisting of the principles (*tattvas*) from Earth up to Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*) behind that [seat], he should turn it face up and place its *kūrca* grass-bundle face up upon it. Meditating on the nectar of the twelve-finger space (*dvādaśānta*), he should fill it with water from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*), cast in nine gems, gold, medicinal herbs, flowers, perfumes, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*), place the leaves of the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*) face up within it, and cover it according to the prescribed method with unbroken grains and fruits.

Having covered him with two white garments and white garlands, and having invoked the Lord of Yoga— who is seated upon a moving and stationary bull-throne, whose form and body are identical to Śiva— into that [liṅga], one should worship him with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings.

Thereafter, at the edge of the pitcher, likewise to the south, when the scattered offerings have been withdrawn, one should fill the *vardhanī* vessel just like the pitcher with the recitation of the weapon-mantra; then, having invoked the Śakti seated upon the lion according to the rite, one should worship her.
(p. 142) Now, regarding this, Brahmaśambhu says:
"Having worshipped, according to rule and in sequence, the gods beginning with Indra and ending with Upendra in all ten directions, starting from the eastern quarter (aindrī)," etc.

Thus [it is said]. Then one should pray to them. Having worshipped the *vardhanī* placed upon a movable or immovable seat, one should thereafter recite the *Aghora* weapon mantra here within the *mañjarī* all around the wall, and then [to] the *vardhanī*.
The preceptor should cause [the water] to flow in a clockwise direction by means of an unbroken stream.

Then, following that same path, another person should take up the Śiva-pitcher, carry it back, and place both the Śiva-pitcher and the Vardhanī vessel in their original positions upon the seat as before.
One should place the root-mantra in the Śiva-vessel; therein, Śiva is to be worshipped, seated upon a firm throne, accompanied by his limbs and forms.
Then, having properly worshipped the divine Umā in that water along with the Tāra and the Pāśupata weapon—
Having touched the Śiva-pitcher with the Liṅga-mudrā using the right hand, one should not touch it with that same fist.
"The right fist is Umā, the base (piṇḍī) is [the other fingers], and the thumb is Hara"—
thus says Brahmaśambhu.
Thus, if one desires enjoyment or liberation, one should first touch the *vardhanī* vessel and afterwards the jar, [reciting]:
"To Umā, who possesses the form of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) and who bears the form of the *liṅga*. (16.38)
Having offered praise with the words, "Salutations to you, O Śaṅkara," he said:
"For you are indeed the Lord of this sacrifice; this power is yours, unwavering. (16.39)
"This is your sword of knowledge; take it as your own weapon.
By me, the sacrificer, this sacrifice of the performers of rites has been set in motion. (16.40)
"O Lord, you must protect this until its completion!
Having thus paid homage to Śiva and properly entrusted him with that sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga), and having worshipped him thoroughly,
he should report that task to the Blessed One and duly worship the Lord of Obstacles (Vighnādhipa) in his own direction for protection.
May this sacrifice for the Lord of the Gods, which has been undertaken by us for the sake of favoring the sacrificial animal,
reach its conclusion without obstacle in your presence.
Having thus paid homage to Gaṇeśa, one should first smear the center of the pavilion with fragrant water and cow dung;
then, having drawn either a *liṅgodbhava* or another auspicious (*bhadraka*) mandala therein, one should worship Maheśa. (16.43)
Then, having meditated upon the infinite seat and having invoked Sadāśiva there according to the prescribed rite, one should worship Him together with the primary offerings and attendants;
and when Śiva is satisfied, one should duly worship the surrounding deities as well.
Regarding "obstructions," the five obstructions are mentioned.
Having established the fire—known as Sadāśiva—in a square sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in the east, that is, in the fire-sanctuary;

It is as follows: having placed the fire according to the manner previously described and having performed the *śivasandhāna*, one should first take out a small portion from the fire consecrated by the five purificatory rites (*pañcasaṃskāra*). Then, having cooked the *caru*—five handfuls of rice grains in the milk of a tawny cow (*kapilā*) that has been ignited on the hearth—according to the prescribed sequence for the initiation of each disciple (increasing the amount for each family), and having duly sprinkled it with clarified butter (*abhighāra*), one should place it upon *darbha* grass to the west of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having offered oblations of clarified butter accompanied by the collection of mantras (*mantrasaṃhitā*) and having poured the remainder into the *caru*, one should transform it into nectar (*amṛtīkṛta*) by means of the *dhenu-mudrā*. Then, dividing the *caru* into four parts: one portion should be offered to the Root-Abode (*mūlasthāna*); another to the Blessed Lord residing in the water-pot (*kumbha*); another to the Fire; and the remaining portion should be set aside for oneself together with the disciples. On this point, Brahmaśambhu says:
Having extracted [the portions] for Śiva, Agni, and the Kalaśa,
one should preserve the remainder of the sacrificial oblation (caru) undisturbed for oneself along with one's disciples.
Thus it is said.

Then, one should offer three portions of the oblation separately, using the sacrificial ladle (sruk) itself, with the root mantra, in sequence, each portion being sprinkled with clarified butter (ājya). || 16-46 ||
Then, having offered eleven oblations mixed with clarified butter using the root mantra,
one should offer them individually and separately, one by one, using the mantras of the Brahma-aṅgas and the Mūrtis.
Here,

one should offer oblations in sequence with clarified butter using the mantras known as Brahma, the six limb-mantras (ṣaḍaṅga), all the attendant mantras (parivāra), and those beginning with Vidyeśvara.

Thus it is stated in the *Mañjarī*: "In that same manner, having offered oblations with sesame seeds, and then having offered them again, one should likewise offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). (16.48)

Having offered the bali-oblation to Rudra and the other deities and having received permission from Śiva, the Guru may initiate one disciple, two disciples, or many disciples according to his authority. (16.49)
This much is the ritual action to be known by the teachers (deśikas) in the initiations of common practice (sāmānyakriyā) and so forth,
beginning with those of the initiate (sāmayī) and ending with those of the adept (sādhaka), in their proper sequence.
The General Section on Ritual Action.

Now, regarding the initiation into the *samaya*, having stationed outside the door the disciples as previously described—who have performed the cleansing of their teeth, completed their bath and the daily twilight rites (*saṃdhyā-nityānuṣṭhāna*), and are wearing white garments and upper cloths—the preceptor himself enters within, bows to the Deity, and makes this request:
"O Lord! These very animals for whose sake this sacrifice to Śiva was commenced by me stand here at the gate, pacified and restrained. (16.51)
"O Śaṅkara, grant me the favor for my entry there!
When the Lord had thus granted his grace, saying, "I shall bestow my favor," [the sage spoke]. (16.52)
Having performed the ritual identification of his own body (sakalīkaraṇa), the Guru, whose form is that of Sadāśiva, reflects: "In all five bases of initiation, I am indeed Śiva alone."
He is the protector of the sacrifice by means of the water-pots, the witness of the ritual action within the maṇḍala,
the locus of the fire-oblation in the sacrificial fire, and the remover of the bonds of the disciple's fetters.
One should contemplate that the teacher, who is intent on bestowing grace, is indeed oneself.

Then, on the mandala in the outer area of the door, the Guru himself, facing north and holding water for the guest-offering (arghya) in his hand, shall look upon the disciple— who is seated upon a lotus-seat made of darbha grass and unbroken rice grains with the syllable Om, standing with palms joined in reverence, body erect, and gazing upward toward the Lord.
On this point, Brahmaśambhu says:
"The Guru, with the vision of the knowledge of reality, should erase [the impurity] from the crest-lock down to the tips of the toenails, and from the tips of the nails up to the topknot."
Thus:
"Now, this Self of his, with the net of bonds loosened, [attains] inner Śiva-hood through the descent of Śiva’s power."
Having meditated thus, having sprinkled it three times with water for the guest-offering (arghya) while reciting the Astra-mantra,
and then having struck it three times on the head with ashes, [he should then strike it] with water.

"Having sprinkled," meaning up to that point: having placed a flower on the head of the disciple, one should draw three lines across from the heart upward with the tips and roots of *kuśa* grass. Bhojarāja says [the lines should extend] upward and downward from the navel. Then, having manifested the form of the bound soul (*paśu*) residing within the triad of the support-power (*ādhāra-śakti*) and endowed with the powers of knowledge and action by means of the mantra, and having projected the body of wisdom (*vidyā-deha*), one should perform the ritual integration (*sakalī-karaṇa*) with the root-mantra, the limb-mantras, and the form-mantras, and worship it. Then, having bound the eyes of the disciple with a white, fine, pure, unbleached cloth—sprinkled, veiled with the armor-mantra (*kavaca*), and consecrated with the root-mantra and the eye-mantra (*netra-mantra*)—one should lead him into the sacrificial hall and cause him to circumambulate the pitcher, the fire, the mandala, and Śiva.
On the right side of Śiva, a lotus seat has been prepared.
One should establish that [deity] along with the four [factors] beginning with dharma,
using the root mantra— which is encapsulated by the seed-syllable of the heart and accompanied by the *haṃsa*— uttered with a leaping resonance.
Having withdrawn its consciousness by means of the *saṃhāramudrā*, the teacher [withdraws] even the net of gross fetters and constituent parts for the sake of attaining the pure fruit. (16.59)
Having meditated upon [the disciple] as residing within his own body, one should purify him with the [mantras] of Bindu;
having purified him through the ritual procedure for the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) by means of dhāraṇās.
In his heart, within the solar disc and the lotuses of Brahmā and the other deities,
he beheld Sadāśiva, enriched by the forms of the network of the five mantras and their kalās, as well as the limbs (of the ritual).

Having mentally worshipped the Teaching together with its embodied form as the body of knowledge according to the prescribed rite, one should indeed offer oblations into the fire of the navel-pit with the intellect.

Having accomplished the purification of the self through meditation on Śiva within the drop at the lotus between the eyebrows, he himself, with his hands smeared with fragrant unguents, [proceeds]. (16.63)
Having formed the *śivahasta* mudrā upon his own left lotus-hand while meditating,
he should indeed worship Śiva along with His limbs (the *aṅgas*) through the sequence beginning with the seat (*āsana*), using his intellect.
Having mentally placed upon that [hand] the seed-syllable of the heart, enriched by the root-mantra and the *haṃsa*,
one should then first place that hand upon the heart of the disciple.
For the purpose of severing the knots of the heart and the other centers, one should sequentially direct [the breath] to the throat,
the palate, the space between the eyebrows, and the crown of the head, in order to attain the state of Rudra.

Thereafter, having placed a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*) scented with perfumes and flowers into the hands of the disciple, he should rise and position the disciple before the deity with his body upright and facing the deity. Standing himself facing north, he should meditate upon the blindfold that conceals the animal (*paśu*), remove the blindfold with the *jñāna-asinā* (sword of knowledge) and the *pāśupata-astra*, and say, "Throw this handful of flowers. He should then cause him to drop that handful into the mandala. Some maintain that he should throw the handful of flowers while still blindfolded. In that regard, whichever form, limb, or other part of the deity the handful of flowers falls upon, one should assign [the disciple] a name ending with that [deity's] name.

The name of a Brāhmaṇa should end with the word *śiva*, that of the other two [castes] with a term denoting a class of deities, and that of a Śūdra should end with the word *muni*; one should assign these names according to this sequence. (67)
Having instructed him in the eight-limbed prostration, one should cause him to bow down.

In this regard, according to the view of King Bhoja, however, after the circumambulation and the offering of a handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*), one should seat the disciple, purify him through the *dhāraṇās*, perform the ritual integration (*sakalīkṛti*), and then apply the Hand of Śiva (*śivahasta*). This is not approved by the root scriptures (*mūlāgama*), because only one who has been purified by the *dhāraṇās* is authorized to cast the handful of flowers upon the specific Śiva situated within the mandala; therefore, the previously mentioned position alone was accepted by Brahmaśambhu. Thereafter, having instructed the disciple in salutation preceded by a handful of flowers toward the Śiva-pitcher and the fire, one should seat the disciple on a seat prepared as before in the north-western quarter of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Having offered oblations with clarified butter (*ājya*) using the collection of mantras (*mantrasaṃhitā*) and poured the remnants back into the fire, one should effect the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) between the disciple and oneself. In that process, taking the base of a *darbha* grass blade at the junction of one's own shanks and placing the tip of the *darbha* in the hand of the disciple—Bhojarāja says this is the reverse order.

Then, having visualized that the disciple’s channels—*iḍā*, *piṅgalā*, and *suṣumnā*—have entered his own channels, he should offer three or five oblations with the root mantra. Having performed the entry and exit [of the breath] for the sake of seizing that consciousness, he should offer one-tenth as many oblations to the limbs (*aṅga*) and the forms (*mūrti*) using the root mantra one hundred and eight times, and perform the full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*). Then, for the sake of expiation, he should again offer one hundred and eight oblations with the root mantra and thereby remove the disciple’s previous birth.
On this point, Brahmaśambhu says:
"One who is not twice-born is not fit for spiritual perfection, nor does he attain liberation."
For since even a twice-born man [is so regarded] by him, one should therefore consider him the best among the twice-born.

Thus, by the elevation of their caste (*jātyuddhāra*), the twice-born attain the status of the "best of the twice-born" (*dvijottama*), and through liberation from the state of being animals, they attain the state of Śiva. Even for a Śūdra, by turning away from the Śūdra-nature and the condition of being an animal, a second birth characterized by the state of Śiva occurs through the elevation of his caste; therefore, such a person initiated [into this path] is no longer a Śūdra. Rather, because the state of Śiva is possible for one born with the *saṃskāra* of Śiva and because his previous birth has ceased, he possesses the fitness for hearing and performing worship according to the Śaiva mantras and tantras, excluding those Vedic mantras.

Now, if it is argued that a Śūdra possesses the status of the twice-born (*dvijatva*) through the extraction of his birth by means of the *Śiva-saṃskāra*, why is he not entitled to the Vedic mantras? To this objection, [the reply is: even for one born of a Brāhmaṇa father and a Brāhmaṇī mother, entitlement to the Veda belongs only to that Vedic twice-born who has been consecrated by the Vedic initiation (*upanayana*), because the effect must correspond to its instrument. Likewise, for one consecrated by the *Śaiva* mantras, once the corresponding status of the twice-born is established, it is logical that his entitlement is restricted only to the *janma-mantra*, worship, and so forth.
In that regard, the Teacher [resides] in the lotus of his own heart, beautified by the couch of Māyā. (68)

One should meditate upon Śiva and Śivā, the lords of knowledge, closely united within the beautiful lamp of knowledge, which is spread over the reality-principle of passion (rāga-tattva) and has the designation of "bound souls" (paśu) as its pillow. (16.69)
Having mentally worshipped those two, he should thereafter extract the life-force from the sacrificial animal;
having sprinkled water upon its heart-lotus and struck it with the weapon-mantra.
Having emerged from one's own head by means of the *suṣumṇā* through the exhaling breath (*recaka*),
and having entered the body of the disciple, [one should unite] the *pudgala* residing in the heart-lotus of oneself with that [of the disciple].
Having severed and detached [the bonds] with the Weapon-mantra (astra) and the goad (aṅkuśa),
one should draw [the soul] upward through the channel (nāḍī) and establish it at the End of the Twelve (dvādaśānta).
Having worshipped Dhruva, Tāra, Haṃsa, and Kāraka,
one should recite [the mantra]— that is to say,
having withdrawn the individual soul (pudgala) from that [place] by means of the saṃhāramudrā. || 16-73 ||

Then, having placed [the deity] within the womb of Śiva and Śivā in the lotus of one's own heart by means of inhalation (pūraka), and having rendered it of one flavor through retention (kumbhaka), having worshipped there mentally, and having contemplated what has arisen therein in the Vidyā, one should lead it upward through the Suṣumṇā by means of exhalation (recaka) to Brahman.

Having sequentially joined [the soul] to Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva, and having transcended them, one should unite it at the *dvādaśānta* (the end of the twelve fingers), worship it with the *dhruva* mantra, and then, using the *praṇava-haṃsa-praṇava*, grasp it with the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā]. Having thus [withdrawn it] through the *suṣumṇā* and placed it within the heart-lotus of the disciple, one should make it of one flavor (*samarasīkṛtya*) by means of the *haṃsa* mantra enclosed within the heart-mantra, and bathe it with the nectar from the *dvādaśānta*. One should then contemplate the disciple as being reborn, stainless, and like a youth.

Having manifested that disciple born [thus], purified by contact with Śiva—who is beyond the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) of Brahmā and the other causal deities—one should establish him in the status of a twice-born (*dvija*). (16–74)
In this regard, the *Makuṭottara* states:
"Just as a bee, having taken another insect wrapped in clay against a wall,
makes it its own kind through humming, buzzing, and so forth."
In the same way, through the purificatory rites of initiation, one becomes stainless and attains the state of Śiva.

Having offered three oblations with the root mantra for the sake of elevating his birth, and then having offered [with] "Oṃ Hauṃ, to Śiva, Svāhā" for the sake of attaining the status of a twice-born (*dvija*), one should offer three oblations with the mantra: "Oṃ, O Blessed One, may this self become a twice-born, purified in its origin, seed, food, state, and place; Svāhā! Then, by offering three oblations with the *purah* (introductory) mantras, one should cause him to attain the state of being a portion of Rudra [with]: "Oṃ, O Blessed One, may this self become Rudra; Svāhā! Regarding the five purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) as being like those of the Śiva-fire, according to the view of Brahmaśambhu, one should worship Sadyojāta and the others individually according to the procedure of the *agnikārya-paṭala* for the completion of the purificatory rites beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*), and offer oblations individually with the heart-mantra (*hṛdaya*) and the rest. This demonstrates the distinction between the purificatory rites of a twice-born person bound to transmigratory existence and those of a twice-born person who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*).
The rite of impregnation (*garbhādhāna*) is performed when [the woman] is known to be capable, based on the removal of impurities;
the seed [is placed] into [her] who has been purified by the touch of Brahmā and others. (16.75)
The manifestation of his sovereignty is the *puṃsavana* (the rite for ensuring a male child);
the knowledge [gained] through the discrimination between *māyā* and the Self is the *sīmantonnayana* (the parting of the hair). (16.76)
Through the abandonment of what is known to be rejectable and the grasping of what is to be accepted,
there occurs for him the rite of birth (*jātakarma*), for that indeed manifests his state of Śiva-nature.

For it has been said that the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*) is thus the fifth of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*); here Brahmaśambhu states [the others] as emerging from the womb, eating, and so forth. (16.78)

Even though these [rites] yield the fruit of worldly existence (*bhava*), they are auspicious on this path to liberation (*śiva*). Having performed for him the purificatory rites (*saṃskāras*) beginning with the extraction from the womb according to the prescribed method, one should then place the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) upon him with the root mantra. Then, for the sake of atonement, having offered a hundred or a thousand oblations of clarified butter with the *Prāsāda* mantra, and having performed the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), one should cause him to bow down before the water-pot (*kumbha*), the fire, and Śiva. Having worshipped Śiva once more and circumambulated him three times, the disciple—his hands not empty of gold flowers and other offerings—should prostrate like a staff before both Śiva and the Guru.
Having raised him up and greeted the disciple with blessings, the teacher [should proceed]. || 16-79 ||
With a clear mind, he should say, "You have been born worthy of the samaya.
