Indeed, initiation into the samaya is said to be for the attainment of goals both in this world and the next;
by means of the elevation of one's birth, a twice-born man becomes a master through reliance on knowledge.

Then he shall become fit for the rites of worship, recitation, and listening, as well as one whose soul is a portion of Rudra and who possesses the virtues of daily worship of Śiva and so forth. || 16-80 ||
On this point, Brahmaśambhu says:
"One should establish the phonemes as they are situated, along with their respective dependencies and one's own stages of life (āśramas),
by never transgressing the worship of Īśa, Agni, and the Guru."
However, the vow of a religious student (*brahmacārin*), whether he be a *bhautika* or a *naiṣṭhika*, ought to be properly undertaken without regard for his previous stage of life.

Thus it is said. From this [instruction], one should consecrate the five insignia—the ash-vessel, the rosary, the loincloth, the staff, and either matted hair or a topknot—using the five Brahmans and their limbs (*aṅga-mantras*), and then wear them.
First there is the fire-offering for the union of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna-homa*); then there is the worship for the satiation of the mantras.
Through the elevation of one's birth and the attainment of the status of a twice-born, one reaches the state of Śakti-consciousness by following the path step by step.
From the ritual refinement (saṃskāra), the attainment of Rudra-hood occurs; following that, the bestowing of the sacred thread (upavīta) is declared.
This atonement (prāyaścitta), the prostration, and the observance (samaya) constitute what is called the initiation of the Samayin (sāmayī dīkṣā). || 16-81½ ||

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, on General Rituals and Initiation into the Observances (*samayadīkṣā*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 16.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Next, the means for accomplishing the ritual procedures such as the initiation into Nirvāṇa is presented;
the true nature of the six paths is described exactly as it is.

The path of reality (tattvādhvan), the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan), the path of mantras (mantrādhvan), the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan), the path of words (padādhvan), and the path of kalās (kalādhvan)—this is the determination of the sixfold path. (17.2)
The five [categories] beginning with *tattva* are the pervaded (*vyāpya*), while the three beginning with *mala* are the pervaders (*vyāpaka*).
Furthermore, the [three] beginning with *mala* are again the pervaded, and the path of *kalā* (*kalādhvan*) is traditionally held to be the pervader.
In that regard, the thirty-six principles constitute the path of principles (tattvādhvan) in reverse order;
the path of phonemes (varṇādhvan) is the sequence of letters beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *a*. (17.4)
The Brahma-mantras beginning with the Sadyojāta, as well as the heart-mantras and so forth, and the root-mantra—the path of mantras—have already been demonstrated here previously. (17.5)
The two hundred worlds beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Śakti, together with the twenty-four cities, are called the path of worlds (bhuvanādhvan). || 17.6 ||

In this [mantra-extraction], those words beginning with *vyoma* that number eighty-one, when taken in reverse order, constitute the path of words (*padādhvan*); this is what has been taught in the extraction of the mantra.
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, Śānti as the fifth, and Śāntyatītā—these indeed are the Kalās; thus has that Path of Kalās (kalādhvan) been shown. || 17-8 ||
Since it has not been mentioned previously in this tantra, the path of the worlds (bhuvanādhvan) is now described:
[the worlds] named Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, and Hāṭaka, as well as those of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. (17.9)
And here, within the Brahmāṇḍa, there are six worlds of Raudra;
at the base of the Brahmāṇḍa is the world of Kālāgni, measuring ten koṭis [of yojanas].
His celestial chariot is one hundred thousand yojanas in extent;
his lion-throne is five thousand [yojanas] and possesses a circle of fire.
In this *Mañjarī* it is said: "And that Kālāgni stands, desiring to incinerate the worlds, with a body ten thousand *yojanas* in extent,
possessing three-eyed, formidable faces from which flames of fire issue forth, and which are radiant with fangs."

He is endowed with various serpent ornaments and possesses arms holding a noose, a goad, a sword, a shield, a bow, arrows, fire, a khaṭvāṅga, a trident, a skull-cup, and making the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons.
Thus it is said; moreover,
he is formidable, with matted locks of tawny hue scattered about, possessing the brilliance of a mass of lightning flashing through a line of not-too-thin firebrands.
Wearing a garland of terrifying severed heads and clad in a skin, his body white with ashes, Kālāgnirudra shines forth. (17.12)
That god was surrounded by seven crores of terrifying Rudras who resembled his own form, as well as the lords of those [groups], numbering ten.
Dhūmreśvara, Kapila, Kālaka, Adhīśvara, Jalada, Cañcala, Artheśa, Īśa, Ananta, and Padmabhū. (17–14)
These lords of groups numbering seventy lakhs each reside in the ten directions, beginning with the east, together with their retinues.
Above the world of Kālāgni lies the world of the Kūṣmāṇḍas;
it is ninety lakhs of yojanas in both its extent and its height. (17–15)
In the midst of that is his abode, five thousand yojanas in extent; there dwells Kūṣmāṇḍa, whose body is a thousand yojanas tall, who possesses three eyes and three faces,
with jagged teeth terrifying from their fangs, and who is full of self-importance with a loud laugh like the flames of fire.
With matted hair tawny like lightning, he holds in his hands a hand-drum, a skull-topped staff, a noose, and a goad;
he bears a trident, a skull-cup, fire, and serpents, and wears a garland of entrails and bones.
Moreover,
with his hair and garments bound by chains of bells, seated upon a corpse-throne, his body smeared with ashes, and adorned with various kinds of serpents;
Surrounded by hosts of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and jambhakas numbering sixty million,
the formidable Lord Kuṣmāṇḍarudra shines resplendent, established in his own abode.
Beneath that, all around, in hells numbering five crores where sinners are cooked in extreme suffering, [there are... 17-18.
Of those as well, there are thirty-two principal hells;
these also consist of three groups, each having its own three presiding lords.

These are Raurava, Kumbhīpāka, and Avīci. Furthermore, there are eleven hells dominated by Raurava, known as Raurava, Mahāraurava, Śīta, Uṣṇa, Santāpana, Vidāraṇa, Paṅka, Mahāpaṅka, Asipatravana, Sūcīmukha, and Kālasūtra, as well as Kṣuradhāra. Similarly, there are [others]: Kumbhīpāka, Aṅgāranicaya, Śvabhaikṣaṇa, Asṛkpūyapaṅka, Krakacapāṭana, Taptaloha, Taptavālukā, Asthibhaṅga, Sūkaramukha, Māṃsabhakṣaṇa, and Vāṅmukhalambana.

There are eleven hells, chief among which is Kumbhīpāka; and ten hells, chief among which is Avīci, namely: Avīci, Kriminicaya, Kūṭaśalmali, Nirucchvāsa, Āmedhyakūpa, Krimikūpa, Andhakūpa, Nirālambanapatanā, Śūlaprotā, and Vaitaraṇī. Kūśmāṇḍarudra is recorded as the lord of all these hells.
The extent of each of them is recorded as ninety lakhs [yojanas].
Indeed, all seven netherworlds (pātālas) are situated one above the other.
Aṭala, Pātāla, Nitala, Gabhastita,
Mahātala, Sutala, and beyond that, Rasātala.
One should know that these [seven netherworlds] are composed, respectively, of gold, ruby, sapphire, topaz, silver, and crystal;
whereas Rasātala is composed of stone and strewn with pearls.
Therein dwell the Daityas, Dānavas, and Nāgas who have performed meritorious deeds in the past.
Dwelling in these netherworlds, they are devoted to the worship of Hara’s feet.
Virocana, Hiraṇyākṣa, Prahlāda, Bali, Śambara, Vṛtra, and other lords of the Daityas, who dwell in the netherworlds and in heaven. (17–24)
And Viṣṇu, who possesses an infinite form and is intent upon supporting the earth,
also dwells in that divine abode, eternally honored by the lords of the nāgas.
Therein is the auspicious city of Vāsuki named Bhogavatī;
it is divine, composed of gold and jewels, and endowed with celestial enjoyments.

In those [lower regions], seven Rudras, the lords of the Pātālas, dwell here and there; they are known by the names Caṇḍa, Vijaya, Jyeṣṭha, Āmaya, Atharvapada, Mahārudra, and Nairṛta. Generally, the god Hāṭakeśvara is the lord of all the Pātālas.
The golden city of Hāṭakeśa is surrounded by divine hosts;
it is equal in width and length, measuring two thousand yojanas. (17–27)

His celestial palace measures two hundred yojanas in extent. In its center sits the three-eyed one, possessing the luster of gold, seated upon a lion-throne, divine in form, and holding with his arms the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, as well as a deer and a water-jar.
(153) Resplendent with a serpent as his armlet, the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, a snake as his bracelet, a garland, and a matted lock of hair;
accompanied by Pārvatī, Hāṭakaśiva is surrounded by divine attendants. || 17-28 ||
He was constantly being worshipped by the daughters of the Daityas, Dānavas, and the lords of the Nāgas, as well as by young boys, with heaps of fragrant flowers.
Indeed, above that world of mortals, extending up to the Satyaloka, there exists the realm of Brahmā, which is said to be sevenfold and filled with the creations of Brahmā.
Its ground is ten lakhs of yojanas in thickness and fifty koṭis of yojanas in extent, situated in the shape of a lotus.
In its center stands Mount Meru, the golden mountain, shaped like a pericarp;
it extends sixteen thousand yojanas below the surface of the earth.
It is likewise eighty-four thousand yojanas in height;
at its base, it is sixteen thousand yojanas in width.
That great mountain extends twice as far again at its summit;
the city of Brahmā is fourteen thousand yojanas [in extent].
In the center here is the divine Mānasī city, blazing with the luster of various jewels.

To its east and in the other eight directions are the eight cities of the world-protectors, Indra and the rest, constructed by Viśvakarman. These are known as Amarāvatī, Tejovatī, Sāṃyamanī, Kṛṣṇāvatī, Śuddhāvatī, Gandhāvatī, Mahodayā, and Yaśovatī.
Slightly to the west there is also the great city of Viṣṇu.
In the same way, on the eastern and western sides, there is a mountain named Jyotiḥśikhara,
measuring eight thousand yojanas in extent.
There, in those celestial palaces, Hara, accompanied by Pārvatī and surrounded by the lords of the Gaṇas, sports, being honored by the gods.
The Gaṅgā, having descended from heaven, flooding the lunar orb,
fell upon that mass of Śiva’s matted locks and emerged from it.
Sītā is renowned as having gone to the eastern direction, Bhadrā to the northern direction, Alakanandā to the southern, and Sucakṣu has gone to the western direction. (17.38)
Having gone in the four directions, they entered the salt ocean; that is to say:
Mandara is in the east, Gandhamādana is to the south of Meru, Vipula is the western mountain, and Supārśva is situated in the north. (17.39)

These four supporting mountains of Meru are each eight thousand *yojanas* in extent, abounding in jewels, and frequented by divine beings. In them, respectively, are celestial gardens and lakes. As it is said: "The Caitraratha grove is in the east; Gandhamādana is in the south; likewise, Vaibhrāja is on Vipula, and Nandana is recorded as being on Supārśva. (17.40)
Aruṇoda, Subhadra, Sitoda, and Mānasa— these lakes,
enjoyed by the gods, are situated in order upon Mount Mandara and the others.
And likewise, among the trees on Mount Mandara and the others, one should know there is a quartet:
the kadamba, the jambu, the pippala, and the vaṭa.
Each of these mountains is two thousand yojanas in width and height.
As for the Jambu tree situated on Mount Gandhamādana, this continent is called Jambūdvīpa after its name. (17.43)
Fruits as large as great elephants, sweet and flavorful, fall from it by the thousands at all times. (17.44)
From that fruit-juice arose a river named Jambūnadī,
frequented by gods, gandharvas, siddhas, and cāraṇas.
By the touch of that water, wood, clay, gravel, and so forth,
become gold known as Jāmbūnada, possessing sixteen colors.
By bathing in and drinking that water, all four classes of living beings become golden-hued, free from decay, and possess a lifespan of ten thousand years.
Surrounding Meru, it is renowned as being one hundred thousand yojanas in extent;
for those regions of Jambūdvīpa are indeed nine varṣas.
(155) This island is surrounded on the outside by the Lavana Ocean;
among the nine regions (varṣas), Ilāvṛta is the central one. (17.49)
And Meru, situated in their center, is joined by the Kesara mountains;
to the south of Ilāvṛta are the regions named Hari and Kimpuruṣa.
(Bhārata consists of) nine regions and three mountain ranges among them; Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat are here in the south. (17.51)
All of them extend from east to west and flow into the eastern and western oceans;
the three regions—Ramyaka, Hiraṇmaya, and Kuru—are equal in size to Ilāvṛta.
In the north, as before, there are three mountains extending eastward—
Nīla, Śveta, and Triśṛṅgin— which are situated at the boundaries of the regions (varṣas).
To the east of Ilāvṛta is the single region known as Bhadrāśva;
to the west is Ketumāla; and between these two are the two mountain ranges that demarcate the regions.
The Mālyavat and Gandhamādana mountains extend as far as the Nīla and Niṣadha ranges;
the inhabitants of Ilāvṛta are lotus-colored and subsist on the juice of jambu fruits.
Their lifespan is thirteen thousand years, and Śaṅkara is their object of worship.
In Bhadrāśva, the humans are white, possess divine forms, and have a lifespan of ten thousand years.
In Harivarṣa, those who resemble safflower in hue and possess a lifespan of ten thousand years worship the god Maheśvara while partaking of divine mangoes.
All the men there worship Viṣṇu and subsist on sugarcane products;
in Kimpuruṣa, the men are golden-hued and have a lifespan of ten thousand years.
Subsisting on the fruit of the *plakṣa* tree, they worship Brahmā;
in Bhārata, however, there are many castes, with various languages, foods, and lifespans. (17.59)
All [these] perform various worship of the gods and likewise perform various rituals:
Māhendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, and the Ṛkṣa mountain.
The Vindhya, the Pāriyātra, and seven other principal mountain ranges are here;
likewise, the principal rivers here are the Gaṅgā and the Godāvarī.
The Yamunā, Narmadā, Tāpī, Kṛṣṇaveṇā, Sarasvatī, Tuṅgabhadrā, Kāverī, Sindhu, Tāmraparṇī, and others likewise. (17.62)
All these rivers are remembered as destroyers of all sins when touched, drunk, or bathed in;
this, indeed, is the land of Bhārata, adorned with nine islands.
This meritorious island situated between Kumārī and Himavat is said to be the land of action for those who proceed toward heaven and liberation. (17.64)
Other islands belonging to Bhārata, which are crowded with barbarian peoples, are Indradvīpa, Kaśeru, Tāmravarṇa, and Gabhastimān. (17.65)
The Nāga, the Saumya, the Gāndharva, and the Vāruṇa is recorded as the eighth;
in this Kumārīdvīpa, however, there are preeminently the celestial sages (devarṣis).
Those places which may exist shall also be mentioned here in brief; furthermore, fifty-six cities among the elements such as water and the rest will be described. (17.67)

Indeed, those very places of Śambhu are seen here as well under names such as Amareśa and others; that is to say, [they are his abodes]. Here, on Mount Mahendra, is the descendant of Jamadagni, and Agastya is on Mount Malaya. (17–68)
In the Sahya mountains dwell Brahmā, Hari, and Īśāna; Kumāra resides on the Śuktimat mountain; Śiva dwells in the Ṛkṣa range; and the Man-lion (Nṛkesarī) resides on the Pāriyātra mountain.
In the Vindhya mountains is Durgā; on the Himavat is the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa.
In Ketumāla, the men are dark-blue and the women resemble blue lotuses.
Those devotees of Rudra who eat milk-rice have a lifespan of ten thousand years;
in the Ramya region, they are as white as silver and live for five thousand years.
Those who dwell in Madhvāśā are devotees of Brahmā, possessing beautiful limbs and eternal youth;
those in Hiraṇyaka are golden-hued, while those in Drākṣāśā have a lifespan of ten thousand years.
Likewise, the men in Kuru-varṣa are devoted to the sun and resemble gods;
those born in Mithuna are dark-complexioned and subsist on the Kalpa-tree.
Their lifespan is twelve thousand years, and the two Śivas are remembered as worthy of worship on Kailāsa, Hemakūṭa, Himavat, and also in the north.
On Mount Triśṛṅga, Mandara, Nīla, and Gandhamādana, as well as in the Karṇikāra forest, are the cities of the Ruler of Cities. (17.75)
For the celestial palaces there are indeed primarily made of gold and jewels;
moreover, on Kailāsa is the auspicious city of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) known as Alakā.
O Vasudhārā, you who are the source of riches for the Vasus and the repository of jewels for the celestial sages;
on Ekaśṛṅga is the hermitage of Brahmā and of Jaigīṣavya.
On Gajaśaila is Durgā; on Sunīla is the city of the Rākṣasas; on Sumegha is that of the King of the Gods (Indra); and on Śvetādri is that of Garuḍa.
And there, on that very Krauñca mountain, on Mount Jārudhi, is the abode of Ṣaṇmukha;
on the hundred-peaked mountain (Śataśṛṅga) are the Yakṣas, and likewise on the three-peaked mountain (Triśṛṅga) is Śrī.
Indeed, on the thousand-peaked king of mountains are the cities of the Vidyādharas;
on Mahālakṣmī’s [mountain] is Parijāta, and on Sarasvatī’s is Supārśvaka.
On Mount Añjana, which is white with apsarases and gandharvas;
on Mount Kumuda, however, belong the Rudras; and on Mount Jārudhi belongs the Sun.
On Mount Piñjara is the abode of Gaṇapati; on Haṃsakūṭa is that of Brahmā; in that very place is the realm of Sanaka and others; and on Pañcaśailaka is the domain of the Daityas.
In the southern salt ocean lies the city of the Rākṣasas called Laṅkā;
in the sugarcane ocean are the islands and cities of Gaṇeśa.
In the Ocean of Wine (Surābdhi) are the cities of Bhadrakālī and the Bhairavas;
there, indeed, are also those of Vīrabhadra, the Mothers, and Kṣetreśa. (17.84)
In the ocean of clarified butter belongs Agni; in the ocean of curds belong the gods and Brahmā; and in the ocean of milk belonging to Nārāyaṇa-Hari is the exceedingly beautiful Śvetadvīpa.
Abounding in celestial chariots made of gold and jewels, extending five hundred thousand [yojanas],
it is filled with four-armed beings of white complexion who bear the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Adorned by men and women who have attained the same form as Viṣṇu,
the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa lies there upon a divine celestial chariot.
On his divine couch of the serpent Śeṣa, the Sovereign (Virāṭ) shines resplendent together with Śrī and Bhūmi,
served by Kumuda and others, as well as by the hosts of Viṣvaksena and the rest.

And there too, certain groups [of beings] exist who possess divine forms and three eyes, are covered in ashes, marked with the triple horizontal lines (tripuṇḍra), and are devoted to the worship of Rudra. (17.89)

In the ocean of sweet water, situated in their respective directions, there are indeed separate cities belonging to the world-protectors and the lords of progeny, which possess various enjoyments. (17.90)
Enough with excessive detail; that which is relevant is now introduced: Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śalmala, Plakṣa, and Puṣkara;
[these are surrounded by] the oceans of salt water, milk, curd, clarified butter, molasses, wine, and fresh water. (17.91)
Thus, in some tantras as well, the sequence beginning with honey and so forth is taught according to the divisions of the two, four, and [other] oceans. (17.92)
Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmala, Kuśa, Krauñca, and beyond that Śāka and the one called Puṣkara— these are the seven continents surrounded by oceans.
The oceans of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk,
and fresh water have been described in their entirety.

Thus, between these two mutually contradictory positions regarding the sequence of continents and oceans, the latter is stated here by relying upon the greater number of authoritative opinions. (17.95)
Beyond Jambūdvīpa lies the salt ocean, which is twice its size;
beyond the salt ocean is the island named Plakṣa, which is twice as large and circular in shape.
In that [continent], there are exactly seven regions and seven mountain ranges. They are as follows: the regions are named Śānta, Abhaya, Śiśira, Sukhodaya, Ānanda, Śiva, and Kṣemaka.

The mountain ranges are named Gomedaka, Cakraka, Nārada, Dundubhi, Somaka, Ṛṣabha, and Vaibhrāja; they touch both the salt ocean and the sugarcane ocean, and all are one thousand yojanas in breadth and height. Therein, however—
The Āryakas, the Kuraras, the Vidaṃśas, and likewise the Bhāvins; || 17-97 ||
The castes shall be exactly four, just as they are here among the Brāhmaṇas and the others;
and they shall have a lifespan of five thousand years and possess enduring youth. (17.98)
Worshipping Mahādeva in the form of Soma, they dwell in happiness;
even the seven rivers of rain here are heated by the nectar of Śiva. (17.99)
The rivers Vipāpā, Tridivā, Nandā, Sukṛtā, and Amalodakā flow there;
Ikṣūda is twice as large as Plakṣa, and Śālmaladvīpa is twice as large as that. (17.100)
And on that island there are seven regions, mountains, and rivers.
As they have said:

the regions are named Harita, Jīmūta, Rohita, Vaidyuta, Mānasa, Haṃsa, and Suprabha. The mountains, named Kumuda, Kumudonnata, Valāhaka, Droṇa, Kaṅka, Mahiṣa, and Kakudman, are straight and elongated, reaching from the Ikṣu ocean to the Suroda ocean.
Yonitoyā, Vitṛṣṇā, Candrā, Śuklā, and Vimocanī. || 17-101 ||
Nivṛtti and Subhadrā—these are the seven rivers in Śālmala;
they are the Kāpilās, Aruṇās, Pītās, and those called Kṛṣṇās, corresponding respectively to the twice-born (Brahmins) and the other castes.
There, mortals with a lifespan of ten thousand years worship Vāyu; they are smoky-colored.
Outside of Śālmaladvīpa is the Suroda ocean, circular in shape and twice its size. 103.
Kuśadvīpa is twice as large as this; in it there are indeed seven regions:
Udbhida, Veṇumān, Suraya, Lambana, and Dhṛti.
Prabhākara, Kapila, Varṣa crowded with prosperous people, Vidruma, Dyutimān, Hema, Hari, Puṣṭa, and Kuśeśaya. (17.105)
And the mountains, including Mandara, are situated amidst the oceans of Surājya; they possess a golden luster, and the inhabitants of those regions live for seven thousand years.
Double the size of Kuśadvīpa is the outer [region], and double that again is Krauñcadvīpa;
it has seven regions, rivers, and mountains. (17.107)
The rainfalls are known as Kuśala, Manohara, Uṣṇaka, Pravara, Andhakāra, Muni, and Dundubhi. The mountains are known as Krauñca, Vāmana, Kāraṇḍaka, Divispṛś, Vivida, Puṇḍarīka, Dundubhi, and Svana.
Gaurī, Kumudvatī, Sandhyā, Rātri, Manojava, Khyāti, and Puṇḍarīkā are recorded as the principal rivers. (17.108)
The Puṣkaras, Puṣkalas, Dhanyas, Tiṣyas, and other Brāhmaṇas and so forth, who worship Śiva, live for eight thousand years. (17.109)
Outside of Krauñca, however, is the Ocean of Curd, which is twice as large;
beyond that is Śākadvīpa, which is twice the size of this [Krauñca], and in it there are indeed seven regions. (17.110)
The ages are named Jalada, Kumāra, Sukumāra-maṇicaka, Kusumottara, Moda, and Mahādruma.
The mountains are Udaya, Raivata, Śyāmāka, Astagiri, Āmbikeya, Ramya, and Kesari. (17–111)
Sukumārī, Kumārī, Nandinī, Veṇukā, as well as Ikṣukā, Dhenukā, and Gabhastī—these are the seven rivers. || 17-112 ||
There, the four castes are the Nagas, the Magadhas, the Vamanas, and the Nandakas; they are yellowish in complexion and live for seven thousand years.
And they worship the form of the Sun.
Outside of Śāka, however, is the Ocean of Milk, which is twice as large as that; beyond this is Puṣkara.
Therein lies a single mountain range of the continents known as Mānasottara. (17.114)
In its middle, this great mountain is circular in shape, fifty thousand yojanas in width, and as many [yojanas] in height.
And on both sides of that [mountain], likewise on the upper terrace,
there is the Mahāvīta forest within and the Dhātakī grove without.
In that region there are no rivers nor castes; all the people are predominantly twice-born, live for ten thousand years, and possess a golden complexion. There, they worship Vāyu in embodied form.
In the center of that Mānasottara mountain stands a banyan tree measuring three thousand yojanas; in it dwells Brahmā together with his retinue.
To the north of that is the abode of Śambhu, whose body is half-Hari;
here Hari-Hara resides, being worshipped by gods and asuras. (17.118)
Twice the size of Puṣkara is the great ocean of sweet water (Svādūda) on the outside;
beyond that lies the land of gold (Hiraṇyabhū), measuring ten crores of yojanas.
Outside the Sweet Ocean (Svādūdaka) is the Golden Earth (Hiraṇyadharaṇī), ten crores [yojanas] beyond the Ten-faced one (Daśāsya).
Beyond that is the Lokāloka mountain, equal in height and breadth to Meru.
Indeed, outside of this is the lifeless darkness (tamas), extending for thirty-six crores [yojanas].
And externally, beyond the shell of the cosmic egg, that [atmosphere] is dense for sixty million yojanas. || 17-120 ||
Enough of this digression. Now, the Bhuvarloka and the other worlds are described. It is as follows:
One hundred thousand *yojanas* above the earth, the path of the sun is said to be located.
The diameter of the sun’s chariot, however, is nine thousand *yojanas*. (17.121)
The orb of light from that [sun] is indeed three times its size in measurement;
the world of the sun (Sūryaloka) should be known as crowded with hundreds of celestial palaces (vimāna).
It is adorned with delightful gardens containing assembly halls and reservoirs of water;
the moon is situated one hundred thousand [yojanas] from the sun, and beyond that is the circle of the constellations.
Therefore, the wise one [Mercury] is two hundred thousand [yojanas] from that; from him, Bhārgava [Venus] is two hundred thousand;
from Bhārgava, Bhauma [Mars] is two hundred thousand; and likewise, Bṛhaspati [Jupiter] is two hundred thousand from Bhauma.
At a distance of two hundred thousand yojanas, Saturn is situated from the Guru (Jupiter).
The chariot of Soma has three wheels, and its horses are as white as jasmine flowers.
Ten horses carry him, and that is known as the world of Soma;
moreover, the chariot of Budha has eight red horses, for that indeed is his world.
The great chariot of Śukra also has eight horses resembling safflower;
the golden chariot of Bhauma indeed has eight horses as red as rubies.
The chariot of Bṛhaspati is golden and renowned for having eight white horses;
the chariot of Śani is also made of gold and has eight brindled horses.
The chariot of Rāhu is smoke-colored and adorned with eight blue horses;
it is recorded that eight horses, smoke-red in hue, are yoked to the chariot of Ketu.
The station of those two, Soma and Sūrya, is indeed declared to be below [the others];
however, their respective worlds are proclaimed to be distinct from one another.
One hundred thousand yojanas above Śani is the mandala of the Seven Sages;
one hundred thousand yojanas above them, Dhruva stands as the central pivot.
The Pole Star (Dhruva) is said to be the impeller of the planets, lunar mansions, and stars.
Above the earth is the Bhuvarloka, which is remembered as extending up to the path of the stars.
Above that, up to the path of Dhruva, is the celestial world called Svarga.
Therein is the auspicious city of Śakra named Amarāvatī. (17.133)
There are thousands of celestial chariots there belonging to the divine sages,
as well as those of the Ādityas, the Rudras, the Vasus, and even the two Aśvins.
The cities and worlds of the Maruts and the Sādhyas, as well as those of the world-protectors and the preeminent royal seers, were likewise situated in their respective directions. (17.135)
The celestial chariots of the Gandharvas and the Pitṛs are by the thousands;
and the abode of others who have conquered heaven is likewise known as Svar.
They enjoy their respective enjoyments right there, in accordance with their own merit.
Even the Śiṃśumāra is the support for Dhruva, situated above Dhruva.
Ten million yojanas from Dhruva is Maharloka, filled with the gods who dwell in celestial palaces (vaimānika-sura).
Two million yojanas above Maharloka, the world known as Janaloka is situated. (17.138)
There, the high-souled sons of Brahmā born of his mind, perfected in their ritual observances and augmented by the power of yoga, dwell. (17.139)
"Until the dissolution of Brahmā" means up to that point.
Three crores [of yojanas] above Jana-loka, Tapo-loka is established. Those gods named Vairājas who dwell in Tapo-loka are they. (17–140)
They too remain until the dissolution of Brahmā.
Sixty million [yojanas] above the world of Tapas, Satya is established;
that is to be known as the world of Brahmā, its duration lasting until the dissolution of Brahmā. (17.141)
The lords of creatures, as well as the stainless Dakṣa, Bhṛgu, and others, and other ascetics who discourse on Brahman and have conquered the world of Brahmā. (17.142)
That abode of Brahmā cannot be described;
above Satyaloka, slightly higher than that, lies the great city of Viṣṇu.
Consisting of light and boundless, it is impossible to describe;
there, in the realm of Brahmā, Brahmā himself always dwells, being worshipped by the gods and others. (17.144)
In his own world, the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu sits upon the seat of Ananta, accompanied by yogis such as Kumuda and others, and by his hosts beginning with Viṣvaksena. (17.145)
Accompanied by all his weapons, such as the discus and others, personified in bodily form,
he is situated ten million yojanas above the world of Viṣṇu.
The world of Rudra stands before him; its power is not capable of being surpassed.
Encircled by a rampart of light, it possesses a radiance equal to ten million suns.
There, the three-eyed god with the moon as his crest-jewel, possessing a divine body,
was accompanied by Skanda, Nandi, Gaṇeśa, and other attendants who also bore divine forms.
Being worshipped by those liberated through attaining a form similar to his who are devoted to the adoration of the Lord,
he dwells eternally with the Goddess Umā in divine celestial chariots.
Enough with further description. From the earth up to the level of the Truths (satyas), there are seven Rudras, each being the presiding lord of his respective realm, as stated in the *Mañjarī*:
"On the earth is Subhadra; in the atmosphere, Vāyuvega; and in heaven, the one known as Mahāvīryaparākrama."
Rudra, Mahastha, Vikata, Parastat, the renowned Mahakala, and Kavaidyuta.
The Lord of the World of Truth (Satyaloka) is Śveta; beyond him is Brahmā, and beyond him is Hari.
Rudra himself is the Lord of his own world, said to reside within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa).

Now, outside the Brahmāṇḍa, in each of the ten directions, there are ten cities of Rudra; their names are to be known by the designations of the hundred Rudras beginning with Kapālīśa. Regarding this, it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"There, in separate locations, are [cities] measuring one hundred thousand yojanas, most radiant;
there resides the power of Rudra, Bhadrakālī, together with her own Gaṇas."
Thus, the worlds beginning with Kālāgni and ending with the city of Bhadrakālī exist individually within the earth-element (pṛthvītattva).
This refers to one hundred and eight worlds (*bhuvana*).
Beyond these, there are indeed worlds situated within the principle of water (*ap-tattva*) and the others;
they are exceedingly vast, most radiant, and great. (17.150)
(164) It would not be possible to describe them according to their true nature even in hundreds of years; therefore, there is a fear that the work would become too voluminous. (17.151)
They are shown in brief for the sake of establishing the path of the worlds (*bhuvanādhvan*):
from the principle of earth (*pṛthvītattva*), the principle of water (*aptattva*) is to be known as ten times greater than that.
The *tejastattva* (fire-principle) is tenfold [in extent] compared to that; from it, *vāyu* (air); and from that, *viyat* (space).

In this manner, one should know the principles (*tattvas*) beginning with earth and ending with *māyā* to have progressively increasing dimensions. The principles of *śuddhavidyā*, *īśvara*, and *sadāśiva* are each increased ten-thousandfold in succession. Because the principles of *śakti* and *śiva* are without beginning or end, their measurement is not stated.
Now follows the arrangement of the worlds (*bhuvanas*) within these principles, beginning with water. (17–153)
In the purification of the paths (*adhvaśodhana*), these should be known separately and in sequence by the teachers;
however, even within the seven principles (*tattva*), the group beginning with Amareśa is not included among those called the eight secret ones (*guhyāṣṭaka*).
In the fire [element] resides the group of eight beginning with Hariścandra, known as the "Secret of Secrets";
in the ether resides the group of eight beginning with Vastrāpada, known as Bhīma;
and in the seven [tattvas] beginning with the subtle element of smell reside those ending with Ahaṅkāra.
The eight [groups] beginning with Śarva, including Ucchuṣma and Gaṇḍa, are situated in the principles (tattvas);
likewise, the eight divine origins beginning with the Piśāca are situated in the intellect (buddhi). || 17.157 ||
The first group of eight, beginning with Yoni, is situated here within Prakṛti as unmanifest and so forth;
whereas that which consists of the eight Sthaleśvaras, beginning with Mahādeva, is [the second]. (17.158)
In the reality of Time (kālatattva) and in Māyā, [the group] should be known as established;
the group of nine beginning with Vāmā and Jyeṣṭhā resides in that which is called Śuddhavidyā.
The eight worlds of the Vidyeśas, known by the names Ananteśa and the others, are to be understood by the teachers as situated within the Īśvara-tattva in their proper sequence. (17.160)
The world known as Sadāśiva is situated within the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva;
the five worlds designated by the names of the kalās, beginning with Nivṛtti, are located within the Bindu.
The pentad beginning with Indhikā is situated in the Nāda;
beyond that, the pentad beginning with Vyāpinī is established in the Śakti alone.
(165) Two hundred and twenty-four worlds, which reside on the path of the principles (tattva-adhvā), have been briefly described as belonging to the deity Vidyā. (17.163)
All these worlds are filled with embodied beings,
brought forth by the will of Śiva through the unfolding of the power of action (kriyā-śakti).
Since bodies extending to the end of the earth are composed of an excess of earthy dyads and other [compounds], they are indeed of an earthly nature.
In the worlds such as Bhuvarloka and others, the auspicious bodies of the gods are recorded as being sometimes composed of water,
sometimes of fire, and sometimes of wind.
The all-pervading space (vyoman) is known to be mixed with the city-of-eight (puryaṣṭaka),
[residing] here among the principles beginning with the mind and ending with Māyā, as well as within the worlds.
Bodies are primarily composed of their respective *tattvas* due to the manifestation of *māyā*.
For individual souls (*aṇu*s), there is a collection of bodies beginning from *śuddhavidyā* and ending with the *śakti*s. (17.168)
He is considered pure, consisting of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*), because of the perception of the pure reality (*śuddhatattva*);
however, at the time of initiation for liberation (*nirvāṇadīkṣā*) and so forth, [he is affected] by past and future karmas. (17.169)
In all these worlds, the embodied soul is that which is to be purified.
Enough with this excessive detail; now the pervasion of these paths is correctly described in their proper sequence. (17–170)
The earth element (pṛthvītattva) and the letter *kṣa* are the two mantras of Hṛdaya and Sadyojāta; furthermore, Kālāgni, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Hāṭaka, Brāhma, and Vaiṣṇava [are associated with them].
Within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa), there are six worlds belonging to Rudra;
outside the egg, the hundred Rudras are stationed in the ten directions.
Kapālīśa, the unborn Buddha, Vajradeha, the crusher;
the pervasive lord, the imperishable teacher, Pinākī, the sovereign of the thirty gods. || 17-173 ||
Agni, Rudra, Hutāśa, Piṅgala, Khanaka, Hara, Jvalana, Dahana, Babhru, Bhasmānta, and Kṣayāntaka. || 17-174 ||
Yama, Mṛtyu, Hara, Dhātṛ, and likewise Vidhātṛ;
he is the agent, the uniter, the disuniter, and indeed Dharma itself. (17.175)
In the same way, the Lord of Dharma stands there as the tenth, situated on the right;
he is Nirṛti, the slayer and destroyer, with a cruel gaze and a terrifying appearance. (17.176)
Ūrdhvakeśa, Virūpākṣa, Dhūmra, Lohita, Daṃṣṭrin, Bala, Atibala, Pāśahasta, and Mahābala. (17–177)
Then Śveta, Jayabhadra, Dīrghahasta, Jalāntaka, Meghanāda, and Sunāda— these ten are stationed in the western quarter.
Swift is Vāyu, Vāyuvega, Subtle, Sharp, the End of Destruction;
the Destroyer of the Five, Pañcaśikha, Kapardin, and Meghavāhana.
These ten renowned Rudras are established in the northern direction (Vāyavyā).
They are the Lord of Treasures (Nidhīśa), Rūpavān, Dhanya, Saumyadeha, and Jaṭādhara. (17–18)
Lakṣmīdhara, Ratnadhara, Śrīdhara, Prasādana,
and Prakāśa as the tenth— these are situated in the northern direction.
Lord of the sciences, omniscient, enjoyer of knowledge, one who has reached the further shore of the Vedas;
lord of the gods, eldest of all, protector of beings, and lover of offerings.
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣadhara, Ananta, Krodhana, Mārutāśana, Grāsana, Udumbarīśa, Phaṇīndra, and Vajradaṃṣṭrin. (17–183)
Śambhu, Vibhu, Guṇādhyakṣa, Tridaśa, Tridaśeśvara, Saṃvāha, Vivāha, Lipsu, Brahmā, and Trilocana. (17–184)
Above those Rudras stands Vīrabhadra;
such is the world of Bhadrakālī, consisting of one hundred and eight [worlds].
The worlds of the Rudras have been described individually according to their own names.

Oṃ, salutations! O Ananta, salutations to Śiva! Oṃ, salutations again and again! O All-bestowing One, O Śarva, O Śiva, O Subtle One, O Subtle One, O Sound, O Sound, O Tawny One, O Tawny One, O Bird, O Bird, O Swift One, O Swift One, O Witness, O Witness, O You who were established from of old, O Unpraised One, O Unpraised One, O Unworshipped One, O Unworshipped One, O Supreme One beyond Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra, O Bringer of Presence to all!

O bestower of happiness upon all beings, O source of existence, exist, exist! O All, All! O First, First! Release, release! O Lord of Yoga, O you of great splendor, O Lord of True Being, O Mahādeva! *Thapra* ¾¾ 28.
From the word at the end of the mantra up to the word "Mahādeva."
The words, numbering twenty-eight, should be [arranged] in reverse order;
thus, the fivefold path is conjoined with the sixth, the *nivṛtti-kalā*.
The sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan) should be contemplated as pervading [all things] according to its divisions:
water, fire, air, space, smell, and taste and form. (17–188)
Touch and sound, speech, feet, hands, anus, and genitals;
and the ear, skin, eyes, tongue, and nose—these are the sense organs. (17–189)
That triad of internal organs, known as mind (manas), ego (ahaṅkāra), and intellect (buddhi),
has as its supreme cause and source Prakṛti, which consists of the three guṇas for all beings.
The twenty-three principles are [indicated] in reverse order by their number: *ha*, *sa*, *ṣa*, *śa*, *va*, *la*, *ra*, *ya*, *ma*, *bha*, *ba*, *pha*, *pa*, *na*, *dha*, *da*. (17–191)
The syllables ya, ta, ṇa, ḍha, ḍha, ṭha, and ṭa—these twenty-three phonemes, as well as the Śiras and the mantra named Vāmadeva, likewise constitute the cities. (17–192)
There are fifty-six [sites] in sequence, known by the names beginning with Amareśa:
Amareśa, Prabhāsa, Naimiśa, Puṣkara, and Aṣaḍhī. (17–193)
Ḍiṇḍī, Muṇḍī, and Bhārabhūti—these eight are in the water-tattva;
as are Hariścandra, Śīśaila, Jalpīśa, Āmrādakeśvara, and [the others]. (17–194)
Madhyameśa, Mahākāla, Kedāra, and likewise Bhairava—
this group of eight worlds is established within the element of fire (tejastattva).
Gaya, Kurukṣetra, Naulakha, Kanakhāla, Vimaleśa, Aṭṭahāsa, Mahendra, and Bhīmakeśvara. || 17-196 ||
Thus there are eight worlds situated within the principle of air (vāyutattva):
Vastrāpada, Rudrakoṭi, Avimukta, and Mahālaya.
Gokarṇa, Bhadrakarṇa, Svarṇākṣa, and Sthāṇu—
these constitute the eight worlds situated within the principle known as Ākāśa.
Chagalaṇḍa, Dviraṇḍa, Mākoṭa, Maṇḍaleśvara, Kālañjara, Śaṅkukarṇa, Sthūleśa, and then Sthaleśvara. (17–199)
Beginning from the subtle element of smell (gandhatanmātra) and extending up to the ego (ahaṃkāra) on the path,
these eight worlds are situated in their respective order.
The Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Yākṣa, Gāndharva, Aindra, Saumya, Prājāpatya, and Brāhma— these are the eight divine wombs for the intellects.
Akṛta, Kṛta, Bhairava, Brāhma, Vaiṣṇava, Kaumāra, Auma, and Śrīkaṇṭha—thus the eightfold yoga is established. (17–202)
But this Bhauvana [world] is situated within the principle of Guṇaprakṛti;
thus, by means of seven groups of eight, it consists of fifty-six [levels] in due order.
Just as the worlds are thus established, so too are these twenty-one words:

Maheśvara, Paramātman, Śarva, Śiva, Nidhanodbhava, Nidhana, Anidhana, Oṃ Svaḥ, Oṃ Bhuvaḥ, Oṃ Bhūḥ, Dhū Dhū Dhū, Nā Nā Nā, Anāde, Abhasma, Adhūma, Anagne, Arūpa, Jyoti Jyoti, Teja Teja, Prathama, Arūpin, Arūpin. (Thus, there are twenty-one.)
Beginning from the one called Maheśvara, it extends up to the state of the formless (arūpi-pada).
Thus, the fivefold path should be considered as being pervaded by the sixth [category], namely the *pratiṣṭhā-kalā*; such is the sixfold pervasion of the paths. (17–205)

Now, within the category of Vidyā (Knowledge), there are Puruṣa (the Person) and Rāga (Attachment), as well as Aśuddhavidyā (Impure Knowledge), Kalā (Limited Agency), Niyati (Necessity), and Kāla (Time). || 17-206 ||
Māyā consists of seven principles joined with the seven vowels;
Ña, Jha, Ja, A, Cha, Ca, Ṅa, and Gha are the two mantras Śikhā and Ghora.
The worlds of Vāma are twenty-seven in number: Vāma, Bhīma, Ugra, Bhava, and Īśāna. (17–208)
Ekavīra and Puruṣa—these six are the lords of the world (bhuvaneśvaras): Pracaṇḍa, Umāpati, Aja, Ananta, and Ekarudraka.
This pentad of worlds, however, is situated within the principle of passion (rāga-tattva);
while Krodha and Caṇḍa are established within the Vidyā principle, which is impure (aśuddhā).
In Niyati [are] Jyotis and Saṃvarta; then those known as Sukara, Pañcāntaka, Ekavīra, and Śiva, who have reached the level of Kalā. (17–211)
And "at the proper time" means up to this point:
Mahādeva, Vāmadeva, Udbhava, Ekapiṅgala, Ekanetra, and likewise Īśāna; after that is Bhuvaneśa. (17–212)
And "thumb-sized" (aṅguṣṭhamātra)—these eight are the Sthaleśvaras;
from the principle of Time (kālatattva) up to Māyā, there are twenty-seven Bhauvanīs.

O Pervasive One, O All-pervading One, in every sky; O Consciousness of the unconscious, O Supreme Refuge of Maheśvara; O You whose form is light, Lord of all Yoga, Sovereign of all sciences, the Deathless One, the Protector, the Secret beyond secrets—*oṃ*, salutations again and again to Sadyojāta, the source of existence; to Vāmadeva, the secret; to Aghora, the heart; to Tatpuruṣa, the face; to Īśāna, the head; to Śiva, the source of all; *oṃ*, salutations to Śiva, whose food is meditation.
From the word "Pervasive One" (*vyāpin*) up to the word "whose food is meditation" (*dhyānāhāra*), there are twenty words here; this constitutes the entire *Vidyākalā*. (17–214)

One should thus contemplate [the universe] as pervaded by the established arrangement of the sixfold path (ṣaḍvidhādhvan). Now, within the power of tranquility (śāntikalā), there are also Śuddhavidyā and Īśvara.
Sadāśiva and the three principles (tattvas) are indeed situated within it;
there are three phonemes (varṇas), namely ga, kha, and ka, which constitute the two mantras of the armor (kavaca) and the person (puruṣa).
In this [system], there are exactly eighteen worlds designated by names beginning with Vāmā:
Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, Raudrī, Kālī, and Kalavikaraṇī; || 17-217 ||
Balavikaraṇī, Balapramathanī, and likewise Sarvabhūtadamanī; the ninth, however, is Manonmanī.
Thus, in due order, they are situated within the principle (tattva) called Śuddhavidyā:
Ananteśa, Sūkṣma, and then Śivottama.
Ekanetra, Ekarudra, Trimūrti, and another, Śrīkaṇṭha and Śikhaṇḍin—these are the worlds called Īśvara. (17–220)
The world known as Sadāśiva is situated within the principle (tattva) of Sadāśiva.

Homage to the eternal Yogi, established upon the seat of yoga (yogapīṭha), to the everlasting, the fixed, the Unsupported (Anāśrita), the Lordless (Anātha), the Infinite Śiva, the all-pervading one whose form is space and who pervades space. Herein, from "the Eternal Yogi" onwards, there are eleven words. (17–221)
Thus, ending with the words "pervading the sky" (vyomavyāpin), they are established in five ways;
they are pervaded by the sixth, the Śāntikalā, according to the wise.
The pervasion consisting of the sixfold path should be understood as occurring in successive order;
likewise, the Śiva-tattva is established within the state beyond tranquility (śāntyatītā).
The sixteen vowels beginning with 'Sa' (Sarga) are the *svara*s; when reversed, they likewise constitute the *astra*, *īśāna*, and *mūla*—for these are indeed the three mantras. (17–224)
Indeed, there are exactly fifteen worlds here, beginning with Nivṛtti:
Nivṛtti, Pratiṣṭhā, Vidyā, and likewise Śānti; || 17-225 ||
For the kalās are indeed beyond peace (śāntyatītā), while the worlds reside in the bindu;
they are Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocis, Mocikā, and likewise Ūrdhvagā. (17–226)
The five [principles] beginning with Bhuvana are indeed the Nāda and Kalās;
they are Vyāpinī, Vyomarūpā, Anantā, and Anāthā. (17–227)
The Kalās, as well as the Śākta worlds, are likewise unattached.
That which begins with the Mantra and the Praṇava is [the first], while that which ends at the Antaka is in reverse order.
In this way, there is one *pada*; this path is said to be fivefold.
One should know that it is pervaded by the *kalā* beyond peace (*śāntyatīta*), according to the sequence of the paths.
Sixfold pervasion has been declared according to the determination of the Śaiva Āgamas;
the worlds (bhuvanas) number two hundred and twenty-four. (17-230)

One who possesses knowledge of the six paths is liberated and can liberate others from the ocean of existence. On one side, there are six kinds of paths; on the other, there are eleven mantras and eighty-one words.
Furthermore, there are thirty-six principles (tattvas), fifty letters, and five groups of kalās.
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, the Determination of the Six Paths (Ṣaḍadhvanirṇaya), in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 17.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter. Then,

for the purpose of the initiation into Nirvāṇa, the Guru— having performed his daily rites, having withdrawn and then emitted [the deities], and having consecrated his own body with the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa— [proceeds].

Having performed the scattering, the throwing away, and the pouring of the previously desired auspicious water-pot and weapons, one should invoke Śambhu into whichever mandala is appropriate and worship him as before.
Regarding this, Brahmaśambhu states:
"One should not cause the destruction of the arrangement of colored powders by means of flowers, nor by fragrance, nor by unbroken grains (akṣata), nor by water."

Thus, on the edge of that mandala, one should worship as on the painted cloth; having worshipped Śiva in the fire-pit and in the fire, one should satisfy him with the prescribed offerings as before. (18.3)

Having scattered the sacrificial offering (bali) and cast aside the purificatory grass (pavitra), the preceptor, restrained in speech, having thoroughly washed his feet and hands, having sipped water for purification (ācamana), and wearing white garments— || 18-4 ||
Wearing a turban, an upper garment, and a ring with a sacred thread (*pavitra*),
and having consecrated his body with the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite as before by means of the general water offering (*sāmānyārghya*).

Having performed all the rites prescribed for the *samayadīkṣā*— beginning with the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), inspection (*nirīkṣaṇa*), smearing with ashes (*bhasitatāḍana*), binding the eyes (*netrabandha*), entry into the pavilion (*maṇḍapapraveśa*), purification of the disciple’s inner organ (*śiṣyāntaḥkaraṇaśodhana*), the casting of the flower-offering (*puṣpāñjalikṣepa*), worship of Śiva, the water-jar (*kumbha*), and the fire (*agni*), and ending with the unification of the channels (*nāḍīsandhāna*) at the edge of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the offering of the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) along with the surrender of the mantras—

thereafter, one should perform the "kindling" (*dīpana*) of the root and limb-mantras in their proper sequence, each individually enclosed by the seed-syllable of the crest (*śikhā*) joined with fire. (18–6)
Having uttered the root syllables and the limbs beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and ending with *phaṭ*, one should offer clarified butter three times; that indeed causes the manifestation of the mantra.
Now, for the disciple of the upper body, there is a thread woven from new fibers;
that thread, which extends the length of the body, is for the purpose of binding the noose.

Having consecrated it with the Astra-mantra, enveloped it with the Kavaca-mantra, and worshipped it, one should tie it to the crest-lock (śikhā) of the disciple. For the sake of worldly enjoyment (bhukti), for a male, one should suspend it while pressing down on the big toe of the right foot; for a female, while pressing down on the big toe of the left foot. For one seeking liberation (mumukṣu), having first tied it to the big toe and afterwards to the crest-lock, one should meditate upon that thread as being identical to the disciple’s Suṣumnā. Then, reciting "Oṃ Huṃ, obeisance to Suṣumnā," one should withdraw the Suṣumnā from the disciple’s body by means of the Saṃhāriṇī [power], join it to that thread, worship the thread as being of the nature of the Suṣumnā, envelop it with the Varma-mantra, and offer oblations three times for the sake of invoking its presence (sānnidhya).

Having sprinkled him with water at the region of his heart and struck him with the flower-arrow, he himself, uttering the syllable *huṃ* with a protracted vowel (*pluta*) through the path of exhalation (*recaka*), [should draw the soul out]. (18.9)
Having entered the disciple’s heart through the channel while recollecting that consciousness—
which resembles a shimmering star— one should sever it from its root with the weapon-mantra.
Having drawn forth [the syllable] situated at the dvādaśānta, augmented by the power of Śiva,
and having grasped it within the enclosure of the heart, one should then [place it] upon the cord with the Saṃhāriṇī [mudrā].
Having joined [the mantras] and meditated on the pervasive [deity], and having veiled it with the armor-mantra (kavaca),
one should worship and then offer three oblations with the root mantra alone.

One should perform acts such as striking and seizing according to the Sūtra, not in a state of conflict; one should contemplate the bonds of impurity and so forth upon this animal according to that Sūtra. (18.13)
Then, one should assign the *kalās*, beginning with Śāntyatītā, to the threads, as they are capable of producing the body which is the locus of experience for the enjoyer. (18.14)
For example:
"The seed-root is said to be located at the crown of the head in the past;
likewise, [the letter] 'sa' with the nasal bindu, situated in the wind, possesses the twelfth vowel. (18.15)
The seed-syllable of peace (Śāntibīja) is known to extend from the forehead to that place, the throat;
the seed-syllable of the crest (Śikhābīja), mounted upon fire, is known as the seed-syllable of knowledge (Vidyābīja). (18–16)
From the throat to the navel is that location where the Vidyā is established;
it consists of the letter ending in *s* (sa) mounted upon the letter ending in *l* (la), joined with the fourth vowel and the bindu. (18.17)
The seed-syllable for the foundation (pratiṣṭhā) is situated from the navel to the ankles;
it consists of the letter 'sa' joined with the long vowel 'ī', ending with the nasal 'm', and topped by a bindu. (18–18)

The seed-syllable and its location are also said to extend from the ankle to the sole of the foot; these are called the "Kalās" (digits), consisting of the seed-syllables of the digits beginning with *Tārā*, each accompanied by the dative case-ending (*caturthikā*). (18–19)
In striking, they should end with *huṃ phaṭ*; in commissioning, they should end with *namaḥ*;
and in the fire-oblation (*homa*), they should end with *svāhā*. One should apply them in this manner according to the Sūtra.

Thus, having struck the aforementioned locations beginning with the *mūrdhan* (the crown of the head) with the Flower-Arrow (*puṣpāstra*), one should withdraw the past and other *kalās* by means of the Withdrawal Mudrā (*saṃhāriṇī mudrā*) and sequentially join them to their respective threads. Thereafter, one should contemplate the relationship of the pervaded (*vyāpya*) and the pervader (*vyāpaka*). In this context, the principles (*tattva*), worlds (*bhuvana*), states (*pada*), phonemes (*varṇa*), and mantras are the pervaded; impurity (*mala*), karma, and Māyā, along with its lords (*īśa*), are the pervaders. Furthermore, impurity and the rest are the pervaded, while the levels such as *śāntyatītā* are the pervaders. Therefore, by the inclusion of the pervaders, the principles and so forth, as well as impurity and the rest, are subsumed; thus, through these [levels] which have been brought forward, present, purified, and cleansed, they become pure.
Then, having worshipped the nooses situated upon the thread with their respective mantras,
the rite of kindling (uddīpana) should be performed according to the sequence that will be described.
Having uttered the seed-syllables of Tārā, Aghora, and Kalā, joined with their names in the dative case and ending with *hūṃ phaṭ*, one should offer three oblations in succession.
Thus, there should be an awakening of the past and other kalās;
thereafter, the binding with fetters (pāśabandha) must be performed according to the sequence of the past and other kalās.

That is as follows: having struck [the thread] as before with the Flower-Arrow (puṣpāstra), one should utter the seed-syllables of the Kalās—past and so forth—enclosed by the root-mantra preceded by the *praṇava*, saying: "O Blessed One! Bind, bind the pervasive [entities] of the Śāntyatīta-kalā—the bonds, impurities, Māyā, Karma, the powers, the principles (tattva), the worlds, the mantras, the phonemes, and the words (adhvan)—huṃ phaṭ! Thus, one should tie a knot in the thread at the location of each Kalā, beginning with the past Kalā and ending with Nivṛtti, in order to bind the bonds (pāśa). Thereafter, having placed the bonds within a pair of shallow bowls (śarāva), one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with their respective mantras.
Having cast [the oblation] into the mandala of Śambhu, the preceptor should present it as an offering and perform worship.
And having led [the disciple] from there for the sake of protection, one should offer him into the *śivakumbha*.

Having performed here the fourteen rites—namely, the illumination of the mantra (*mantradīpana*), the suspension of the thread (*sūtrāvalambana*), the union with the *suṣumnā* (*suṣumnāsaṃyoga*), the joining of the disciple’s consciousness (*śiṣyacaitanyayojana*), the resolution regarding the impurities (*malādisaṅkalpa*), the striking (*tāḍana*) beyond the *śāntā*, the grasping (*grahaṇa*), the union (*saṃyoga*), the offering of worship (*pūjāsamarpaṇa*), the kindling (*uddīpana*), the binding of the fetters (*pāśabandhana*), the immersion (*sampāta*), and the offering into the *śivakumbha* (*śivakumbhasamarpaṇa*)—one should thereafter cause the naming (*praṇāma*) of the *kumbha*, the *Śiva*, and the fire. (18–25)
Outside the pavilion, to the east, for the disciple who has sat down facing east upon three separate small mandalas in sequence; || 18–26 ||
One should cause [the disciple] to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), a portion of the sacrificial porridge (caru), and a tooth-stick;
for the sake of liberation, [he should eat] from a palāśa leaf, and for the sake of enjoyment, from an aśvattha leaf. (18.27)
In that regard, some say one should cause [the initiate] to consume only eight mouthfuls of the sacrificial porridge (caru), and not more.
The auspiciousness or inauspiciousness of this [act] is to be known by the falling of the tip of the tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha).
A fall toward the directions of Soma (North), Indra (East), or Īśa (Northeast) is auspicious; in other directions, it is inauspicious. (18–28)
One should perform a pacification homa for inauspiciousness with the root mantra, the limb mantras, and the sacrificial fees,
upon a well-smeared ground covered with a layer of *darbha* grass and an upper cloth.

On the eastern ground obtained by a hundred [repetitions of] the weapon-mantra, one seeking enjoyment should sleep with the head toward the east; one desiring liberation should sleep on a bed of ashes with the head toward the south. (18.30)
One should touch him with the Heart-mantra, bind his topknot with the Heart-mantra,
and cover him with a fine white cloth using the Astra-mantra.

Having drawn three concentric circles outside the bed using wash-water from sesame and mustard seeds as if they were a rampart, and having offered the bali-offering to the spirits with the Astra-mantra, [one should proceed].
And having himself consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and so forth, and having sipped water for purification, the Guru should sleep there.
Then, having risen in the morning, bathed, and performed his daily obligatory rites, [he should proceed].
Having brought the disciple, authorized by Śiva, he should examine his dreams;
having approved them if they are auspicious, but if they are inauspicious, for the sake of their pacification. (18.34)
Having offered sesame, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, and white mustard seeds one hundred times with the combined mantras,
as well as with the Aghora and Astra mantras, and having given the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), [one should proceed].
One should have the twice-born and those bearing sectarian marks recite, "May there be a good dream.
Now, auspicious and inauspicious dreams are described: heard, seen, experienced, desired, and likewise related. (18–36)
Dreaming is traditionally said to be of seven types: [the dreamer], the one who has already occurred, the one yet to come, and the indicative;
among these, the first five are fruitless, while the last two—the one yet to come and the indicative—are productive of results.
The falling from a height of one's own limbs, hair, and nails; of teeth, palaces, and houses; and likewise of deities, the moon, the sun, trees, and oneself. (18.38)
(175) Shaving, oil massages, and marriage; being harmed by horned animals, fanged beasts, or birds; or riding on donkeys, camels, horses, or swings. (18.39)
A journey facing south, sinking into pits, mud, or water, failing to rise from there, and the manner of proceeding for one who has fallen—these are [the omens]. (18.40)
Or by widows, or by shaven-headed women, or even by those who are deformed;
by those who are exceedingly dark and extremely fierce, wearing black and red garments and iron ornaments. (18.41)
Embracing and hugging women who are adorned yet ungentle, and the draining of rivers, streams, and oceans. || 18-42 ||
The extinguishing of lamps, fire, or light; the breaking of images and lingas; and the wearing of black garlands, garments, ointments, red clothes, and so forth. (18.43)
The application of turmeric ointment causes obesity and the breaking apart of the limbs of the body;
likewise, [the consumption of] cotton, sesame, oil-cakes, gold, black pepper, and food [is similarly destructive]. (18.44)
Gain and purgation, clarified butter and fish, [the teaching], the drinking of honey, oil, sugarcane juice, and buttermilk, as well as singing and dancing. (18.45)
Separation from beloved ones, union with the undesired, [reproach] from gods, brahmins, ancestors, and even ascetics, as well as threats, beatings, and the like. (18.46)
Eating cakes, parched grain flour, or dry food with water and such;
extinguishing a lamp or the like; or the falling off of the leather of one's feet. (18.47)
Beholding and touching those who are naked, those who are unseemly, those with shaven heads, those dressed in black, those wearing saffron robes, and monkeys; 18.48.
Mounting a donkey, camel, boar, buffalo, or the like, or riding in such a vehicle; bathing in cow dung, smearing oneself with it, or associating with those who are ungentle or infants. (18.49)
In a dream, such things as being embraced by the dead in social gatherings, drinking parties, and the like, bring about the suffering of fear regarding one's own destruction. (50)
Even for those who are healthy, [such dreams] may lead to disease or even death.
Hereafter, auspicious dreams that indicate success are described. (18.51)
(176) The gathering of white garlands, garments, ointments, lamps, and mirrors;
and of curd, milk, clarified butter, betel, fruits, rice, and cloths. (18.52)
There is the acquisition of rice, śāli rice, barley, conch shells, pearls, and women; as well as the obtaining of those with handsome forms and white attire, and being drenched in blood. (18.53)
Crossing a river or the waters of the ocean, seeing a blazing fire, touching the moon, the sun, or the stars, and mounting a human vehicle. (18.54)
Even for humans and cattle, there is an ascent to trees, mountains, elephants, palaces, planks, milky trees, bones, lofty celestial mansions, and the earth. (18.55)
Bestowing grace upon eminent ascetics, the foremost of Brahmins, the ancestors, the gods, and others;
and the collection of distinctive emblems such as the *liṅga*, rosaries, images, and specific ritual weapons. (18.56)
Setting fire to one's own limbs, clothing, house, and so forth; wrapping oneself in entrails, or smearing one's own body with excrement. (18.57)
Death, or the touch of a corpse, or the eating of raw flesh;
or being bitten on one's own right hand by a white-colored serpent. (18.58)
In a vessel made of lotus or gold, one should partake of a meal of milk-rice with ghee;
or consume curd and milk, and drink either wine or nectar.
The acquisition of a full water-pot, or the pursuit of a woman who is forbidden; the acquisition of a crane, a hen, a curlew, or a female swan, signifies the arrival of a son. (18.60)
The acquisition of mantra-texts, sciences, lutes, or medicinal herbs; the obtaining of parasols belonging to the Asuras; and bathing at sacred fords (tīrtha). (18.61)
Seeing such things in a dream indicates the attainment of success, prosperity, and happiness; likewise, the sight of Brahmins, gods, ancestors, and ascetics [is auspicious]. (18.62)
"Whatever they say in a dream will indeed come to pass exactly so.
Thus concludes the section on dreams.

Now, having led the disciple—who has bathed, performed his twilight devotions (*sandhyopāsana*), offered salutations and worship to Śambhu, the water-pot (*kumbha*), and the fire of Śiva, and who holds the *pāśasūtra* as before—into the pavilion by the command of Śiva, [the teacher] approaches the vicinity of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
Having seated her and invoked her into the fire with the mantra "Oṃ hām, obeisance to Ādhāraśakti," one should offer clarified butter three times with that same mantra ending in *svāhā*.
Then, one should deposit the five paths (*adhvapañcaka*) within that Ādhāraśakti. (18.63)
The cessation that pervades that [earth] is also described as its differentiation;
the earth-element (pṛthvītattva), the letter *kṣa*, and the two mantras of the Heart and Sadyojāta.
Twenty-eight steps, starting from the last one in reverse order,
comprise one hundred and eight worlds, beginning with Kālāgni and ending with Kālī.
Having withdrawn the Nivṛtti-kalā from the thread by means of its own mantra,
and having offered it into the fire along with the Śakti, one should offer three oblations for the sake of invoking her presence.

Having offered oblations with that very [mantra] ending in *agnipriya*, one should there contemplate the impurity (*mala*) and karma [as being removed] from the fettered soul (*paśu*) once again by means of the bond consisting of Māyā.
And by the will of Śiva, having conceived various embodied wombs within these worlds, [He] brought about the generator of the state of being an enjoyer, the body of enjoyment, and so forth. (18.68)
To those who are in accordance with the worlds, who have their limits, and who arise from karma,
and to Vāgīśī, who pervades them— Oṃ Hāṃ, salutation to Vāgīśvarī.
Having invoked [the deity] with this, one should worship.

Having offered oblations three times with this very mantra ending in *svāhā*, one should pray: "O Blessed One, O Mistress of Speech! Be present for the sake of favoring the sacrificial animal (*paśu*). Then, having sprinkled [the disciple] with the water of the *arghya* while reciting the *astra-mantra*, and having struck him in the heart with the *puṣpāstra-mantra*, one should enter the disciple's heart through the *suṣumnā* by means of the *recaka* (exhalation). Having severed that consciousness with the *astra-mantra* and drawn it out with the *aṅkuśa-mudrā*, one should join it to the form of the *bindu* at the *dvādaśānta* by means of the root mantra. While pronouncing the *haṃsa* mantra encapsulated by the *praṇava*, one should bring that consciousness of the disciple to the lotus of one's own heart by means of the *pūraka* (inhalation). Recalling the root mantra and performing *kumbhaka* (retention), one should then grasp it with the root mantra and lead it to the *dvādaśānta* by means of the *recaka*. Thereafter, with the *bhava-mudrā*, one should simultaneously effect the union of the disciple's consciousness with all the infinite matrices (*yoni*)—whether born from a womb, an egg, sweat, or a sprout, or even those of mental origin—as previously described, in the form of the manifestation of assuming a body. Following that:
This seven-syllable mantra of Śivā’s husband, beginning with *tāra* (oṃ) and *mūla* (hūṃ), is declared to be the mantra for the union of the womb, conception, birth, and so forth. (18.70)
O Blessed One! At the conclusion of this [practice], one should recite this mantra: "May you effect the simultaneous conjunction of this self with all wombs—do it, do it!"

(p. 178) In that regard, following the word *ātmanaḥ* (of this self), at the point where it says "conjunction in all wombs," one should perform the rites to be described—such as the formation of the embryo and birth from the womb—by joining them with their respective names and uttering "do, do. Having offered three oblations everywhere with the root mantra (*mūla*) and three times with the seven-syllable mantra, and having uttered "O Blessed One" and so forth three times, one should pray. Therein, having sequentially accomplished the conjunction in all wombs, the formation of the embryo, and the birth from all wombs, [one should proceed].
Then, from the beginning, there is a simultaneous growth of all the bodies.
Having recollected past karma and future karma for the sake of the accomplishment of experience,
one should remember the acquisition of the karma of experience within all bodies born from every womb.

Therein, having offered oblations as before, one should first perform the acquisition of karma that bestows various enjoyments by reciting "kuru kuru" (*perform, perform*). In the *lokadharmikā* [rite], one should visualize and offer the acquisition of karma consisting of past and future dharma and adharma.

Furthermore, during the initiation of the practitioner, while recollecting the past and future karma, one should offer oblations for the bodily, sensory, and active functions attained at that place and time. (18.73)
Through differentiation, there arise various forms of pleasure and pain for this self, which is embraced by the state of being an experiencer, as a result of past and future karmas. (18.74)
Recalling that this enjoyment is subject to sensation and dependent upon attachment to sense objects, one should offer three oblations with the root mantra and the four-syllable mantra.
In that regard, one should say for this sacrificial animal: "Bring about the accomplishment of all enjoyments!

Bring about! On this point, Bhojarāja states: "In the case of initiation for a householder (*lokadharmika*), one should offer oblations after contemplating various forms of enjoyment according to the distinctions of place, time, body, and objects produced by past and future merit and demerit. In the case of initiation for an aspirant (*sādhaka*), the offering of oblations should be performed after contemplating various forms of enjoyment according to the distinctions of place, time, body, and objects produced by past karma alone.
Then follows dissolution (*laya*) within those enjoyments, characterized by supreme delight.
One should offer oblations with this intention, as before, for the sake of causing absorption into that.

"Perform, perform absorption (laya) in the form of supreme delight in enjoyments. Thereafter, for the sake of accomplishing the latent impressions (saṃskāra) of caste, lifespan, and enjoyment, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Heart-mantra; here Brahmaśambhu has stated the purpose. (18.77)
Just as an autumn cloud is light once its water has been used,
so too is purity prescribed for this reality when karma has been exhausted.
It is said that [the rite] consists of non-reproduction and expiation;
for that purpose, one should offer a hundred oblations with the *hṛdaya* [mantra].
Thus, having offered oblations three times with the root mantra and with the seven-syllable mantra beginning with "Bhagavan," one should pray, "Perform the purification of all actions, perform! and,
having resolved upon the absence of worldly enjoyment, one has emerged from the noose of *māyā*.
And having contemplated the separation from that [state], by means of the seven root syllables and so forth. || 18-78 ||

Then, having offered [the oblation], one should contemplate the impure body characterized by attachment to sense objects as its state of being an enjoyer; for the sake of its purification, one should perform ten offerings.
Having resolved upon the separation of impurities by means of the root mantra, one should offer three oblations;
likewise, for the sake of the purification and separation of even ritual action, one should offer three oblations.

Then, with the root mantra and the seven syllables, and again with the name of the Lord [Bhagavan], one should perform the severance of the three bonds (*pāśatraya*) consisting of *māyā*, impurity (*mala*), and karma by saying "sever, sever" (*viśleṣaṃ kuru kuru*). Having thus effected the severance of the bonds, one should offer oblations three times with the weapon-mantra (*astra*), the root-mantra, and the seven-syllable mantra for the bond of cessation (*nivṛttipāśa*), which pervades the principles (*tattva*) such as impurity. Then, with the name of the Lord [Bhagavan], one should contemplate the cutting of that bond by saying "cut the bond of cessation, cut it" (*nivṛttipāśacchedaṃ kuru kuru*).
Thereafter, because all matrices and bodies have been destroyed, [one effects the liberation] of the Self residing therein. || 18-81 ||

Then, having meditated upon oneness, one should offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) with the root mantra joined with the syllable *vauṣaṭ*, preceded by the *tāra* and ending with "namo brahmaṇe. (18.82)
Having spoken thus, having invoked and worshipped [the deity],
and having offered three oblations with the mantra: "Oṃ brahman, accept sound and touch, svāhā!"— thus having offered the three oblations.
Thereafter,
O Lord of Causes, may he who has gone to that state free from affliction not be obstructed by you.
"An obstruction must be established; this is the command of the Supreme Lord.
Having thus given the command of Śiva, he should dismiss Brahmā, the lord of the causes such as the *nivṛtti-kalā* and the *pāśas*.
In this way, the consciousness of the disciple becomes pure, with the luster of crystal. (84)
Having remembered [the soul] as liberated from the fetters of *nivṛtti*, one should perform the extraction (*uddhāra*).
Having offered oblations as before with the mantra beginning with "O Bhagavan," one should say, "Perform the extraction from the fetters of the *nivṛtti* kalā!
Having extracted that consciousness by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [mudrā], one should [draw it up] by means of the inhalation (*pūraka*). (18.85)

Having established [the disciple] within himself, the Guru should then, in an instant, draw him up by means of exhalation (recaka) and join him to his own thread-body; for the sake of stability, he should offer oblations three times.
Then, having worshipped Vāgīśvarī and offered three oblations with her own mantra,
one should dismiss her and then unite the pure *kalā* with the impure.
Then one should utter the short seed-syllable of the pure Nivṛtti;
subsequently, the names of the completely pure Pratiṣṭhā, ending with the long vowels, [should be uttered] in sequence. (18.88)
Having first honored the compound ending in the dative case with the word "namaḥ," one should then offer oblations three times with this very mantra, ending with the wife of Agni (svāhā).
One should contemplate the dissolved, purified withdrawal within the stage of establishment (*pratiṣṭhā*).
Thus ends the purification of the *nivṛtti*-kalā.
Herein, the sequential order of the aforementioned rites is prescribed. (18–90)
And that which serves for the purification of the kalās beginning with Pratiṣṭhā is the foundational power (ādhāraśakti) and the principle (tattva); it is not of a single origin with Vāgīśī. (18.91)
The undertaking of the disciple's self, the conjunction in all wombs, the completion of the embryo and its birth, and thereafter the acquisition of karma. (18.92)

Sovereignty, the attainment of enjoyments, dissolution, expiation, the separation from impurities and the like, and the severing of the bonds—all these are accomplished through the *pūrṇā* [offering]. (18.93)
The offering to the Lord of Causes, the extraction, the taking up, the unification, and thereafter the further application within the body of the Sūtra, as well as the dismissal of Vāgīśvarī. (18.94)
"The light of the nature of the pure reality occurs during the ritual of the unification and worship of the *kalās*;
thus, the sequence of ritual action is the same even for the *kalās* beginning with *Pratiṣṭhā*. (18.95)

Then, having propitiated Śakti with her own mantra, having performed the installation (pratiṣṭhā), invoked her presence, and established her, he should worship her and offer oblations three times with that [mantra] for the sake of her proximity—[oblations] which consist of the bonds of impurity (mala), action (karman), and illusion (māyā), and which produce the state of being an enjoyer, the body of experience, and so forth.

(p. 181) Having contemplated that [the universe] is pervaded by *Pratiṣṭhā*, one should meditate upon the fifty-six worlds (*bhuvana*), twenty-one words (*pada*), and twenty-three phonemes (*varṇa*) within the path of principles (*tattvādhvan*) from Earth (*ādi*) up to Nature (*prakṛti*) as being pervaded by *Pratiṣṭhā*, along with the *Śiraḥ* and *Vāma* mantras. Having offered oblations three times with the root-mantra and the seven-syllable mantra, one should say: "O Lord, bring the impurities and other principles of this self into proximity (*sannidhi*) within the category of *Pratiṣṭhā*—do, do! Thereafter, having visualized the various types of wombs (*yoni*) within the fifty-six worlds, one should invoke, install, and worship Vāgīśvarī, who pervades them. Having offered oblations three times for her presence, and having performed the sprinkling, striking, entry, cutting, attraction, grasping, and so forth as before, one should, by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), concentrate the consciousness of the disciple residing in the self, and by means of exhalation (*recaka*), seize it as it reaches the end of the twelve (*dvādaśānta*). Then, as before, having simultaneously manifested it in all the wombs, one should offer oblations three times with the root-mantra and the seven-syllable mantra. With the mantra beginning "O Lord," one should separately perform—as before—the acts of union, conception in the womb, birth, the acquisition of karma, experience, and dissolution within all the wombs. Having offered a hundred oblations with the *Śiraḥ* mantra during the rite of expiation (*niṣkṛti*), and having brought about expiation as before, one should effect the separation [of the soul] from the bond of *Māyā* due to the absence of experience and its emergence from it, offering oblations as before; then, meditating on the separation from the effects of impurity (*mala*) such as the state of being an enjoyer, one should effect that specific separation by offering oblations as before; and likewise, one should effect the separation from karma. Having offered oblations three times with "Oṃ Viṣṇo! Take the *puryaṣṭaka* (eightfold subtle body) of this self, Svāhā!", and having proclaimed the command with "O Lord of Causes, etc.," one should dismiss [the deity]. Then, having offered oblations as before with the root-mantra and the seven-syllable mantra, and having extracted [the soul] from the bond of *Pratiṣṭhā* with the mantra beginning "O Lord," saying "perform the extraction, perform," one should place that consciousness back in the self as before and cause it to enter the thread-body (*sūtra-śarīra*). Having worshipped and dismissed Vāgīśvarī, and having performed the connection of the categories (*kalā-sandhāna*) through the utterance of their respective seed-syllables and so forth according to the *Pratiṣṭhā* and *Vidyā* rites, one should worship and offer oblations, and contemplate *Pratiṣṭhā* as dissolved into *Vidyā*. Now, in order to purify the category of *Vidyā*, one should worship the Power (*Śakti*), invoke, install, and worship the category of *Vidyā* with its own mantra, and offer oblations with it three times while observing its pervasion. One should contemplate that the seven principles from Puruṣa to *Māyā*, the seven phonemes, the twenty-seven worlds, the two mantras *Śikhā* and *Ghora*, the twenty words, and the triad of impurities (*mala*) and so forth—all are pervaded by the category of *Vidyā*. Having invoked, installed, and worshipped Vāgīśī, who pervades all wombs, with her own mantra, one should offer oblations three times for her presence.
