Then, having performed the sprinkling, striking, and so forth, and having offered oblations three times each with the root seven-syllable mantra for all the actions ending with the union in all wombs, conception, birth, experience, and dissolution, and having performed the appropriate rites with the mantra beginning "O Lord," one should offer a hundred oblations with the *Śikhā* mantra during expiation. One should effect expiation as before with the root seven-syllable mantra, saying: "By this expiation, perform the purification of all bonds, do, do! Likewise, having performed the oblations for separation, the cutting of the bonds, and the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) as before, one should then invoke Rudra with "Oṃ, obeisance to Rudra," install and worship him, and offer oblations three times. Then one offers three oblations with: "Oṃ Rudra! Take form and smell, Svāhā. Thereafter, having proclaimed the command with "O Lord of Causes, etc.," and having dismissed him, one should extract [the soul] from the bond of the *Vidyā*-category as before, place it in the self, and from the end of the twelve, cause it to enter the thread in the body.

Having offered oblations three times for the sake of stabilization, having worshipped and offered oblations to Vāgīśa, and having dismissed him, one should join the short and long *vidyā* and *śānti* seeds as before, effect their presence, offer oblations three times with the root mantra, and visualize the *vidyā* dissolved into the *śānti*-kalā; then one should purify the *śānti*.
Thereafter, having worshipped and offered oblations to Śakti with the seven-syllable mantra, one should invoke the *śānti* with its own mantra, establish it, worship it, and offer oblations. (18.96)

Having offered oblations with the root mantra for the sake of bringing [the deities] into proximity, and having meditated upon the fivefold path—the principles (tattvas) ending with Sadāśiva and the eighteen worlds (purāṇi)—[one should proceed]. (18.97)
In this [mantra], there are eleven words, two mantras—the Kavaca and the Pūruṣa—and three phonemes; these are to be understood as being pervaded by Śānti, each individually.
Then, recollecting Vāgīśvarī, the progenitor of various wombs,
one should invoke her, worship her, and offer oblations with the root mantra as before.

Thereafter, having performed—as before—the rites of sprinkling, striking, entry, cutting, drawing forth, seizing, joining, birth, the cleansing of karma, sovereignty, enjoyment, and dissolution; and having offered a hundred oblations with the *varman* mantra during the expiation (*niṣkṛti*), one should conclude by performing the purification of all fetters (*pāśa*) with the root mantra and the seven-syllable mantra, preceded by "O Lord," ending with the words "perform the expiation, perform the purification of all fetters" (*niṣkṛtya sarvapāśaśuddhiṃ kuru kuru*).
Then, through the root mantra and the seven-syllable mantra, etc., one effects the separation from all enjoyments and from both impurity (*mala*) and karma upon exiting from the state of enjoyment.
Having offered oblations for the purpose of separation, and likewise for the severing of the bonds with the weapon-mantra,
one should offer oblations from the seven-syllable root mantra of the Lord, whose nature is the primordial source.
Having completed [the rite] with "Cut! Cut!"—which severs that which pervades the principles (tattva) beginning with Māyā—and having offered the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as before, [one recites]:
"Oṃ, obeisance to Īśvara."
One should invoke and worship this [deity],
and having offered oblations to the intellect and the ego, one should say, "Accept [this]," using its specific name.
Having offered oblations three times and caused [the disciple] to hear [the mantras] beginning with Kāraṇeśa,
he should then dismiss that disciple— who has been liberated from the bonds of peace— unto the Lord (Īśvara).

"O Bhagavat, by means of the homa of the seven-syllable root mantra, perform the extraction from the bond of the peaceful kalās of the primordial self, as previously described, saying 'Do it! Do it! (18.104)

Having extracted that [soul] by means of the *saṃhāriṇī* [breath], and having joined it to the Self by means of the *pūraka*, one should cause it, extracted by the *recaka*, to enter the body of the thread of bonds (*pāśasūtra*). (18.105)

Having stabilized [the deity] with the root mantra and offered oblations, and having likewise worshipped and offered oblations to Vāgīśvarī, one should release [her] and perform the conjunction of the kalās.

As before, having offered [oblations] for both the short and the long [mantras], according to the distinction between pure and impure, and likewise for Śānti and Śāntyatītā, he should perform the fire sacrifice.
Having performed the pacification (śānti) for the dissolved [deity] in the past, one should purify that which has passed;
then, having invoked Śāntyatītā, established her, and worshipped her, one should offer oblations.
As before, one should here recollect the pervasive pervasion (vyāpti) as being mixed with impurity (mala) and karma.
The path [consists of] up to Śakti; there are three mantras, sixteen phonemes (varṇas), and indeed one word (pada).
Indeed, there is one [world] of the worlds that is to be contemplated, and there are fifteen;
these are manifested by the Transcendent (Atītā) as Bindu, Nāda, Kalā, and Śakti.
Then, once these have been pervaded by its presence, he should offer oblations three times with the root mantra;
having invoked Vāgīśī, who pervades these worlds, he should worship her.
For the sake of bringing them into proximity, one should offer clarified butter three times as before.

Thereafter, having offered oblations with three offerings each for [the stages of] sprinkling, striking, cutting, drawing forth, union with the womb, birth, childhood, sovereignty, enjoyment, and dissolution—using the root mantra of seven syllables—and having performed these while intending those respective acts by addressing the Lord as "O Bhagavan," one should offer a hundred oblations with the root mantra during the expiation (*niṣkṛti*). Then, as before, saying "Perform the expiation! Perform it!", one should meditate on the separation [of the soul] from the bonds of *Śāntyatītā* due to its emergence outside of them. Having offered three times with the root mantra, and then three oblations with the *praṇava* (OM) for the bond of *Atītā* which pervades the impurities (*mala*) and so forth, one should say: "O Bhagavan, perform the severing of the *Śāntyatītā* bond of this self! using both the root mantra and the seven-syllable mantra. Having offered the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) with the root mantra, one should purify the bond of conventional conduct (*samayācāra*) along with its injunctions, having resolved upon it for the sake of purifying the *kalās*, by means of the [mantra] beginning with *Sā*.

Having invoked [the deities] with "Oṃ, obeisance to the hosts who are lords of the noose of the conduct of the pledge and the pledge," and having established and worshipped them, one should offer oblations three times with this [mantra] ending in *svāhā* for the purpose of making them present. Then, with the seven-syllable mantra, and thereafter with the *praṇava*, the root-mantra, and so forth—up to the portion of the eight names of Sadāśiva—one should offer oblations three times with "O Mind, grasp [it], svāhā. Then, having made [the disciple] hear [the command] with "O Lord of Causes," and so forth, one should dismiss him. Thereafter, having withdrawn [the impurity] from the past noose by means of the *śivāstra* mantra enclosed by the *praṇava* and the exhaling breath (*recaka*), and having rendered both the self and the disciple utterly stainless, one should place a drop of water upon the disciple's head.

Having offered [the oblation], worshipped Vāgīśī, and gratified her, one should address her: "O Blessed One! You have been fatigued by the five principles; now please return to your own domain. Having thus dismissed her and meditated upon the Śāntyatīta-kalā as dissolved into the Śakti-tattva, one should establish the Ātma-tattva up to the limit of the Māyā-tattva. Having brought it into presence with the formula beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ), namely "Ātma-tattvāya namaḥ," and while loudly reciting the seven-syllable mantra, one should offer a hundred oblations; in this way, there shall be purification from the karma of ritual deficiencies.

Then, having invoked, established, and worshipped the *vidyā-tattva* ending with Sadāśiva by means of its own mantra, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations while reciting that same mantra in a low voice (*upāṃśu*); thus, any deficiency in the recitation of the mantra is purified. Next, having approached, invoked, established, and worshipped the *śiva-tattva* ending with Śakti, one should offer one hundred and eight oblations while reciting it mentally; thus, one is purified from deficiencies in mental cognition.
Thereafter, one should contemplate the Power (*śakti*) which pervades the entire cosmic path (*viśvādhvan*) and resides within the path. (18–112)
And having visualized the disciple before him as possessing the form of all causes, resembling a pure gem, the Guru should worship him. (18.113)
Having consecrated the razor with the *śikhā-mantra*, one who desires worldly enjoyment should cut the topknot at a distance of twelve finger-breadths;
however, for the sake of liberation, one should cut it beyond eight finger-breadths.
Having cut off his topknot with [the blade of] his own topknot, the disciple should bathe for the sake of purification;
and the guru, having washed his hands and feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), becomes pure through the sprinkling [of water].
Then the Guru, having entered within together with his disciples and performed the ritual of self-protection (sakalīkṛta),
should place the topknot along with the cord of the noose upon a ball of cow dung that has been covered.
Having performed the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) as prescribed with the large ladle (sruc) and the small ladle (sruva),
and having offered it, he should then go outside and wash both the *sruc* and the *sruva*.
Having sipped water with the *kartarī* and having especially worshipped Śiva, he should make this request:
"O Blessed One, by your command, let there be the purification of the path (*adhvaśuddhi*). (18.118)
"O Lord! Since the crest-lock and the bonds of this soul have been severed by you, may he attain the state of Śiva and the supreme abode through your grace. (18.119)
"Let the command be given to me for the application of the quality of Śiva-hood to this [disciple].

Do so," he said. Thus authorized by the Blessed One, he was overjoyed; holding the vessel of *arghya* in his hand and accompanied by his disciple, he sat down near the fire and performed, as before, the rites of sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), striking (*tāḍana*), internalization (*antahkaraṇa*), the rite of making the body complete (*sakalīkaraṇa*), the unification of the channels (*nādīsaṃdhāna*), and the libation with mantras (*mantratarpaṇa*).

(185) Having performed the *sakalīkaraṇa* (the ritual integration of the limbs) and purification for each of the *saṃhitā-mantras* with a single oblation (*āhuti*), he should unite the consciousness (*caitanya*) of the disciple with the Self of Śiva (*śivātman*). Then, the Guru—himself established in the principle of *vidyā* within the seat of the *bindu-tattva*—should contemplate the external instruments [of perception]: Indhikā, Dīpikā, Rocikā, Mocikā, Ūrdhvagāminī, Sūkṣmā, Susūkṣmā, Amṛtā, Ṛtā, and Śakti; as well as the powers of *nāda*, the *kalās*, their pervader (*vyāpinī*), the one whose form is space (*vyomarūpā*), Anantā, Anāthā, and Anāśritā. Having purified the internal instruments and made his body full of the three principles—the pure Self-principle (*śuddhātmatattva*) and the other two—he should perform the filling (*pūraka*) and retention (*kumbhaka*) breaths. Joining the tongue to the palate, with the mouth slightly open, not touching the teeth with the teeth, and with the body straight, he should unite the disciple’s consciousness with his own. Unifying the other channels with the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*) within the *suṣumnā*, he should visualize the disciple’s self along with the mantras as resembling pure crystal. Reciting the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) and the *haṃsa*, he should transcend Brahmā and the other lords of the causal realms located at the heart, throat, palate, *bindu*, and the crown of the head. By means of a full oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*) and the retention of breath (*bahiḥ-kumbhaka*), he should unite the disciple’s self with Śiva. Meditating on the disciple as having become Śiva, he should bestow upon him the six qualities pertaining to Śiva through the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*). They are as follows: [The text here proceeds to list the six qualities.]

Having offered an oblation of clarified butter (ājyāhuti) with the mantra: *oṃ hūṃ ātman! sarvajño bhava svāhā*, and likewise having offered individual oblations with the mantras: *anādibuddha*, *svatantra*, *aluptaśakti*, and *anantaśakti*, one should visualize the disciple as having become Śiva, endowed with the qualities of omniscience and the rest. Then, having consecrated him with the root-mantra and water for respectful offering (arghya) accompanied by the collection of mantras, one should inform him of the eight pledges (samayas).
They are as follows: [one should honor] the devotees of Maheśvara and those who practice the observances and conduct prescribed in their scriptures. (18.120)

This first [rule] is: one should not revile Śiva, the Guru, or their devotees; nor should one step on the shadow of a celestial chariot, a Guru, or a Liṅga, nor that of those who bear the Liṅga or of cows. (18.121)
One should not step over the remains of an offering (nirmālya), nor should one eat with those who have fallen from their status or the like.
One should not eat food touched by a woman in her menses, a female messenger, or one in a state of impurity, nor should one touch them.

This is the second commitment. One should not have the commitments, the practices of the commitments, or the mantra-tantras written down by those who have not been initiated, nor should one cause them to be heard; this is the third commitment. (18.123)
Having worshipped Śiva and the Guru either twice a day, thrice a day, or even once a day, one should then eat; this is the fourth rule of conduct (samaya).

One should not initiate those whose powers have not yet descended, nor those who have fallen [from their state], nor atheists, nor those of sinful character; this is remembered as the fifth rule. (18.125)
One should not partake of food, drink, flowers, or anything else that is dear to Śiva, Agni, the Guru, or the Vidyā, without first offering it. (18.126)
In the same way, having satisfied children, women, the elderly, those afflicted by disease, the wretched,
and guests with food, drink, and other necessities according to one's ability, || 18-127 ||
"One should give food out of favor to parrots, crows, dogs, and *caṇḍālas*";
this is to be known as the sixth vow of observance (*samayavrata*) for the Śaivas. (18.128)
On the days that are parvan-eighth (aṣṭamī), one must avoid shaving, oil-massage, and women;
as well as eating from bell-metal vessels, drinking [intoxicants], and consuming fish, meat, and honey.
To be avoided in every way and at all times—this is the seventh commitment:
the practice of the restraints (yamas) and observances (niyamas) according to their appropriate application. (18.130)

On the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, on festival days, during planetary eclipses, at the solstices and other such times, as well as on occasions such as the Pavitra and Caitraka rites, one should perform worship according to the specific injunctions.
Having made a single resolution regarding his meal, he may eat either at night or during the day;
[he should provide for] those who have come for refuge, those afflicted by disease, travelers, and those who are terrified and distraught. (18.132)
Furthermore, one should protect, according to one's capacity, devotees of Śiva, other virtuous people, cows, Brahmins, dependents, servants, and so forth; this is the eighth [duty]. (18.133)
"This is indeed the samaya that has been declared; it must be observed with great effort.
Having thus received the instruction regarding the guru’s samayas, the disciple, having satisfied the guru with wealth and humble prostrations as desired by him, [should proceed].
Having performed a prostration and received his permission, one should constantly perform the worship of Śambhu, being intent upon what is pleasing and beneficial [to him]. 18.134½.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on Nirvāṇa-dīkṣā, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 18.
Now begins the nineteenth chapter.

Next is described the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), who has been initiated by the initiation involving ritual action (*kriyāvatī-dīkṣā*) and has correctly understood the Tantra.
On this point, Brahmaśambhu states:
"That disciple who understands the Saṃhitā— which consists of three categories and four sections, and which brings about the fruit of both worldly enjoyment and liberation— is worthy of initiation."

Thus: On the appointed day and at the auspicious hour (*muhūrta*), having duly performed the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*) of the disciple, and having caused the worship of the water-pot (*kumbha*), the mandala, and the fire, one should proceed as follows: In a square pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) measuring nine, seven, or five cubits, situated in the east, northeast, or north, one should install upon a square altar (*vedikā*)—which is one and a half, three, or two cubits high, and upon which svastikas are drawn in the four corners with unbroken rice or barley—either a set of nine water-pots presided over by the Vidyeśvaras and Sadāśiva, or a set of five water-pots presided over by Brahmā and the Kalās beginning with Nivṛtti. Having filled them with water from sacred sites (*tīrtha*) mixed with all kinds of gems, medicinal herbs, and perfumes, and having covered them with two white cloths; having placed bundles of *kuśa* grass, leaves of the holy fig tree (*aśvattha*), mango sprouts, and citron fruits (*bījapūra*) upon the mouths of the pots; and having worshipped Śakti, Śiva, and the mantra to be employed (*sādhyamantra*) therein; Then, having seated Śiva to the south of the altar, one should perform oblations (*homa*) in sequence with white mustard seeds, unbroken rice, sesame, *dūrvā* grass, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge (*caru*), using the *sādhyamantra*. Next, one should pour the residual clarified butter (*sampātājya*) into the water-pots. Following the procedure taught for the Nirvāṇa-initiation, one should purify the triad of Kalās beginning with Nivṛtti within the body of the disciple. Then, having purified the Śāntyatītā Kalā, one should meditate on Sadāśiva as the body of knowledge (*vidyādeha*), invoke him into the heart of the disciple, establish him there, perform the ritual of integration (*sakalīkaraṇa*), worship him according to the sequence of the seat (*āsana*) and so forth, offer the final oblation (*pūrṇāhuti*), and then purify the Śānti Kalā. Thereafter...

Then, the Praṇava and the Root-mantra joined with the word "Ātman" [are recited], ending with the mention of the qualities beginning with Aṇimā; these [become complete] by means of the wife of Agni (the Svāhā). || 19-2 ||
Having separately proclaimed the qualities beginning with *aṇimā*,
and having offered eight oblations, he should endow the disciple with the eight supernatural powers (*aṣṭaguṇa*).
Aṇimā and mahimā, as well as laghimā and prāpti;
likewise prākāmya, īśitva, and after that vaśitva. (19.4)
The eightfold qualities of sovereignty consist of the power to resolve at will wherever one desires;
thereafter, the disciple is made complete (sakalīkṛta) through the ritual application of the limbs along with the object of accomplishment.
Then, having worshipped with perfumes and other offerings that form which is presided over by Śiva and likewise by Śakti, accompanied by song and instrumental music— || 19-6 ||

Having performed the *nīrājana* ceremony with garments made from colored powders, with [images of] Vajra and others placed upon vessels, and with abundant lamps, [the officiant], facing north, [should perform it for the disciple] who faces east. (19.7)
Thereafter,
having cleansed [the area] with curd, cow dung, white mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, sandalwood paste, lotuses, anthill earth, and protective herbs, all saturated with water; || 19.8 ||
Having worshipped him with offerings ending in incense, one should consecrate him with water-pots joined with their respective mantras, in the sequence beginning with Ananta and Nivṛtti.
One should contemplate the entry of that mantra-form by means of the *suṣumṇā*, as it pours forth streams of nectar into identity with this [deity]. (19.10)
One should meditate upon the mantra-form, which has washed away all impurities with the flow of supreme nectar and is pervaded by consciousness within the heart-lotus.
On this point, Brahmaśambhu says:
"The nectar is the water, the support is Śakti, and her Kuṇḍalinī;
Śiva is to be known as the one who sprinkles, while the individual soul (pudgala) is the one to be sprinkled."

Thus [it is said]. Then, having seated the disciple—who has changed into white garments, washed his hands and feet, and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana)—on the eastern side of the deity’s altar upon a prepared infinite seat made of *śrīparṇī* wood or similar materials, facing east; and having performed the purification of the elements (*bhūtaśuddhi*), adorned him with a sacred thread, ornaments, perfumes, and flowers, and having consecrated him with the ritual of the parts (*sakalīkṛtya*) and worshipped him, he should wave the *ārātrika* lamp three times while it is honored with curd, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*). He should then cause the disciple to touch the "Eight Auspicious Things" (*maṅgalāṣṭaka*) along with a salutation, using three handfuls of cool water. These are: yellow pigment (*rocanā*), sandalwood paste, *dūrvā* grass, jasmine flowers (*sumanas*), curd, and milk-rice (*pāyasa*).
Barley and white mustard seeds—this is declared to be the eightfold auspicious substances (maṅgalāṣṭaka).
Then he should invest the disciple with authority through the ritual implements:
a bracelet, an upper garment, a parasol, a fly-whisk, and sandals. (19.13)
A book, a rosary, a water-pot, vehicles and mounts, and whatever other royal insignia there may be—all these the practitioner deserves. (19.14)
This same entitlement regarding the retinue applies to the Ācārya as well;
his distinction, however, consists of the crown, the turban, and likewise the ritual instrument (karaṇī).

(p. 189) Thereafter, the Guru, having taken the disciple’s right hand with his own right hand, shall enter by the western door and cause him to perform three circumambulations and worship of the Śambhu-vessel, the maṇḍala, and Śiva. Then, while the disciple has descended to the ground in prostration with both knees, the Guru, having recited the mantra to be mastered (*sādhyamantra*), shall place water mixed with fragrant flowers into the disciple’s joined palms and bestow the mantra along with its oral instructions (*upadeśa*). The disciple, in turn, placing that joined-palm gesture upon his own head and bowing to the Guru, shall bring [the mantra] down via the *suṣumnā* path in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), deposit it in the lotus of his own heart, bathe it with the nectar from the "End of the Twelve" (*dvādaśānta*), and offer oblations of clarified butter with the mantra-complex (*mantrasaṃhitā*). Then, having invoked and established the mantra together with its limbs (*sāṅga*) upon a lotus seat to the south of the Śiva-vessel and the fires, and having worshipped it as if it were Śiva himself, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) should extract the mantra from that [seat] and, visualizing it in his own body according to the sequence beginning with *Śakti*, he should establish it there.
As Brahmaśambhu states:
"From Śiva [comes] Śakti, from that the Bindu, from the Bindu the Nāda,
and from the Nāda the Half-moon, the letter *ha*, and likewise the sixth primary vowel (*ā*)."
That, moreover, is the two-footed Brahman, the cause of the parts, the imperishable;
it is the seed-mantra that is not to be uttered, the cause of creation and dissolution.

Thus it is said. One should know that there are nine locations for these knots (*granthi*): the *dvādaśānta*, the aperture of the crest (*śikhā-randhra*), the forehead, the space between the eyebrows, the palate, the throat, the heart, the navel, and the bladder (*vasti*). Having meditated upon them in sequence within the lotuses at these locations, one should flood them with nectar (*amṛta*). Then the Guru should cause him to adopt the rules of conduct (*samayācāra*). These are declared for one initiated for liberation (*nirvāṇa-dīkṣita*) and are exactly the same for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) as well. In brief, they consist of: maintaining the vow of service (*sevā-vrata*), assuming a specific sectarian mark (*liṅga*), consuming pure food, renouncing social attachments, indifference toward both punishment and favor, avoiding what is prohibited, and not abandoning prescribed duties.
Then, having gratified the fire with the Saṃhitā mantras, one should dismiss it;
by his command, one should then unite the fire residing in the mandala with the Śiva-kumbha.
Then, having scattered an offering (bali) to the beings in the various directions with their respective mantras,
he [the teacher] should then seat the disciple as before upon the throne and worship him.
With auspicious rites and the auspicious jar (śivakumbha), the preceptor should consecrate him according to this very procedure for the attainment of royal fortune and victory. (19.18)
Or, for the sake of longevity, health, good fortune, and the nourishment of sons, wives, and [the kingdom], one should consecrate the king, other men, and women as well. (19-19)
A devotee of Śiva attains all that by effortless means, and not otherwise;
moreover, having received the initiation mantra and then obtained permission from the Guru... (19–20).

The practitioner should accomplish the mantra for the attainment of both visible and invisible fruits, especially during auspicious asterisms, lunar days, and weekdays that are favorable to himself. (19–21)
Having approached the sacred field of Śiva, which abounds in flowers, kuśa grass, and water,
one should carefully avoid a linga that has its openings toward the south and north.
The Liṅga is indeed fixed with stakes, joined by Brahmā, Skanda, Indra, Nandī, Śiva, the Bull, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśvara, the Mothers, Bhāskara, and Durgā.

The meaning is that one should avoid [such things]. Furthermore, one should avoid a *liṅga* worshipped by others, one consecrated by a human being, one devoid of worship, one defiled by Mlecchas or outcastes, one corrupted by defects such as being displaced or broken, and one with multiple *liṅgas*. A single *liṅga* with a western-facing door and a self-manifested (*svayambhū*) *liṅga* are excellent. Those established by gods (*daiva*), sages (*ārṣa*), or Bāṇa are middling. Those established by Asuras, Rākṣasas, Piśācas, and so forth, are inferior. Among these *liṅgas*, because they are common to all purposes and mantras, there is no confusion of mantras; therefore, having projected one's own mantra onto them, one should worship. In the case of *liṅgas* whose mantras are unknown, one should project either the *praṇava* or the *mātṛkā*, bring it into one’s own heart by means of inhalation (*pūraka*), lead it to dissolution at the "twelfth end" (*dvādaśānta*) by means of exhalation (*recaka*), and then, having projected one's own mantra according to the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhā*), one should worship. In the event that these three types of *liṅgas* are unavailable, even a *liṅga* possessing power (*sānnidhya*) that has been installed by a Guru, by oneself, or by another, should be resorted to—this is the fourth position. Thereafter...

Having performed the ritual of the weapon (astrayāga) together with its ancillaries, having offered oblations of clarified butter and sesame seeds, and having first performed the worship of Vāstu while it is protected by the deities of Vāstu; || 19–24 ||

One should bury eight sesame seeds, each the size of a cubit, empowered by the weapons of the World-Guardians (lokeśa) with their respective mantras, in the cardinal directions for the protection of that sacred field.
One should encircle the exterior with a thread, a protective amulet, and a peg;
then, one should again scatter seven seeds all around with the hand. (19–26)
One should draw a line with ashes and also with sesame seeds mixed with barley;
having thus fashioned a boundary wall there, one should likewise offer the bali-oblation to the spirits.
Eating once a day in measured amounts food that is uncultivated, free from pungent salt, pure, and light, he was devoted to bathing three times a day. || 19-28 ||
Having fully restrained the collection of his senses, he should accomplish the desired mantra.
Once the mantra is mastered, he should again worship Śiva therein with devotion. (19.29)
Having cast away the kīla, the world-lord, and the weapons, and having bowed to Śiva and requested his permission,
one should go to a desired place or reside right there.
The Chapter on the Initiation of the Aspirant (Sādhaka-dīkṣā-adhikāra).

Now, the preceptor (ācārya) worthy of consecration should be one who possesses established conduct, is virtuous, pure, born in a praiseworthy land, learned, and endowed with the auspicious characteristics prescribed [in the scriptures]. (19–31)
One who has been properly initiated by means of the initiation with seed (sabījadīkṣā), whose senses are conquered,
and who has correctly mastered the mantra, is capable of both restraint and grace.

One who has understood the entire meaning of the tantras, who is noble and possesses the essence of compassion, who is devoted to the worship of Śiva, tranquil, and a protector of the conduct of the samaya. || 19-33 ||

Having departed from his home, he should first undertake a pilgrimage to sacred fords (tīrthayātrā), proceeding in due order according to the requirements of place, time, age, strength, and capacity. (19–34)
Having completed his pilgrimage to the sacred fords on the banks of rivers such as the Gaṅgā,
or in a sacred field of Śiva or on a mountain, he should there observe the vow of an Ācārya.
When the sun has entered its northern course, during the bright fortnight on an auspicious day,
having worshipped Gaṇeśvara and the Guru, one should worship Śiva with special rites.
Having performed the sacrifice with the *astra-mantra* and being devoted to bathing at the three periods of the day,
he should likewise bathe for a period of three days using cow’s urine.
By eating once a day, by eating only at night, and likewise by eating only what is unasked for;
and furthermore, by subsisting solely on the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) or on the consecrated sacrificial porridge (siddhacarū).
And one should spend three days separately in fasting;
likewise, for a fortnight, one should eat only at the fourth meal-time, and similarly at the sixth meal-time.
Thus, for three days beyond the two fortnights,
he should spend his time constantly lying on ashes and *darbha* grass, always devoted to bathing in ashes.

Having eaten barley-food that is free from pungent substances and salt according to the prescribed sequence, at the conclusion [of the rite], one should honor the initiated Brahmins with food, clothing, and other gifts. (19.41)
Having gratified [the recipient] according to one's ability, saying, "May he be pleased with this instruction," one should then,
in a pure location as previously described and cleared of all thorns, [proceed].
Having constructed a very beautiful pavilion nine cubits in size, or likewise seven or five cubits, and half a cubit in height.
The archways from the east onwards are made of Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa;
likewise, Palāśa, Āmalaka, Madhūka, and Bilva.
One should fashion archways (toraṇas) with those [materials] in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya),
and banners (dhvajās) distinguished by the colors and emblems of the ten guardians of the directions.
And the canopy of the pavilion was variegated, white, and pure,
resplendent with a network of bells, small tinkling bells, and strings of pearls.
It was adorned with border-cloths, jeweled balls, and yak-tail whisks, and provided with protective amulets made of fine silk and other materials. (19.47)
One should construct a fire-sanctuary for him in the east and a beautiful sacrificial pit;
at its doors, one should place water-pots and vessels for the germinating seeds.
Having performed the worship of the site (vāstupūjā), one should then cause the declaration of an auspicious day (puṇyāha) to be recited;
then, after first scattering the ritual offerings (vikira), one should worship the water-pot and the weapon (kumbhāstra).
Having established the lords of the world and the weapons such as the vajra in the directions,
and having prepared the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the sequence prescribed for the five compartments.

Having consecrated the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with the eighteen purificatory rites (saṃskāras) as prescribed, and having duly established the Śiva-fire therein and offered libations, one should invoke Sadāśiva according to the rules, worship Him, and offer five oblations each of fuel-sticks (samit), clarified butter (ājya), parched grain (caru), and sesame seeds (tila). Having performed the final full oblation (pūrṇāhuti), one should draw an auspicious Sarvatobhadra or Bhadraka diagram in its center.
This should be measured respectively by five, four, three, two, and one cubits for the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas.
Even with those very same powders, a white lotus in their center is prescribed as the primary door for the Brahmins and the other castes, situated in the directions starting from the east. (19.52)
On the outer path of the pedestal, one should draw creepers, leaves, and so forth;
outside the mandala, in the cardinal directions, one should draw eight very white conchs.
Their names, O Ānanda, were Sunanda, Nanda, and Nandivardhana, as well as Śrīmukha and Vijaya. (19.54)
Tāra and Sutāra—these three mantras should consist of the Praṇava (Oṃ), the long vowels beginning with Ā, accompanied by the Anusvāra, and their own names. (19.55)
Having invoked with these words "Obeisance to the Self," one should perform worship;
in the central regions of the conchs, one should draw eight jars.
And that [mandala] facing the mandala is white and variegated with colors;
it is Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sunanda, and Puṣpanandaka. (19.57)
Then Jaya, Vijaya, Pūrṇa, and Pūrṇakumbha follow in sequence;
one should assign their mantras according to their respective names, just as one does for conch shells.
Likewise, for the eight archways (toraṇas), there are separate [mantras] associated with the names of the World-Guardians (lokeśa).
In this regard, the specific [mantra] is as follows: *oṃ āṃ īṃ rūṃ nyagrodhātmane surādhipatoraṇāya namaḥ*.
In the same way, the mantras for the palāśa and other trees are indeed formed.
Then, on the path outside the pedestal, one should place sixteen conch shells;
outside of that, one should set down eight water-pots located in the cardinal and intermediate directions.
One should fill these conch shells and jars with all kinds of gems, medicinal herbs, seeds, clay, and water, each according to its own mantra. || 19-61 ||
Their necks were adorned with garlands of garments, and they were smeared with sandalwood paste and unbroken grains of rice;
their mouths were formed from the five types of sprouts, and their faces were like the citron fruit.

Here, the names of the sixteen conchs and the eight jars are stated—those which, beginning with the *praṇava* (OM) and the three long vowels and so forth, and ending with the word *namaḥ* for each respective deity, constitute their respective mantras. They are as follows:

(194) The sixteen conches (*śaṅkha*)—Āyata, Ānanda, Nandyāyata, Sunanda, Mahākukṣi, Nandi, Sunābhi, Nandivardhana, Hrasvanābhi, Śrīmukhanābhi, Maṇḍalī, Vijaya, Sughosha, Tāra, Uttāra, and Sutāra—are to be filled. The jars (*kalaśa*)—Manthara, Subhadra, Pṛthuloṣṭha, Sudanta, Hrasvoṣṭha, Mantharagrīva, Jaya, and Vijaya—should each be placed separately upon seats made of *śāli* rice and *darbha* grass. Now the medicinal herbs (*auṣadhi*) are described: Jayā, Vijayā, Jayantī, Aparājitā, Viṣṇukrāntā, Śaṅkhapuṣpī, Hemapuṣpī, Nākulī, Viśālā, Balā, Atibalā, Gandhanākulī, Sahā, Sahadevā, Vārāhī, Śatāvarī, Medā, Mahāmedā, Vṛddhi, Ṛddhi, and the one known as Kākolī; these herbs should be taken according to their availability. The gems (*ratna*) are ruby, pearl, *gomeda*, emerald, topaz, diamond, sapphire, coral, and crystal. The seeds (*bīja*) are seven: *śāli* rice, barley, mung bean, black gram, sesame, *sidhārtha* (white mustard), and wheat. The eight fragrances (*gandha*) are sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, camphor, costus, spikenard, *kaccora*, and vetiver. The eight types of earth (*mṛd*) are to be taken from the top of an anthill, from a fragrant mountain peak, from a riverbank, from the confluence of great rivers, from the root of a *bilva* tree, from an elephant’s tusk, and from a cow’s horn. Having mixed these substances, one should fill the conches and jars with water from sacred bathing places (*tīrtha*). One should fill the conches in sequence with the sixteen vowels. One should invoke the eight groups of letters (*aṣṭavarga*) into the jars, the eight forms (*mūrti*) beginning with Earth in the eight directions within the conches, the eight powers (*śakti*) beginning with Vāmā in the intermediate directions of the conches, and the eight Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) in the eight outer jars; having invoked and established them all, one should worship them according to the rules. In the center, upon the pericarp of the lotus, in a jar made of gold, silver, copper, or clay—whichever is suitable for the power (*śakti*) and provided with all herbs, seeds, gems, fragrances, and flowers, along with gold—one should fill it with sacred waters while reciting the mantra-collection (*mantrasaṃhitā*), remembering the nectar of the "twelve-ends" (*dvādaśāntāmṛta*). Having duly invoked the power Manonmanī, the embodied form with its limbs (*sāṅgamūrti*), the Root Mantra, and Sadāśiva in the sequence of the throne (*āsana*) and so forth, and having placed *kūrca* grass, sprouts, and fruits everywhere, one should adorn the neck [of the jar] with unwashed cloths and garlands, and worship it properly up to the offering of food (*naivedya*). The mantras for the insertion of the gems and other items therein are stated: *Oṃ āṃ īṃ ūṃ, salutations to all gems whose essence is the universe.* As before: *Salutations to all seeds whose essence is Indra.* As before: *Salutations to all herbs whose essence is the Moon.* *Salutations to all fragrances whose essence is Earth; salutations to all earths whose essence is Earth.* Thus one should arrange them. Having thus consecrated the jars, conches, arches (*toraṇa*), gems, and so forth, and having worshipped them, one should employ them. Thereafter, the disciple—who has observed a fast, performed his daily ablutions and rites, completed his regular worship of Śiva and the fire-sacrifice (*agnikārya*), is dressed in white garments, and has washed his hands and feet—is made to circumambulate the pavilion. Having performed worship of the arches of the doors of the Peaceful Kalās (*śāntikalā*) starting from the east, he is led through the eastern door, which corresponds to the appropriate metal, and is made to offer worship and prostration to the jar of Śiva, the weapon (*astra*), and the fire. Then, [the officiant] himself, by means of the mantra-collection... *(Note: The text provided ends abruptly here.)*

Having satisfied the Śiva-fire with individual oblations and brought it [to the disciple], he should place an *audumbara* or *śrīparṇika* auspicious seat (*bhadrāsana*) covered with a matching cloth upon a lotus drawn to the south of the pavilion. Having seated the disciple—who is intent on the recitation of the Gāyatrī—upon that Ananta-seat, the Guru, accompanied by sixteen or eight Mūrtidharas of the first caste who have been initiated with the seed-syllable (*sabījadīkṣā*), should, while the sounds of auspicious instruments such as conchs and drums and the chanting of Vedic hymns by Brāhmaṇas in all directions drown out other noises, "churn" the disciple using seeds, arrows, variegated mouthfuls, joined palms, elephant-ears, unbroken buds, and torches. Thereafter, having smeared his entire body with the aforementioned earth-clays while reciting the respective mantras, he should first bathe him with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), with powders of *bilva*, lotus filaments, and *priyaṅgu*, and then with the decoction-water of *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, *vaṭa*, and *bilva* kept separately in jars. Having washed him, performed worship ending with incense, and effected the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkṛta*), he should bathe him with the Vidyeśvara jars using their respective mantras, again performing worship ending with incense. Then, likewise bathing him with the sixteen conchs, and again performing worship ending with incense, he should finally bathe him with the Śiva-jar over which the root-mantra of the Mūrtis has been recited. While doing so, he should contemplate the entry and pervasion of Śiva into the disciple’s heart through the *suṣumnā* channel in the order of emanation (*sṛṣṭikrama*), [Śiva] being accompanied by the Vidyās and Vidyeśvaras, together with His Śaktis, endowed with all the mantras arising from the sequence beginning with the Bindu, and possessed of qualities such as omniscience.

Then, having performed protection around him with the *astravardhanī* [consecrated water], he should likewise perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with the *śivakumbha*. Then, after the disciple has changed his garments, he should give him a sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*) according to the number of the colors [of the elements]. Having bestowed the insignia—such as a turban, crown, necklace, mirror, ring, parasol, fly-whisk, elephant, horse, palanquin, water-pot (*bhṛṅgāra*), sandals, and so forth—and having honored him with the sounds of elephants, drums, and other instruments, he should perform the *nīrājana* ceremony for him with auspicious musical sounds, using lamps made from the powder of weapons such as diamonds placed in vessels of gold and the like, brought forward by maidens and brides.
Thereafter, having led him facing toward Śiva and caused him to perform a prostration accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), he should make this request regarding what is to be given:
"O Blessed One! By Your grace, through Your command, this person has arrived;
from this day forward, let him be the Ācārya for the Great Consecration."
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods, he was told by Śiva, "So be it.
Then, having bid farewell to the god, the fire, the water-pots, the conch-shells, and the arches, [he departed].
Having worshipped the world-protectors according to his desire, he should cast the bali offering;
then he should dismiss them, as well as the bearers of the images and the ascetics.
Having satisfied the Brahmins with gold, garments, and food, as well as the poor and the helpless according to his ability, he should then appoint this very Guru to his own office. (19.66)
This place, these teachings, and these collections of books, as well as these female and male servants and others, must be protected just as before. (19.67)

One should initiate people with initiations according to their respective capacities, setting in motion the wheel of ritual action beginning with the plowing of the site and ending with the consecration. (19.68)
The scriptures must be explained to those who have been initiated and not otherwise;
while observing the rules of conduct, be intent on bestowing grace.
Having thus instructed him, the former preceptor should then worship Śiva with special care and recite the root mantra ten thousand times.

By this very procedure, one should worship for the sake of obtaining a kingdom for one desiring sovereignty, for the restoration of lost power and sons, and for a woman’s attainment of good fortune. (19.71)
One should consecrate devotees of Śiva after having initiated them, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the section on the Great Consecration of the Ācārya.
[This applies] even for one who desires the status of an Ācārya but is unable to perform [the rites] in this manner. (19–72)

For one who has completed the vow of an ācārya but is thus unable to fulfill that vow, [the rite is performed] after he has given a double gift according to his means and by appropriate means. || 19-73 ||
Having drawn the auspicious Sarvatobhadra maṇḍala within the pavilion,
one should place and worship the water-pot (kumbha) and the weapon (astra) in the northeast by scattering the ritual offerings (vikira).
One should worship Śiva properly within the central lotus of this [mandala], while the area outside the mandala is adorned in the cardinal directions with svastikas and other ornaments. (19.75)
Having placed five jars according to the prescribed rite in the western, northern, southern, eastern, and northeast directions, [representing] earth, water, fire, wind, and space; 19–76.
They are worshipped with the limbs of the kalās, such as Nivṛtti, and with [the mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta;
they are provided with all kinds of jewels, medicinal herbs, seeds, earth, perfumes, and flowers.

Adorned with golden plates, brushes, and the aforementioned fruits and sprouts, and provided with garments, garlands, and ornaments, they should be arranged in the sequence beginning with the seats. (19.78)
Having invoked the *kalās* in sequence at the end of the process of supreme transformation (*paramīkaraṇa*),
and having fully worshipped the forms (*mūrti*) and the limbs (*aṅga*), one should likewise worship the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) as before.

Having performed the sacrifice by offering five oblations with the names of the elements beginning with Earth, preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ), the heart-mantra, and the root-mantra for the limbs, the forms, and the digits.
Having offered fuel-sticks, clarified butter, sacrificial porridge, parched grain, and sesame seeds, one should cast the oblation;
then, having established the auspicious fire and performed the full oblation as prescribed.

Having obtained permission from Śiva, [the teacher] should then place the disciple— who has performed his daily rites— upon a well-adorned lotus to the south of the maṇḍala, decorated with svastikas and other auspicious symbols.

Having performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkṛtya*) as before upon the auspicious and infinite seat, one should worship with *sidhārtha* seeds, curd, clay, ashes, *dūrvā* grass, and balls of cow dung. (19.83)
Having churned [the substances], washed them with scented water, and honored them while incensed, one should [place] those jars—
each obtained from a hundred roots— with their respective mantras.
Having consecrated him, dressed in new garments, and seated upon the Anantāsana throne,
one should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, worship him, and bestow the means of accomplishment such as the uṣṇīṣa and so forth.
Having announced his authority, he should offer it to this Śiva;
then, having obtained permission from Śiva, he should go back again to the vicinity of the sacrificial pit.
Then he offers five oblations of clarified butter for each of the five digits,
and having offered the final full oblation, he takes hold of that [disciple's] right hand.
One should mark [the hands] on the little finger and the others with the five limbs using a *darbha* torch;
as before, one should likewise dismiss Śiva, as well as Agni, the water-pot (*kumbha*), and the weapon (*astra*).
Then, having satisfied those people with gold, garments, food, drink, and other gifts,
he should exercise the authority obtained by the command of Śiva and the Guru.
Thus, the initiations along with their consecrations, as established in the Tantras, have been duly described here according to their primary importance;
by means of these, one shall attain the destruction of all worldly afflictions, as well as enjoyments, sovereign powers, and even liberation without effort. (19.90)

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Initiation of the Aspiring Practitioner and the Consecration of the Preceptor," in the section on ritual practice (*kriyāpāda*) of the *Uparibhāga* within the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Paddhati* of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 19.
Now begins the twentieth chapter.
Next, for the sake of pacifying the faults of negligence, transgression, forgetfulness, lapses, and those committed in previous births, the rite of atonement (*prāyaścitta*) is here proclaimed.

If the *liṅga* falls from the hand, or is touched by others who are uninitiated (*adīkṣita*), one should perform ten thousand recitations (*jāpa*) of the Aghora mantra; by means of special worship, one becomes pure. (20.2)

By the term "special worship" (viśeṣārcana), it is meant that one should perform the worship up to the end of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), the five nectars (pañcāmṛta) bath, the great food offering (mahānaivedya), and the fire ritual (agnikārya).
If [the image] falls from a height of two cubits after the final consecration (samprokṣaṇa), one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times;
if it falls from a greater height, one should be a reciter of two or three hundred thousand [times]. (20–3)
If the *liṅga* or the pedestal (*pīṭha*) is broken, no expiation exists;
therefore, one must protect it with great effort and without negligence. (20.4)

Likewise, for the pacification of a mortal sin such as the destruction of a linga or other [sacred object], one becomes purified by performing a tenfold expiation through the kṛcchra penance. || 20-5 ||
If the Lord has not yet been dismissed and a disturbance occurs at the sacrificial ground or elsewhere,
one should offer oblations and then recite the Aghora mantra five thousand times, followed by a tenth part of that as a concluding offering.

If the *liṅga* is lost, burnt, fallen, or stolen by thieves and the like, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times, sprinkle it with water, and if it can be recovered, one should worship it again. (20.7)
In the absence of that, one should install and worship another linga.
However, upon the omission of the twilight prayers (sandhyā), one who is free from disease should fast and recite [the mantra] one hundred times.
If the ritual implements, the fire, or the feet are touched by [impure] contact or stepped over,
one should recite five thousand [mantras] and purify them by washing.
One should discard flowers, water, fragrance, clay, the vessel, milk, food, and clarified butter [if they have been touched by an impure person].
In the event of the omission of worship for one day, one should fast for three nights and perform the recitation of mantras (japa).
One should likewise accumulate [the penance] at a rate of one thousand repetitions for even a single day's omission of worship;
if the lapse exceeds five days, one should perform six times that amount.
One should perform a thousand recitations; that number is prescribed for Brahmins.
For those of mixed caste who act unintentionally, however, one should recite five hundred Brahmans.
Fasting and pure, having consumed the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), he performs oblations;
if a mixture of discarded offerings (nirmālya) occurs therein, he should recite the Pañcabrahma mantra one hundred times. (20.13)
If one consumes it unintentionally, one should recite [the mantra] one thousand five hundred times;
if intentionally, through the sacrifice of Ananta and the initiation of the path of the feet (padādhvan). || 20-14 ||
However, it becomes pure; one should neither eat nor even touch the *nirmālya*.

The sacrifice known as the *Anantayāga*—the sacrifice of Śiva, who is surrounded by the Lords of Knowledge (*vidyeśvara*) such as Ananteśa—is specified in this very chapter, which will be described later.
Now the varieties of *nirmālya* are stated; they are also sixfold, as follows: [Verse 20-15]
The property of the deity, the wealth of the deity, the food offering that has been presented, the substance belonging to Caṇḍa, and the remains of the offering— their characteristics are now stated.
Clothing, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth are traditionally known as *devadravya* (the property of the deity).
*Devasva* (the wealth of the deity) refers to villages, fields, cattle, and the like that belong to the deity. (20.17)
Furthermore, that food and other offerings prepared for the sake of the deity is called *naivedya*;
that which has been offered is termed *nivedita*, and what remains from it is the substance belonging to Caṇḍa.
One should not touch the floral offerings (nirmālya) cast outside the inner sanctum;
furthermore, one should never utilize the sixfold types of such offerings.
Regarding this, King Bhoja states:

"One should not smell, step over, eat, or sell even the six kinds of *nirmālya*. By eating it, one becomes a carnivore; by stepping over it, an outcaste (*mātaṅga*); by smelling it, a wolf; by touching it, a woman; by selling it, a *caṇḍāla*; and by [selling] it, a *śabara*.
The *nirmālya* of the Sun (*saura*) given to Caṇḍa is even more [forbidden] than that of Śiva."

[The offering] does not become *nirmālya* (remnant of worship) when placed upon the teacher, a book, fire, *yakṣas*, *nāgas*, lords of yogins, the host of Mothers, or Gaurī; nor when it is on immobile [liṅgas] in the ten locations during the time of the teacher’s exposition, in the *śivakumbha* (the Śiva-pitcher), or during the circumambulation of the deity. Even when the deity has been dismissed (*visarjita*), the worship remains in the case of a stationary liṅga. King Bhoja states that for a mobile liṅga, an unjoined liṅga, an installed liṅga, one made of painted gems, one made of gold, or any other [material], there is no *nirmālya* until the fourth ritual act (*caturthī-karma*)—that is, until the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) is complete.
(p. 200) Regarding the sight or unintentional inhalation of the scent of perfumes, incense, and so forth during worship: || 20-20 ||

There is no fault in touching [objects] brought by the current of a river and so forth; nor is there any fault for one who has been initiated, or for one who has eaten during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity. (20–21)

One who has fasted should not recite the Vāmadeva mantra a thousand times out of desire; therefore, for the sake of purification from an act committed out of desire, it is traditionally taught that the recitation should be threefold.
When there is impurity related to oneself, one should not touch that person personally;
one should eat separately and perform rituals such as bathing and worship.
The wise one, initiated into Nirvāṇa, should act as before, free from doubt;
or likewise, even one initiated by the *nirbīja* initiation or by the *sāmāyikī* initiation.
One should not touch the liṅga oneself; rather, one should have it worshipped by another—either by an initiated disciple, or by sons and other kinsmen. (20–25)
Having performed the worship, fire-oblation, and other rites, bathed, and restrained his speech and mind,
he should perform the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa and the rest while mentally reciting the mantras.
Having made offerings with handfuls of flowers to Śiva within the prepared maṇḍala, having worshipped him mentally, recited the mantra, and bowed down to the fire; || 20–27 ||
One who eats separately from others may pass the days of birth-impurity and the like;
however, one possessed of perfect knowledge is not defiled even by hundreds of such impurities of birth.
Just as a fire covered by a heap of grass and wood blazes forth, so too one who has eaten during the impurity caused by birth or death due to negligence shall fast for one day. (20–29)
One who desires [to purify himself] should recite it one thousand times; having eaten, he becomes pure by reciting three times that number.
However, having eaten during the period of impurity following a birth or death (sūtaka), he indeed becomes as impure as that [period] itself.
But from the end of that day for as many days as there were [in the offense],
he should eat only barley-gruel at night, bathe three times a day, and recite [the mantra] three hundred times every day.
This same rule is prescribed even for eating forbidden food;
if one should emit semen at night, one should recite the Puruṣasūkta a thousand times.
Therefore, one should give twice as much fodder for the cows each day;
among the castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, the lords of the species are the males and so forth. (20–33)

p. 201) Herein, if one who is himself impure by having remnants of food (ucchiṣṭa) touches another person of the same caste who is also impure by remnants, purification occurs by bathing and reciting the mantra of one's own clan-lord (svajātīśvara) one hundred times. Upon touching the remnants of one who is uninitiated (adīkṣita), one should recite it two hundred times. Upon touching the remnants of one of the caste immediately lower than oneself, however, one should fast for one day and, having combined the mantra of one's own clan-lord with that of the clan-lord of the touched caste, recite it one hundred times. In that case, upon touching the remnants of one caste separated by one degree, one should fast for one day and, having combined the mantra of one's own clan-lord with that of the clan-lord of the touched caste, recite it one hundred times. In that regard, upon touching the remnants of one separated by two degrees, one should fast for two nights; upon touching one separated by three degrees, one should fast for three nights and recite as before. For touching these [persons] when they are uninitiated, the penance is doubled. Likewise, even upon touching the remnants of a caste higher than oneself, the recitation and fasting should be performed reduced by a quarter and a half respectively. If one who is himself impure by remnants should touch an outcaste (antyaja) who is also impure by remnants, he should fast for three nights, bathe, and recite the mantra of his own clan-lord ten thousand times.
If [the guest] leaves one morsel remaining, it shall be half of that; if he eats in the natural order (anuloma), it shall be half of that again.
Those born in the inverse order (pratiloma) are the outcastes (antyajas), such as blacksmiths, dyers, and so forth. || 20-34 ||
Upon touching the remnants of food from a Caṇḍāla at a sacred bathing place (tīrtha),
one becomes pure after completing the Kṛcchra penance, reciting the Aghora mantra ten thousand times, and giving a gift according to one's capacity.

In this regard, if one who is himself not impure (anucchiṣṭa) touches those mentioned above who are impure (ucchiṣṭa), he should perform a quarter of the prescribed penance. However, if he himself is impure and touches those who are not impure, he should perform half of the penance. Alternatively, having eaten the food of others that is impure, he should worship the Brahmās within the *pañcabrahma-maṇḍala* and initiate [the person] by means of the "Elevation of Birth" (*jātyuddhāra*). That *maṇḍala* should be made four cubits in size with four doors. Having established Puruṣa and the others in it according to their directions, and having duly worshipped Īśāna—the Lord of his own caste—in the center, he should purify [the person] with the mantra of the Lord of his own caste ending in *phaṭ*. Having elevated the birth, he should cast [the person] into the Lord of his own caste situated in the *maṇḍala* using that same mantra ending in *svāhā*, and after lifting and purifying him, he should likewise unite him with his own self. Having thus elevated the birth, the Guru should initiate him through initiation by means of his power. If the Guru is not present, he may initiate himself. If he lacks the capacity to initiate in this manner, he should fast for six days, subsisting on forest fare, and mutter the mantra of the Lord of his own caste one hundred thousand times. In this context, having eaten the food of an impure member of the same caste, he should fast for one day and mutter it one hundred times; for one of the next lower caste, he should fast for two days and mutter it one thousand times; for one separated by one caste, three days and two thousand times; for one separated by two castes, the recitation is double, namely ten thousand times. A Brāhmaṇa, having eaten the food of an impure Śūdra, becomes pure after fasting for five nights, being initiated by the "Elevation of Birth," and muttering the mantra one hundred thousand times along with a *kṛcchra* penance. This same penance should be understood for those born in the direct order (*anuloma*) as well. In the case of eating the food of an outcaste (*antyaja*), there is no penance and one simply falls [from grace]; therefore, one should avoid that with effort. Likewise, upon eating the food of those belonging to another sectarian mark (*paraliṅgin*), one should mutter the mantra of the Lord of that particular caste ten thousand times. These are the Arhatas, Śākyas, Pāśupatas, and Kāpālikas; their Lords are Sadyojāta and the others respectively. Among them, having performed a *kṛcchra* and a *cāndrāyaṇa* penance upon eating the food of a Kāpālika, and having muttered the mantra of Īśāna one hundred thousand times, one should worship the Lord of the other sect's mark within the *maṇḍala* of the Lord of one's own caste.

One who has been initiated for the removal of birth is purified. If one eats food provided by those associated with other sectarian marks (*anyaliṅgin*), one should perform three hundred thousand recitations (*japa*) and the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.
For a householder dependent on others, the recitation is double that of one who is independent. It is indicated that for an independent teacher (*ācārya*), this very same [penance] applies. (20.36)
Half [of the penance] is prescribed for one who merely observes the commitments (samayin), while three-quarters is for a spiritual son (putraka).
Furthermore, regarding the commission of unmentioned sins that cause the loss of intelligence: || 20-37 ||
The expiation for an intentional act is remembered as being double that even [of an unintentional one].

In that regard, the performance of each of the following—eating once a day (*ekabhukta*), eating only at night (*nakta*), eating food obtained unasked (*annāyācita*), and fasting (*upavāsa*)—three times in succession constitutes what is known as the *kṛcchradvādaśarātra*. The *Cāndrāyaṇa* is performed by beginning on the first day of the bright fortnight, bathing three times a day (*triṣavaṇa*), with senses restrained, starting with one morsel of food and increasing the number of morsels daily until fifteen morsels are eaten on the full moon day. Similarly, in the dark fortnight, beginning on the first day and decreasing the number of morsels daily, one eats only one morsel on the new moon day; this is the *yavamadhya* (barley-shaped) *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Conversely, if one begins on the first day of the bright fortnight by eating fifteen morsels and decreases the number daily until eating only one morsel on the full moon day, and then begins the dark fortnight by eating one morsel and increases it daily until fifteen morsels are eaten on the new moon day, this is the *pipīlikamadhya* (ant-shaped) *Cāndrāyaṇa*. For all misdeeds, even those not specifically mentioned, expiations (*prāyaścitta*) such as vows, fasts, *kṛcchra*, *Cāndrāyaṇa*, recitation (*japa*), oblations (*huta*), gifts (*dāna*), visiting sacred sites (*tīrthasevā*), and worship of Śiva, as prescribed in the Dharmaśāstras, must be performed according to the gravity of the respective fault. These are not written here for fear of excessive length. In cases of expiation, if one is unable to perform the fasts, recitations, and so forth due to illness or extreme old age, one may have them performed for one's sake by a disciple, son, brother, maternal uncle, father, nephew, or others.
The expiation for those faults has thus been declared for their purification;
having understood them with his intellect, the wise man should avoid them with effort, just as avoiding contact with mud is superior to washing it away. (20.38½)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, on Expiation, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 20.
Now begins the twenty-first chapter.
A wise person should perform the rite of the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) every year; it fulfills all deficiencies, omissions, lapses, and errors in the procedures of worship.
If one does not perform the *pavitraka* rite out of negligence or ignorance, he suffers a fall from his spiritual attainments and is overcome by obstacles. (21.2)

(203) Since its fruit consists of the removal of obstacles, the fulfillment [of desires], and so forth, the *pavitraka* must indeed be performed by teachers (*deśika*), practitioners (*sādhaka*), spiritual sons (*putraka*), and others. (21.3)
Because it purifies that which has been performed with the faults of omission or error in worship, recitation, fire-rituals, and so forth, it is therefore called *pavitraka* (the purifier). 21.4.
If one does not perform the purificatory rite (pavitra) due to delusion or negligence,
he should recite the mantra of Kṛṣṇa three hundred thousand times and offer clarified butter as oblations ten times that number.
In this *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Worship performed without the purificatory rite (*pavitra*) is proclaimed to be *tāmasī*;
and it would be *rājasī* if it lacks the act of making [the deity] supreme like Indra."
Desiring to attain great merit, one should daily fashion a purifier for Śambhu using either leaves, flowers, or kuśa grass.
Thus, this is the perpetual purification; now the occasional [purification] is described:
in the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, and in both the bright and dark fortnights of Śrāvaṇa.
One should prepare the fragrant *pavitraka* on the seventh or the thirteenth day;
furthermore, it is traditionally prescribed that the *pavitra* must certainly be made on the fourteenth day (*bhūtā*) of the month of Āṣāḍha.
One who desires his own welfare should not perform the initiation (dīkṣā) and the installation (sthāpana), nor the Pavitraka rite and others for Indra (Śatakratu), during an intercalary month.
Where three lunar months should occur without a solar transit (saṅkrānti), that is to be known as an intercalary month (adhimāsa), excluded from all ritual acts.
Thus:
"Where two *sinīvālī*s occur within the interval of a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*), that should be known as an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*), excluded from all ritual acts. (21.6)
Furthermore, in the Pauṣkara:
"In the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, the fruits of the Pavitraka rite are declared to be excellent, middling, and inferior respectively; at no other time is it desired."
Thus, just as the Vedic injunction "one should sacrifice in the spring seasons" indicates the exclusion of other times and not [prescribes] anything else; || 21.7 ||

(p. 204) Therefore, on the eighth or fourteenth day of both the bright and dark fortnights of the months of Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada, the *pavitra* (sacred thread) of Śambhu should be prepared. That too should be performed by those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*) during the dark fortnight, and by those seeking worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) during the bright fortnight. For other deities as well, the *pavitraka* should be performed on their respective lunar days.
Regarding the materials for the thread: in the *Kṛta* and subsequent ages, gold, silver, or copper is prescribed; however, in this age of *Kali*, a new thread made of cotton is recommended. (21–8)
For the sacred thread (*pavitraka*), the primary thread should be neither too thick nor too thin, free of loose hairs, white as snow, and spun by the daughters of Brahmins.
The middle [grade] is with Kṣatriya and Vaiśya women, while that with Śūdra women is recorded as the lowest.
And the thread marked as lowest may be accepted according to one's capacity. || 21-10 ||
In the absence of thread, one should provide a purifier made of *darbha*, *muñja*, or other such materials;
that purifier must by all means not be omitted.
It is stated in the Gandhasūtra that elsewhere it may consist of nine threads;
having prepared it on the day before, or on the seventh or fifth day from that date. (21.12)
Having properly performed the offering of the sprouts, one should collect the necessary materials and have an auspicious pavilion constructed, square in shape and with four doors.
The ground should be eight cubits or five cubits wide at minimum,
provided with four archways, and elevated by half a cubit.
Having fashioned that [shrine] with canopies, adorned with strings of pearls, and covered with fine silk cloths, divine garments, or white raiment; || 21-15 ||
It was hung with various kinds of fruits, flowers, and garlands;
the floor, as smooth as the surface of a mirror, was smeared with cow-dung and water. (21.16)

To the east of that, one should construct a beautiful fire-chamber (agnyagāra) containing an Aindra-pit covered with a garland of Darbha grass, as well as a *sruk* and *sruva* ladles possessing the prescribed characteristics.
The water-pots, the ritual jars, the large vessels, the vardhanī, the bowls, and the buckets;
hair-free garments that have not yet been worn, as well as the sacrificial ladles and other such implements. || 21-18 ||
Sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, guggulu, clarified butter, honey, sugar, parched grain, white mustard, sesame, śāli rice, barley, and so forth. (21.19)
White grains of śāli rice, sacrificial fuel, kuśa grass, and fruits, as well as lamps, incense, food offerings, and whatever else may be useful. (21.20)
Having prepared the person who performs that rite, he should employ him there;
then, having taken the thread and gone to abundant, pure water, he should remain purified.
Having thoroughly purified it with alkaline water and washed it by pure Brahmins,
one should place it upon a pedestal accompanied by songs, instrumental music, and so forth, and perform its worship.
Having worshipped Gaṇeśvara with the general offering (sāmānyārghya) and perfumes and other articles,
one should wash the thread with the Sadyojāta mantra and dry it with the Aghora mantra.
Having worshipped it and placed it in a golden vessel or a bamboo one,
he should mount it upon a vehicle such as an elephant, adorned with an umbrella and chowries.
Adorned with the sounds of conchs, trumpets, and other instruments, along with the auspicious music of songs,
it was graced by men and women wearing ornaments and beautified by raised banners.
Having slowly performed a circumambulation of the village or the city or another place,
one should go to the door of the sacrificial hall and have the Brahmins recite auspicious blessings (*svasti*).
Having placed the thread upon the pedestal, one should then recite the *puṇyāha* formula;
one should then visualize the deities within the nine strands of the thread.
The Praṇava, the Moon, Fire, Brahmā, the Nāgas, Guha, the Sun, Śiva, and all the gods—these are the nine deities of the threads. (21–28)
The eight forms beginning with Earth, as well as Śiva, are the presiding deities;
their powers are Vāmā and the others—one should meditate upon these nine powers. (21–29)
One should worship these with their names, ending each with "namaḥ," and then [worship] Kālātman within the thread and the ninefold division among the strands.
One should sacrifice the *tuṭi*, the *lava*, the *nimeṣa*, the *kāṣṭhā*, and even the *kalā*; likewise, one should sacrifice the *ghaṭikā*, the *muhūrta*, the day, and the night. (21–31)
One should worship, in successive order, the lunar mansions, the lunar days, the weekdays, the two fortnights, the months, the seasons, and the year, as they are situated within the threads.
One should worship with one's own names beginning with "Tāra" (Oṃ) and ending with "Namaḥ," and then offer this prayer:
"Salutation to that Self of Time (Kālātman), who consists of moments and so forth up to the year, who is all-pervading, omnipresent, without beginning or end, and eternal. (21.33)

Thus, according to the Sūtra, one should worship the god Śiva, who is the essence of the principle of Time (kālatattva), while recollecting His presence until [the soul] is projected into Śiva. (21.34)
Thereafter,
having placed the hand of Śiva before him and accompanied by the act of supreme unification (paramīkaraṇa),
one should perform the construction of the *pavitra*, while reciting and remembering Vāmadeva.
In that regard, the fragrant purifier (gandhapavitra) should have a single knot and consist of few threads;
some say it should be equal in number to the little finger [in length], and it is fashioned from three strands.
The *pavitraka* for lingas measuring from one cubit up to nine cubits should consist of twenty-eight strands, beginning there and increasing up to one hundred and eight.
One should prepare the *pavitra* with nine threads according to the sequence of tenfold increase; for this is the secondary rule, while the primary rule is now being declared. (21–38)
For all stable lingas, whether unmanifest (avyakta) in particular or mobile (cala), it is prescribed according to one hundred and eight threads. || 21-39 ||
Alternatively, there is the excellent method with eighty-one threads, the middling with fifty thereafter, or the inferior method with thirty-six threads. (21.40)
It has been declared for those with the smallest liṅgas and those whose capacity for worship is minimal;
therefore, one should prepare the pavitraka according to one's own capacity.
For fixed lingas here,
one should fashion a triple head-purifier (śiraḥpavitra) from the measurement of the top of the linga, consisting of the three principles (tattvas).

One should fashion the fourth [mark], which pertains to all principles (sārvatattva), as the descent of the Gaṅgā (gaṅgāvatāraka); it should extend from the top of the liṅga down to the point where it touches the entire base (piṇḍikā). || 21.43 ||

It is explained that for movable liṅgas and sacrificial altars (sthaṇḍila) during the pavitraka rite, there shall indeed be an expansion according to the distinctions in worship, beginning with the superior [grade]. (21.44)
The sacred threads (pavitra) shall be of superior, middling, and inferior quality respectively, with widths of twelve, eight, and four finger-breadths (aṅgula).
(207) "Twelve finger-breadths, eight finger-breadths, and four finger-breadths—thus says King Bhoja.
The triad of head-purifiers (*śiraḥpavitra*) constitutes the three [types] beginning with the *uttama*;
that should be employed upon a single liṅga in the form of a crown. (21–46)

One should fashion the *gaṅgāvatāraka* there, equal in measure to the *tattva*-finger-breadths. Regarding the measurement of the knots of the purifier (*pavitra*) here, Somaśambhu states: "Ten knots should be made, or else according to the number of *tattvas*."
The intervals between the knots should be made equal, measuring one, two, four, or more finger-breadths as desired, or according to what is aesthetically pleasing.
And he states the names of the ten knots:
Prakṛti, Pauruṣī, Vīrā, and the fourth is Aparājitā;
the fifth is Jayā, the sixth is Ajitā, and the seventh is Kriyā.
Śivā, Manonmanī, and Sarvatomukhā as the tenth; thus [are the ten].
Furthermore, there are twelve knots for the Gaṅgāvatāraka. (21.47)
Or they may correspond to the number of threads [in the main cord], or it should be made according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
one should prepare four purifiers (pavitra) with their characteristic marks unmanifested.
In the same way, for the face-emblems (mukhaliṅgas), one should perform [the rite] for each one individually among those that are manifest,
as well as upon one's own image, the Lord of the Gaṇas, the lineage of gurus, and the sacred book.

One should likewise provide a single sacred thread (*pavitra*) for the auspicious water-pot, the weapon-vessel, the weapons of the world-protectors, and the bull, as well as one for each of the lords of the gates.
One should fashion those [ornaments] hanging down from the neck for Gaurī, Mahālakṣmī, Durgā, and among the eight Mothers (aṣṭamātṛs) in their manifest forms. (21.51)
One should prepare three purifiers for each of Sarasvatī;
that is to say, excluding those [purifiers] associated with the descent of the Gaṅgā.
[One should also prepare them] for Viṣṇu, Bhāskara, and Vahni, as well as for Caṇḍeśa, Skanda, and Vedhas. (21–52)
p. 208) A fourfold set of purifiers, equal to Śiva, has been described separately.
Having thus prepared the purifiers, one should then dye their knots. (21.53)
Having ground camphor, saffron, turmeric, yellow pigment (rocanā), agallochum, and red ochre together in equal parts according to availability, one should color the person with it.
Now, having discarded the old collection of vessels made of clay, wood, bamboo, and so forth, everything new that is suitable for worship should be accepted.
"Even an old *sruk* ladle is not defective; one should make a new and auspicious *sruva* ladle," so it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*.
"O Śakra! having set aside the *sruk* and *sruva*, one should discard everything that is ancient."
Thus it is said in the *Mohaśūrottara*.

Thereafter, on the seventh or thirteenth lunar day, having observed a fast and performed the rites of bathing and *sandhyā*, and having performed the specific libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the mantras and so forth according to the procedure taught in the "Chapter on Bathing" (*Snānapaṭala*), one should encircle the entire sacrificial ground and its surroundings with a triple-stranded thread. Having worshipped the Sun in the eastern portion of the enclosed area according to the rules, and subsequently worshipped Śiva and the Fire according to the daily ritual (*nityavidhi*), one should worship and employ pure Brāhmaṇas learned in the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva Vedas at the east, south, north, and west of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*). With the words, "The recitation must be performed by you as an auspicious limb of the Pavitrāropaṇa rite," one should honor them with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings and engage them in recitation.
