Then, having washed one's hands and feet, and having sprinkled the doors of the sacrificial pavilion with the Weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*) for the sake of the occasional worship (*naimittikapūjā*), one should worship the door-deities: Śāntikalā at the eastern door, Vidyā at the southern, Nivṛtti at the western, and Pratiṣṭhā at the northern. One should worship these using their respective names preceded by the *Tāra* (Om) and the Heart-seed-syllable (*hṛdbīja*), ending with "namaḥ. Furthermore, one should worship the two door-keepers belonging to each respective Vedic branch, such as Nandīśa and others, using their names ending in "namaḥ."
One should worship Nandīśa, Mahākāla, Bhṛṅgīśa, Gaṇanāyaka, Vṛṣabha, Ṣaṇmukha, Devī, and Caṇḍa, starting from the east.
Then, at the western gate, one should worship the gatekeepers as prescribed for the daily rite;
thereafter, one should employ the iron-arrow weapon (nārācāstra) and strike three times with the heel.

Having dispelled the obstacles with snapping fingers and threatening gestures, and having taken recourse to the southern branch, he should enter the interior of the house while reciting the weapon-mantra as before.
Having placed [the deity] in the middle of the threshold and circumambulating clockwise,
one should worship Vāstupa and Vedhas, and likewise take one's seat as before.

(p. 209) Then, having sat upon the altar facing north, having performed self-purification (*ātmaśuddhi*), having effected the ritual integration of the limbs (*sakalīkṛtya*), and having worshipped the special *arghya* water, he should sprinkle his own head and the ritual implements with the *arghya* waters using the *astra-mantra*, enclose them with the *varma-mantra*, and perform the purification of the mantras residing in the substances as previously described. Wearing a *tripuṇḍra* mark of ashes, a tilaka of sandalwood, and white flowers, and wearing an upper garment, holding the sword of knowledge (*jñānakhaḍga*), and having prepared the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in the five squares according to the path taught for initiation, he should sequentially perform the rites of inspection, sprinkling, striking, moistening, digging, scattering, filling, leveling, pouring, pounding, sweeping, smearing, and making [the ground] adamantine (*vajrīkaraṇa*) using the *hṛdaya*, *astra*, *varma*, and root mantras respectively. Having thus consecrated the pavilion by sprinkling it with the *pañcagavya*, and having worshipped the mobile and immobile jars (*kumbha* and *vardhanī*) situated on their seats according to the path taught for initiation—preceded by the scattering of offerings—he should then, within the pavilion, invoke and worship the world-protectors (*lokapāla*) in jars filled with water placed over grain upon which mandalas have been drawn in the respective directions, each adorned with three threads, sprouts and fruits of mango and other trees, perfumes, unbroken rice, flowers, and tufts of grass (*kūrca*). He should also invoke their weapons and cause the command of Śiva to be proclaimed to them.
O Śakra! By the command of Śiva, you must remain vigilant in your own quarter for the sake of pacifying obstacles, until the conclusion of the sacrifice. (21.60)
Having thus addressed the lords of the world, and having circumambulated the weapon-vessel and the water-pot,
and having recollected the fortress of the weapon, one should worship while remaining in a steady posture.
And having recollected their union with the previously assumed mudrā,
he should offer that sword of knowledge to Kumbheśa and pray to Śiva.
O Śambhu! O Śaṅkara, Lord of Yoga! You must remain here until the end of the sacrifice, together with Śivā, along with your sons, your attendants, and the Lord of Yoga.

Having thus made the request, offered the concluding oblation, performed worship, and restrained [the deity], he should seat [the disciple] in their proper place. Then, having bathed the Śiva residing in the *liṅga* according to the procedure taught in the chapter on ritual services (*upacāra-paṭala*)—beginning with the purification of the *liṅga* and including the invocation (*āvāhana*), the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), and ablutions with perfumed water—and having presented garments, ornaments, perfumes, and so forth, and worshipped Him up to the final offering; then, either in the center, the northeast, or the north, within one of the mandalas such as the *Bhadra-liṅga*, he should worship Śiva up to the final offering, omitting the bathing, by means of the seat, invocation, and other rites. Then, having established the fire in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) to the east according to the procedure taught in the chapter on fire-rituals (*agnikārya-paṭala*), and having invoked and worshipped Śiva therein, he should satisfy Him properly. He should then contemplate the light emerging from the crest of Śiva situated in the mandala as being in the form of a flash of lightning, and having joined it through the path of his own central channel (*svanāḍī*) with the light emerging from the fire-nose of Śiva residing in the fire, he should worship Śiva in the heart of the fire. Thereafter, he should cook the sacrificial porridge (*caru*).
p. 210) It is as follows:

Having smeared the hearth to the west of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), or to the south, one should scratch it with the Astra-mantra, sprinkle it with water, and enclose it with the Kavaca-mantra. || 21-64 ||
Having cleansed and smeared the hearth, one should then visualize Śakti,
whose entire body is thus fashioned with the arms of both dharma and adharma.
Having worshipped with perfumes, incense, and other offerings, one should then place the fire— which was previously drawn out and consecrated by the five purificatory rites— into that hearth.
One should again worship both Śiva and that Śakti;
[and prepare] a vessel for the sacrificial porridge (caru), made either of udumbara wood or of clay, which is free from any blemish.
Having washed it with the Astra-mantra, veiled it with the Kavaca-mantra, and gazed upon it, one should sprinkle it, drench it, strike it, smear it with fragrance, and fumigate it.
Having wound a cord of kuśa grass around his neck, he should place him within the mandala;
it is then sprinkled with water while reciting the Astra-mantra, enclosed by the Kavaca-mantra, and consecrated with the Astra-mantra.
One should place her face downwards upon a seat of six-fold darbha grass;
having worshipped Śiva along with his limbs upon her, one should turn her face upwards and smear her with clarified butter.
One should fill [the vessel] with fresh milk from a cow that has pure milk;
having placed that [vessel] on the stove, [one should add] white *śāli* rice grains.
One should place five times the amount of strained [substances] into milk;
then, sitting in the southeast, one should perform the shaking and opening in due order.
One should prepare it once with the ladle while reciting the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), constructing a small pavilion;
then, having cooked that sacrificial porridge (*caru*) within the vessel while reciting the collection of mantras (*mantrasaṃhitā*).
Having said, "Become well-sweated," one should sprinkle it with ghee;
having thus performed the sprinkling over the heated [substance], [one should place it] upon a seat of darbha grass within the maṇḍala.
Having removed that sacrificial porridge (caru) onto the second [fire] again with the Saṃhitā-mantra,
he should perform the "cooling-consecration" (śītābhighāraṇa) by pouring clarified butter over it while reciting, "Become cool."

Having cleansed the vessel on the outside with clay and water, protected it with the Astra-mantra, marked it with three lines (tripuṇḍra), and rendered it immortal by means of the [Amṛta] mudrā. (21.76)
To the west of the pit, one should place a small mandala as before;
having worshipped it with the Heart-mantra, one should offer clarified butter, sacrificing once each time with the limbs of Śiva.
One should pour [clarified butter] over that sacrificial porridge (caru) one hundred and eight times with the root mantra;
having offered it and poured [the remainder] over it, one should subsequently divide that porridge into three parts.
Having combined one's own portion with honey and clarified butter for Śiva and the fire,
and having worshipped the portion belonging to Śiva with the *hṛdaya-mantra*, one should perform the ritual placement (*vinyāsa*).

Thereafter, having gone near the deity and offered the eight-fold flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should arrange and worship the following items: a tooth-stick and betel-leaf with the *puruṣa* mantra in the east; ashes, a rosary, a staff, a loincloth, and an alms-bowl with the *aghora* mantra in the south; earth, *kuśa* grass, water, and sacrificial materials with the *sadyojāta* mantra in the west; myrobalan fruit, yellow pigment (*rocanā*), saffron, a probe, *kaṅkatika* wood, and collyrium with the *vāmadeva* mantra in the north; and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), sandals, an umbrella, a yoga-mat, and a seat with the *īśāna* mantra in the northeast. Whatever among these is unavailable, one should mentally visualize it.
But the *caru* portion for the gods should be sprinkled with weapons and protected by armor.
Having worshipped with the heart-mantra and consecrated it as nectar, one should offer it with the Brahma-mantras.
Then, taking the sacred threads (pavitra), one should place them in a vessel made of gold, bamboo, or other materials.
One should place [the image] upon a seat covered with a black antelope skin, silk cloth, and so forth, while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*.
Having sprinkled it with water using the *astra-mantra* and touched it with the *saṃhitā-mantras*, one should worship it and meditate upon it.
[He meditated upon] Śambhu, whose nature is the year, the sole witness of all actions,
the imperishable protector, and the bestower of the fruits of worldly enjoyment and liberation.

One should then visualize within the purifiers (pavitras) the fulfillment of all actions— those performed, those left undone, and those abandoned— as well as those that have been ploughed over, according to the number of the primary elements.
Having offered oblations into the fire there with the root mantra, one should pour clarified butter upon those [materials];
having thus purified them by the pouring of the residue (saṃpāta), one should then worship them with the Saṃhitā-mantra.
One should offer a fragrant purifier (gandhapavitraka) to the Sun who has been previously worshipped;
it should be well-perfumed with incense, accompanied by flowers, and consecrated as nectar from the primary pitcher (mūlakumbha).

Having performed the ritual rinsing of the mouth with the root mantra ending in *recānta*, and having raised the *ārātrika* lamp while uttering the *sarvātman* mantra ending in *antaka*, he should thereafter rinse his mouth again and sanctify his body through the *sakalīkaraṇa* rite. (21.87)
One should wrap the entire temple and the pavilion with three threads;
likewise, one should wrap the entire collection of ritual implements for worship with the Tārā mantra.
Having offered fragrant purifiers (gandhapavitraka) to Nandin and the other gatekeepers, as well as to Vāstupa and Brahmā, and to the world-protectors (lokeśa) along with their weapons; 21.89.

Thereafter, taking the *pavitra* threads from the vessel near the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and placing them before the *śivakumbha*, one should offer them for the sake of protection to Śiva residing in the jar with this [mantra]:
"O Blessed One! These consecrated *pavitra* threads are here according to the prescribed rite."
I offer them here to you; protect them, O Śaṅkara! || 21-90 ||
Thus one should offer [the pavitra].

Thereafter, taking the fragrant pavitras from that [offering], one should place them upon the Śiva-kumbha, the Astra-vardhanī, and the rows of Gaṇapati and the Gurus with their respective mantras ending in "namas" and "sarvatattvātmane. Having separately performed the ārātrika rite and seated oneself facing the deity upon the prepared maṇḍala, one should place the pavitra upon one's own self with this [mantra]:
Oṃ.
In this vow that brings completion to the annual sacrifice,
I, whose soul is purified, wear the purifying Pavitraka.

Having spoken thus, and having dissolved [the deity] into himself with the mantra ending in *namaḥ* addressed to Tāra-mūla-Śiva, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*). Then, sitting facing the deity, he should take in his joined palms (*añjali*) the fragrant purifier (*gandha-pavitraka*) prepared for that purpose—smeared with fragrant paste, well-perfumed, and accompanied by *dūrvā* grass and unbroken rice (*akṣata*)—and, having rendered it nectar-like (*amṛtīkṛta*) through the collection of mantras (*mantra-saṃhitā*), he should consecrate it and offer it with this [verse]:
"Oṃ! To you, the Lord who fulfills all deficiencies in the ritual procedure, I address myself today regarding my transgressions; O Cause of the attainment of my desires! (21.92)
O Lord of the conscious and the unconscious, grant success to me who am performing this sacrifice!
O Śambhu, salutations to you in every way and at all times; be gracious unto me. (21.93)

Thus, having rendered [the deity] immortal through *recaka* (exhalation), and having uttered the root *tāra* (oṃ) ending with "namas śivāya," one should offer the sacred perfumed cloth (*gandhapavitra*) to the Blessed One. Immediately thereafter, having performed the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), one should pray with this:
Oṃ!
You are invited, O Lord of Gods, together with the Goddess and the lords of the Gaṇas.
Accompanied by the lords of mantras, the guardians of the world, and their retinues.
"I announce to you that at dawn I shall perform the *pavitraka* rite;
and by your command, O Supreme Lord, I shall observe the religious observance (*niyama*). (21.95)

Having thus prayed for auspiciousness and being granted permission by Śiva with the words "So be it," he should thereafter present a special *naivedya* to the Lord according to his means. After honoring Him with offerings ending in betel and mouth-fresheners, and celebrating with songs, dances, and the like, he should exit once permitted by the Blessed One. Having gone outside, he should place the fragrant *pavitra* upon the girdle of the fire-altar (*agni*), offer a portion of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) into the fire, and having cast the remainder of that as a *bali* offering near the fire, he should seek permission and go outside again. There, with water containing fragrant flowers, incense, and lamps, he should offer a *bali* in the ten directions using the remnants of the vessel's food while reciting the *saṃhitā* mantras.
With [the mantras] beginning with "Oṃ, accept this for Indra, obeisance," and so forth; and again:

Saying "Oṃ, svāhā to the dwellers of the eastern and other directions, to the lords of the quarters, the hosts of spirits, the Mothers, Rudras, Kṣetrapālas, and others," he should scatter the *bali* offering in the ten directions. Having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*), he should perform the expiation for any defects by offering oblations three times with the *mūrtis*, five times with the *mūla-mantra*, ten times with the *aghora-mantra*, and one hundred and eight times with sesame, white mustard, parched grain, and ghee. Then, having offered the *pūrṇāhuti* and offerings to Agni, Soma, Agni-Soma, and Agni Sviṣṭakṛt using the *vyāhṛtis*, and having worshipped the Śiva residing in the fire, he should unite that Śiva with the Śiva in the *maṇḍala* through the channel of the *saṃhitā*. Having worshipped the Deity, he should place the fragrant *pavitra* upon the seat of knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) presided over by the book of the Siddhānta—which has been worshipped like Śiva with the names of the Vidyās—and upon which the ten-syllabled Vāgīśvarī is present. He should conclude the mantra with "namas" to the essence of the *praṇava*, the heart, and the root-vidyā. Then, having removed the *ārātrika* lamp, he should place the great *pavitra*s in a vessel covered by the armor (*varma*) and weapon (*astra*) mantras. Having consecrated them with the *mantra-saṃhitā*, protected them with the *astra* and *varma* mantras, and worshipped them, he should inform the one stationed in the *kumbha* of the protection and bow to the Blessed Lord. Having offered the ritual service (*kriyā*) and requested, "May this rite of mine be free from defects," and being authorized by the Blessed One, he should go outside and partake of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and the tooth-stick according to the path taught in the initiation (*dīkṣā*) within the three eastern *maṇḍalas*.

In that case, because the fast is mandatory and because the consumption of the remainder of the sacrificial porridge (caru) is already established, one should consume only five mouthfuls as the oblations of breath (prāṇāhuti).
Regarding this, it is stated in the Pauṣkara:
"But when the fast is mandatory and the consumption of the remainder has arrived..."
One who eats only the measure required for the Prāṇāgnihotra is not considered to have broken his fast.
Thus [it is said].
Also elsewhere, in the section on *śrāddha*:
"When fasting is obligatory and a *śrāddha* occurs as an occasional (*naimittika*) duty..."
Then, having smelled that which was used by the ancestors, one should observe a fast.

Thus it is said. Then, having sipped water (ācamana), one who desires worldly enjoyment (bhoktu-kāma) should sit upon a bed of *darbha* grass with his head toward the east, while one who desires liberation (mumukṣu) should sit upon a bed of ashes.
On this point, Somaśambhu states:
"Having sipped water, equipped with the mantras, and having performed the vigil with songs..."
Desiring to enjoy [the fruits of his penance], he sat upon a bed of darbha grass, recollecting the Lord.
"In this very manner, one desiring liberation should also lie down,
solely upon a bed of ashes, fasting and composed in mind.
Since it has been stated that "the vigil with music has been performed," sleep must not be indulged in.
And in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"Having performed the offering of ritual action before Śiva, one should pass the night intent on recitation and meditation,
or else devoted to hymns and songs."
Thus it is said. Therefore, one should remain awake before the deity upon a seat of *darbha* grass while observing a fast.

Then, having bathed before sunrise and completed the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*), one should worship with the general *arghya* offering, beginning with the perfumes and threads in their proper order. (21.96)
Without having dismissed the Lord, one should place him within the northeastern mandala;
then, having bid farewell to the deity with due regard and having removed the used floral offerings (nirmālya), [one should proceed].
Having sipped water for purification (ācamana) and performed the purification of oneself and so forth as before,
one should then worship the Sun, followed by the worship of the door-guardians, the world-protectors, and the weapons.
One who is constant in the daily ritual should worship the deity with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and other offerings;
having sacrificed to the water-pot, the weapon, the lords of the maṇḍala, and the fire, one should likewise offer the full oblation (pūrṇāhuti) and the bali.
Having thus constantly completed the obligatory rites, one should then commence the occasional rites.

(p. 215) There, while the deity has not yet been dismissed, one should remove the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) from the fire and the tooth-stick (*dantakāṣṭha*) and other items, placing them in their proper locations. Having adorned the deity according to one’s means with the *yantra*, the *liṅga*, golden balls (*hemagolaka*), cloth, garlands, perfumes, and so forth, one should offer the expiatory oblation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of one hundred and eight repetitions of the *Aghora* mantra, followed by the *pūrṇāhuti*. Then, having offered the great purifiers (*mahāpavitra*)—which have been fumigated—to the Sun with his own mantra, and having performed the waving of lights (*ārātrika*), one should sip water for purification (*ācamana*). As before, one should offer the purifiers to the Lords of the Gates (*dvāreśa*), Vāstu, Brahmā, the Lord of the World (*lokeśa*), the [deities of the] weapons (*astra*), Gaṇapati, and the Gurus, using their respective mantras. Then, as previously, one should offer the purifier to one's own self with the mantra, sip water, and sit facing the deity, identifying oneself with Sadāśiva. Having offered the *arghya* and worshipped with the eightfold flowers (*aṣṭapuṣpikā*), one should contemplate the Self as Time (*kāla*), whose body consists of the moments of *truṭi*, *lava*, *nimeṣa*, *kāṣṭhā*, *ghaṭikā*, *muhūrta*, day and night, fortnights, months, seasons, solstices, and years, and who is the cause of all activities involving the body, the senses, and their objects.
The sole witness to all actions performed, unperformed, or abandoned, as well as to those that are afflicted.

With a pure mind, recollecting Śiva— who is the protector of the field, the Lord, the refuge, and the pure-minded— one should first take the head-purifier (śiraḥpavitra), fumigate it with flowers, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and the tips of dūrvā grass, and having addressed Śiva facing the pitcher with this [verse], one should offer it: Oṃ.
O God! That which was seen by you in the form of Time within my ritual procedure—|| 21.101 ||
May that which was done by me—whether it be joined, released, held, or concealed—be free from affliction;
may what has been done be unafflicted, perfected, and well-honored.

O Śambhu! By means of this entirely pure [thread], through Your will—*oṃ pūraya pūraya maghavrataniyameśvarāya svāhā*; with this, having first placed one *pavitra* [on the head] with the root-mantra *tāra* and "to Śiva, the Lord of the Śiva-tattva, obeisance," one should likewise place another two *pavitras* with "obeisance to the Lord of the Vidyā-tattva and Ātma-tattva. In the Śiva-tattva, ending with Śiva, protected by the cause of Rudra. (21.103)

Having recited [the mantra] from the Root (mūla) up to Śiva, one should place the purifying thread (pavitra). But in the case of the Vidyā-tattva, at the end of the Vidyā-mantra, it is protected by Viṣṇu as the cause.
Having uttered [the mantra] up to Īśvara, one should place the second [syllable] upon it;
[this is done] within the principle of the Self (ātmatattva), ending with Prakṛti, which is protected by Brahmā as its cause.
The root mantra should extend up to Sadāśiva; one should then superimpose the third [mantra], which extends up to the Lord of all Tattvas and is protected by all the Causes.
Having recited the root mantra up to Śiva, the descent of the Gaṅgā should be bestowed;
for one desiring worldly enjoyment it should be thus, but for liberation it should indeed be the reverse. (21.107)
One should install the purificatory vessels with the principles (tattvas) of the Self, Knowledge, and Śiva;
then, having presented the ārātrika lamp, the wise one should address the Deity.
You are the refuge of all beings; you abide in everything that moves and is stationary.
O Supreme Lord, you are the witness of all through your internal movement.
By deed, by mind, or by speech, there is no other refuge for me than you.
Whatever has been performed deficient in mantra, deficient in ritual action, or deficient in materials— [may it be perfected]. (21.110)
O Maheśvara! Whatever daily rite of yours has been performed by me devoid of recitation, fire-offerings, and worship, and lacking praise and devotion—please fulfill that deficiency.
O Lord of the Gods, you are perfectly pure, the purifier that destroys sin;
by you, the entire world, both moving and unmoving, has been made holy.
O Lord! Whatever vow has been broken by me through the occurrence of deficiency—may all of that become whole again, joined together by the thread of your command. (21.113)

At the conclusion of this, having made the formal declaration: "Obeisance to Śiva, the self of all principles (tattvas), the witness of all actions, the fulfiller of all, the bestower of all fruits, the omniscient," one should offer the worship of the sacred thread (*pavitrapūjā*) and dedicate oneself at the lotus-feet of Śiva with a handful of flowers accompanied by water, and prostrate like a staff.
[One should do this] for four months, three months, two months, or even a fortnight;
or for seven days, five nights, two nights, or even a single night. (21.114)
Having made a formal resolve (saṅkalpa) before the deity, saying, "I shall perform this much," and having been told by Śiva, "So be it," he departed with his permission.
Having worshipped the World-Protectors (Lokapālas), the weapons, Nandī and the others who stand at the gates, with purificatory offerings (pavitrakas),
one should place the purificatory threads upon the fire and upon the seat of knowledge (vidyāpīṭha).
Then, having offered oblations to Agni with the *vyāhṛtis*, and also to Soma and to Agni-Soma, one should likewise cast the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and the *bali* as before.

(p. 217) Now, while the Guru is present, having honored him like Śiva and satisfied him with garments, ornaments, wealth, and so forth, one should place a most beautiful *pavitra* upon him; in his absence, one should worship and place it upon his sandals or similar items. Then, taking the fruits of the recitation (*adhyayana*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), and other rites into one’s own hand with water, and offering them at the lotus-feet of the deity, one should give them their sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the sacred threads (*sūtra*). Having given the sacred threads to initiated Brahmins, ascetics (*liṅgin*), and kinsmen, and having satisfied the initiated Brahmins and ascetics with gold, garments, and other gifts, one should give gold and other wealth according to one's ability to all supplicants, including the poor, the blind, and the wretched. After feeding everyone, one should offer the entire fruit of that act of providing food to Śiva through this [mantra].
Oṃ,
may Sadāśiva be pleased by this gift given with devotion, free from stinginess regarding wealth, and according to my capacity. (21.118)
Thus, one should offer the gifts and other offerings at the lotus-feet of Śambhu.

Until the conclusion of the vow, one should worship daily with such grandeur; having removed the previous offering (nirmālya), performed the cleansing of the temple, and lifted the first binding thread from its base, one should hang new sacred threads (pavitra) over the deity.
Then, at the end of the vow, having worshipped with special rites:
Oṃ,
the vow of the purificatory rite (pavitraka) has been performed by me according to my resolve.
"By your grace, may this rite lead to the attainment of its fruit.
Thus, one who desires worldly enjoyment or even liberation should offer [the ritual] to Śambhu.
"One should offer [the oblation], saying: 'May my karma not be binding.

Thereafter, having performed the rites up to the satiation of the mantra and having offered the *pūrṇāhuti*, one should unite the Blessed One residing in the fire with Śiva through the path of the channels (*nāḍī*)."
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya, if he is learned in the Vedas, [he should perform the rite] with the Jaya and other [oblations]. || 21-121 ||

Having offered oblations into the fire with Vedic mantras and performed expiatory rites (*prāyaścitta*), he then withdraws the mantras from the fire, leads them to the *dvādaśānta*, and establishes them within his heart. Having likewise joined the Fire-god (*vahni*) at the *dvādaśānta*, he dismisses those [deities] seated upon the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass (*viṣṭara*). Having sipped water for purification (*ācamana*) and performed the ritual of self-protection (*sakalīkaraṇa*), he enters within. There, having withdrawn the mantras of the Śiva-pitcher (*śivakumbha*), the weapon (*astra*), and the *vardhanī* vessel, he joins the Śiva residing therein with the Śiva established in the *liṅga*. Having also dismissed the guardians of the quarters (*dikpāla*) and others, if Caṇḍa is present, he shall deposit the sacred threads (*pavitra*) using the seven-syllabled mantra of that deity.
Having invoked [the deity] upon the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) and worshipped him, one should offer all the remains of his offerings (nirmālya) and so forth without exception to Caṇḍanātha.
Alternatively, one should worship Caṇḍa seated upon a pedestal (pīṭha) on the sacrificial ground.
Thus says Somaśambhu.
Oṃ, whatever annual rite has been performed by me, whether deficient or excessive... [21.122]
"May all that be fulfilled by your command, O Caṇḍanātha!
Thus one should pray to him, and afterwards worship him with perfumes and other offerings.
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa) to him, and having bowed and praised him, one should dismiss him;
all his remains, such as the floral offerings (nirmālya), should be cast into a blind well or into water.
One should especially cast the threads into the abundant [water] after reciting mantras and cutting them;
then, one should purify the ground with water saturated with cow dung. (21.125)
Then, one should bathe the deity according to the prescribed method with one hundred and eight jars, or according to one's capacity, or even with nine.
Having honored it with special distinction, one obtains the complete fruit.

He who performs this *pavitra* ceremony every year with devotion, fulfilling whatever omissions may have occurred, attains the entire fruit of worship and other rites, and goes to the imperishable and auspicious abode of Śambhu. (21.127½)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, on the Installation of the Sacred Thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 21.
Now begins the twenty-second chapter.
Now is described the springtime worship of the *dāmanaka* flower, which brings satisfaction to the Moon-crested Lord (Śiva),
during which time the God dwelt for a long duration in the Himalayan hermitage, separated from the Goddess.
Accompanied by Nandīśvara and other lords of the Gaṇas, and being worshipped by hosts of eminent sages,
he constantly manifested the *samādhi* of *sabīja-yoga* (meditation with seed-syllables), beholding his own Self within the Self.

Then, at that time, it is said, the lord of the Asuras named Tāraka—extremely fierce and resembling the sun at the end of a kalpa—having conquered the king of the gods along with the hosts of deities, tormented them intensely. (22.3)

p. 219) Then, entreated by Indra and the other gods and by the lords of sages for the sake of pacifying that [obstacle], the Creator spoke to the gods: "Exert yourselves to make Gaurī pleasing to Giriśa, who is self-restrained. (22.4)
There is no other means in this world for the pacification of the splendor of the lord of the Daityas than the power of Śiva and Pārvatī;
for this great task was accepted by the gods after they had been addressed by the Great God himself.
Thereupon, commissioned by all the Maruts headed by Indra to accomplish that task, Kāma went to the hermitage of Sthāṇu in the Himalayas together with his friend Vasanta. || 22.6 ||

Even while dwelling among sensual desires, he who had exerted himself toward the breaking of meditative concentration found his companionship provided by forests in full bloom and by gentle breezes that stirred the lotuses. (22.7)
Even Giriśa, standing before Gaurī, reflecting slightly on the cause of his mental agitation and perceiving the immodesty of Smara, did not wish to restrain the anger that had arisen.
Then, from his third eye, a fierce fire emerged;
it became Bhairava, three-eyed and holding a trident and a skull in his hands, and he reduced Kāma to nothing but ashes.

Beholding that terrible deed of Bhairava and his fearsome, loud laughter as he roared, all—the gods, asuras, siddhas, and yakṣas—though self-controlled, were suddenly struck with fear and despondency. || 22-10 ||

Even Rudra, the best of gods, beholding that Bhairava, was pleased and addressed him: "Since the three worlds have been thoroughly subdued by you today through your very act of burning, you shall therefore be known by the name Damana."

Then, having come there to attend upon Gaurī along with the wife of Smara, the celestial women beheld the destruction of Rati; knowing her husband’s dissolution, she fell down overwhelmed like a severed plantain tree.

There, Pārvatī, beholding the Tathāgata’s delight and the god of love, Anaṅga, in an instant, cursed Bhairava with her mind alone out of anger: "For a long time, become a creeping plant moving upon the earth! (22.13)
Thus cursed by Ambikā, he instantly became known as Vīrudhamana;
with his exceedingly delicate limbs, he possessed a delightful fragrance born from the sprinkling of Rati’s tears upon the ashes of Smara’s body.
Then Śiva, perceiving that excessive delight of the Goddess and her expressed approval,
smiling and allaying her anger, the most excellent one granted a boon to the *damana* creeper.

"From this day forward, those people here who worship me during the spring season together with Vasanta and Manmatha, shall enjoy their desired objects through the leaves of the *damana* plant and other offerings that have become part of your own body. (22.16)
"O dear one, since you have worshipped me along with Umā, a second boon is granted to you once again.
Likewise, may Hari and the deities headed by Brahmā, being worshipped by you, grant you all that you desire. (22.17)

"Those men who, transgressing my command, do not observe the Dāmana festival in the spring—accept all the merit born of the spring resulting from their worship, which is granted through my grace. (22.18)
Having thus granted a boon to Damanaka, the Bull-bannered Lord then ordained the ritual procedure for him;
that too is well-known in the Svacchanda Tantra, and has been observed by other Śaiva traditions as well. (22.19)
On this point, Somaśambhu states:
"Although it has been declared thus in the *Svacchandabhairava-tantra*,
nevertheless, because of its conciseness, it is also taught here in the Siddhānta."
Thus it is said:
"For example, on the eighth or fourteenth day of the first fortnights of the months of Madhu and Mādhava, the Dāmanaka offering to Śambhu bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (22.20)

Prior to that, within seven days or five days, one should perform the planting of the sprouts (aṅkura) and gather the required materials, such as the pavilion and other necessities, as they have been prescribed.
On the seventh or the thirteenth lunar day, having performed the prescribed rites of daily worship,
one should decorate that sacrificial hall with canopies, garlands, fruits, and other ornaments.
Then, having gone to the Damanaka grove adorned with Aśoka trees, he went to the foot of a beautiful and decorated Aśoka tree.

In the absence of that [image], one should perform the springtime worship in the shrine room or even in a place where a temporary structure has been built, using these mantras in their proper sequence.

Having invoked Gaṇapati in the southwest and the Guru in the northeast, and having worshipped them, he should then recite: "Oṃ, salutations to you, Aśoka, the destroyer of the sorrow of desire and women!
Constantly remove my affliction of grief and produce joy within me. (22–25)
Having thus worshipped the Aśoka tree with perfumes and other offerings up to the lamps, [one should recite]:

"Salutation to that self of Time (Kālātman), who is imperishable and all-pervading, whose form is time ranging from a moment (truṭi) up to a yuga, who is beginningless, and who indeed brings about the manifestation of all things. (22–26)

Having thus invoked and worshipped the Soul of Time (*Kālātman*) at the foot of an *aśoka* tree, one should place two jars—drawn with lines upon grain, fumigated, filled with scented water and other substances, containing gold, *kūrca*-grass, and flowers, and adorned with fruits, garments, garlands, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*)—within two mandalas formed to the south and north of that very spot. In the southern jar, one should worship Vasanta (Spring), and in the northern, Kāma (Desire), each upon their respective seat consisting of a lotus made of the qualities of passion (*rajas*), darkness (*tamas*), and goodness (*sattva*), along with the foundational power (*ādhāra-śakti*), the seat of Ananta (*anantāsana*), and the [spiritual] throne (*pīṭha*). Their respective names are used for worship, and the root mantra is: *oṃ vasantāya namaḥ*. Having assigned the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) together with the ritual gestures (*mudrā*) using the long vowels starting from *oṃ vāṃ hṛdayāya namaḥ*, and having performed the purification of the hands with the weapon-mantra (*astra-mantra*), one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs starting from the heart up to the little finger; then, one should perform the placement of the limbs on the head, face, heart, private parts, and feet, as well as in their respective locations starting from the heart. With the root mantra, one should meditate upon Vasanta—who is seated on the worshipped throne in the jar, holding a lotus, a boon-granting gesture, and a gesture of fearlessness, golden-hued, adorned with red garments, perfumes, garlands, a golden crown, earrings, necklaces, armlets, and so forth, and youthful—and invoke him from one's own heart. Having performed the rites of installation, presence (*sānnidhya*), and so on, one should invoke Padmāvatī to his right and Kusumāvatī to his left—two goddesses of red and white complexion, beautifully adorned—and worship them with the root mantra, beginning with the offering of water (*arghya*) and ending with perfumes and other offerings.
Oṃ!
Homage to you, O Spring, beloved of trees, shrubs, and creepers!
O you who possess a thousand mouths! O kinsman of Kāma, let there be homage to you! (22–27)

Having thus worshipped Vāsanta together with the two goddesses by means of these three handfuls of flowers, one should worship his Śaktis, the forest deities (vanadevatās), upon the tips of the petals of that lotus:
Āhlādinī, Gandhavatī, Surabhī, Mālinī, Madirā, Madayantī, Ramā, and likewise Puṣpavatī. (22–28)
And one should also worship Vāsantī as the ninth [goddess] in sequence by her own name;
all of them are well-adorned with garments and ornaments, possessing graceful limbs and smiling faces.

Thereafter, one should worship Damanaka situated in the grove. Therein, one should meditate upon Bhairava—red in color, holding a trident and a skull-cup in his hands, adorned with red perfumes, garlands, and garments, wearing a freshly severed garland of heads from noble warriors, with tinkling anklets and small bells, standing upon the sandals of his beloved, holding a sword, a trident, a *ḍamaru* drum, and a noose in his hands, and whose head is marked by abundant, sprouting *damanaka* flowers; having thus visualized him, one should worship him with these offerings (*arghya*) and so forth, as well as with perfumes and other articles.
*Oṃ, O you who have arisen from the ashes of Kāma! O you who are bathed in the tears of Rati!*
O you who enchant the sages, gandharvas, gods, and others—homage be to you! || 22-30 ||

(222) Having worshipped the *damanaka* with "Oṃ daṃ, obeisance to the *damanaka*," one should then worship the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) within the *kāmakubha*, beginning with Śakti and ending with Sattva. The root mantra is "Oṃ klīṃ, obeisance to Kāma. With the mantras "Oṃ klāṃ, obeisance to the heart" and so forth, using the long vowels combined with the [six] ritual gestures (*jāti*), one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) of the limbs as before upon the fingers of the hands, the body, and one's own respective locations. Then, having worshipped the seat of Kāma with "Obeisance to the seat of Kāma" using a handful of flowers, one should worship the powers (*śakti*) situated at the tips of the petals.
Saubhāgyā, Hlādinī, Harṣā, Dhṛti, Prīti, as well as Unmadā,
Saṅgamā, Nirvāṇā, and the ninth, Madhyagā Rati.

"Oṃ klīṃ, let us know Manmatha; let us meditate upon Kāmadeva; may that Gandharva inspire us!"—this is the Anaṅga-Gāyatrī. Now, having meditated upon Anaṅga while offering a handful of flowers, one should invoke him:
"Red in color, wearing red garments, youthful, with polished earrings, adorned with necklaces, armlets, bracelets, a crown, earrings, and anklets... (22–32).
Adorned with other divine ornaments, garlands, and perfumes,
he further held a flower-bow and arrows, as well as a noose and a goad.
With Rati seated upon his left lap, he stands in the midst of a host of young women,
adorned with beauty, charm, loveliness, and tenderness.
Having meditated thus, one should worship the desired deity with water for the guest-offering (arghya), perfumes, and so forth, in due order,
using both the root mantra and the Gāyatrī, up until the offering of food (naivedya) according to the prescribed rite.
Following that: "Oṃ, salutations be to you, the one with flower-arrows, who brings delight to the world;
to Manmatha, the eye of the universe, the bestower of pleasure and love. (22-36)
Having worshipped him with these handfuls of flowers, one should pray to him again;
outside [the mandala], one should worship the lords of the world belonging to spring, desire, and the *aśoka* tree.
Then one should worship the weapons in those directions; this worship grants all desires.
Thereafter, taking up Damanaka, along with Vasanta, Aśoka, and Manmatha—
Having worshipped with the aforementioned enclosures (āvaraṇas), one should then consecrate the *damana* plant with the mantra:
"Oṃ!
Born from the grace of Hara, you have been invoked by me. (22-39)
"O Damana, you must not go; remain present at the worship of Śiva by the command of Śiva.
Having thus addressed Damana, [recite] *oṃ*.
O you who have become beloved by the world through the abundance of spring flowers! || 22-40 ||
Accompanied by Smara (the God of Love), you should serve the Lord together with Umā.

Having addressed them both with the mantra "Oṃ Vaṃ Klīṃ, obeisance to Vasantaka and Kāma," and having requested their permission and performed protection there, one should go to one's own home and eat.
Thus ends the section on the worship of Vasanta.
Then, having risen in the morning and performed his daily rites, he then—
Having gathered the appropriate sacrificial materials in the evening,
one should go to a grove of *damanaka* plants and take a large quantity of *damanaka*.
Having uprooted some [of the plants] together with their roots and placed them all in vessels,
he also set aside the two jars of Vasanta and Smara, whose presiding deities had not yet been dismissed.
Having raised it up, one should place the entire assembly upon elephant-vehicles and the like,
together with dancing, singing, instrumental music, auspicious umbrellas, and chowries.
Having adorned it, one should proceed by way of cities, villages, dwellings, and so forth;
having had the Brahmins recite auspicious benedictions (*svasti*), one should then enter within the pavilion.

Having placed two water-pots on both sides of the deity and worshipped them as before, one should then bathe; having completed the libation (tarpaṇa) as previously described, one should worship the Sun.
One should worship Śānti, Vidyā, Nivṛtti, and Pratiṣṭhā like the doors;
having worshipped the deities of the door as prescribed for the daily rite at the western door.
Having entered within by means of kicks with the heels and the discharge of flower-arrows,
one should place the weapon at the threshold and worship Vāstveśa and Vedhas.
Having assigned the world-protectors to the directions, having worshipped the obstacle-remover and likewise the Guru,
and having first performed the scattering of the *vikira* offerings, one should perform the worship of the jar and the weapon-mantra.
After circumambulating that [fire] and having worshipped it, holding the sword of knowledge, one should worship Śiva specifically in the sacrificial pit, the mandala, and the liṅga. (22.50)

As before, one should perform the joining of the channels (*nāḍī-sandhāna*) and then the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*). It is as follows: with the *Sadyojāta* mantra, place the root of the *damana* plant together with clay in the west; with the *Vāmadeva* mantra, place its stalk and *gandhāmalaka* in the north; with the *Aghora* mantra, place its leaves and ashes in the south; with the *Puruṣa* mantra, place its flower and tooth-stick in the east; and with the *Īśāna* mantra, place its fruit and fragrant powder in the northeast. Having arranged all other sacrificial materials (*yāga-dravya*) in their respective places, fill the hollow of one’s joined palms (*añjali*) with the five parts (*pañcāṅga*) of the *damana* plant, pray to the Blessed One, and install [the deity] with this [mantra] ending in *tāra-mūla-śivāya-namaḥ*.
Oṃ!
O Lord of Gods, O All-pervading One, you have been invited by me at the time of dawn.
The Dāmana rite should be performed in full according to one's capacity by your command.
Then, having offered the ārātrika lamp, one should worship until the conclusion of the food offering (naivedya). || 22-52 ||
Having offered oblations according to the rite for the *pavitraka*,
one should pour the clarified butter into a vessel filled with *damanaka* flowers, which has been consecrated and protected by the *astra-mantras*.
Having covered him with armor and seated him before Kumbheśa,
one should offer him food and perform a hundred oblations of the Aghora mantra.

Having scattered the *bali* offering outside and without having dismissed the deities, he should then eat for the sake of consuming the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); or else, for the sake of liberation, he should even fast.
Meditating or reciting prayers, one should keep a vigil at night with musical performances;
then, having bathed at dawn and performed worship through the gateway of the Sun (Sūryadvāra), [one should proceed].
Having bid farewell to Śambhu with a lingering look, preceded by the five purifications, one should worship Śiva as in the daily rite within the water-pot, the fire, the liṅga, and the image. (22.57)
Having removed the floral remains (nirmālya) but not yet dismissed the deity,
he should perform a special worship of Śambhu according to his means.
Having placed the *damana* upon the sun [mandala] with his own root mantra,
[he should worship] Īśvara, Antaka, the Lord of the Gate, Brahmā, the Lord of the Vāstu, the water-pot (*kumbha*), the weapon (*astra*), and Gaṇanāyaka.
Having worshipped the gurus with *damanaka* flowers using their own root-mantras ending in *Īśvara* and *Antaka*,
he himself should perform the waving of lights (*ārātrika*) before the deity in the mandala.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa, one should place the *damana* plant upon one's own head;
then, having gone outside and performed the ceremonial rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*), one should re-enter and sit down. (22.61)
One should worship Śambhu with the sprouts of *damanaka* according to the sequence beginning with the seat (*āsana*).
Then, one should offer those five limbs to Śiva in the order beginning with Sadyojāta.
Thereafter, one should worship with the five-fold aggregate of the five Brahmans;
again, with the five-fold aggregate of *damana* flowers, accompanied by perfumes, *dūrvā* grass, and unbroken grains (*akṣata*).
Having properly filled his joined palms (añjali), he should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva with the principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, according to the ritual procedure for the Pavitraka.
One should gradually offer three handfuls of *damanaka* to Śambhu;
then, having filled a fourth handful of *damanaka* along with unbroken grains of rice...
Oṃ, to the Lord of Sacrifice, fulfill the sacrifice, fulfill it; obeisance to the wielder of the trident!

At the conclusion of this, one should perform the ritual installation with the *praṇava* and the root-mantra, saying: "Obeisance to Śiva, the Lord of all principles (*tattva*s). Then, having presented the *ārātrika* lamp and the great offering (*mahānivedya*), and having offered oblations into the fire, one should worship those [deities] situated on the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*) and the sacrificial grass seats (*viṣṭara*) with *damanaka* flowers. Having also placed *damanaka* into the fire with the *sruva* ladle, just as for Śiva, and then upon the Seat of Knowledge (*vidyāpīṭha*) with its own mantra; thereafter, if one's own Guru is present, one should worship him with garments, ornaments, and so forth, as well as with *damanaka*. Having given *damanaka* to the initiated, the wearers of sectarian marks (*liṅgin*), the twice-born, and kinsmen, and having fed them as appropriate, one should satisfy all supplicants with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and gifts. Finally, with this handful of *damanaka*, one should pray to the God.
Oṃ!
O God of gods! Lord of the universe! Sovereign bestower of desired objects!
O beloved of Kāmeśvarī, fulfill the desires dwelling within my heart! (22.66)

Having offered a *kāmyāñjali* (an auspicious handful of offerings) at the lotus-feet of Śiva with the mantra "Obeisance to the gentle Śiva, whose root is the *praṇava*," and having presented the fruit of the Dāmanaka worship, one should pray once more as follows:
"O Blessed One, whatever has been done by me in excess or deficiency, may all that become complete; O All-pervading Lord, may this Dāmanaka festival be perfect for You! (22.67)
Having thus informed the Lord of Gods who resides in the fire within the auspicious mandala,
he should unite him with Sadāśiva, who resides in the linga and in the water-pot.
Having applied [the fire] to the heart-lotus, and having bowed to and praised Maheśvara,
one should prostrate, saying "Forgive me," and dismiss him as before.
One should join the Lords of the Worlds, such as those of the weapons and the gates, to their respective places;
having performed this Dāmanaka festival, one should worship Caṇḍa. (22.70)
One should worship Śiva daily upon ground smeared with cow-dung and water;
thus is described the sacrifice performed in spring along with the Vasanta-yāga, for the Dāmanaka festival concludes at its end.
Just as the *vasantatilaka* tree is delightful with its blossoms, so too does this [tantra] here bear fruit in accordance with the desires of the mind. (22.71)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on the ritual procedure for the Damanaka festival, in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the Siddhāntasāra, the manual of the venerable Lord Īśānaśiva. 22.
Now begins the twenty-third chapter.
Now, the earth is the source of sustenance for all castes and likewise their refuge,
since within her the wheel of ritual activities, such as consecration and the like, proceeds.
Therefore, its characteristics are correctly described here in brief:
the earth is endowed with sacred fields, river-banks, holy fords, mountains, and so forth. (23.2)
Since it bestows supreme accomplishment, the wise man should take refuge in it;
it is naturally filled with black antelopes and adorned with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grasses. (23.3)
It was frequented by twice-born ones who were knowers of the Vedas, surrounded by sacrificial trees, sloping toward the northeast, delightful, and possessing abundant reservoirs of water. (23.4)
Land that is free from fissures, very fertile, endowed with fuel, flowers, and fruits, and filled with its own gardens and herds of cattle, is praised as being suitable for all [four castes]. (23.5)
The ground is of four kinds—Pūrṇā, Supadmā, Bhadrā, and Dhūmrā—in successive order; their characteristics are now described. (23.6)
It is joined with aṅkola, aśoka, bakula, śiṃśapā, nimba, and kiṃśuka trees,
as well as mādhavī creepers and niṣpāva plants, and possesses small reservoirs of water.
The ground that bestows nourishment is one that is full and where [the earth] rests upon mountains and marshlands;
it is [perfumed] with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, kadamba, arjuna, and kesara flowers. (23.8)
The ground in the north, adorned with *tilaka*, *ketakī*, and *kunda* trees, as well as with reservoirs abounding in lotuses, is "Supadmā" (well-lotused) and should slope toward the east. (23.9)
It should be near the ocean or a river, possessing excellent bathing places and reservoirs of water, and adorned with sacrificial fruit-bearing trees situated to the west. || 23-10 ||
The Bhadrā region, situated to the south and characterized by fields, bestows happiness;
it is marked by *snuhī*, *śleṣmātaka*, *arka*, *pīlu*, *veṇu*, and *vibhītaka* trees. (23.11)
It was covered with saline soil, parched and harsh, strewn with pebbles and stones,
and swarming with hawks, vultures, boars, bears, crows, and jackals.
A land named Dhūmrā is censurable, bringing about grief, suffering, and fear;
one should not install a liṅga there, nor should one practice mantras there either. (23.13)
People of the four castes should not find pleasure in residing there;
it is triangular in shape, deep in the middle, resembling a trident in luster, and shaped like the mouth of a serpent. (23.14)
Resembling a winnowing basket, or like the back of a tortoise, hexagonal, or waterless;
flowing toward the directions of Yama, Agni, Marut, and Rākṣasa, and perpetually muddy. (23.15)
That river which is constantly buffeted by fierce winds, whose waters swirl counter-clockwise, which is foul-smelling, and which is defiled by hair, insects, bones, ashes, and anthills; (16)
That land is called "mixed" (saṅkīrṇā), being censured by all castes; now the earth is described as being fourfold according to the distinction of castes, beginning with the Brahmins.

It is white, fragrant with the scent of clarified butter, sweet, adorned with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass, glossy with rafts from the north and northeast, and provided with *palāśa* and *udumbara* trees. (23.18)
Land belonging to a Brahmin is said to be square in shape and bestows peace;
it is red, has the scent of blood, is astringent, and slopes toward the east. (23.19)

A *kṣatriya* stone is said to be marked with *aśvattha* leaves, having a height exceeding one-eighth of its width, yellow in color, rich in the scent of cow’s urine, and possessing a bitter or sour taste. (23.20)
The Vaiśya land is declared to be rich with Plakṣa trees, sloping toward the east, extending by more than six parts, and adorned with various crops. (23.21)
(228) That ground which is black, sweet-smelling, pungent, and slopes toward the east or toward the west should be known as belonging to the Śūdra caste. (23.22)
The Govīthī path is to the east; the earth is sloping toward the fire (Agni) and is thus called Anala.
The Yāmyā path is to be known as sloping toward Yama; the Nāgavīthī, however, is in the southwest (Nairṛta).
The Vāruṇī path has its slope toward the west; the Bhūtavīthī has its slope toward the northwest;
the Dhanavīthī has its slope toward the north; and the Dhānyavīthī has its slope toward the northeast. (23–24)

For the Brahmins and other [classes] as well as for the gods, pathways sloping toward the east, northeast, or north are recommended; the remaining ones should be avoided, because they are inauspicious.
Thus has the definition of the ground been stated in general; now it is described in detail as residing in sacred grass, mountains, distinguished peaks, holy fords, sacred fields, and forests.
Acquired solely through righteous means, auspicious, well-crafted, uniform in color, and even;
white when not available, it is beautiful and brings benefit to all castes. (23–27)

It should be free from blameworthy things, not saline, devoid of snakes, anthills, and outcasts; it should be free from cremation grounds and charcoal, and provided with water of excellent taste. (23–28)
The Nyagrodha, Udumbara, Aśvattha, and Plakṣa trees are auspicious when located in the eastern direction; Kesara, Āmra, Punnāga, Nāga, and pomegranate trees are auspicious everywhere. (23–29)
On Mount Manasa are beautiful campaka trees, betel-nut palms, and coconut trees;
for the mountain in the east is forbidden, as its shadow falls upon the rising sun.
Even where it falls, a village or similar location is not recommended;
water contained in a jar is best, while that from Pisces and Aries is middling. (23–31)
When the sun is in Capricorn or Taurus, it is debilitated; having worshipped and placed a jar full of grain upon the village or the dwelling, one should perform the rite. (23–32)
One should pour a kuḍuba measure of cow’s clarified butter into an unbaked earthen bowl;
one should place pure wicks made of cotton threads in the four directions.
The four [lines] are white, red, yellow, and black, arranged symmetrically;
they turn toward the east, south, north, and west, corresponding respectively to the Brahmins and the other castes.

One should light lamps made of substances such as human fat and the like, consecrated with those specific mantras; having visualized them, one should also worship them with perfumes and other offerings. (23.35)
Having set a limit of one watch (yāma), one should place [the lamp] upon a well-smeared ground;
whichever wick corresponds to whichever color, that burning [wick] brings happiness.
If they are extinguished, they should be avoided in the construction of celestial palaces and such;
however, if all of them blaze, they bring happiness to all castes.
One should dig a pit one cubit deep and even; if it is then filled again with that same earth, the ground is excellent if there is an excess of soil, and middling if it is exactly level. (23–38)
If it is deficient, she is of the lowest class and should be abandoned; thus one should determine the three types.
Alternatively, having filled that pit with water, one should walk away a hundred paces.
When returning again, as before, if it is full, the ground is excellent;
if it is less by a barley-corn, it would be middling; if it is less than that, it should be abandoned. (23.40)
Having thus reflected upon the earth— free from the aforementioned defects and endowed with the praised qualities— and finding it most delightful,
one should establish there that which brings about the attainment of the desired fruit.
The sacrifice and the temple of Śiva [should be constructed] according to the prescribed path. || 23-41 ||

Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, on the characteristics of the ground, in the section on ritual practice (kriyāpāda) of the latter part of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 23.
Now begins the twenty-fourth chapter.
Then, when the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and at an auspicious time of sunrise,
one who has acquired the site for a dwelling should dig it, extract any hidden impurities (śalya), and purify it.
Having made the ground level on all sides, resembling a mirror,
its center should be even with the surrounding water up to the height of a staff.
For example: Having placed a jar with a hole in its middle, filled with a load of water, upon a support for a mechanical device, one should set it down level in the middle of a dry spot. (24.3)

Then, when the ground has been sprinkled with the flowing waters, one should understand the arrangement [of the site] to be neither deficient nor excessive, just as it is known from those waters. (24.4)
Having made a mark at the center of the ground, one should place a level gnomon upon it.
As it has been stated by others:
"A gnomon (*śaṅku*) made from ivory or from solid wood, with its circumference fashioned by turning,
having equal parts for the base and the tip, straight and even, free from flaws, six-sided, with a flat top, twelve *aṅgulas* in height, is recommended here."
Thus:
"Between the tip of the prongs and the tip of the tail, [the line] is equal, as thick as a barleycorn, and long. (24.5)
One should fashion two iron needles for the purpose of determining the midpoint of its shadow;
then, having placed a thread equal in length to the measure of the gnomon upon that point, one should fix it there.
One should rotate it all around until it forms a perfect circle while remaining fixed on the *bindu*;
then, at sunrise, one should place that gnomon upon the *bindu* in the center of that circle.

When the tip of the gnomon's shadow reaches the circumference-line of that circle during the twenty [muhūrtas] of the forenoon due to its diminishing, one should mark the tip of the shadow there. (24.8)
Likewise, in the afternoon, when the shadow is emerging from the mandala and touching its line, one should mark that point there as well, just as before.
One should stretch a straight thread between those two marks at the east and west;
thus the directions east and west are established, for that is indeed remembered as the Brahma-line (the east).

Having placed the thread situated at the western mark toward the south from the eastern mark, according to the measurement of half a rakṣoghna, that direction is called the eastern (aindrī) one. (24.11)
Likewise, that which is to the north of the northeast (prāgaṅka) shall be the eastern quarter (aiśī kāṣṭhā).
Some maintain that in the construction of temples for Śiva and the like, the eastern direction is actually the northeast.
Others have declared that in the construction of dwellings for Brahmins and others, the direction should be Aindrī; however, all agree that it is indeed Brāhmī, as evidenced by various Tantras.
"Some say that this determination of the directions would apply to places like Laṅkā which are devoid of latitude; therefore, [the method] for a place with latitude is now being stated. (24.14)
p. 231) There is indeed a distinction among the various regions due to the sun’s recession [from the equator].
And it has been stated by others:
"The sun moves at every moment along an oblique orbit toward the southern and northern directions."
Therefore, that direction appears straight; moreover, it would be straight by means of the arc of its departure.

Thus: one situated on the northern hemisphere moves toward the north by means of the apakrama-maṇḍala (the declination circle); one situated on the southern hemisphere moves toward the south by means of the apakrama-maṇḍala. Therefore, that direction appears non-straight. Consequently, in order to demonstrate the straightness of the direction now by means of the *apakrama-jyā* (sine of declination), he says: "The difference between the sines of the declinations (*ākramajīvā*) of the sun at the times of the entry and exit of the shadow's disappearance, multiplied by the hypotenuse (*saśravaṇa*) and divided by the *lambaka* (the sine of colatitude), shall be the result in finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and so forth."

Thereafter, one should move the point (bindu) from the solar solstice by means of this [calculation] in reverse order; or else, due to the precession of the equinoxes, one should displace the eastern point forward.

Thus: the time at which the shadow of the gnomon touches the circle and the time at which it emerges from the circle—these are indeed the moments of entry and exit of the shadow. The difference between the sines of the sun's amplitude at those two times is what is called the "measure of the sun's ghatis" (the duration in time units). That [difference], multiplied by the hypotenuse of the shadow at the times of entry and exit and divided by the radius (lambaka), that is, divided by the sine of the colatitude (lambajyā), results in a fruit in finger-breadths (aṅgulas). By means of that fruit, one should move the point reached at the back by the measure of finger-breadths, because of the reversal of the sun's solstice (ayana). The meaning of the reversal of the solstice is that one should move it to the south during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), and to the north during the southern solstice (dakṣiṇāyana). A thread struck in that manner, having touched the true location, becomes the east. Now, another method for the determination of the directions, even without the sun and the radius, is stated:

The point where the two lines—one touching the middle of the circle arising from the tips of the three shadows and the other being the north-south line—intersect is the direction of the meridian; it lies toward the south in the northern hemisphere and toward the north in the southern hemisphere, respectively. (24–15)

Having observed the three tips of the shadows on either the eastern or the western side of the gnomon’s base, and having drawn three circles with those [distances], two fish-figures (*matsya*) are produced; one should stretch a cord from the point where the two cords following the mouths and tails of those two meet, down to the base of the gnomon. That becomes the north-south direction. When the sun is situated in the northern hemisphere, the south is from the base of the gnomon; when it is situated in the southern hemisphere, the north is from the base of the gnomon. This is now stated clearly as follows: on ground leveled with water...

(p. 232) Having fixed a gnomon (*śaṅku*) of the prescribed measure, one should mark three points at the tips of the shadows when they coincide during either the forenoon or the afternoon. Then, having placed one point in the center, one should draw a circle with a desired radius. Using that same [radius] and taking the second point as the center, one should likewise draw a second circle; then, having placed the third point in the center, one should draw a third circle. One should draw these circles with that same measure such that the circle centered on the middle point produces two segments of the two side-point circles. When this is done, two "fish" figures (*matsya*) are produced. The two [fish] whose mouths are in the direction where there is a great distance between them, and whose tails are in the direction where there is proximity, should have fine pegs inserted into their mouths. Having tied strings to those [pegs], one should pull them out from the middle of the tails and lead each along its own path. Where the intersection of those two strings occurs according to the movement of the mouths and tails, that is the southern direction, provided the sun is situated in the northern hemisphere relative to the base of the gnomon; then, when the sun is in the southern hemisphere, it is the opposite. Likewise, the point of intersection of the two strings passing through the center is the northern direction starting from the base of the gnomon. Thus, having stretched a string from the base of the gnomon through the intersection point, one should draw a line; that is the north-south direction. Then, having placed each point in the center, one should produce two fish by means of two circles. The string passing through the mouths and tails of that [fish] is the east-west direction. Thus the determination of directions has been explained for a place with latitude (*sākṣadeśa*). However, in a place without latitude (*nirakṣadeśa*), the east-west direction is exactly as previously stated. Standing at the central point of that string, having marked the east and west points at a distance of ten finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) along the middle of the string, and having placed a string equal to the interval between those two marks, one should rotate it toward the south and north. By stretching the string across the two fish thus produced, the south-north direction is established. This suffices. Furthermore:
And the sun's recession should be inferred according to the movement of human shadows. || 24-16 ||
Having calculated it like the bowstring, one should know it for the two paths of the Sun;
the shadow is diminished by half a finger in Taurus, Gemini, and Virgo. (24.17)
In Libra, Gemini, and Sagittarius it would be increasing; in Cancer, Capricorn, and so forth, it would be decreasing.
And that occurs day by day.
Two, one, not one, and two, according to the number of eyes, fires, and Vedas (2, 3, 4).
By the measure of two Vedas and two fires, there are two; by one, nothing at all.
Not by the number of one eye, four oceans, three eyes, two pairs, or five seasons. (24.19)

Measured by six, seven, and eight, and by the number of eight, seven, and six; and likewise measured by six seasons, five arrows, and four Vedas, and by four Vedas, three fires, and two eyes, respectively. (24–20)

p. 233) By a measure of half and half a quarter [of a verse] for each of the twelve signs beginning with Aries, one should discard the measurement of the human shadow during every set of ten days. (24.21)
Having observed here the movement of the sun along with its zodiacal signs, one should discard the previously mentioned finger-measure (aṅgula) here according to reason;
then, having grasped the direction (kāṣṭhā) by its power and released the thread, one should properly establish the site.

The ground is level when it stands straight according to a suspended plumb-line due to the influence of water; there is equality of the arms when they are horizontal and straight by means of cords. (24.23)
From the eastward line, the other directions extending along the square are established. This concludes the section on the gnomon's shadow.

[The measures of length] are determined by eight successive units: the atom (paramāṇu), the speck of dust (rajas), the hair-tip (roma), the nit (likṣā), the louse (yūkā), the barley-corn (yava), and the finger-breadth (aṅgula). 24–24.
The *mānāṅgula* (measurement finger) is to be known [as the standard]; twelve *aṅgulas* constitute a *vitasti*.
Twelve *mānāṅgulas* indeed make a *vitasti*, and two *vitastis* are known as a *hastaka*. Four *hastas* would be a *dhanus*, and that same measure is also called a *daṇḍa* by name. (24–25)
A distance of fifty daṇḍas is declared to be half a gavyūti. || 24–26 ||
Twice that [gavyūti] is a gavyūti; two of those are called a krośa.
A yojana consists of four krośas, and half a yojana is two krośas.
On this point, Āryabhaṭa says: Twenty fingers plus four make one hasta; four hastas make one daṇḍa;
two thousand of those [daṇḍas] make one krośa; and four krośas make one yojana.
Thus: The hand called *prājāpatya* should be twenty-five finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) long;
the bow-grip (*dhanurmuṣṭi*) and the bow-hold (*dhanurgraha*) should be twenty-six and twenty-seven [finger-breadths] respectively. (24–28)
A fist that is closed up to the joint is declared to be a *ratni* (cubit); that same measure is designated as an *aratni* if the little finger is extended. (24–29)

The *prādeśa*, *tāla*, *gokarṇa*, and *vitasti* are, respectively, the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tips of the fingers when extended, starting from the index finger (*tarjanī*) and ending with the little finger (*kaniṣṭhā*). (24–30)
That which is measured by the length of the middle joint of the middle finger is the *mātrāṅgula* in its longitudinal dimension;
that same measure, by way of the joint, is the *mātrāṅgula* in its transverse dimension, and it is designated as *tata*. (24–31)

That which is perceived as a finger-measure (*aṅgula*) on the body should be understood in images according to the logic of measurement. A rope consisting of eight *daṇḍas* is prescribed for boundary lines and the like.
By means of the *kiṣku* and the *hasta*, one accomplishes vehicles, beds, and other such implements. (24–32)
Regarding this, Maya said:
"In vehicles and beds, the *kiṣku* is used; for celestial chariots (*vimāna*), the *prājāpatya*;
for buildings, the *dhanurmuṣṭi*; and for villages and the like, the *dhanurgraha*."
"For all types of sites, the measurement shall be either a *kiṣku* or a *hasta*.
Furthermore, one should construct villages, settlements, and so forth, as well as cities, market towns, and ports, using the *daṇḍa* as the standard measure.
The measurement for houses and other structures is said to be by the hand, or else by small finger-breadths (aṅgula) or barley grains.
One should indeed construct temples, houses, and other such structures using the *mātrā-aṅgula* measurement.
The construction of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and other mandalas everywhere shall be according to the measurement of the *mātrāṅgula*.
In this regard, the accomplishment of the specific distinctions of those various ritual actions has been correctly explained. (24–35)

Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Fingers of the Shadow of the Gnomon and Other Measures," in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudeva-paddhati*. 24.
Now begins the twenty-fifth chapter.
Now, therefore, the arrangement of the steps (padavinyāsa) is described for the sake of accomplishing the goal:
the entire *pecaka*, the *pīṭha*, the *mahāpīṭha*, and the *upapīṭhaka*.

The fierce seat (ugrapīṭha), the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), the frog (maṇḍūka), the one who lies on another (paraśāyika), and the posture (āsana)—these ten constitute the practice of the fierce installation (caṇḍita) in villages and other locations. (25.2)
Within the space between the four boundary lines, there should be one complete square;
by increasing the first line toward the east and north, that becomes a four-square grid. (25.3)
In this manner, one should gradually increase the rows of squares from the northeast;
a four-square figure is known as a *pecaka*, while a nine-square figure is remembered as a *pīṭha*.
The great seat (mahāpīṭha) consists of sixteen or twenty-five squares; the secondary seat (upapīṭha) shall consist of thirty-six squares, as shall the fierce seat (ugrapīṭhaka). (25.5)
The sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) indeed consists of forty-nine squares and is formed by eight sets of eight;
it is known as a field of eighty-one plots, the supreme resting place.
The board (āsana) consists of one hundred squares; by means of these, the village and other units are established.
A square plot of land measuring eight daṇḍas is a kākaṇī, and four times that [is the next unit]. (25–7)
A *māṣa* is one-fourth of a *vedaguṇa*; from that, there is what is called a *vartanaka*. Five times that is a *vāṭī*, and four times that is a *kuḍuba*. (25.8)

Thus the measurement of the *bhūmāna* has been explained; now the measurement of the *daṇḍa* is being described: the extent of a superior great village (*mahāgrāma*) is one hundred thousand *daṇḍas*. (25.9)
Therefore, by a gradual reduction of the twenty-thousand-fold staff, the measurement of villages is fivefold; thus has the primary [system] been declared. (25.10)
From the twenty-thousand-danda [village] down to the five-hundred-danda,
the measurements of the villages decrease in sequence from the twenty-thousand-danda down to the five-hundred-danda.
Indeed, there are forty varieties when [the land] is being measured;
this is remembered as the measurement of the boundary for villages, inhabited areas, fields, and so forth. (25.12)

The measurement of the boundaries for the inner enclosure, the chariot-paths, and the dwellings is stated here; namely, the village (grāma), the hamlet (kheṭaka), the market town (kharvaṭa), and the fortified city (durga). 25-13.
The city, the royal capital, the port, the mouth of the valley, the camp, the divisional headquarters, the provincial seat, and the outpost. (25.14)
Then the nigama is specified, and after that the śākhānagara;
the characteristics of these fourteen are now described individually. (25.15)
A village measuring eight times eight *daṇḍas* in extent is considered the lowest of the low; villages twice and thrice that size are recorded as the middle and the highest, respectively. (25.16)
Two hundred and fifty-six cubits are recorded as the measure for an inferior *kheṭa*;
one of medium quality is measured by three hundred and twenty cubits, and [one of superior quality] by eight hundred and forty. (25.17)
With three hundred [daṇḍas] it would be the highest; thus the *kheṭa* is remembered as being of three kinds.
Likewise, there are forty-eight *daṇḍas* and four hundred [of the next kind]. (25–18)
In an inferior market town (kharvaṭa), it should be known as [one hundred]; in a middling one, more than five hundred;
and in a superior one, twelve hundred, increased by six, seventy, and five hundred [respectively]. (25.19)
A fortress that is inferior is provided with six hundred and forty [dandas];
a medium fortress, however, has seven hundred and four dandas.
This excellent fortress here is [measured] by seven hundred and sixty-eight,
by one hundred and thirty-two, by nine hundred and six, and by eight hundred.
Indeed, the three cities of Nīca are [located] at nine hundred and six,
one thousand five hundred, and two thousand [yojanas], respectively.
In the three middle [categories], there are inferior, middling, and superior cities;
in the three highest [categories], there are cities consisting of three, four, and five thousand [houses] respectively. (25.23)
With six, seven, and eight thousand *daṇḍas*, there are the three types of cities—namely, the highest, the higher, and the middling—respectively, for those three categories of cities. (25–24)
Furthermore, by increasing the staff for each modification ninefold, the measurements for villages and so forth indeed become greater than those previously stated. (25–25)
The measurement of royal capitals and the like should be as in the case of cities.
This same measurement is prescribed for villages and so forth among human settlements. (25–26)
The measurement of the cities of the gods, asuras, and others is not known by men;
it may be one-quarter, one-half, three-quarters, or double the width. (25–27)
The width of their faces should extend from the villages up to the cities;
these [buildings] are formed by pairs of staff-like (daṇḍaka) widths that are broad.
Therefore, the remaining ground for the movement of the garden should be laid out;
one should establish villages on the southern bank or other such banks of rivers and the like. (25–29)
Between two villages is a *kheṭa*; in the midst of a kingdom is a *kharvaṭa*.
A *durga* (fortress) may be situated within a mountain, in a forest, by the ocean, or surrounded by water. || 25–30 ||
Fortresses are of seven kinds: mountainous, forest-based, water-based, as well as those involving enemies, divine, desert-based, and artificial. (25–31)
A city is traditionally defined as being in the midst of a kingdom or near a river;
it should be difficult to assault, protected by stakes, mud, and moats. (25–32)
Its high walls, watchtowers, and gateways were surrounded by catapults and *śataghnīs*, and its lofty battlements were strewn all around with them.
A royal capital is said to have one, two, three, or four gates;
it is filled with various goods and wealth, and is situated on the coastal marshlands of the ocean. (25–34)
They describe a port as one frequented by seafaring merchants;
that very same place is called a harbor when vessels arrive there at the confluence of the ocean and a river. (25–35)
The wise know Droṇamukha as a place frequented by merchants traveling between different continents;
it is situated either in a foreign kingdom or within one's own country and is provided with the fourfold army.
The camp of one who desires victory is called a *śibira*;
it should be situated not too far from that of another king when the two are about to fight each other. (25.37)
