A military encampment situated separately is known as a *skandhāvāra*;
it is accompanied by the king's forces and located on the side of either a mountain or a river. (25–38)
The wise know that which protects the borders of the kingdom as *sthānīya*;
the dwelling of farmers and others at the edge of a village is called *viḍambaka*. (25.39)
A *nigama* is traditionally defined as a place endowed with artisans of the four castes who subsist by various crafts, as well as with merchandise, wealth, grain, and other such goods. (25.40)
Whether in a forest or on the outskirts of a city,
surrounded by urban people and endowed with fields, groves, and mines, it is considered a branch-city (śākhānagara).
By thousands of twice-born men numbering eight hundred, sixty, and eighty respectively, there are the best-of-the-best, the best-middle, and likewise the best-lowest villages. (25.42)

Villages consisting of seven, six, or five thousand [houses] are classified as middle, superior, and so forth; those with four, three, or two thousand houses belong to the three lower categories. (25.43)

(238) Among the brahmins, villages of the lowest, highest, and other classes exist in numbers ranging from seven to one hundred and ten; furthermore, those small villages are recorded as being of eleven types.
By means of four hundred, three hundred, two hundred, and eight hundred;
and also by means of eighty-four, sixty-four, fifty-two, thirty-two, and twenty-eight. (25–45)

And by Brāhmaṇas numbering as many as the sun’s rays (vikārāditya), who were settled there, [the villages] beginning with Ekadvija and ending with Daśa were established; these ten [villages] had one enjoyer and so forth, up to ten. (25–46)

O you who are skilled in the installation of villages and other sites, when the entire sequence from the primary seat (ādyāsana) to the end is completed, the paths (vīthīs) occur in pairs of threads; when they are odd, they occur in rows of squares (padapaṅktis).
One should not cause a confusion between these two, for such confusion leads to ruin.
[The types of seats are] the staff-like (daṇḍaka), the cross-shaped (svastika), the spread-out (prastara), and the miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka). || 25-48 ||
The Nandyāvarta, the Parāga, the one called Padma, and the Śrīpratiṣṭhita—these are the eightfold common arrangements for villages and other settlements. (25.49)
The street at the edge of a village is known as a *maṅgalavīthikā*;
in a city it is the *janavīthī*, while in market towns (*kheṭaka*) and the like, it is called a *rathyā*. (25.50)
The width of the pathway (vīthī) shall be one, two, three, four, or five rods (daṇḍa). The middle [section] is bound by a *kakārī* from the eastern and northern pathways. (25.51)
The city called Daṇḍaka is richly provided with ramparts extending to its four gates;
that [city] in which there is only a single street running eastward is also known as Daṇḍaka.

In the village [of the grid] consisting of twenty-five squares, one should erase two separate squares each in the four directions starting from the east, beginning from the central square of that [grid]. (25.53)
Therefore, by omitting the two outer positions starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, the arrangement in the form of a swastika is clearly accomplished. (25.54)
Three lines extending eastward and westward, and three toward the north, constitute the paths;
four, five, six, or seven are prescribed for the sacrificial strewing (prastara).
In the *prakīrṇaka* [section], there may be four eastern streets and twelve northern streets, measured by eleven, ten, nine, and eight [respectively]. (25.56)
To the east and west, there should be five avenues, and to the north, thirteen;
these are commensurate with the Śakvarī, Atiśakvarī, Aṣṭi, and Atyaṣṭi meters. (25–57)
Indeed, in the Nandyāvarta layout, the eastern streets of the village and other areas prevail,
numbering six, while those to the north are numbered according to the sequence beginning with Dhṛti (16).
Where the squares extend as far as the Ākṛti-line, that is called Parāga;
there are seven eastern streets starting from the twenty-third square in sequence. (25-59)
Oṃ: Twenty-seven gentle [deities] are prescribed for placement in the lotus;
there should be eight eastward paths starting from the twenty-eighth.
Up to the thirty-second [deity], there are those of the North in the arrangement established for prosperity:
[the deities] Mahendra, Gṛharakṣa, Bhallāṭa, and Puṣpadantaka. (25–61)
There should be great gates, and if there are side-gates, they should be located at Bhṛśa, Pūṣan, the one called Bhṛṅga, Dauvāra, Śoṣa, and Nāga. || 25-62 ||
Even when Parjanya has ceased raining, water-channels originating from the direction of Indra (the east) are recommended as far as the bolt of Īśa (the northeast),
provided they slope toward the north and east.
In the Sun is Sūrya; in Bhṛśa is Viṣṇu; in Agni is Kālī; in Yama is Guha;
and in Varuṇa, who is in the center of Viṣṇu, is Sugrīva, the abode of the Sugata.

In the northeast is Bhṛṅgin, in the east is Jina, in the northwest is Vāyu, in the southeast is Caṇḍī, in the north is Kubera, in the southwest is Mahākālī, and in the moon [the northwest] are the Mothers. (25–65)
In the east, the temple of Vāstu-Cāmuṇḍī is recommended; in the northeast, there should be a shrine for Śiva; or in the southwest or the southeast, there may be the house of Vighneśa. (25–66)
Alternatively, others have declared the arrangement of the deities;
in the center of that village, city, or kingdom, there shall be the house of the Brāhmaṇa.
To the east or west of Viṣṇu, or facing toward villages and other settlements,
the temple of Śiva for human beings should be situated with its face turned away [from them], or in the northeast.

Whether it be self-manifested (svayambhu), divine, or composed by a seer (ārṣa), or situated anywhere at all—it shall not lead to fault; yet even such [texts], their opening portions should be avoided by those seeking auspiciousness. (25.69)

p. 240) To the east, in the northeast, or in the center is the abode of Gaurī; that of Sūrya and Śrī is to the south; and that of the Mothers, of the Teacher (Śāstṛ), and of Kālī is in the southwest. (25.70)
For Ṣaṇmukha, however, [the worship is] in the west; immediately after that, for Jyeṣṭhā, in the northwest and the north;
and for Durgā, in the respective domains of the world-protectors.
Alternatively, the abode of Kṣetrapāla may be situated between Indra, Īśa, and Soma;
in this way, it brings prosperity to countries, villages, cities, and the like. (25.72)
The cowshed should be to the south or the east, while the pond should be in the northeast or likewise to the north;
water is auspicious everywhere, and a flower garden should be in the north.
To the south is the quarter for courtesans, surrounded by those born of the Śūdra caste;
to the east are the Vaiśyas and merchants, and in the center shall be the royal marketplace.
To the northeast are the houses of potters and barbers;
there, in the northwest are the houses of net-makers, and in the west are the houses of slaughterers.
In the north, there should be sellers of oil; in the northeast, carpenters; in the southeast, artisans and the like; and in the west, weavers. (25.76)
Within two *krośas* or even one *krośa*, there should be a settlement of Caṇḍālas outside;
however, beyond one *krośa* to the northeast, there should be a cemetery.
In the same way, one should determine the residence for other [deities] not mentioned by means of logical reasoning.
In the royal capital, the king’s residence is located in the sector other than that of Brahmā’s portion.
To its east, however, is the outer enclosure, provided with Indra’s treasury and assembly hall;
the kitchen is in the intermediate space, the bedchamber in the southeast, and the guardhouse in the southwest.
The armory should be in the direction of Nirṛti, the dining hall in the direction of Varuṇa;
the recreation hall should be in the direction of Vāyu, and the treasury storehouse in the direction of Bhallāṭa. || 25-80 ||
Likewise, a storehouse should be placed in the north; physical exercise is prescribed for the northeast (Argala);
a bathing hall in the southeast (Parjanya); and a house for fire-offerings and worship in the northeast (Īśa). (25–81)

The dance hall should be in the Gāndharva quarter; the elephant stable in the Pūṣan quarter; and the stables for horses and women in the Diti and Aditi quarters, in the west and the north-west respectively. (25.82)

In the center, one should cause a water-shed or a pavilion to be constructed by appropriate means, as well as other [structures], for Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and even for the wealthy. (25.83)
However, those temple-pavilions (prāsāda) of various types that will be described hereafter as the abode of prosperity may,
for those who are unable [to construct them], be built as halls (śālā), fashioned according to their respective requirements.

Thus has been declared the entire measurement of villages, cities, and so forth, as well as their characteristics, just as they were proclaimed by Brahmā, Agastya, and Purandara, and as they were uttered by Tvaṣṭṛ and Maya;
having understood which, all the immortals established their abodes according to the prescribed rule.
Thus the Lord, the husband of Mṛḍānī, is to be worshipped by sages as well as by men.

Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Characteristics of the Placement of the Footprints, the Village, and the City," in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 25.
Now begins the twenty-sixth chapter.

Now, regarding the construction of the temple for the purpose of the installation of the *liṅga*, the cycle of rites beginning with the plowing (*karṣaṇa*) should be known; it is described here. (26.1)
In this matter, one must pay particular attention to obtaining a virtuous place and time;
for a seed sown in a fertile field at the proper season indeed sprouts. (26.2)

And that [temple], which grants desired fruits through rites such as the sprinkling of water, [is established] in a temple endowed with the proper characteristics, once the activities beginning with the plowing of the ground have been accomplished. (26-3)
When the *liṅga* has been installed according to the prescribed rite in an excellent location and at an auspicious time, Śiva manifests his presence for the welfare of the practitioner.
In this regard, the period of the northern solstice is fixed for activities such as plowing;
the months should not be deficient, the fortnight should be the bright one, and the lunar days (tithis) should be auspicious. (26.5)
Those days which are free from the Parvan, the Aṣṭamī, the Viṣṭi, and the Pratipad, as well as the Karaṇas— excluding Viṣṭi, Śakuni, and Catuṣpada— [are auspicious].
Excluding the lords of the Nāga (Saturn) and Kiṃstughna (the last Navāṃśa), the days, decans, and degrees of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are praised as bestowing happiness. (26-7)
The ascendants and aspects of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are auspicious; the degrees, days, decans, ascendants, and aspects of the malefic planets are [inauspicious]. (26-8)
All the *horās* (ascendants) are inauspicious; all planets are auspicious when they have gone to the eleventh house.
Malefic planets are commended when situated in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses, but are not desired elsewhere than those. (26–9)

Venus situated in the sixth, seventh, or tenth house is not desired, though it brings auspiciousness elsewhere; all planets are undesirable when placed in the eighth house, yet Venus is auspicious even there. (26–10)
The Moon is favorable when in the second, fifth, and ninth houses; Mercury when in the seventh, ninth, and fifth;
and Jupiter when in the second, seventh, fifth, and ninth—these bring about auspicious results. (26–11)
The asterisms of Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Āditya (Punarvasu), Aśvinī, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Hasta, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), the three Uttaras,
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Svātī, and Maitra (Anurādhā) are indeed the auspicious lunar mansions.
One should discard that which is released by a planet, joined with a planet, or sought after by a planet;
for example:

A meteor fall occurring in the tenth lunar mansion from the Sun portends an earthquake; in the seventh, it is the "Staff of Brahmā" (brahmadaṇḍa); in the fifteenth, it is fruitless. From Venus, death occurs in the seventh lunar mansion, as does the eleventh from Rāhu. The tenth, sixth, and twentieth mansions from the mansion occupied by Saturn are "fragmentary" (khaṇḍa) mansions and should be avoided. From Mercury, the eighth, eighteenth, twenty-fourth, and third [mansion] are known as the "Great Throat" (mahākaṇṭhaka). From Mars, the fifth, seventh, ninth, fourteenth, and third mansions, as well as the ninth from Jupiter known as "Disease" (roga), and the "Flaming Fire" (jvālāgni), should be avoided. Furthermore:
In Aśvinī, Citrā, Rohiṇī, Dhaniṣṭhā, and likewise in Uttarā; || 26-13 ||
The Arkādi-yoga is called "burnt" (dagdha) when it occurs on Jyeṣṭhā or Pūṣa;
likewise, it is burnt when the twelfth lunar day falls on the eleventh, or the fifth on the second.
The sixth, eighth, and ninth lunar days are burnt when joined with the sun and other planets; likewise, the constellations Anurādhā, Viśākhā, Śatabhiṣaj, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, and Āśleṣā. (15)
Indeed, through conjunction with the Sun and other planets, the Hasta constellation becomes a death-yoga;
so too do Makhā, Viśākhā, Ārdrā, Mūlā, and Śatabhiṣak. (26–16)
Rohiṇī with Uttarāṣāḍhā is a Viṣa-yoga caused by the signs beginning with Aries;
on a Sunday, there is the Agni-pañcamī yoga; and on a Monday, Citrā with the second lunar day [is a Viṣa-yoga].

On Tuesday, Rohiṇī and the full moon; on Wednesday, the seventh lunar day with the southern asterism (Pūrvaphalgunī); on Thursday, Jyeṣṭhā and the first lunar day; on Friday, the sixth lunar day and Śravaṇa. (26.18)
On a Saturday, the conjunction with the eighth lunar day of the asterism Revatī is a "death-yoga"; one should avoid these.
On the third lunar day, the asterism Rohiṇī (Prājāpatya), and on the sixth, the asterism Mṛgaśiras (Saumya) and Puṣya (Tiṣyabha). (26–19)
On the tenth day, the Dvādaśī [nakṣatra] is Maitra; likewise, on the fifth day, Śravaṇa;
on the seventh day, Pauṣṇa; and on the eighth day, Yāmya—these are known as the Ugra [nakṣatras].
Citrā and Viśākhā belong to Agni; Ajaikapād and Vaiṣṇava (Anurādhā); Śatabhiṣaj and Āhirbudhnya (Śravaṇa); the two Aśvins (Aśvinī) and likewise Bharaṇī. || 26-21 ||
Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, and the asterism of Aditi (Punarvasu) are void among the signs beginning with Aja (Aries);
these twelve asterisms are likewise to be avoided in the twelve months respectively.
In these yogas—Viṣkambha, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Atigaṇḍa, Vajra, and Vyāghāta—the [birth] is measured by three, five, six, and four *ṛtus* (seasons) respectively. (26–23)
Excluding the first nine *ghaṭikās* of these [nine yogas], the subsequent ones are auspicious;
specifically, the first [periods] of Viṣkambha and Śūla, and the middle [periods] of Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa.
At the end of Vyāghāta and Vajra, one should abandon the stated nāḍīs;
one should also entirely avoid Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti.
One should avoid the roots of the Arka and Āra trees, as well as the stars corresponding in number to those roots,
and one should also avoid burnt wood, thorns, pillars, and the like in rites such as consecrations.
The asterisms of Āśleṣā, Aśvinī, Maghā, and Revatī; Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla; Bharaṇī, Pūrvābhādrapadā, and Anurādhā; and Puṣya, Pūrvāphālgunī, and Uttarāṣāḍhā are mutually in opposition. (26–27)
Śroṇā, Prajeśa, Śatabhiṣaj, Hasta, Ārdrā, and Svāti are mutually [joined] as a quarter-nakṣatra by a quarter-part, and as a half-nakṣatra by a half-part. || 26–28 ||
Having understood the piercing (vedha) caused by the planets situated in these [lunar mansions], one should avoid them;
likewise, in various yogas, according to their respective numbers, they are joined with the lunar days (tithis) of the two fortnights.
In this [system] divided by the number of Munis (seven), the following should be known as the Śrīdivasas and so forth:
Śrīdivasa, Kalidivasa, Nandīdivasa, and Kālakarṇī. (26–30)
The day of victory, the day of slaughter, and likewise the ocean of wealth—these seven, along with Kali, Kālakarṇī, and the one known as Slaughter, are to be avoided. (26–31)

By enumeration, one should abandon the nāḍīs called Yama, Nāga, Sana, Pāra, and Khala, which correspond in form to the lunar days (tithis), in sequence within the [sixty] nandā and other periods. || 26–32 ||
Hārī, Sānumayaḥ, Netram, Sūnuḥ, Maunī, Kapiḥ, Paṭuḥ;
Haraḥ, Hārī, Naraḥ, Saṃjñā, Mānyaḥ, Mṛtyuḥ, Paṭuḥ, Nariḥ. (26–33)
One should not stay with a naked army; earth suitable for those seeking ritual marks (saṃjñā) should be used;
one should avoid places where an old sage is far away, and one should also avoid those shaped like bears.
In the case of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, two *ghaṭikās* at the end of the number of *ghaṭikās* stated in the [respective] verse must be avoided.
Two *ghaṭikās* at the end of the asterism, five *nāḍikās* at the end of the day, two days at the end of the month, and three days at the end of the solstice [are to be abandoned]. (26–35)
One should avoid [the following] during the fortnight and at the end of the year in rites such as consecrations:
Nāga, Nābhi, Vara, Kopa, Nīla, Nīra, Naga, and Naga. (26–36)

Araṃ means "quickly"; dayā means "compassion"; kharaḥ means "donkey"; krūraḥ means "cruel"; pāpaḥ means "sinful"; bhūyaḥ means "again"; nayaḥ means "policy"; bhayam means "fear"; nārī means "woman"; priyā means "beloved"; naraḥ means "man"; nīpam means "a kind of tree"; nāram means "human"; deyam means "to be given"; dvayoḥ means "of two"; bhayam means "fear. || 26-37 ||
The [lunar] days, the directions, and the "excellent" (vara) are said to be the poison-nāḍīs;
one should avoid four nāḍīs at the end of the statements for Kṛttikā and the other [nakṣatras]. (26–38)

One should recognize the *ardhaprahāra*, the *vesara*, the *mandagīta*, the *yamakaṇṭaka*, the *sākṣācchiva*, the *gurupada*, and the *gulika* by means of the junctions of the eighth parts of the days of the week, beginning with Sunday. (26–39)

The Yoginīs, beginning with Brahmāṇī, are to be known by the [elements] earth, air, water, and peace; [the deities] starting with the Sun, Fire, and Durgā are to be worshipped on the lunar days (tithis) beginning from the east.
During the journey for the formal acquisition of land and similar occasions, as well as during the taking possession of the foundation stone and other rites,
one should always proceed by avoiding travel directly toward the Yoginī.
In the three sets of ten lunar days beginning with the new moon (amāvāsyā), the numbers of the lunar days are nine, ten, and eight;
these correspond to space and the subterranean realm (rasātala).
One should not perform auspicious rites in the sky or in the netherworld (pātāla), nor at those other times of fault determined by the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra). (26–43)
One should avoid the five defects, the half-circle, the sixty-four openings, as well as the eclipses, the equinoxes, the transits, and the solstices. (26.44)
However, a day free from all defects is not easily found by itself;
therefore, one should resort to a *lagna* (ascendant) that possesses many virtues and only few defects. || 26-45 ||
The Guru, situated in the ascendant, pacifies one hundred thousand defects;
Venus, five thousand; and Mercury, five hundred. (26-46)
Therefore, when a benefic planet is strong and situated in the ascendant,
one should perform activities such as plowing for the sake of increasing the landowner's estate, as well as for the sake of the patron and the architect.
When auspicious conjunctions are possible, one should perform the installation and other rites;
for example:
the *mūla* [nakṣatra] with the second lunar day under the Sun, and the *śroṇā* [nakṣatra] with the first lunar day under the Moon.

On a Tuesday, the third lunar day and the constellation Āhirbudhnya; on a Wednesday, the eighth lunar day and Kṛttikā; on a Thursday, the fifth lunar day and the constellation Aditi; and on a Friday, the fourth lunar day and Phalgunī. (26–49)
Saturn and Svāti on the seventh day—these yogas are immortal and auspicious;
so too are Hasta, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Aśvinī, Maitra (Anurādhā), Puṣya, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), and Rohiṇī. || 26-50 ||
When conjoined with the days of the week beginning with Sunday, these Siddhi-yogas are considered auspicious.
And it has been stated by others: "Of Agni, Vāyu, Citrā, Revatī, Varuṇa, Śeṣa, Gaṇeśa, and Nirṛti, [one should take] one from each in sequence."
If Nandā enters into conjunction with either the Sun or Mars,
it becomes Parayoga, which is the cause for the accomplishment of all undertakings.

Thus it is said. Therefore, one should perform rites beginning with plowing and ending with consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) at an auspicious time endowed with qualities—whether all or some of them as applicable—such as the enjoined month, fortnight, lunar day (*tithi*), *karana*, asterism (*nakṣatra*), day of the week, planetary conjunctions (*yoga*), and the favorable divisions of the zodiac (*grahāṃśaka*), *horā*, decan (*drekkāṇa*), aspect (*nirīkṣaṇa*), and ascendant (*udaya*).
This concludes the section on Place and Time.
The patron (*yajamāna*), endowed with virtues, seeking the consecration of the *liṅga*... (26–51)

One who possesses the means of wealth, grain, and so forth, acquired through righteous methods and purified [of wrongdoing], [should seek] a teacher of pure intention, adorned with the aforementioned characteristics and ornaments. (26.52)
Having worshipped him with gold, garments, perfumes, garlands, and even fruits, one should request him for the purpose of installation on the onset of an auspicious day favorable to oneself. (26.53)
Having established him in a temple or a delightful riverside,
[he should be attended] by practitioners who have received initiation and are endowed with the most excellent characteristics.
Accompanied by eight pure Brahmins who bear his forms,
one should worship him with these mantras, beginning with water for the feet (pādya) and ending with incense (dhūpa).
In this *Mañjarī*: "Then,
having envisioned those eight forms and their respective guardians,
and having worshipped them in due order with these mantras preceded by prostrations, one should satisfy them with garments, ornaments, and other offerings."
Thus:
Oṃ, the earth supports the worlds; the worlds are said to consist of the earth.
O you whose form is the earth! Salutations to you, the all-pervading form of the earth. || 26-56 ||
Oṃ!
Agni sustains the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of Agni.
O you whose form is Agni, who are all-pervading—salutations be to you! (26.57)
Oṃ!
The Self indeed sacrifices through sacrifices; the worlds are remembered as being composed of sacrifice.
O You whose form is sacrifice! Salutations be unto You, who are omnipresent and the embodiment of sacrifice. (26.58)
Oṃ!
The Sun sustains the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of the Sun.
O you whose form is the Sun! Salutations to you, who are all-pervading and whose nature is the Sun. (26-59)
Oṃ!
You sustain the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of water.
O you whose form is water! Salutations to you, who are all-pervading and whose nature is water. (26-60)
Oṃ, Vāyu sustains the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of Vāyu. O you whose form is Vāyu! Homage be to you, whose form is all-pervading Vāyu! (26-61)
Oṃ! Soma sustains the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of Soma. O you whose form is Soma! Salutations to you, who are all-pervading. || 26-62 ||
Oṃ!
Space sustains the worlds; the worlds are remembered as being composed of space.
You are all-pervading and have the form of space; O you whose body is space, homage be to you! (26.63)
Thus, the eight forms of Śiva—designated as Earth, Fire, Self, Sun, Water, Wind, Moon, and Sky—are said to be the drivers of the machine of the universe. (6.64)
Śarva, Rudra, Paśupati, Īśāna,
as well as Bhava, Ugra, Mahādeva, and Bhīma— these are the eight guardians of the forms (mūrtipās).

Having thus worshipped eight Brahmins— who embody the forms of Earth and the others, as well as Śarva and the rest, and who are the lords of the embodied— by means of perfumes, flowers, garments, and other offerings.
Having especially honored and bowed down to the preceptor, the patron, with a serene mind, should then choose these [officiants]. (26.67)
"For the purpose of installing the Śiva-liṅga, I choose you as the preceptor;
together with these bearers of the forms [of the deities], O All-pervading Lord, grant me your grace! (26.68)
Having spoken thus, the patron should bow to them and make his request;
together with the preceptor, they should say to the patron, "So be it. (69)
Then, in a location determined by his own intention, on an auspicious day and so forth,
having ascertained the boundary of the enclosure for the ground, he should perform the ritual of formal possession (*parigraha*).
For example:

having constructed a pavilion that is square, four cubits in size, and supported by four pillars to the northeast of the interior of the temple, one should fashion a beautiful sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 26.71 ||
Having worshipped the doors and entered within, having placed the fire in the sacrificial pit,
one should offer clarified butter with the Saṃhitā mantras as well as those called the weapons of the world-protectors.
Then again, with the Aghora-weapon mantra, one hundred or indeed a thousand [times].

Then, having drawn a lotus in the center of five compartments within the pavilion and four svastikas in the cardinal directions, one should place five water-pots upon heaps of the seven grains. Having filled them with sacred waters according to the rules and having cast into them gold, gems, perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice, and auspicious herbs; and having adorned them with the five sprouts of the *bilva*, *aśvattha*, and other trees, with *kuśa* grass tufts, fruits at their mouths, garments, and garlands around their necks; and having duly worshipped Śiva—invoked therein along with His limbs and primary seat—in the sequence beginning with the seat; and having installed the *Śiva-kumbha* (the pot of Śiva) according to rule upon the heap of seven grains on a lotus-seat within a mandala prepared to the northeast of those pots, having filled and decorated it, and having invoked and worshipped Śiva with His limbs upon its mobile or immobile seat; and having united Śiva with His limbs, who was stationed in the fire, with the waters of the pots; and having sprinkled the interior of the temple with the waters from the northeast pot; and having sprinkled the eastern, southern, western, and northern boundaries of the temple with the waters of the eastern and other pots, [consecrating them] with the Puruṣa-sūkta and other mantras; and having had the artisan, facing north, dig a pit in the location of the fire-pada on the consecrated site using a basket made of bamboo or cane; and having removed the earth from that spot and thrown it seven times onto the *nairṛta* (southwest) pada; and having filled the pit with the water remaining in the pots; and having bathed the spade and other tools with the leftover water; and having lifted the *Śiva-kumbha* and placed it upon the head or shoulder of a Brahmin who has bathed and is wearing unwashed garments; and having led the pot to the eastern boundary of the enclosure wall accompanied by the witnesses of many people, preceded by songs, instrumental music, and the chanting of the Vedas; and having stayed there for a moment; and having carried the pot around in a clockwise direction starting from the southeast and ending in the northeast through the four corners of the boundary; and having fixed four stakes at the four corners of the boundary; and having scattered an offering (*bali*) to the spirits in the various directions at night with the *bhūtakrūra* mantra; the Preceptor should cause the spirits stationed there to depart elsewhere for residence with this [mantra].
Oṃ! Bhūtas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas! || 26-73 ||
And whoever else remains here, let them all depart from this place;
for from this day forward, this shall be the abode of the trident-bearing God.

Having dismissed the host of spirits with the mantra *oṃ haḥ huṃ phaṭ*, and having again scattered the sacrificial offering (*bali*) for those who are departing, one should perform the plowing at a favorable moment when the night has turned to dawn. It is as follows:
with tawny or white, strong, and auspiciously marked bulls, yoked to pairs of milk-tree poles made of *khadira*, *āsana*, or *lāṅgala* wood. (26.75)
When all those men have bathed, put on new garments, and are fully adorned, the preceptor, having touched that plough, should consecrate it with the Ajāta mantra.
Then, one should have them perform the plowing with lines drawn toward the east;
having recited the Vāmadeva hymn, one should sow the seven grains.
Having sprinkled [the grains] with water using the Aghora mantra, one should perform protection with the Īśāna mantra.
Once those grains are ripe, one should have them fed to cows by means of the Vaktra mantra. (26.78)
Now, in this *Mañjarī*:
"Having again placed a cow-hide there and having let it remain for a year, one should sow pulses and other grains there once more according to the previous sequence."

Then, after having consumed those [remains] along with the sacrificial animals during a pure moment, one should dig up the ground where the stake was removed and restore the earth very firmly once more.
Thus ends the section on plowing. Having leveled the ground as far as the boundary of the palace site, one should proceed.
Resembling the surface of a mirror and smeared with cow-dung and water.

Having determined the directions here by means of a gnomon according to the sequence prescribed above, one should [erect] stakes made from firm and highly auspicious trees such as the Punnāga, Nāga, and others. (26.80)
One should [place] nine [pots], well-rounded, with a circumference equal to one-fourth of their height; these, beginning from the middle one, should be worshipped with perfumes and other offerings.
Some say that one should place eight [stakes] in the directions starting from the east, and others in the directions starting from the southeast;
first, the Guru, having fixed the stakes at the boundaries of the temple, [proceeds].
One should strike with an iron mallet or a mace of equal weight;
one should not strike with stone nor with wood, for that would cause harm.
For the accomplishment of the eight auspicious signs, one facing east should strike [the ground] with the tip [of the staff];
thereafter, the artisan may strike the pegs with the mallet as desired.
If the peg enters suddenly, it is an omen of doubt; if it does not enter at all, it creates an obstacle.
If the peg enters slowly and straight, one should declare that there will be success in the ritual action.
If [the tree] is split, withered, or broken, there will be the death of that person or his son;
if it leans toward the east or other directions, there is wealth, danger from fire, and death.
One should indicate loss of wealth, fear, disease, prosperity, and happiness [respectively].
If the flame is unbroken and rising, one should predict an increase in status.
A cord made of cotton thread should be excellent, very firm, and even; or it may be made of hemp, silk, or muñja grass. With that [cord], one should stretch out the thread. (26.88)
A line following the thread should be clearly drawn with a golden rod,
or else with silver, or even with curd, or with unbroken grains (akṣata), according to the respective directions.
When the one appointed for the casting of the thread, whether he be the sacrificer or another,
remains free from agitation, one should designate the ground as being free from defects.

One should indicate the presence of a foreign body (śalya) by such deformities as scratching and so forth, as well as by the sudden appearance of dogs, jackals, goats, cows, horses, and other animals. (26.91)
If one should see [a mark] below there, one should indicate that a splinter is present;
for example:

For scratching the head, there is a skull-bone at a depth of two *tālas*; for touching the mouth, a piece of wood or a skull-fragment at two cubits; for the neck, an iron chain at three cubits; for the forearms or upper arms, that bone at two and a half cubits; for the forearms or knees, a bed-leg, a skull, or a bone at the height of the knees; for the waist, iron upon touching the waist; for the thighs, a bone or wood at that same measure; for the chest and heart, that bone at that same measure; for the knees, a pillar at one cubit; for the shanks, a barber’s tool or a shank-bone; for the feet, an elephant-bone; for the big toe, a small jar or bell-metal; for the fingers, a horse-hoof or bell-metal at one and a half *tālas*. One should declare the omen to be a mixture of these when the actions are mixed. For a cat leaping over, there is a bone of a wild animal (*rabhasa*) at that same measure; for a dog, a cow-bone; for a goat, a goat-bone or a dog-bone; for a horse, a buffalo-bone; for a buffalo, a jackal-bone; for a jackal, a boar-bone; for a boar, a tiger-bone; for a tiger, an elephant-bone; for an elephant, a human bone; for a human, a donkey-bone; for a donkey, a goat-bone. One should likewise declare it by the crossing of a thread, the entering of a field, or by sight and mention thereof. One should indicate ashes, chaff, charcoal, and so forth, from the entry of birds.

If one were to construct a temple or a house while such thorns (śalyas) have not yet been extracted, there would be a loss of the deity’s presence (*sānnidhya*) therein, and for the builder and his lineage, there would arise defects such as lack of prosperity, calamities, disease, exile, the destruction of grain, and affliction. These are not explained in detail here for fear of making the text too voluminous. Furthermore, there are auspicious thorns; regarding this, Brahmaśambhu says:
"A living fish brings the acquisition of grain; a tortoise promotes the practice of yoga; a frog brings constant fortune; and a mouse brings a virtuous character."
Furthermore:
"One should not extract fish, frogs, tortoises, gold, mercury, or gems from a pit; if one should extract them, it will cause misfortune. (26.92)
Thus ends the section on the extraction of the splinter.
Now, having extracted the splinter here, one should proceed with the worship of Vāstu.

Regarding this, Brahmaśambhu states: "Vāstu is the Daitya Vastutanu; he was born from the anger of the Daitya ministers. This is heard in the sciences of architecture (vāstuvidyā) as well as in the Śiva-āgamas."
Thus it was:
in ancient times, during the war between the gods and the asuras, the gods led by Purandara were defeated by the asuras; however, through the very abundance of Viṣṇu’s power, the asuras perished.
Their preceptor, the son of Bhṛgu, becoming exceedingly incensed by their agitation,
offered an oblation into the fire and sacrificed a single goat endowed with auspicious marks.
As he was offering oblations to dispel his sweat, that which fell upon the consumer of the oblation—
by its splendor— that goat became the demon Chāgavaktra.
Covering both the earth and the heavens with his terrifyingly vast body, he rose up before the best of sages and said, "What shall I do? (26.97)
The son of Bhṛgu addressed that yawning and terrifying being:
"You shall cause the gods, whose wisdom is unawakened, to fall from heaven. (26.98)
Thus addressed, threatening with roars and emitting flames from his own mouth,
as if scorching the three worlds, he rushed toward the gods.
Even Bhava, out of fear of him, along with his own manifestations that had been cast down,
approached the all-pervading Śambhu, who is free from fear and adorned with ashes.
Even Bhava, due to his defeat by Bhārgava, was utterly terrified of them;
then, for the welfare of those who were broken, fire arose from his third eye.
Having commanded that elemental form to tear apart the son of Bhṛgu,
you should then consume the cruel and grown-up Chāgāsura.
Thus addressed, the fire, being unattached to anything, rushed toward Bhārgava;
fleeing in fear, he too wandered through the three worlds.
p. 252) He found no one who could grant him safety, except for the one adorned with ashes.
Then, by means of his yogic power, he made his own body exceedingly small. || 26-104 ||
For the sake of Śambhu’s well-being, he entered the auspicious body [of Viṣṇu] by means of hearing;
having entered the belly of that Śaṅkara, he brought him auspiciousness.
The entire world was seen to be trusting and reassured;
and the god, possessing divine vision, having heard that he had come for refuge, [acted accordingly].
Without astonishment, the three-eyed Lord, smiling, said to the yogi:
"Do not fear, O Bhārgava! I am pleased with this wisdom of yours regarding right conduct."
"You have dwelt here long enough, my son; depart from here at your own will.
The foremost station of the planets has been granted, along with that great sovereignty of yours. (26.108)
"Thus, you must constantly cause right conduct and misconduct, as well as rain and drought, to prevail throughout the three worlds," having spoken thus to him, the Three-eyed One [departed]. (26.109)
He was emitted through the white path (the left nostril), and from that he became known by the name Śukra.

Then Śukra, having bowed to the Lord and understood his desire, made this request: 26-110. He was emitted through the white path (the left nostril), and from that he became known by the name Śukra. Then Śukra, having bowed to the Lord and understood his desire, made this request:
I have achieved my purpose and am favored; who else besides me is so fortunate, since I have been thus greeted with grace by the God of gods? (26.111)
Having spoken thus to Śukra, who was bowing down, the Lord whose crest is the moon of his curved face, being pleased, said to that brahmin: "Choose another boon. (26.112)
In that place, he also granted a boon to the terrified Chāgāsura of old,
who had previously been struck down by the feet of the Enemy of Tripura (Śiva), for the sake of his welfare.
Then, to the Daitya who was bowing his head and prostrating on the ground like a staff, the Lord, being pleased, spoke: "I grant you freedom from fear; choose whatever boon you desire."
"O goat! Let that which you desired be yours," said Śambhu; thus addressed, the asura informed him: "O Lord! That which I have performed so poorly was done out of ignorance. (26.115)
You ought to forgive that; by your grace, may I dwell upon the earth.
Grant me this boon: that I may live without conflict with the gods.
"May the gods, beginning with Brahmā, dwell within me, honored [by me].
Hearing this, even though he held a trident in his hand, he said: "An excellent boon is granted by you for [my] dwelling. (26.117)
Since I have been chosen by you, therefore you shall be known by the name Vāstupa; may it be so for you.
From the root *vas*, meaning "to dwell," you shall dwell upon the earth, Vasuṃdharā.
And may the deities, headed by Śatānanda, dwell in you with affection;
from this day forward, whether divine or otherwise, in the world of mortals.
Those who construct a dwelling for the purpose of habitation should first worship you with flowers,
incense, lamps, and various kinds of offerings.
"You and the deities residing within your body shall be worshipped in due order;
thus has the worship of Vāstu been ordained by me for those who perform it. (26.121)
May there be prosperity for those dwelling in temples, houses, and the like;
yet, without performing the Vāstu sacrifice, one should not construct palaces, mansions, and so forth. (26.122)
"Whatever has been done by the Asuras, and whatever has been done there [by you], let all that become [as it was].
Having thus granted the boon separately to Śukra and Vāstu, the God [departed]. (26.123)
Having appointed the gods to dwell in this place, he vanished right there;
at whatever region or direction the Asura was cast down while bowing to Śambhu, [that became his abode]. (26.124)
By the grace of the Lord, it became inhabited by the gods and Śukra at that very moment;
likewise, even today the foundation remains with its face turned downwards and its head toward the northeast.
Stretching out his feet toward the southwest, he lay down upon the earth;
for thus had the boon been obtained by Vāstoṣpati, the lord of the city, which was his heart's desire:
that this sacrifice should be as pleasing to the gods as it was to men in the performance of the rites for celestial chariots and other offerings.

Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, concerning the determination of place and time, the extraction of the ritual stake, and the rules for the origin of the site (*vāstu*), in the *Kriyāpāda* of the *Uparibhāga* of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 26.
Now begins the twenty-seventh chapter.
Herein, one should perform the worship of Vāstu and of Vāstoṣpati, as well as of the deities residing therein;
and having scattered the bali offering with their respective names and with the materials to be described hereafter, according to the rule: 27-1.

In the designated place, having first smeared it with water mixed with fresh cow dung into a square shape, one should then divide that into eight parts; thus, as it has been said, it shall consist of sixty-four squares.
When that [space] is divided ninefold and the lines are drawn, it is mixed with rice-flour paste;
that which consists of eighty-one squares is said to be for the temples of the gods as well as for kings. (27-3)
Having fashioned it with sixty-four squares and having fixed the thread at its corners, one should then worship Brahmā in the center of the four central squares. || 27-4 ||
In the two eastern cells, he is named Marīci; in the southern, Vivasvat; and in the western, Mitra.
Mahīdhara resides in the pair of northern cells. Now I shall describe the deities in the pairs of half-cells at the corners. 27–5.
Sāvitra and Savitṛ shall be in the southeast; Vahni and Harita shall be at the half-step [of the corner]; Indra and Indrajaya are renowned in the direction of the Rākṣasas (the southwest);
likewise, Rudra and Rudrajaya are in the northwest; and Āpa and Apavatsa are in the direction of Īśa (the northeast).
Furthermore, I shall describe the eight deities in the four external corners as well.
Śarva, Skanda, Aryaman, Ahi, Jambhaka, Pilipiñjaka, Carakī, Vidārī, Pūtanā, and Pāparākṣasī. || 27-7 ||
Now, the deities of the thirty-two squares of the peripheral four-footed grid are to be known in the fourfold manner, proceeding in order from the east in each of the four directions. (27–8)
In the east, there are eight deities— Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Indra, Arka, Satya, Bhṛśa, and Antarikṣa— to be worshipped in clockwise order.
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama the guardian of the house, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and the one named Mṛga are also in the south. (27.10)
Nirṛti and Dauvārika, as well as Sugrīva and Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta and Asura, Śoṣa and Pāpayakṣman are in the west. (27.11)
Māruta, the two chief Nāgas, Bhallāṭa, Niśākara, Argala, Diti, and likewise Aditi are situated in the north. (27.12)
The head of this Vāstoṣpati was placed in the northeast; his two hands were in the northwest and the southeast, and his pair of feet was stationed in the southwest.
Parjanya was in his eyes, Aditi in his mouth, and Apāpa and Vatsa in his throat.
And Diti was in his ear, while Jayanta and Indrārgala were at his shoulders. || 27-13 ||
The Sun and the Moon are on the two arms, while Bhallāṭa and Satya, along with Sāvitra and likewise Rudra, are stationed at his sides.
Caturānana (Brahmā) should be at the navel, and Bhūbhṛt and Marīci at the two breasts.
And Mitra was also within that womb by Vivasvat, as was another, Guhyendra.
Gandharva, Pūrva, and Traya are placed upon his thighs and shanks; Dauvārika, Sugala, and likewise Varuṇa are situated on the remaining [limbs].
Therefore, one should not perform the placement of the deities within the limbs of the Vāstu-body.
If one should perform it out of ignorance, then it brings about the destruction of everything. || 27-15 ||

The worship of Īśāna should be performed with ghee, unbroken rice, and water; that of Parjanya with water scented with blue lotuses. The banner of Jayanta shall be yellow; one should worship Mahendra with red food and lamps.

The worship of Sūrya should be performed with yellow food and canopies; likewise, that of Satya with ghee and boiled rice; that of Bhṛśa with wheat cakes; and that of Antarikṣa with meat and beans. (27.17)
Having worshipped Agni with the sacrificial ladle (sruc) and likewise Pūṣan with parched grains (lāja), and Vitatha with gold;
one should worship the deity named Gṛharakṣaka with honey and boiled rice, and Yama with meat and boiled rice.

Having worshipped the Gandharvas with fragrant flowers, one should then offer *pakṣijihvā* at the *bhṛṅgarāja* plant; for the worship of the Mṛga [deity], one should use sesame or barley seeds, and for Nirṛti, *kṛsara* (rice and peas) should be prepared according to the rules.
Having worshipped Śobhanadanta with auspicious tooth-sticks and grains of barley along with incense,
and likewise Puṣpadanta with pillars of *kuśa* grass, one should worship Jaleśa with white lotuses.
For Asura, worship should consist of honey and parched grain; for Śoṣa, food mixed with clarified butter;
for Pāpayakṣman, however, food made of wild rice (nīvāra); and for Vāyu, there should be cakes made with clarified butter. || 27-21 ||

One should perform the worship of Nāga with *nāgapuṣpa* flowers, and that of the Principal [Deity] with *modaka* sweets; for the one named Bhallāṭa, food prepared with meat; and for King Soma, honey, milk-rice, and clarified butter.

Having worshipped Argala with unbroken grains of *śāli* rice and Ditī with well-colored *śāli* rice and ghee, and having duly worshipped Aditi with food offerings of black gram (*māṣa*), one should thus worship the thirty-two [deities] in sequence. (27.23)
One should worship Āpa with milk, and likewise the Apavatsa with curd, ghee, and sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka).
Having worshipped Sāvitra with kuśa grass and rice mixed with jaggery, one should perform the sacrifice for Savitṛ.
For Indra, yellow rice with ghee is prescribed; for Indrajaya, pure rice alone is recommended. For Rudra, cooked meat is ordained, whereas for Rudrajaya, raw meat is prescribed.
Then Samarīcikā and the others are to be worshipped with sweetmeat balls (laḍḍuka) and red and white rice,
as well as with black gram (māṣa) and ghee, according to rule and in due order, each in their respective place.

Having first worshipped Brahmā with clarified butter, unbroken rice, the five products of the cow, flowers, perfumes, sacrificial porridge (caru), and sesame seeds, one should then worship the one named Śarva, Skanda, with ghee and milk-rice (pāyasa).
To Yama and Aryaman, one offers meat and ghee; then, to Jambhaka, yellow garlands and meat in the southwest; and to Pilipiñja in the north.
One should thus cause the bali-offering to be presented with thick red flowers and food;
in the northeast, the bali for Carakī consists of meat, rice, ghee, and cakes.
Outside, in the southeast direction, an offering is made with bile and flesh for Vidyārī;
and for Pūtanā, in the southwest direction, an offering is made with curd, blood, and rice.

Having reached the Vāyavyā Rākṣasī, one should worship all [the others] with milk, bile, bone, blood, and food, using their own names ending in "namaḥ," accompanied by the ritual offerings (upacāra). || 27-31 ||
Then, outside, one should offer a bali-oblation to the eight classes of beings;
if the aforementioned substances for each are unavailable, [one may use] flowers and unbroken grains (akṣata).

The *bali* offering is prescribed with fragrant incense, lamps, and pure food. Having performed worship to these [deities] with their own names, preceded by the *praṇava* (OM) and ending with "namaḥ," one should offer the *bali* at night, dressed in white garments and possessing a pure disposition, using the five types of ritual services (*pañcopacāra*). || 27–33 ||
In this manner, the deities residing within the body of the dwelling, having been properly worshipped, [grant their favor]. (27–34)
And they bestow success in various rites as well as pacification (*śāntika*).
Having placed this Vāstoṣpati in the eighty-one squares as before,
one should worship him in the center and the Creator (*vedhas*) in the nine squares within that, and outside of that—
In the corners here, within two squares each, the deities beginning with Sāvitra are attained; in their center, the four deities beginning with Samarīca are said to be situated in sequence. (27–35)
In the directions starting from the east, thirty-two deities headed by Īśa (Śiva) should be worshipped in order, each situated in a separate outer enclosure as previously described.
Outside, the others are excluded from their squares; Carakī is in the northeast (Īśa), and Vidārī in the southeast (Anala).
In the corner is the Rakshasi Putana; and in the direction of the wind is the Rakshasi Pavanasya.
The four beginning with Śarva and Skanda stand outside, excluding the [central] square. || 27-37 ||
One should worship [the deities] in the east, south, west, and north in sequence;
having resorted to one of these two paths, one should invoke Vāstupa.

One should also worship, in due order, the deities residing in the limbs and the words [of the mantra]. This concludes the section on the worship of Vāstu. Having thus worshipped the Lord of Vāstu, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas there. (27–39)
And he should [provide] those wearing sectarian marks (liṅgin), as well as artisans and laborers, according to their capacity.
Then, that entire area of ground extending to the boundary of the temple (prāsāda) [should be prepared].
Having dug a pit one man’s height deep with arms raised, one should remove the earth and discard it;
some say that one should dig until reaching water or gravel.
In this *pratiṣṭhāpaddhati*:
"One should have the excavation made for the temple of the deity ending either at the level of gravel or at the level of water;
or, in the case of a house, for the sake of human welfare, as far as the ground remains pure."
Thus, having sprinkled the excavated pit with the Astra-mantra, one should first fill it with eight aṅgulas of pure earth— free from clods and the like, and neither discolored nor impure. (27–42)
Then, having gradually spread out round stones covered with clay and water to the measure of a cubit, one should again cover it with sand and then with clay.
Then, having flooded it with water, one should cause elephants to trample the ground with their firm and level feet, fashioned from the wood of excellent trees.
One should pound [the ground] and rub it down, and then pile up the site very firmly.
When the excavation has been reduced by one-fourth, one should place the first brick. (27.45)
Having constructed a square pavilion to the north of the palace,
it should have four doors, four pillars, and be adorned with four archways.
Having performed his daily rites and bathed, the Guru, accompanied by those who embody the deities,
should first offer the general *arghya* and then worship the lords of the directions at the entrance.
Having discharged the weapon-mantra and entered within, one should cause the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be recited there;
the Guru, bearing the sword of knowledge, possesses the mantra of the station of the pure self.
The pavilion entrance has been sprinkled with the special *arghya* offering of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*).
In the center are Vāstveśa and Padmajā; in the east are Lakṣmī and Gaṇeśvara.
One should worship Durgā in the south, Kṣetreśa in the west, and [the deity] in the north;
this is preceded by the scattering of the *vikira* offerings and followed by the worship of the water-pot (*kumbha*) and the weapon (*astra*).
One should install the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the jars and the weapons in the banners;
one should cause them to hear the command of Śiva with the mantras of Bhīma, Oṃ, Śakra, and the others.
After the rotation of the weapon-vessel (astrakumbha), once the vessel and the weapon have become stable, one should worship;
having touched the vessel with the mudrā, one should consecrate the sword of knowledge (jñānakhaḍga). || 27-52 ||

Having offered clarified butter into the fire within the Veda-triangle-shaped pit in the east— where Śiva has been invoked— with the Saṃhitā mantras and with the five-syllabled mantra, [he should offer] fuel-sticks.

Then, having offered oblations of clarified butter three times each with the five-syllable mantras— preceded by the *tāra* (oṃ) and ending in *svāhā*— separately for the *tāra*, the *dādhāra*, and the *ājyabhāga* portions.

Having offered fuel-sticks, clarified butter, and sacrificial porridge separately with each of the five Brahma-mantras a hundred times each, he should then offer clarified butter a hundred times with the Vyāhṛtis.
With the mantras of the world-protectors (lokapālas), two oblations each are offered;
then, to the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), to the spirits (bhūtas), and to the serpents (nāgas), one oblation each is offered.
Having offered oblations to all the individual deities by their respective names,
ending each with "namas" and "svāhā," he should then offer again with the five-syllabled mantra.
Having offered clarified butter with the *vyāhṛti* mantras, preceded by the *sviṣṭakṛt* oblation, and having scattered the *caru* offering there, one should recite the eleven-fold [mantra]. (27.58)
Then, on the ground of the temple, one should draw the corner-lines upon a square area divided into four compartments, which consists of five syllables and that same number [of units].

Having laid out eighty-one squares there, one should delineate the vital points (*marmāṇi*) and the veins; one must not place foundation stones upon those parts that constitute the limbs of the site (*vāstu*).
One should not place the first pillar, nor any [pillar] at the vital points (marmans) and so forth.
The eastern thread is called the "upper beam" (ūrdhva-vaṃśa), and the beams are the cords of the corners.
The ribs and the backbone constitute the north-south thread; its veins are considered to be the [other] threads.
The joints therein are the vital points (marmans); the arrangement of the limbs is as previously described. (27–62)

Since those [locations] must be avoided during the initial placement of the bricks and so forth, the limbs of the Lord of the Site (Vāstveśa) are stated once again as follows: In the northeast is the head; the two vital breaths (prāṇas) are in the southeast and southwest; Parjanya and Aditi are the two eyes; Āpa is the mouth; Āpavatsa is the throat; Aditi is in the two ears; Jayanta and Argala are the two shoulders; Sūrya, Soma, and others are the two arms; Rudra is the back; Sāvitra and Savitṛ, as well as Roga and Śoṣa, are the two forearms; Brahmā is the navel; Bhūbhṛt and Aryaman are the two thighs; Mitra and Vivasvat are the belly; Indra and Indrajaya are the private parts; and Nirṛti is the two feet. Having avoided these deities who constitute the limbs of the Vāstupuruṣa, as well as the veins (sirās) and vital points (marmas), one should place the first bricks. Likewise, one should place the first pillar in pavilions, houses, and other such structures.
Regarding this, Viśvakarman says:
"If one should place a stone on a structural member (vāstvaṅga) out of ignorance or negligence,
there will be the destruction of the site, suffering for the builder, or even death."
Thus: To the south of the door, within the space between the two arms of the beam, one should place the first bricks in the excavation that remains after the foot-measure has been set aside. (27–63)
(260) Those whose limbs are well-proportioned with respect to the head and back, who are free from defects and possess auspicious marks,
whose hands are long, and whose width is half that length and eight finger-breadths high— || 27-64 ||
The first bricks should be well-baked, red in luster, free from cracks and other defects, and they should be nine or five in number. (27–65)

This procedure for the *aiṣṭaka* (brick) type has been declared for the temple of the most excellent of the excellent *liṅgas*; now, [the procedure] for the excellent and other [categories] is being described.
The Jagatī, Paṅkti, and Anuṣṭubh [verses] are long in number of finger-breadths respectively;
their width is half that [length], and their height is half the width.
The first bricks for the *uttama* and other types of pavilions have been specified; a brick thick at the base is female (*strī*), while one thick at the top is neuter (*napuṃsaka*).
The brick for men should be equal in length and thickness on all sides;
some say that bricks for men are best when they are male-shaped, while those for women should be female-shaped.
Indeed, a brick made of pumīṣṭikā alone bestows the fulfillment of all intentions for everyone.
Whether on stone or in a temple, bricks made of śaileya shall be the first bricks.
Then, in the middle of the pavilion, upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila) made of rice grains,
and on a seat prepared with darbha grass, one should place those bricks.

There, having sprinkled the bricks with the general *arghya* water, struck them with the *astra-mantra*, scraped them with the *kavaca-mantra*, and washed them with earth; then, having bathed them with cow dung, cow urine, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), gold, gems, fruits, and scented water—each separated by offerings of water and incense—having anointed them with perfumes, bound each one with a golden thread and a *kautuka*-cord, covered them with new cloths, and placed them on the prescribed sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) according to their respective directions, one should meditate upon the three sections within them. Therein, one should invoke and meditate upon the eightfold city (*puryaṣṭaka*) beginning with intellect (*buddhi*) and ending with smell (*gandha*), the eight forms (*mūrtyaṣṭaka*) beginning with earth and ending with space (*vyoman*), and the eight guardians of form (*mūrtipāṣṭaka*) beginning with Śarva and ending with Bhīma, together respectively with the principles of Śiva, Vidyā, and Ātman, and with the causal lords Rudra, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā. Each should be invoked individually upon the eight bricks at their base, middle, and top, using their respective names preceded by the *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*, with the dative case added to each name. One should worship them starting from "oṃ buddhaye namaḥ" up to the end of the scent offering. Then: "oṃ śivatattvāya namaḥ, oṃ śivatattvādhipataye rudrāya namaḥ"—these at the bases of the first section. "oṃ pṛthivīmūrtaye namaḥ" and so on, up to space, for the eight [forms] at the middles. "oṃ vidyātattvāya namaḥ, vidyātattvādhipataye viṣṇave namaḥ"—these in the middle [sections]. And "oṃ pṛthivīmūrtyadhipataye śarvāya namaḥ," and so on, up to Bhīma. Oṃ... *(Note: The text provided ends mid-sentence regarding the final invocation.)*

"Salutation to the reality of the Self; Om, salutation to Brahmā, the lord of the reality of the Self"—having thus touched the base, middle, and top of the bricks with the *kuśa* grass blade at their front parts, one should then install and worship [the mantra] upon the central brick with: "Salutation to Śiva, the lord of the three principles—the reality of all principles, the form of all forms, and the lord of all forms."

Having performed protection all around with *rakṣā*, *darbha*, and sesame seeds, and then having sat down in front of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should satisfy the triad of principles—the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth, the earth (*pṛthivī*) and so forth, and Śarva and so forth—as well as the lords of the petals by their respective names, preceded by the syllable *tāra* (oṃ), followed by the dative case ending, and ending with *svāhā*, using clarified butter (*ājya*) in three oblations for each. Having poured the remainder of that [offering] into a vessel, one should pour it onto the bricks; however, in the case of the three-fold division, one should pour it there.

Then, for the purpose of invoking their presence (*sānnidhya*), one should perform the *tattvasandhāna* (union of the principles). Reciting: "Oṃ Ām Īm, salutation to the *ātmatattva* and *vidyātattva*; Oṃ Īm Ūm, salutation to the *vidyātattva* and *śivatattva*," and having thus performed the union, one should prepare nine or five copper treasure-pots (*nidhikumbha*) filled with the three sweets (*trimadhura*). In the case of nine pots, one should invoke the eight treasures (*nidhi*)—known as Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, Kacchapa, Mukunda, Ananta, Nīla, and Śaṅkha—into the eight pots named Subhadra, Vibhadra, Sunanda, Puṣpadanta, Jaya, Vijaya, Jayanta, and Pūrṇa. Then, in the central Ananta-pot, which is joined with the Śakti-treasure, one should worship Ananta at the base, mounted upon salt, and Brahmā above him, using the root-mantra. Into these treasures, one should invoke and worship the eight world-protectors (*lokapāla*), beginning with Indra. In the case of five pots, one should invoke the five treasures known as Padma, Mahāpadma, Makara, Śaṅkha, and Samudra into the pots named Dharma, Jñāna, Vairāgya, Aiśvarya, and Sarvasiddhi, which correspond to the lunar days (*tithi*) of Nandā, Bhadrā, Jayā, Riktā, and Pūrṇā. One should then invoke the five lords of the causes (*kāraṇeśa*), beginning with Brahmā, into these five treasures, worship them thoroughly, and cast the nine gems (*navaratna*) or the five gems (*pañcaratna*) into all the pots according to the respective directions. Having established them in the pits up to the mouth, one should worship the treasures, the world-protectors, or the lords of the causes with offerings such as *arghya*.

Now, having sequentially brought the bricks placed upon the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), one should place them at the openings of the treasure-pots (*nidhikumbha*) during the prescribed auspicious moment (*muhūrta*), using the names of the respective world-protectors (*lokapāla*) associated with each treasure, beginning with the *tāraka* (the sacred syllable) and ending with the word "namas" (salutation), oriented first toward the east and then toward the north. Moving clockwise from the east to the northeast, and in the case of five [treasures], from the east to the north, one should pile them all so that they are perfectly level, free from depressions or elevations. If they are uneven, it brings fear to the kingdom and suffering to the patron and the site. Therefore, having piled them level and bathed them with the water from the *śiva-kumbha*, one should fill the pit with scented water, cast a single flower into it with the *praṇava* (Om), and observe it. If it turns clockwise, it is auspicious; if it turns counter-clockwise, one should perform pacification rites (*śānti*) through fire-offerings (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and gifts. Then, having constructed the foundation of the site with stones or bricks as specified, rising to the height of the prescribed cubits and making the surface even, one should worship the preceptor and the sculptor who bears his form. Having seen a dream on a bed of *darbha* grass at night, one should perform a pacification rite if the dream is inauspicious. If the dream is auspicious, however, one should again perform the Vāstu sacrifice and then proceed with the laying of the foundation (*garbhanyāsa*).
Thus ends the section on the first brick.
Now, one should perform the placement of the embryo within the sanctuaries and other sites;
for that which is the seed and the primordial nature (prakṛti) bestows prosperity. (27.72)
Between Indra and Pāvaka, on the ground to the south of the door, all castes should perform the deposition of the embryo (garbhavinyāsa) for the sake of prosperity. (27.73)
Above the mat for Brahmins, above the footstool for kings,
and on the ground for Vaiśyas and those of the fourth caste— so say some.
One should make a firm copper vessel as a receptacle for the embryo;
regarding this, the *Mañjarī* states:
"It should be eight finger-breadths in circumference and half that in height, with a height at the top measuring three-quarters of that."
The bowl should be of the highest quality, with a length equal to the span of a hand; its height should be determined here by the rule of three proportions.
Thus it is said;
one should, however, make that [pedestal] solid with a lid, consisting of one-twentieth part. || 27-75 ||
The height of the walls of the inner chambers (koṣṭha) shall be one-fourth of the width;
however, some authorities maintain that the best [type] has a height equal to its length.
The middle [type] shall be three-quarters [of the height], and the inferior one shall be half as high;
the lid shall be one-third [of the height], and in all cases it should be level and firm.
Having washed the vessel with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), one should fashion a pit therein while reciting the *hṛdaya-mantra*;
then, having smeared it with cow dung, one should cause the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha*) to be made.
Having drawn an infinite number of serpents with flour paste upon their hoods,
one should place the vessel containing the embryo upon them, four finger-breadths outside of that.
Having prepared a sacrificial mound with rice grains, one should draw upon it, using clay from the ocean,
the earth consisting of the seven continents and oceans, together with its mountains.
Within the central cell at the base of the *garbhapātra*, Brahmā is situated in the middle cell, with [the other deities] in the eight cells surrounding it. (27–81)
Samarīcaka, Sāvitra, Vivasvat, Śakra, Mitra,
Rudra, Pṛthvīdhara, and likewise Āpavatsa are situated within the compartments (koṣṭha).
Outside of that, situated within the squares of the vowels, are sixteen deities.
They are as follows: Īśāna, Jayanta, Sūrya, and Bhṛśa in the east; || 27.83 ||
Agni, Vitatha, Kīnāśa, and Bhṛṅgarāja are in the south;
behind them are Nirṛti, Sugrīva, Varuṇa, and Śoṣa. (27.84)
Vāyu, Mukhya, Soma, and Aditi are situated in the north;
likewise, there are diamonds, pearls, lapis lazuli, conch shells, and emeralds.
One should place crystal, great sapphire, and coral in sequence; one should place eight [gems] beginning with *samarīca* in the [deities] starting with Indra, and place ruby (*māṇikya*) in Brahmā.
To the east, one should place barley, realgar, rice, and green malachite;
then wild rice, collyrium, and Tuvara along with Priyaṅgu. (27.87)
One should place [the substances] in the south; that is to say:

one should place millet (śyāmāka), lead (sīsaka), black gram (māṣa), and saurāṣṭra in the west. One should place kula-stha, yellow pigment (rocanā), and flat beans (niṣpāva) along with red ochre (gairika) in the north. || 27-88 ||
One should place gold, silver, copper, iron, lead, tin, tortoise-shell, and lotus, as well as a trident, in the cardinal directions and the intermediate corners respectively.
One should sequentially place golden images of a skull-topped staff (khaṭvāṅga), a crescent moon, a bull, a Pināka bow, a lotus, and an axe, as well as a deer and a discus, in the position of Brahmā.
Having likewise placed earth from mountains, sacred fords, rivers, and lakes in the directions starting with the east, [he should then take it] from the Kārkaṭaka cave.
Having placed earth from an anthill, from the far shore of the ocean, from the horn of a bull,
and from an elephant's tusk in the directions beginning with the southeast (the fire-corner), [one should proceed].

One should place the lotus, the blue lotus, the white water-lily, and the *utpala* in the soft [tastes] arising from the horns of a bull and the tusks of an elephant, while the middling [tastes] are to be placed in the others. (27.93)
One should place the roots of *tagara* in the cardinal directions and in the center.
Then, with the [mantras] beginning with Sadyojāta, one should offer sacrificial fuel, clarified butter, cooked rice, and sesame seeds into the fires of the cardinal directions.
The image-keepers (mūrtipās) should offer oblations two by two, and they should perform recitations (japa) according to their respective divisions,
in the fire into which Śiva has been invoked within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) to the south of the pavilion (maṇḍapa).
The preceptor, having offered three oblations of clarified butter each with the *mantra-saṃhitā*,
should separately offer eleven oblations of fuel-sticks (*samidh*), clarified butter, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), and parched grain (*lāja*).
Having offered oblations with the five-syllable mantra, as well as with the ten-syllable *vyomavyāpin*,
and with the thirty-eight *kalās* and the *brahman*-mantras, each once.
Then, having offered clarified butter, and then each once the gems, the seeds, the herbs,
the minerals, the roots, and even the earth.

[He recited] the names of the Lords of the World, as well as those of the Weapons, the Lamps, the Oceans, and the Directions, and also of the Netherworlds and the Nagas, preceded by all their respective names. (27.99)

With their respective names beginning with "Tārā" and ending with "svāhā," preceded by the dative case, one should pour the remainder of all the oblations into a vessel; that clarified butter [is thus collected]. (27.100)
Having cast [the seed-syllable] into the womb with the syllable *TĀREṆA* and meditated upon it as consisting of earth,
one should then worship it with perfumes and other offerings, touch it, and recite the five-syllabled mantra.
On a night when the moon is in a non-declining constellation, in a fixed zodiacal sign endowed with auspicious qualities,
[he should offer] that vessel (phelā) as the goddess Earth, together with its seven continents and oceans.
One should meditate upon [the site] as being endowed with the fourfold classes of beings, both mobile and immobile,
and as consisting of the essence of the seed and the womb of the aforementioned abode and so forth.

Oṃ hāṃ hlāṃ, obeisance to the Earth, the supporter of all beings! Having invoked her with this mantra, one should establish her with the Sadyojāta mantra; having restrained her with the Aghora mantra, one should worship her with the Vāmadeva mantra. || 27-104 ||

Then, having veiled [the deity] with the *seśāna* mantra, one should worship again with perfumes and other offerings: "Oṃ, O bearer of all beings! O beloved! O you adorned by mountain-breasts! (27.105)
"O Goddess, Earth, whose garment is the ocean! Take up this embryo!

With these words, following the previously mentioned mantra, one should consecrate the earth, which has been placed upon a raft, so that it becomes firm. In this regard, the *Mañjarī* (p. 265) states:
"Having thus recited this mantra repeatedly and having meditated upon the circle of the earth..."
Having filled the pit with cow urine according to the rules and having placed the embryo therein,
and having performed this rite of conception (garbhādhāna) according to the injunctions while satisfying the preceptor with wealth,
one should then have a very firm temple constructed by artisans, endowed with all auspicious characteristics.

Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Worship of the Vāstu and the First Brick: The Deposition into the Foundation," in the Kriyāpāda of the Upper Section of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the manual of the venerable teacher Īśānaśiva. 27.
Now begins the twenty-eighth chapter.
Herein, the characteristics of temples for gods and others, as well as for men, are briefly described—in which [temples] they may dwell for a long time due to their beauty. (28.1)
Minds become serene; therefore, they are celebrated as *prāsādas*.
Because it is constructed according to various rules of measurement, it is called a *vimāna* according to the scriptures. (28-2)
Just as in former times the Grandfather, the sages, and Maya described the principal celestial chariots and others in their proper sequence.
Those [mantras] which are here described briefly for the gods and others—among those, there are twenty principal mantras for the primary deities, namely Īśa, Brahmā, and Viṣṇu. (28.4)
There are thirty-two other classes [of vimānas] belonging to all the gods;
furthermore, there are exactly twelve classes of vimānas for the twice-born.
For kings, there are sixteen types of weights; likewise, eight for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.
Indeed, when lacking the capacity [to carry larger loads], all these are prescribed as being known by the names "small" or "insignificant."
Therein, the names of the ninety-six principal celestial palaces (vimānas) are as follows:
Nalina, Pralīna, Svastika, and Caturmukha.
From that, there arises the Sarvatobhadra [mandala], which is as radiant as the back of an elephant.
The Śrīcchanda, Vṛttabhadra, Śrīkānta, Śrīpratiṣṭhita, Śivabhadra, Śivacchanda, Aṣṭāṅga, and the one shaped like a lotus (Padmaka). (28.8)
The Viṣṇucchanda and Saubhadra for the Kailāsa and Rudra [mandiras], and then the vimāna called Lalitabhadra—thus there are twenty. (28–9)
Meru, Mandara, Kailāsa, Jayāṅga, Vimalākṛti, the one called Kumbha, Vimalāṅga, Vṛṣacchanda, and Sudarśana. (28–10)
The Haṃsacchanda, the Padmakānta, and the Garuḍacchanda;
the Bhogicchanda, the Padmabhadra, and then the Kailāsakāntaka. (28.11)
Rudrakānta, Skandakānta, Yogabhadra, Maṅgala, Vindhyacchanda, Merukūṭa, Mahendra, and Citrakūṭaka. || 28-12 ||
Then there is Śrīmaṇḍana, Saumukhya, the blue one known as Niṣadha, followed by the one called Lalitakānta, Vijaya, and likewise Śrīkara. (28.13)
Śrīviśāla has been described, as well as Jayamaṅgala;
these, along with others, are the thirty-two celestial palaces of the denizens of heaven. (28.14)
There are thirty-two celestial palaces for the deities (*devika-vimāna*).
In the *nāgābhāgāhvaya* style, there are the *kuḍyāvarta*, the *trikūṭaka*, the *śrīvardhana*, the *padmagṛha*, and likewise the *prekṣāgṛhamukha*. (28–15)
These twelve palaces of the twice-born are exceedingly radiant like the sun and the moon, beautiful, and increase the merit of sacrifices; they are all circular in shape. (28.16)
There are twelve palatial abodes of the Brāhmaṇas:
Catuṣkuṭa, Mantrapūta, Āvantya, Māhiṣa, Tantrīkānta, Karṇabhadra, Vijayāṅga, and Viśālaka. (28.17)
Viśālabhadra, Gaṇikāviśāla, Karṇaśālaka, Padmāsana, Indrakānta, and thereafter Sarvalalita. || 28-18 ||
Then there are the types called *yoga*, *pratyantaka*, and *kānta*, followed by *utpalapatraka*, the meter named *mahārāja*, and after that, *mālāgṛha*.
Then there shall be the Pṛthivīvijaya, as well as the Nandiviśālaka;
furthermore, there is the Sarvāṅgasundara and the Chāyāgṛha.
Thus, the twenty-four [types] beginning with Rativardhana are recorded.
There are twenty-four palaces for the Kṣatriyas:
those named Viśālālaya and Catuṣpādika, and so forth. (28.21)
Likewise, there is the horse-faced [arrangement], as well as the harlot’s cluster;
then the hawk-pattern, the lotus-tip, and thereafter the cock’s tail.
(Beyond that, there is the celestial mansion known as Muṇḍaprāsādaka.
Thus, these eight are the residential mansions for Vaiśyas and Śūdras;
they are the eight celestial mansions for the Viṭ and the Śūdra.
Now, the ornamentation of the aforementioned celestial mansions is described. (28.23)
First, for the one named Nalinaka, there is a square, even, and auspicious foundation;
the inner sanctum (garbhāgāra) is one-third of that [foundation] and half of that [sanctum].
The *ardhārikā* should be a necklace; then, from nine parts, the interior (*garbha*) is formed. It should be elongated and circular, with a spire (*śikhara*) consisting of three *stūpis*.
The neck should have the appearance of a peak, measuring one-fourth of the width of the altar (vedī) and half of the portion of the architrave (arika);
from there, the projection of the central dome (bimba) should extend beyond the inner sanctum (garbhasadman).
The *sphuṭitaka* is placed in front, protruding by one-fourth [of its width];
from that, the broad nose (*pṛthunāsikā*) extends with a projection and width double [that of the preceding part]. (28–27)
In front and on both sides there are sixteen [channels] with small nostrils;
those situated at the back have one nostril and emerge from half the width of that [central channel].
When the half-arch has emerged halfway from its width, it should be twice as long;
one should fix it upon the nostrils, the side chambers, and the top of the central pillar.
From the midpoint of the house's core mass, the ascent should be internal;
the staircase should proceed clockwise, step by step, for each successive floor.
The *gṛhapiṇḍī* (the residential block) has eight *nāsikās* (projections) and is provided with great arches (*mahāhārakriyā*).

Regarding this, Parāśara states: "Below the *gṛhapiṇḍī*, one should construct the palace (*harmya*) by means of penthouses (*kūṭa*), storehouses (*koṣṭha*), lattices (*pañjara*), elephants (*gaja*), circular pavilions (*vṛtta*), split-pavilions (*sphuṭita*), small halls (*kṣudraśālā*), archways (*hārātoraṇa*), pillars (*stambha*), gate-arches (*toraṇa*), finials (*kumbha*), creepers (*latā*), and so forth. From the palace down to the base of the foundation, one should join these according to their appropriate proportions.
[Verse 28–31: "The pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) for the temple (*prāsāda*) should be equal [in size] to it, or three-quarters, or half."

One should decorate it with the same proportions as previously stated up to the measurement limit, having three, two, or one storey, and with ornaments equal to those of the temple and its constituent parts being likewise identical. (28–32)

One should decorate the temple with floors starting from the third floor according to one's desire, whether on the corner, in the middle, within the wall, or on the exterior, following the measuring line (mānasūtra). || 28-33 ||

One should construct [the temple] endowed with the parts described as the *nirgata*, the *ukta-māna*, the *kūṭa*, the *koṣṭhaka*, and the *pañjara*, as well as those mentioned for the back of an elephant (*gaja-pṛṣṭha*) and so forth.
Above the neck, it should be four-cornered, circular, or eight-cornered;
it rests upon the ears, has a central single nose, and is provided with a stūpikā.
The wise call the component part of a temple "kūṭa.
It is elongated, provided with a front panel, possessing distinct corners in the middle, and lacking a [central] nose.
The *śakti* and the banner are likewise three-faced; indeed, the side-chamber has many peaks. (28–36)
By the word *śikhā*, the *stūpikā* is meant;
at the entrance, there is the *śālāmukha* and the *stūpikā*, which is like the back of an elephant. (28–37)

Parāśara states here that what is called the *pañjara* (cage) is indeed the *pāśamukha* (noose-mouth) and the *hastituṇḍa* (elephant-trunk), consisting of a small compartment (*kṣudrakoṣṭha*) situated between two main compartments (*kūṭakoṣṭha*). Between the two main compartments, a *hārā* (pendant) should be made with one part or half a part.
