Even the *vṛttasphuṭitaka* (round-fluted) should be like the *pañjara*, having the form of a circle protruding by half its size;
for everything indeed has an equal neck, pinnacle, and dome (*stūpika*). (28–38)
This is, in brief, the sequence for the construction of palaces:
a corner cell, a central pinnacle, and within that, the penthouse (pañjara) and so forth.
That which contains an internal substrate is called conceptual construction;
for that manifestation is indeed mixed with those very [elements] in an entirely uniform manner. (28.40)

One should arrange the beauty of the palace façade like the moon reflected in water; indeed, there is a distinction among the celestial palaces (vimānas) based on the difference in their structural forms.
By the differentiation of the pinnacle (śikhara), one should indicate the differentiation of all [other parts];
everything else is traditionally held to be equal, according to what is appropriate and what is beautiful. (28.42)
One should arrange the path of the Maruts according to its beauty and as is appropriate;
for that [arrangement] would be fitting at every opening of the great mouth and on both wings. (28.43)
Floating in the sky like a bird from two and a half bays (koṣṭhas), this lotus-shaped celestial chariot (vimāna) is said to be the favorite of Śiva. (28-44)
The *nalinaka* [plan] has a square base for the central sanctuary (*adhiṣṭhāna*). When that span is divided into eight parts, the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) shall consist of three parts. (28–45)

On the peak of the womb, which is shaped like a Veda, there should be a long protrusion extending half the length of the womb; in front, there should be a large nose, and on the two sides, small nostrils.
And in another part, there are four [small] sections, and one large section with a single nose;
it is twice as long as the width of the portion occupied by the womb. || 28-47 ||
On the two sides and at the top, extending from the interior by one-quarter of the *rāma* measure, there should be a *khaṇḍaharmya*;
its length is twice that [width]. (28–48)
The inner staircase, however, rises halfway up the mass of the house;
the inner chamber is situated between the two halves of the entrance, level with the turret (nirvyūha).
In one case, there should be a *talpa*; in three cases, it becomes an *aptala*.
The *kuṇḍya* should also be made as beautiful as possible; the remainder should be joined together as previously described. (28–50)
On both sides of that base, on the elephant-trunk-shaped staircase,
there is the wing-binding, the umbrella-top, the house-pediment, and the great structure.
On that [platform], there should be eight small noses (alpanāsya), all of which are adorned with svastikas;
the supports for the cross-beams (pratibandha-adhiṣṭhāna) should be square pillars (stambha). || 28-52 ||
Having a form resembling a bird seizing its prey while floating, one should decorate it with artificial limbs and so forth, using the same method as before. (28.53)
With two half-cells on the sides and six nose-projections on the top, it stands like a bird swooping down to seize its prey. (28.54)

The temple of Śiva is endowed with one to ten stories and is characterized by its dissolution (pralīnaka). Its foundation is that of a svastika, extending for a portion equal to the width of Vyāsa’s foot. (28–55)

That [mandala] is square; from its width, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall be two parts out of eight and nine parts respectively, while the structural elements such as the wall-pediments (gṛhapiṇḍī) and so forth are as described previously.
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be long and have four corners; it should project out from half the measure of the inner sanctum (garbha), and the side-nose (pārśvanāsikā) should be half of that.
On the summit, one should join eight small noses, all of which, along with the [main] nose, are auspicious;
one should also arrange the chambers and the turret-houses so that they have the appearance of svastikas.
One should cause all the components, such as the pinnacle and the chamber, to be made as previously described.
It should be a svastika-shaped temple, perfectly circular from the base (adhiṣṭhāna) up to the spire (śikhara), and possessing four faces. (28–59)
Beginning with the *nālīgṛha* and *ardhārika*, according to the measurements prescribed for the *svastika*,
there are four great nostrils (*mahānāsya*) in the cardinal directions, extending out by one-quarter part from the center.
In the middle of those [pinnacles] is a crest; with half that measure, there are small noses (alpanāsikā).
It should be equal to the width of the tube-house (nālīgṛha) and have a projection of one-eighth of its own parts.
One should arrange the house-pavilion in the four directions and in the center;
one should construct four equal halls for the corners and the assembly, all being perfectly symmetrical.
One should arrange the *kūṭa*, *koṣṭha*, and so forth as before, according to what is aesthetically pleasing;
it should have four faces, joined with *bhadra* projections shaped like mouths on the four sides. (28–63)

The base of the Sarvatobhadra [temple] is four-faced and square; its inner sanctum (garbha) should be determined by dividing that [base] into eight parts according to the directions, using four, three, and two [parts] respectively.
The house, the *piṇḍī*, and so forth are as before; the *piṇḍī* has sixteen *sauṣṭhikas*.
On the eight-sided [structure], there should be a neck and a crest; therein are eight nostrils. (28.65)
In each of the four directions, the center should be endowed with the *bhadra* (projection);
this is for the purpose of the five-fold iconographic arrangement, according to the measurement of the interior width.
One should join the gable-pinnacles (karṇakūṭa) in those directions so that they have the appearance of three faces;
there should be four halls there, and the gables, chambers, and so forth are as described previously.
One should join the *kūṭas* (peaks) and other elements together with Bhadrā from its own half-diameter;
or else, one should install nine *liṅgas* in its eight directions or in the center.
For those whose gender is unmanifest or manifest, the *sarvatobhadra* (auspicious on all sides) is prescribed.
The *sarvatobhadra* is a four-cornered [structure] with a base shaped like the back of an elephant, and it is elongated. (28–69)
The house-piṇḍa and so forth are traditionally taught as being derived from a portion of Vyāsa’s feet, as before;
one should assemble all the components, such as the kūṭas and koṣṭhas, as previously described. (28–70)
The back should be rounded with its peak submerged; it should be symmetrical, even, and auspicious, having the appearance of a standing elephant and a face shaped like a *śālā* (hall). || 28-71 ||
On both sides and at the back, there should also be three nostrils each; they have a width of four parts of the inner sanctum and project out by half of that.
One should adorn it with banners at the gateway of Brahmā and with pigeons and other such ornaments;
this temple of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Īśa may consist of one or many stories.

The *hastipṛṣṭha* (elephant-back) is known as the base for a brilliantly radiant [temple]; it has four equal sides. Its inner sanctum (*garbha*) is one-third of that [base], and its pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) is half of that third part.
One should construct the *alinda* and the *hāra* according to that same measurement;
the *nāsikās*, which have a width equal to one-third of the *garbha*, should have a projection (*nīprā*) of half that measure. (28–75)
There should be four [large] nostrils, and half that number—namely two—smaller nostrils; the shape at the peak of the forehead is circular, and there are sixteen [minor] nostrils on the cheeks.
Below the house-mass, having separately adorned the base level with turrets and other ornaments, one should embellish it with great chambers in the four directions. (28.77)
One should construct the foremost maṇḍala of the artisans as the principal pavilion; indeed, it should face inward, and one should perform the remainder of the rites as previously described.
On this point, Parāśara says: "That temple of the Lord of All is brilliantly radiant, endowed with the excellence of perfect circularity and a beautiful neck;
adorned with auspicious śāla trees and decorated in all its parts, it bestows victory, prosperity, fame, and splendor, and is truly enchanting."
It is brilliantly radiant. The foundation of the Śrīcchanda [mandala] is also a square of equal sides;
it should have eight corners at the pinnacle (śikhara) and likewise eight nostrils (nāsikā) on the neck (gala). (28–79)
It should have eight corners with a well-formed tip and be provided with a parrot-beak;
the remainder should be made like a blazing flame—this is dear to Śiva.

The Śrīcchanda [mandala]: from the base up to the summit, it is circular with auspicious circles; in the center is a circular nāligṛha, and in its middle, in the four directions, [are the other elements]. (28.81)
The storehouses should be symmetrical and auspicious, as should the main building; one should decorate the space between those two with an equally wide exit.

On this point, Parāśara states: "In the space between those two, the entrance pavilion (mukhamandapa) should be adorned all around with elephant-backs, small chambers, and so forth, within the great layouts; it should be provided with auspicious features (bhadra), aligned with equal lines, and possess many proportions—it is indeed highly praised for all deities. This is the circular auspicious form (vṛttabhadra).
Furthermore, the foundation of Śrīkānta is remembered as being square (four-sided).
When the width is divided into eighteen parts, the inner sanctum (garbha-mandira) should be two or three parts [from the center].
The half-arches or half-necklaces may consist of half-parts according to the division;
the womb-chamber (garbha-bhavana) is four-cornered, and its pinnacle has a half-protrusion.
On the pinnacle (śikhara), there should be twenty-four faces with small noses; on the body-mass of the temple (gṛhapiṇḍī), there are sixteen faces, along with four corner-turrets (karṇakūṭa).
It should be square, octagonal, and circular; within that, one should arrange small compartments with protruding lattices in the center and in the four directions.
With small chambers, elephant-trunk-shaped niches, half-cages, and lattice-work; with archways, staircases, and also pedestals for bases.
One should appropriately adorn this temple of Śrīkānta, which is dedicated to all the deities.
The base and the pinnacle of the Śrīkānta [temple] should be circular when it is established on a square foundation.
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall be one part from three or four parts of the width; one should likewise fashion the wall-mass, the portico, and the hall, each with a single part.
The Garbha-vedīs and the Aṃśa-vedīs have an extent equal to their width; they possess auspicious nose-like projections (*nāsikā*).
In the *gṛhapiṇḍī*, there should be sixteen small nose-like projections (*kṣudranāsyas*), as before. (28–90)
The external structure is square, with its growth coiled within; it possesses chambers that extend outwards by half the width of the interior on all four sides. (28.91)
One who should join together the limbs of the measurement and the construction, which are beautiful and excellent, [this] temple of Viṣṇu is known by the name Śrīpratiṣṭhitaka Vimāna. || 28-92 ||

This is the Śrīpratiṣṭhita layout. For that Śivabhadra temple, the square base is divided into eighteen parts in width; two or three of those parts constitute the sanctum (garbha-mandira). || 28-93 ||

One should construct the sanctum (garbha) as square, rectangular, circular, or with a spire (śikhara), having four faces like a nose; its width and the projections of its faces should each be one-fourth of the sanctum's dimension.
The three elements, beginning with the *gṛhapiṇḍī*, should each occupy one-third of half the *garbha*;
these should be adorned on all sides with *khaṇḍaharmyas* and *kūṭas*.
The sixteenfold vital breath (*prāṇa*) within the body-mass (*piṇḍī*) is marked with the *tilaka* and *svastika*;
having adorned the palms with various bases (*adhiṣṭhāna*), feet, and so forth. (28–96)
One should join the corners of the ears at the tips of the Vedas (four), Vasus (eight), Vasus (eight), and Śruti (four) [units].
One should arrange the square cells in two, three, or [more] *daṇḍas*, making them perfectly symmetrical.
Then, there shall be a staircase for it known as "the hidden elephant" (antarlīna-hastisaṃjña),
and in front of it, there should be a pavilion (maṇḍapa) provided with the architectural members of a palace.

It may have a single or multiple level, joined with projections and counter-projections; one should likewise construct a *khaṇḍaharmya* (detached pavilion), which is remembered as the "Auspicious" (*śivabhadra*) type. || 28-99 ||
Śivabhadra.
For Śivacchanda, however, the foundation and so forth should be as before;
the cells in the center are indeed non-auspicious (abhadrāṇi), [but they are made auspicious] by means of the pañjarabhadras.
They should be joined with many levels; one should apply them according to the prescribed logic.
This is the *śivacchanda* of Śiva himself, endowed with all ornaments. (28.101)
The Śivacchanda:
The foundation of the eight-limbed [temple] shall be equal to the Śivabhadra;
the inner sanctum and so forth are likewise, though the specific distinction here is now being declared. (28.102)
There are sixteen [pilasters] with auspicious forms provided with pigeon-cotes;
likewise, there are two at the mouth and two above the neck, which constitute the *śīrṣaka*.

It should have the shape of an *āmalaka* fruit; there, eight nostrils (*nāsya*) are equal [in size], with a width of four parts of the interior and an outward projection equal to half of that. (28.104)
Likewise, there are eight small mouths; in the center, there should be a square.
As before, one should take the house, the *piṇḍī*, and so forth, extending upwards from the two wings in front. (28–105)
One should construct the central door, adorned with elephant trunks at the corners of the staircases and featuring the eight auspicious symbols (aṣṭamaṅgala), along with an archway (toraṇa).

One should also employ a staircase for the elderly that is hidden within this [structure], along with various *masūraka* moldings, pillars, altars (*vedikā*), and so forth, by means of aerial passages (*marutpatha*). (28.107)
One should join the eight-cornered *sauṣṭhika* at the ear; here, one should apply the various types of *talas*, from those with few to many components, endowed with three or four *talas*.
Indeed, this eight-limbed temple of the deity is adorned on all its parts.
Regarding the eight limbs: the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is square, with a length of thirty-two and four parts (36 units). || 28-109 ||
In the Vasunandāṃśaka, the nālīgṛha is said to consist of two or three parts; it should also be elongated and circular, or, as before, half as long as that [the previous type]. (28–110)
The house-piṇḍyas in the four directions have bases that are auspiciously shaped like a nose;
however, the pinnacle (śikhara) upon them is broad and elongated, measuring half a part of the inner sanctum (garbha).
The Sabhadrakas and Mahānāsas are as previously described; the Kūṭādikas and others are likewise remembered.
In Gṛhapinyā there are sixteen Kapotas, who have noses like sesame seeds.
One should decorate it with ear-pinnacles (*karṇakūṭa*) and so forth, as before, in the form of a lotus; this is the lotus-shaped [temple].
And for the *viṣṇucchanda* type, the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is elongated as before.
The six-cornered sanctum has its interior chambers measuring three, four, and three parts;
the base is in the lotus arrangement, and the upper part consists of four corners with excellent proportions.
The house-pedestal and so forth are as previously described, and the pinnacle is hexagonal;
there are exactly six nose-projections on it, and the neck is also hexagonal. (28.115)
The *khaṇḍaharmya* and the *sauṣṭhika* should project out by half the width of their own [respective] bases;
they should be concealed by Brahma-doors and banners, and endowed with secret architectural features.
Furthermore, even in the Kapota [style], there should be no *nāsikas*, and it should be auspiciously balanced on all sides;
it is endowed with a pleasure-ground and adorned with the construction of wooden structures.
In the four corners and in the center, according to the ritual for the five forms, there are auspicious [structures] in the four corners with circular and elongated tops. (28.118)
Indeed, this Vaiṣṇava Viṣṇucchanda temple is adorned on all its parts;
and at every level of the kūṭas, the pinnacle is circular and elongated.
Rich with the work of bricks and wood, adorned in all its parts, it is the Viṣṇucchanda style.
The foundation of the Saubhadra temple is also a perfect square. (28–120)
The width of the inner sanctum (garbha) shall be one part out of thirty-four;
from that [total], the house-walls (gṛhapiṇḍī) and so forth shall be formed in sequence by two parts, three parts, and one part respectively.
The pinnacle (śikhara) is square and has the form of a hall facing the four directions; the bhadra-projections and nose-ornaments extend from one-fourth of the inner sanctum's width.
It has four small [projections] and eight large ones; all of them are auspicious and excellent.
Everything, including the peaks and the inner chambers, is characterized by the *bhadraka* style with one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters [of its dimensions].
The pillars should have eight, sixteen, or thirty-two facets and be circular, following the sequence from the base;
they are adorned with the aforementioned ornaments, including water-trays and balconies.
The Saubhadra [temple type]: the square *masūraka* of the Kailāsa-chandaka is also [used here].
The inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*) is on all sides equal to three parts of one-eighth of the total width. (28-125)

With the remaining [parts], there should be the house-piṇḍī and so forth; the womb-chamber (garbhamandira) should be four-cornered, while above the neck it should be eight-cornered, distinct, and possessing eight small nostrils.

On the pedestal of the *gṛhapiṇḍī*, it should be double [the previous measurement]; then, at the tip of the ear, there should be a *sauṣṭhika* ornament, appearing as four-sided, eight-sided, or circular, joined with a nose-piece on each pedestal.
The central ornament should project out by half the width [of the base] as its portion;
having adorned that interior with a lotus-stalk known as the "glorious bond" (śrībandha), [it is completed]. 28-128.
It also featured large enclosures, small halls, elephant-faced [ornaments], various lion-thrones, pillars, altars, lattices, and archways. || 28-129 ||

As previously stated, having adorned the *khaṇḍaharmya* with its constituent parts according to what is appropriate, one should apply them in increasing order from one to the number of stories, assigning them to each progressively lower level. (28.130)
Furthermore, with banners at the gates of the Brahma-chamber, as well as with gables, storehouses, and so forth,
it should be constructed in front with intermediate spaces, resembling the components of a palace.
The excellent pavilion has many stories with internal staircases,
and is constructed by joining all its parts in sequence, such as the various types of meters and their variations.
With its peaked chambers rising and falling, featuring central *bhadra* projections and various types of spires,
it resembled Mount Kailāsa.
The Kailāsa meter is prescribed as being auspicious for Śiva alone.
Regarding the Kailāsa meter:
the base (adhiṣṭhāna) is a square, as in the case of the Rudra meter previously described. (28–134)

The *nālīgṛha* (tube-house) and other such features are to be arranged as before on the corner, the middle, and the interval; likewise, the *kūṭa* (pinnacle), *koṣṭha* (cell), and so forth are to be joined with a projection equal to one-fourth of the width.
The Brahmadvāra, however, should extend by one part and rest upon the piṇḍikā;
it should have a high pinnacle as its ornament and be adorned with various limbs and chariots. || 28-136 ||
The ground levels, beginning from the base, should respectively be square, octagonal, sixteen-sided, and circular, preceded by the foundations, pillars, arches, seed-vines, and gateways. (28.137)
The neck and the rounded summit should be at the front and the sides, while the three nostrils—
each with a width equal to one-third of the interior— should be located at the rear.
With half of that measure, there should be two on the nose and three on each side;
provided with *tilaka* marks, one should apply the remainder according to the *rudracchanda* pattern.
The Rudracchanda [plan] is described as having a square base in the Lalitāmadraka style;
in its width, divided into eight and nine parts, the inner sanctum (garbha-mandira) occupies two and three parts respectively.
The *gṛhapiṇḍī* and other elements are formed by the remaining portions;
the corners are square, and for the eight-cornered [structure], there is a pinnacle with small and large eight-fold nostrils.
In the four directions, there are chambers with exits and entrances equal to their own width; in the center of these, halls extend for one-third [of that width], possessing three openings. (28.142)
The central *bhadra* should be as wide as one-third of the width of the *karṇa-prāsāda*,
and its projection should be half of that [one-third] within that interval.
One should also employ small chambers such as the lion-cage;
that [structure] should have a pinnacle with ears and be shaped like an octagon. (28.144)
In this manner, one should apply the Svastikābha and Tilakanāsa ornaments;
the construction of the temple body (gṛhapiṇḍī) and so forth is as before, and one may also decorate it with kūṭas and other features.
The *Lalitabhadra* consists of an inner *hastisopāna* (elephant-staircase) alone;
thus, the *Nalina* and other [mandalas], endowed with their ornaments, have been described in brief.
These celestial chariots are worthy of Śambhu, and those of Viṣṇu, who is born from the lotus, are likewise preeminent.

Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, concerning the characteristics of the primary vimānas and other structures, in the Kriyāpāda of the *Siddhāntasāra*, which is part of the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 28.
Now begins the twenty-ninth chapter.
Next, the characteristics of the celestial palaces known as the Jāti and Itarā, beginning with Meru, are declared; these grant the accomplishment of their respective realizations.
The circular foundation of the Vedāśrama of the one known as Meru is at the throat,
and that peak is endowed with four nostrils.
The mouth-nose (mukhanāsī) is one large [unit], with its exit equal to half the interior;
however, when the width is divided into thirteen parts, the interior chamber (garbhamandira) consists of five parts. || 29-3 ||
The house, the *piṇḍya*, the *alinda*, and the *hāra* are each one part respectively;
the *kūṭa* is one part, the *koṣṭha* is three parts, and then [the remainder] is one part.
The remaining portion, the *nīḍa*, consists of the *hārāṃśa* part, with its central axis aligned with the pinnacle (*kūṭa*) and other elements;
it resembles the *svastikābandha* and has three, four, or five storeys (*bhūmikā*). (29–5)
One should diligently adorn Mount Meru with various bases, pillars, altars, lattices, and archways, as well as circular, cracked, and hollowed-out nests and other such features.
The Meru palace; that same [palace] at the neck and on the summit is square, namely Mandara. Mandara.
That very [body] had the peak of Mount Aśvagala as its ears and Vasu as its nose. || 29-7 ||
And that which has eight pentagonal pinnacles is desired by name as Kailāsa; indeed, that very same [structure] is the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) with a base shaped like a lotus petal. 29-8.
The vimāna known as Kumbha is celebrated for its beautiful nose (nāsikā);
it is the Kumbhavimāna. That which has a square inner sanctum (garbhageha) is called Jayāṅga, and it is the Sabhadraka. (29–9)
The Jayāṅga:
that same [structure] becomes the Viśālāṅga when it is circular at the summit and the neck.
This is the Viśālāṅga.
Having omitted that same portion from the middle, it should be joined with a cell by means of two parts.
It has eight-cornered peaks and necks, as well as eight throats and nostrils;
it possesses eight cage-like pinnacles and is endowed with sixty-two tilakas.
Whether with a railing or without a railing, consisting of three, four, or five stories, this wondrous celestial palace is indeed known for its stainless form. (29.12)
[It has] a stainless form. (p.
280) That entire enclosure extends out by half its own width.
On each floor, there are two great mouths on the sides, like half-cells. (29–13)
This most beautiful chariot, the Haṃsacchanda, has been described. This very [chariot] has its neck in the shape of a Veda (four-cornered) and its top in the shape of a Veda (four-cornered). 29-14.
The remainder is entirely as previously stated; this is known as the *vṛṣacchanda* meter. That same [meter] is the *garuḍacchanda*; now the *vimāna* meter is described.
The front face should have beautiful corners, while the two wings are like half-cells;
the sides have two nostrils each, and the neck is circular and clearly defined.
The remainder is shaped like Mount Meru and follows the *garuḍacchanda* style;
that very same [style] has an eight-sided neck and furthermore an eight-sided pinnacle. (29-17)
The head [of the structure] resembles a lotus, and its limbs are like lotuses; it is the abode of Brahmā.
Its limbs are like lotuses; that very same [structure], extending from Vyāsa, forms the central cell in the four directions.
That which has a head like a lotus bud is known as Padmabhadra; such is Padmabhadra. That same [shape], when rounded at the neck and peak and possessing a broad nose, [is so called]. (29-19)
On each face, at the two sides, there are three equal nostrils;
every part of the *sabhadrāṅga* base is adorned with *tilaka* marks throughout.
It may have six doors or even no door, and it is as beautiful as Kailāsa through yoga; (p.
281) its width is eleven cubits, and it consists of seven, eight, or nine parts.
The house for the *nālī* (water-clock) should be on all sides three, four, or five parts;
the remainder should be adorned with pearl-string borders, pinnacles, cells, and so forth.
The Sabhadra temple has a circular pinnacle, four protruding noses, two stories, four peaks, and four halls, and is adorned with *tilaka* ornaments on all sides. (29.23)
A celestial mansion with well-rounded ear-tops and a beautiful pinnacle is called Rudrakāntaka; that same structure, when its component parts are auspicious squares, is termed Yogabhadra. (29–24)

Yogabhadra: That same [structure], when its four-cornered head is adorned with a pinnacle (sauṣṭhika) at the top, and its summit has eight small noses, shall be known by the name Bhogicchanda. (29–25)
The desire for enjoyments [is located there]. That very same [place], being a hexagon at the peak of the throat, is the Sudarśana;
they declare that to be the abode of Sudarśana or of Viṣṇu. (29–26)
The Sudarśana:
that very [mandala] is the Skandakānta when adorned with sixty-four [deities];
endowed with its limbs as prescribed, it is a celestial palace (vimāna) dear to the Six-faced One (Kārttikeya). (29.27)
The Skandakānta: that same [plan] entirely octagonal, with ears, pinnacles, and a neck; possessing Bhadrāṅgas and four nostrils, it is the Vindhya-chanda style, two stories high. (29–28)
The Vindhya-chanda [plan] has a width of nine and seven karas, is provided with a seventh and sixth part [of the length],
is endowed with four kūṭas and four halls, and has a circular head and neck. (29–29)
It possesses four small and large gate-towers (toraṇa) with eight enclosures,
and it is endowed with central auspicious tilakas and masūra-shaped pillars.
The celestial palace named Merukūṭa, together with its pedestal and foundation, beautiful with various architectural members, is adorned with primary peaks and other structural parts. (29–31)
Merukūṭa.
There, excluding the central *bhadra*, the *koṣṭhaka* should be made with a *kakara*;
the remainder is to be adorned as before. This is Citrakūṭa, beloved by Hari. (29–32)
Citrakūṭa:

that very same [structure], when joined with eight *sauṣṭhikas* and possessing eight additional *nāsikās*, becomes the Śrīmaṇḍana vimāna; it is auspicious, brings prosperity, and is suitable for all deities. (29–33)
The Glorious Ornament (*Śrīmaṇḍana*). That very thing is indeed the *saumukhya*, which has eight peaks and eight halls.
The *saumukhya*.
That very [stūpa], with its square-shaped summit, is the Jayamaṅgala. || 29-34 ||
Victory and Auspiciousness! That very [mountain] with eight-sided peaks is known as Nīlaparvata;
it is Nīlaparvata.
That very same [structure], when devoid of the gabled halls (kūṭaśālā), is the "eight-celled" (aṣṭapañjara) temple. || 29-35 ||
The Niṣadha temple is known to have its roof shaped according to one's desire;
it is the Niṣadha. Its base is four times as long [as it is wide], and it is endowed with a pinnacle in the form of a hall. (29–36)
Adorned with gables, balconies, turrets, and all other architectural members, and enriched with various supporting pillars and bases, it was a celestial palace named Maṅgala.
Auspiciousness to Śrī Śrīdhara, Dharā, Durgā, Gaurī, and the host of Mothers. (p.
283) The square base is provided with auspicious features and has a circular top. || 29-38 ||
The one-story pavilion with four faces, known as Vijaya, is dear to Hari.
That same [pavilion], when provided with a *sauṣṭhika* [pedestal] and having an octagonal neck and capital, is called Vijaya. (29–39)
The *lalitakānta* is appropriate for all its limbs and is sacred to all deities;
it is the *lalitakānta*.
That same [meter], when having a rounded peak (*vṛttaśikhara*), is the *śrīkara*, beloved by Śrīdhara. (29–40)

The Śrīkara [temple] is that same [structure] with a square front pinnacle and eight penthouses; however, when it is devoid of corner pinnacles (karṇakūṭa), it is called the Śrīviśāla, which is dear to Śiva. (29–41)
The Śrīviśāla [is the thirty-second]. Thus, thirty-two types have been described in general and in detail:
the celestial palaces (*vimāna*) of all the inhabitants of heaven, belonging both to those of noble birth and others. (29–42)
Regarding this, Parāśara says:
"By means of these very ornaments, [the status of] the *kaniṣṭhā* may also apply even to those who are of little merit;
they are called by those same names according to the specific variety of their adornment."
Thus it is said. And those minor, small celestial palaces (vimāna) are described hereafter.
This concludes the section on the ornaments of the various celestial palaces.
Now, the ornamentation of the *jāti* celestial palaces is being declared.
Now, the abode of the Soma-chanda is the Vedāśrama. || 29-43 ||

The inner sanctum (garbhageha) shall be one-sixth [of the total width], the pedestal of the shrine (gṛhapiṇḍikā) half of that [inner sanctum], and the water-course (ambutala) together with the pedestal;
the remainder is for the surrounding area.
The *khaṇḍaharmya* and the *cūḍaharmya* should likewise be on all sides; the staircases are elevated within, and the constituent parts are as before. (29–45)
One should employ the form of a hall with a pinnacle there;
thus, for fifty-two years, it should be provided with pavilions in front.
This *somacchanda*, suitable for the twice-born, consists of one or many squares;
it is the *somacchanda*.
The *nāgacchanda* is rectangular and shaped like a sun-window (*asūraka*). (29–47)
There, one should fashion the womb-extension (garbhavyāsa) by a third part of that [measurement], and from that as well,
one should arrange the surrounding structural mass (gṛhapiṇḍi) by a third part.
The pavilion (maṇḍapa) should be similar [in design] up to the end of the broken-edged cornice (khaṇḍaharmya);
the staircase should extend from half the height of the broken-edged cornice, and the spire (śikhara) may be circular or oblong.
The shape of the assembly hall before him has a broad nose from half the height of the womb; from half of that, the nostrils extend all around, all equal and resembling serpents.
The clear measurement of the base should be at the front of the nose, as well as at the ground-level foundation and above;
there should be pillars with eight or four corners, and one should perform the remainder as previously described.
One should apply the absence of desire, as well as the empowerment and so forth, as previously described for the wall-circuit;
having carefully adorned it with the Brahma-door and the banners, one should complete the remainder. (29–52)
Therein, the inner recess, the feature known as the elephant, the staircase, and likewise the pinnacle, should be shaped like a hall; the nose should be made with twenty-four parts.
With large nostrils at every opening and tilaka-like nostrils on the sides—
this is declared to be the *kuḍyāvarta* style, suitable for the twice-born.
The *kuḍyāvarta* [plan]:
the foundation and the inner sanctum (*garbhāgāra*) of the two-storeyed structure are as described before;
the remainder consists of the water and land areas, adorned with multi-storied pavilions, turrets, and so forth. (29–55)
In front of the vimāna, however, there should be a pavilion (maṇḍapa) according to the measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha);
on the two sides, there should be structures in the form of assembly halls (sabhā), and in the middle, sacrificial altars (vedaśālā).
It should not have a *nāsī* provided with a pinnacle; rather, there should be sixteen *nāsīs* on the *piṇḍī*.
The hall and the assembly chamber should have a pinnacle, and there should be four *nāsikās* there.
The foot-binding is the foundation; all the pillars are conceptual constructions. It is joined with obstacles and counter-obstacles, and provided with an elephant-staircase.
Having adorned the vimāna with lattice-work and other ornaments, it shall be of the *dvikūṭaka* type.
For the *śrīvardhana* as well, the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and other features are the same as previously described. (29–59)
The pinnacle (śikhara) should have the form of a hall (sabhākāra) and be elongated; in front of it there should be one nose (nāsikā), and there should be two on each of the two sides.
One should decorate it with railings, lattices, and so forth, as appropriate; this is the Śrīvardhana. A circular and elongated base is prescribed for the Padmagṛha. (29–61)
In that Vyāsa [plan], with the Vasu (8) and Nanda (9) parts, the inner sanctum (garbhamandira) is formed by two and three parts respectively;
the remainder should be applied as before, and there shall indeed be sixteen nose-projections (nāsikā).
The pinnacle is circular and elongated, and there are four nostrils therein;
there are eight small nostrils here, four of which are adorned with *tilaka* marks.
The Lotus House:
Even for the face of the Hall of Spectacles, there should be a long foundation;
the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be half the width of the square [main hall]. || 29-64 ||
By the measurement of the central sanctum (garbha), there are four pavilions on its sides;
the spire (śikhara) is shaped like a square cell (koṣṭhaka), and there are exactly six nostrils (nāsya) therein.
In the Kapota [section], those [lines] are twelve in number; one should apply the remainder as previously described.
Furthermore, the altar should be adorned with lattices and pathways for the wind.
The assembly hall (prekṣāgṛha). (p.
286) The foundation of Kratuvardhana’s [temple] is also a square with a length equal to its own half-diagonal;
however, the inner sanctum (garbhamandira) is one-third of that [foundation’s] width. (29.67)
From all sides, half of the portion of the inner chamber's area shall be the *ardhārikā*;
the remainder shall be the seven-storied palace (*saptalacūḍīka-harmya*) provided with a paved floor (*kuṭṭima*).
At each opening of the vimāna, there is a pavilion equal in size to the inner sanctum;
its exterior ground is like that of a temple, provided with a pinnacle and a watch-tower.
There are four *karṇakūṭas*, a pinnacle (*śikhara*), and a large chamber (*koṣṭhaka*);
there are four half-assemblies (*ardhasabhās*) therein, and indeed *garbhakūṭas* at the entrance.
In front and at the back, there should be a hall with intoxicated elephants and a pavilion;
four subsidiary halls should be constructed, and the remaining parts are to be made as before. (29–71)
Outside, there should be a lattice-work with exposed pillars on all sides;
indeed, it should have internal recesses provided with stairs, which increases the merit of the sacrifice.
It is an increaser of ritual merit (*kratuvardhana*).
The circular base of the circular temple should have a rectangular foundation; its spire (*śikhara*) should be of that same form, and it should possess four broad noses (*pṛthunāsikā*). (29–73)
The small [type] has exactly these same proportions for its base-pedestal (gṛhapiṇḍī) and so forth, as described previously.
On its back is the measurement of the womb (garbha), while the two pedestals (piṇḍikā) are half of that, being auspicious (bhadra).
Twenty-four nose-projections should be applied to the mouth;
it should be a circular house (*maṇḍigṛha*).
Its foundation is long and square, belonging to that which is as radiant as the sun. (29–75)

The inner sanctum (garbhageha) shall be formed from half the diameter; the remainder shall be used for the temple-pedestal (gṛhapiṇḍikā), the water-platform (aptala), the pavilion (khaṇḍaharmya), and the twelve-sided spire (śikhara).
In this Gṛhapiṇḍī there are twelve nāsikas, and likewise sixteen sabhās; in the middle of that are four great koṣṭhas.
The staircase of the elder would be hidden within the sun-gem (*bhānukāntaka*). The sun-gem is indeed a square base of extreme brilliance. (29.78)
The sanctum (garbhagṛha) is one-third [of the total width], and the spire (śikhara) is half [the height]; it has the form of an assembly hall (sabhākṛti).
Furthermore, there are half-architraves (ardhāryaptalahāra) and [ornaments] made from two parts on the corners (karṇaka).
The assembly hall for the Vedas is equal to the womb, with great inner chambers;
and around the pigeon-house, there are also sixteen tilaka-nāsikās.

One should adorn the remainder as is appropriate; this is exceedingly beautiful. It is exceedingly beautiful. The *masūra* [shape] is elongated like a moon-gem (*candrakānta*), yet circular in form. (29.81)
The inner sanctum (garbhageha) shall be [measured] from half the diameter; the remainder shall constitute the pedestal (piṇḍī) and other elements.
The spire (śikhara) shall be oblong, and there shall be eight broad noses (pṛthunāsikā) therein.
And with a small nose, one should decorate the remainder as before;
this is the *candrakānta* [type].
This concludes the section on the *brāhmaṇa* vimānas.
The consecration of the fourfold manifestation should be long and extended, as before. || 29-83 ||
From the feet of Vyāsa, one should fashion the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*), half the inner sanctum (*garbhārdha*), and the pedestal of the house (*gṛhapiṇḍikā*);
with what remains, one should arrange the *āptalaka*, the *cūḍā*, the *khaṇḍa*, and the *harmya*. (29.84)

The pinnacle is shaped like a small chamber; from the middle of the womb [of the temple], there is a central nose (central spire), and on each side are two large noses. The kūṭas, chambers, and so forth are as described previously.
On the pillars, however, there should be pedestals, lattice-work, and so forth;
in front [of the main hall] is a pavilion equal [in size], but outside of that is one with interior pillars.
One should decorate the wall, which is shaped like a plough, according to its beauty; it may consist of three stories or more, not just one, and is clearly defined by four [sides]. (29.87)
The fourfold clarity: (p.
288) For one purified by mantra, the *masūraka* should measure the length of the Vedas and stages of life (*āśrama*).
The part called the *garbha* is half the width; from the remainder, the *piṇḍī* is formed on the water and dry land. (29.88)
It should have a series of necklaces (hārāvalī), and its pinnacle should be shaped like an assembly hall;
it is adorned with internal pillars and external walls, beautified by various lattice windows.
One should decorate the cardinal and intermediate directions with false balconies (kūṭa) and storehouses (koṣṭha), and so forth;
on the pinnacle (śikhara) there should be sixteen mouths, while on the cornice (kapota) there are hanging spouts (lambanāsikā).
There should be twenty-four doors in the four directions;
in front [of the shrine] is a pavilion equal in size to the inner sanctum (garbha), and there is a wall on the exterior.

One should construct an *alinda* (veranda) and a *khaṇḍaharmya* (pavilion), as well as assembly halls reaching to the *karṇa* (corner) and the *garbha* (central core); one should adorn the space between them with large chambers, gables, and other such features. (29.92)
It is purified by mantras.
Even for the Āvantya [temple], the foundation is a square with a length equal to its own half-diagonal;
the inner sanctum consists of one-eighth and one-sixteenth [of the total], while the three parts beginning with the *piṇḍī* consist of [the remaining] units.
And for the Piṇḍī [temple], there is a wall in the form of a ploughshare at the four corners; and within that, its śikhara is enriched with pillars at the eastern corners. || 29-94 ||
It has the form of an assembly hall with four nostrils, endowed with a Bhadra-assembly at the front;
on the two sides there should be small nostrils, while those in between are broad-nosed. (29.95)
One should employ a staircase hidden within a circle of creepers;
it is manifold, joined with walls and pillars for secret and non-secret rites.
One should decorate the multi-storied structure with pedestals, lattice-work, and so forth;
this is the Āvantya style.
The base of the Mahiṣa style, however, should be elongated and angular. (29-97)
The sanctum (garbhagṛha) is one-third [of the total], and from the remainder, the three parts beginning with the *piṇḍikā* [are formed];
and in front of that, as well as behind it, in the middle of the courtyard (*maṇḍapa*), [the other structures are placed].
And on all sides around the Khaṇḍaharmya, there should be excellent gables and lattices, situated between the base pavilion and the neck with elephant-stairways. (29.99)
Others [describe it] as having the form of a bamboo-thicket like a svastika in front;
however, on the summit there is a nine-nosed face of a buffalo, like a hall.
Having adorned the remainder with altars, lattices, and so forth as previously described, [the altar] for Mahiṣa should be square and elongated; likewise for Tantrīkānta and Masūra. || 29-101 ||

Half of that [measurement] shall be the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha); the remainder shall be the body of the temple (gṛhapiṇḍikā), as well as the water-course (aptala), the turret (khaṇḍaharmya), the spire (śikhara), and indeed the chamber (koṣṭha).
The front face should be at the front, and the mahānāsa at the back;
there should be sixteen nāsīs there, and eight tilakanāsikās.
At the great gate, there are ten lion-cages in sequence;
below the pigeons, there is the emergence of the sabha known as the Vedakarṇa and the Lāṅgala.
The center should consist of four great thrones provided with facing platforms; it should extend outward from the spacious main house according to one's preference.
They declare that which is adorned with peaks and other features by its own limbs to be *tantrīkānta*.
Regarding that *tantrīkānta*, its foundation is a long hermitage, and it belongs to Vijayāṅga. (29–106)
One-third of the total width is called the *garbha* (inner sanctum); the remainder constitutes the *piṇḍī*, the *aptala*, and so forth.
The *śikhara* (spire) should have eight faces and consist of *kakara* and *koṣṭhaka* compartments.
In the Kapota style, there should be twenty-four *tilanāsya* elements;
the staircase should be recessed within, and there should be a pavilion on each successive level of the ground.
The measurement of the inner sanctum (garbha) should be followed by a series of outer pavilions (khaṇḍaharmya);
having adorned the remainder with limbs according to the proper method, it is known as the Vijayāṅga.
The limb of Vijayā: (p.

290) The foundation of Viśālabhadra is as before; when the width is divided into ten parts, two parts are the extent of the womb-chamber (*garbha*), and with the remainder, one constructs the pedestal of the house (*gṛhapiṇḍikā*).
One should fashion the Brahmadvāra, the Cūḍaharmya, and the Khaṇḍaharmya;
in front [of these], there should be a pavilion (maṇḍapa) that is quadrangular and as long as the inner sanctum (garbha).

On both sides, there is a wall and a water-platform; the *khaṇḍaharmyaka* (fragmented palace), the *cūḍīka*, the *karṇa-prāsāda* (corner temple), the *śṛṅga* (pinnacle), and the *kakara-koṣṭhaka* (niche for the *kakara*).

The *kapotaśālā* (dove-cot) is the *piṇḍī*; furthermore, that which issues from the *piṇḍī* and has the form of a projected canopy (*samarpitasabhārūpa*) constitutes the middle ornament (*madhyama-maṇḍana*). || 29-113 ||
The womb (garbha) is one and a half times its own width, and its length is twice that;
for a structure extending outward with elements such as the *hārā* and *pañjara*, it takes the form of an assembly hall (*sabhā*).
In front of the temple pavilion, at the back, and on its sides, it should be provided with foliage;
the spire (śikhara) should have eight projections (nāsa), and there should then be sixteen tilakas.
Above the pavilion (maṇḍapa), there should be a colored platform (raṅga) consisting of one or more stories; this is the Viśālabhadra type.
Its base (ādhiṣṭhāna), however, is four-cornered and its length exceeds its width by four parts.
In the extensive [layout] beginning with the *gaṇikā* type, the remainder is obtained for the *ardhārika*;
and the *khaṇḍaharmya* occurs in the middle of the *karṇaprāsāda*.

As before, pillars should be placed in the middle of the arches and the side-walls of the maṇḍana, as well as within the interior; and in front of the house-pediment (gṛhapiṇḍī), there should be a pavilion (maṇḍapa).
The central stage should be equal in length to the interior of the hall;
the remainder outside is the terrace of the palace, featuring a paved floor adorned with latticed windows.
The *piṇḍī* shall be a *kapotajāla*; within it there are sixteen *nāsikās*.
The *śikhara* shall be a *koṣṭhaka*, and in the city [of the temple] there is the *kakarabhadra*.
p. 291) Therein, on the side, are eight types of *nāsikas*: the *sabhadra* or the *vibhadraka*;
these, with one or more desired storeys (*talaka*), constitute the residence for royal women. || 29-121 ||

The Gaṇikāviśāla [temple] should have a pinnacle shaped like an assembly hall (*sabhākāra*), complete with four-faced spires (*nāsikā*). Furthermore, for Karṇabhadra, there should be the same foundation and other features as previously described. (29.122)
The inner chambers should have their noses [projections] concealed within the space between the wall-piles and the floor;
the stairs should be concealed within the pillars, and there should be a single nose [projection] for the pigeon-hole.
The *karṇaprāsādakas* are situated upon the *cūḍaharmya*, extending as far as the interior;
they are adorned with pigeon-cotes, lion-cages, and projecting balconies.
With concealed and unconcealed structural supports, walls, doors, and archways,
it is provided with *bhadra* projections at the four corners and endowed with *bhadra-sabhās* (auspicious halls) in the cardinal directions.
The *karṇabhadra* is adorned with the *svasti*, *bhadra*, *jāla*, and other [ornaments]. Regarding the *karṇaśāla*, its base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth are prescribed as before. (29–126)

One should duly arrange the four-cornered *bhadraśālā* pavilions, the intermediate gate-towers, and the assembly halls, as well as the application of different structural loads according to the rules.

A *gṛhapiṇḍī* is that which is closely joined with and internally recessed; an *alindaka* is a porch. A *piṇḍī* is a pigeon-house (*kapotaśālā*), while a *kaṇa* is a wall with a plow-shaped [projection]. (29.128)
One should place a pillar in the middle, with its nose resting against that wall;
one should employ the form of an assembly hall, with its peak rising above the neck.

The body of the gateway should have the face of a *kakarī* (a type of bird) and be shaped like a pair of yokes; it may be three stories or seven stories high, according to one's preference, and provided with small windows (*nāsikā*) for light and ventilation.
It is endowed with desired components such as altars, lattices, and so forth;
it is the Kaṇaśāla, the long quadrangular base of the lotus seat. (29.131)

The inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) is one-fifth [of the total width], and the base-mouldings (*gṛhapiṇḍikā*) are half the size of the sanctum; with the remainder, the *āptala*, *cūḍīka*, and *khaṇḍaharmya* sections are made like the sanctum itself.
In the intermediate directions, joined together and extending as far as the ears [of the mandala],
there are four palaces, each equipped with its own separate pavilion.
Like a stage with various pillars, there should be a wall outside of that;
it should be provided with lattices, altars, and doors, and there should be porticoes on the exterior.
In the four corners, one should indeed construct separate gables enriched with equal projections; and in their center, one should join together square cells.
It has four ears and a plough-shaped wall in the middle of the courtyard, with square pillars inside and an internal portico recessed within. (29.136)
On the summit of the assembly hall, there should be small Mahānāsa pavilions for the Vedas;
outside the corner-eaves, there should be twelve entrance-halls on all sides.

This Padmavasantaka [pavilion] is endowed with its constituent parts as appropriate; the floor of the Indrakānta [central hall], which is three-quarters as long as the width, is shaped like a lotus. 29-138.
From that, one part of Rāma constitutes the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha), while the remaining parts form the structural mass of the temple and so forth;
the Vedas (four) form the auspicious assembly hall (sabhā) in the cardinal directions, and the four ears (karna) form the spires (nāsikā).
They have spouts at the mouths of the pigeon-houses, and there are sixteen on the house-pediment; the pinnacle is shaped like an assembly hall.
Between the *karṇahala* and the *bhitti*, there should be a pillar-projection (*stambhaniryūha*).
The face-ornament (*mukhaśobhā*) and the small nose (*alpanāsya*) should be eight [units]; the remainder should be decorated as previously described. (29.141)
The Indrakānta [plan] is long-sided; it is also the foundation for the Yogakānta, situated above. The inner sanctum (garbhamandira) is circular and elongated, measuring one-eighth of the total width.
With half [the measurement], there shall be a *hārā* consisting of half-portions, which is a series of broken palaces;
the spire (*śikhara*) is long and circular, with two nostrils (*nāsikā*) at the front. (29.143)
Half of that size behind it, there should be one [pedestal] with small nostrils on all sides;
these, numbering seventy-four, constitute the staircase for ascending the back.
This [type of seat], which is inwardly recessed, is pleasing for yoga and suitable for kings.
Indeed, even for one who is entirely graceful, the *masūraka* is long-sided. (29.145)
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be one-third of the total width, and the pedestal (gṛhapiṇḍikā) half of that;
one should then construct pigeon-eaves (kapotaśālā) at the corners and auspicious halls (bhadrasabhā).
And in that interval, there should be halls, concealed as desired;
these two should be in the pavilion with a portico, both in front of and behind it. (29.147)
The pinnacle should have the form of a hall, be auspicious, and possess a prominent nose;
one should adorn it with many or even few of the remaining members.

The Sarvalalita [temple] has its foundation at the edge of the beautiful [site] and is perfectly square; it should be surrounded in the center by pillars occupying one-fourth [of the area], with half of that [measure] for the [remaining] space.

Its *gṛhapiṇḍī* (domed roof) should be at the ears, with a *halakuḍyaka* (wall-like structure); and from the two *gābhās* (pillars/bases), there should be an *aptala* (flat roof) and a *khaṇḍaharmya* (small pavilion) at the tips of the ears.
In their center there should be assembly halls, and within those, a group of four *bhadraśāla* pavilions;
one should adorn the middle sections with lattice windows, balconies, and other such features.
The middle of the site should be shaped like an assembly hall and provided with a front hall;
on the pinnacle, one should adorn it with eight small noses and auspicious peaks (bhadrakūṭas). || 29-152 ||
It is beautiful at its extremities. The foundation of the *viśāla* [temple] is oblong;
from one-third of its width, the inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) shall be formed, and with the remainder, the water-platform (*ambutala*) shall be made. (29-153)
In the *cūḍikākhaṇḍaharmya* [type of temple], the pinnacle (*śikhara*) is shaped like a small chamber (*koṣṭhaka*).
In each city [of temples] with six eyes (*ṣaṇnetra*), one should employ two *nāsya*s there. (29.154)
In the *gṛhapiṇḍī* there should be sixteen [pillars], as well as in the corners and in the center;
one should further adorn it with *viśāla*, *sama*, and *bhadra* types, as well as with *kūṭa* and other features. || 29-155 ||
The *viśāla* [type] should be like the petal of a blue lotus; the *masūraka*, however, is long and angular.
The *nālīgṛha* is one-third [of the width], and from the remaining portion, the *gṛhapiṇḍikā* [is formed]. (29.156)
It should resemble a pigeon-house; outside of that, there should be a plinth and so forth, and the spire should have the shape of a hall, wherein three nose-ornaments (nāsīs) are to be placed.
In the Kapota [style], there should be thirty-eight small [elements] around the nose;
one should adorn it with altars, lattices, stairs, archways, and so forth. (29.158)

The lotus petal; the base (adhiṣṭhāna) of Mahārāja is also elongated and polygonal; the stalk-house (nālīgṛha) according to Vyāsa; and the remaining parts, such as the pedestal (piṇḍī) and the plinth (talā), [are as previously described]. (29.159)
The *koṣṭhaka* and the *śikhara* project out by half the width of the central sanctum (*garbha*); their configuration is like that of the front of a hall, both in front and behind. (29-160)

In the *gṛhapiṇḍī* and the *ardhahāra*, there are four small *nāsikās*; the great halls (*mahāśālā*) extend in the four directions, reaching the corners with a measurement equal to the central core (*garbha*).

The assembly halls (sabhās) should emerge from their respective divisions, with internal recesses and ascending passages; there too, they should be provided with half-niches (niryūhas), along with chambers that are elevated and depressed.
One should likewise construct enclosures that are like the shape of a swastika;
there should be four staircases for the elephants and other [beings], arranged clockwise.
The two pillars named Śrīkhaṇḍa and Citrakhaṇḍa should be at the lower level;
the lotus-throne, the pedestal, and the pillar-base are on the upper levels. (29.164)
One should employ the *nandyāvarta*, the *gajākṣa*, the *gavākṣa*, and the *marutpatha* on each successive level; likewise, the subsequent [ornament] is threefold.
Likewise, there are three kinds of railings, as well as archways and altars;
it is enriched with replicas of all its bodies and adorned with all its limbs. (29.166)
The dwelling called Mahārājāhvaya is for universal monarchs (cakravartins); it is known as the Mahārājacchanda, the foundation of the Mālīgṛha, which is rectangular. (29-167)
The sanctum may be one-fourth [of the total width], the pedestal of the sanctum half of that;
the water-course, the pinnacle-shrine, and the fragmentary shrine are made from the remainder. (29.168)
There should be a pinnacle and a long hall in front, with two "noses" (projections);
at the rear, there is one in the body of the house, and eight "noses" as appropriate.

The *mālīgṛha* (pavilion) is provided with multiple stories and features such as gables equipped with exits; its base is broad like a drum (*nandīviśāla*), and its square shape is elongated by one-third [of its side]. (29.170)
The portion known as the *garbha* (inner sanctum) is derived from the parts of Vyāsa and Rāma; the remainder is obtained by dividing by half and then by eight.
It is joined with the *cūḍīka*, *khaṇḍa*, and *harmya*, as well as the *kūṭa*, *koṣṭha*, and other elements. (29.171)
From the interior at the front of the multi-storied palace (khaṇḍaharmya), the Karṇaprāsādaka should be equal [in size];
on both sides and at the elephant-trunk (hastituṇḍa) there should be two gṛhapiṇḍikās.
Furthermore, on the pinnacle there are indeed twenty-eight [parts];
one should adorn the entire pinnacle, the chamber, and the peak with various architectural members.
The Nandīviśāla [temple] has a floor for the Vedāśra (quadrangular) layout belonging to the type known as Pṛthivījaya;
its sanctum (garbhageha) is one-fourth [of the total], and its wall-mass (gṛhapiṇḍi) is half of that.
The pinnacle and the central chamber should have their colored floor according to the measurement of the inner sanctum;
at each entrance there should be a pavilion, and the remainder consists of the palace, the upper stories, and so forth.
In the chamber situated at the front and back, which is like a cluster of houses,
as well as on both sides and at the top, there are tilakas on the nose.
This [type of temple], which possesses both *ūha* and *pratyūha* and consists of many stories, is known as the *pṛthivījaya*.
Even if it is beautiful in all its limbs, if it is elongated and angular, it is called *masūraka*. (29.177)
The *nālīgṛha* (tube-house) is derived from one-eighth of the height of the beautiful women [the pillars], and the *gṛhapiṇḍikā* (pedestal of the house) from half of that;
the remainder is for the water-course, the ground-level, and likewise for the series of pavilions with crest-projections.
Within that space, there should be four palaces with a height equal to the width of the *karṇa*;
one should join together the *vedī* and *koṣṭha* sections, whose length is twice their own breadth.
On the long-pointed peak, there are indeed six large nostrils; surrounding those, there are eight small ones, making forty-four nostrils in total. (29.180)
In front [of the temple], there should be a pavilion adorned with two types of arches and the like;
it should have hall-fronts, chambers, and stairs consisting of equal sections.
It is endowed with three tiers and a base, beautified by networks of altars and the like;
it is possessed of all its limbs, both those explicitly mentioned and those unmentioned, and is beautiful in every part.
Beautiful in all its parts,
the base of the shadow-house (chāyāgṛha) is rectangular, half as long as that [other dimension];
the tube-house (nālīgṛha) is like a pavilion (maṇḍapa), joined with a gabled upper chamber (śiroharmya).
The half of the interior space shall be the structural mass of the house, adorned with elements such as pinnacles (kūṭa) and the like;
together with the altar-platforms (vedikā), lattices (jālaka), and so forth, this is known as a shadow-house (chāyāgṛha). || 29-184 ||
The shadow-house (chāyāgṛha) and the base (adhiṣṭhāna) of the Rativardhana [temple] are elongated quadrilaterals.
From half the width, the inner sanctum (garbhageha) should be formed; the remaining portion shall be the ground for the ardharikā. (29-185)
Furthermore, one should adorn the Cūḍīka, Khaṇḍaharmya, Karṇa, Madhya, and Antara,
as well as all other parts such as the kūṭas, vedikās, and so forth.
The spire (śikhara) should have its interior (koṣṭha) shaped like a crow's beak (kakārī) and possess eight "nostrils" (nāsikā).
In front of it, there should be a pavilion (maṇḍapa) whose length is equal to the width of the inner sanctum (garbha).

(297) It is provided with broken arches (*khaṇḍaharmya*) and the like, adorned with many pillars, and on the *piṇḍī* [pedestal] it is joined with *tilaka* ornaments and twenty-four spires (*nāsikā*). (29-188)

Abounding in bodily ornaments that follow the form of the body, it becomes an increaser of delight. There are twenty-four celestial palaces of the Kṣatriyas. *Rativardhana*. There are twenty-four celestial palaces of the Kṣatriyas.
Its corners were as long as its own width, and its paved floor was vast and extensive.
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall consist of two parts out of eight divisions of the total width [of the temple];
half of that [shall be] the area for the Brahma-door, the śobhā, the dhvaja, and so forth. (29.190)
The pinnacle (śikhara) should be long and circular, with three nostrils (nāsikā) at the front;
all around it, there should be eight and twenty nostrils with equal projections.
The peaks emerging from the expansion are the surrounding chambers;
the remainder [is adorned] with tilakas, nāsas, hāras, pañjarakas, and so forth. (29.192)
This, known as the Viśālālaya, consists of one, two, or three stories;
it is the site for a large hermitage belonging to a four-pillared structure. (29-193)
With Vyāsa and Rāma as its long dimensions and a single portion of Rāma for the womb,
it is quadrangular in shape like an assembly hall, possessing a pinnacle with nine nostrils.
On both sides, there should likewise be two side-chambers (koṣṭhaka) with a length twice that of the width;
and by means of the remainder, there should be two [structures] called Āpta and Lakhaṇḍa in front of that temple.
On the back, there should be a pavilion with exposed pillars and decorative arches;
from its sides, a *khaṇḍaharmya* (pinnacled structure) should emerge at the tips of its corners.
There should be four threshing floors within the divisions of width and length;
indeed, there are eight staff-halls within the intervals between the corner-pinnacles.
There are fourteen compartments (koṣṭha) of the temple both externally and internally;
the remainder should be decorated as appropriate for the Viṭ and Caturtha [classes].
It has four sides. (p.
298) The foundation of the horse-faced deity is rectangular;
the inner sanctum shall be one-third of its width, and the side-walls shall be half of that. || 29-199 ||
The *aptalam* and the *khaṇḍaharmya* should be formed according to the remaining proportions;
within the cardinal directions, the inner sanctum (*garbha*) and the assembly hall (*sabhā*) are situated from the middle of the *karṇa*, *kūṭa*, and other elements.
There should be chambers, and its pinnacle should have the form of an assembly hall;
in front of that, it should have the shape of a horse's mouth and an assembly hall, with a nose-like projection at the front.
The staircase should be recessed within; one should join the ancillary parts as before.
[This applies to] the horse-faced [shrine]. The base and so forth for the pedestal of Gaṇikā are as before.
Half of the *garbha* (inner sanctum) shall be the structural mass of the house; the remainder shall be for the water-channels, courtyards, and so forth.
In the center, facing the four directions, there should be assembly halls (*sabhās*) according to the measurement of the *garbha*.
On the exterior, there is a pinnacle and a chamber provided with its own desired auspicious hall;
the staircase is indeed recessed within, and there are four broad pediments.

The pavilion (maṇḍapa) is measured from the eastern womb; its spire (śikhara) is shaped like a small chamber (koṣṭhaka). Its pedestal (adhiṣṭhāna) has a long back and is of the "hawk-pattern" (śyenacchanda) type. || 29-205 ||
One should form the inner sanctum (*garbha*) from three-sixteenths of the width, and the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) from half of that;
with the remainder, the *āptalaka* and the *khaṇḍaharmya* should be formed all around.
Likewise, one should fashion the two nostrils in the shape of a hawk at the tip of the crest;
on the crest, there should be twenty-eight small nostrils in number.

The Śyenacchanda [plan] is as before; however, the foundation for the *kukkuṭapuccha* [type] is that same extent. The inner sanctum (*garbhagṛha*) is one-third [of the total], and the pedestal of the house (*gṛhapiṇḍikā*) is half of that. (29–208)
The *aptala*, the *cūḍaharmya*, and the *śikhara* in the form of an assembly hall (*sabhākṛti*) should have their stairs concealed within; it shall possess twenty-eight *nāsikās*. (29.209)
The *kukkuṭapucchaka* [mandala] is joined with the previously mentioned parts beginning with the *kūṭa*;
the *kukkuṭapucchaka*. The base for the *utpala* [lotus mandala] is a square extended by half the diameter. (29–210)
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall be one part of that [total], and the remaining portion shall be for the body and pedestal of the temple.
Its pillars should be open, and its spire (śikhara) should have eight "nostrils" (nāsikā).
In the Kapota [plan], there are sixteen [parts] for the nose; the assembly hall should have four sides in the east;
the dance stage should be in the center; and the remainder is for the water-level and so forth.
The temple called Utpala should be provided with features such as kūṭas and vedikās; however, the base (adhiṣṭhāna) of the Muṇḍaprāsādaka is elongated and quadrangular. 29–113.
The lotus-petal (nālīka) shall be one-third of the width of Vyāsa, and the pedestal of the chamber (gṛhapiṇḍikā) half of that;
the pavilion (maṇḍapa) in front should be square and equal in size to the inner sanctum (garbha).
The pinnacle, the chamber, and the nose-ornament (nāsya) shall each measure twelve units on all sides;
the remainder shall be the pigeon-eave (kapotaśālā), joined with the crest-pavilion (cūḍaharmya) and other such features.
The dwelling known as Muṇḍaprāsāda, consisting of one, two, or three stories and provided with a terrace for the gods, is for Vaiśyas and Śūdras.

The Muṇḍaprāsāda. Thus, the rules for ornamentation have been briefly stated for temples known by their generic names as well as those called after specific [deities], whether they are suitable for gods or suitable for men. (29–217)
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Rule for the Ornamentation of the Jāti and Other Castes," in the Kriyāpāda of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmad-Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 29.
Now begins the thirtieth chapter.
Now, from twelve stories down to three stories,
there are the various types of celestial palaces (*vimāna*) previously described, categorized as superior, middling, and so forth.
The measurement of the height and the width is here stated separately in cubits;
among those, the excellent Ādityatala should be one hundred cubits in height.
The principal [image], though of noble birth, should be seventy cubits in width;
furthermore, according to the sequence, that which is ninety-three cubits in height should be sixty-three cubits in width.
But by the highest measure, it would have eleven stories;
likewise, it would be eighty-four cubits high and fifty-seven cubits in extent. (30.4)
This excellent abode, beautiful by its own measure, is known as having ten stories;
it is seventy-five cubits in height and fifty-one cubits in width. (30–5)
That nine-storeyed [temple] is indeed the principal one, when constructed according to the proper rule;
it is sixty-six cubits high, and forty-five [cubits wide]. (30.6)
The expansive and auspicious abode of the Karās should have eight stories, reaching a height of fifty-seven cubits, consisting of thirty-nine [parts]. (30.7)
The extensive abode of the Karas is proclaimed to have seven stories;
its width is thirty-three cubits and also forty cubits.
That which is as high as eight cubits (nandahasta) shall be five-storied;
that which is thirty-one [cubits] in height and width shall be four-storied.
By its very nature, it is in the *atiśakvarī* meter, three stories high, and lofty in its extent;
thus, beginning from three floors up to twelve stories.
One should decrease two cubits from each stated measurement for every successive level;
thus, there are ten intermediate vimānas here in sequence.
Similarly, by decreasing the middle palaces by two cubits each,
the smallest and other palaces are established up to the surface of the ground.

Alternatively, by means of pairs of hands, beginning with that which causes transformation, the celestial chariots (vimānas) arise from the [categories] such as caste (jāti), ending with the seventh case. 30-13.

p. 301) These [measures], beginning with *tritala* and ending with *arkatala*, constitute the section on the *jāti* vimānas. Starting from eighty-seven cubits (*atyaṣṭi-hasta*) up to sixty-three cubits (*triṣaṣṭi-kara*). (30-14)
In this [system], the *chandāni* begin from the five-fold stage and extend down to the level of the sun;
there are three sets of eight, beginning with the smallest (*kaniṣṭha*), each increasing by two cubits.
The Section on the Palace of Desire (Chandavimāna):
From a width of thirteen cubits and a length of fifty-five, by increasing [the width] by two cubits as before, there are twenty-one variations. (30.16)
The celestial palaces of conceptual construction (vikalpavimāna) range from eleven cubits up to forty-seven cubits in extension;
by increasing the height by two cubits at each step, as before, there are nineteen in number.
Those known as the Ābhāsa [palaces] begin from the fourth level and extend up to the level of the Sun and Mars;
they are indeed the Ābhāsa vimānas.
They are arranged in rows with an even or odd number of hands (cubits), starting from nine cubits and so forth in sequence.
The best and other [types of villages] have seven, eight, six, and five cubits [respectively], while those called "small" (kṣudra) have four, three, and two stories in their sequence. (30.19)
Alternatively, in small dwellings with an extent of three or four cubits,
one should employ a single story or two stories according to what is appropriate.
One should group the *nīca* (low) and other types by increasing [the dimensions] by two cubits at a time.
Regarding this, Pitāmaha states:
"In this context, the best [type] is that which is spread over nine cubits in length and twelve cubits in width."
It should be one story high, with a height of eight and seven cubits for the middle section.
The smallest [structure] would consist of three stories with five seasonal [units] each;
thus ends the section on small celestial palaces (*kṣudravimāna*).
Alternatively, [this is] a summary of all types of celestial palaces. || 30-21 ||
The height should be twice the width, or it may be one-eighth more;
alternatively, for those of smaller stature, the height should be seven parts of the width. (30.22)
The height of the palaces here is six parts more for the middling ones, five parts more for the middle ones, and three parts more for the superior ones. (30.23)
According to their respective authority, they bestow prosperity upon the gods and others,
as well as the supreme [status] of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and universal monarchs (cakravartins).
The twelve-storied [temple] is prescribed for [the worship of] the thirty-three gods, as well as for the lords of the Yakṣas, the Nāgas, and the Creator (Brahmā); it is not ordained for others.
An eleven-storied palace is recommended for the Moon and the Sun;
for Great Kings of Kings, the celestial chariot (vimāna) should have nine floors.
A palace of eight stories is suitable for Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas;
one of seven stories bestows prosperity upon the foremost of the twice-born and upon kings. (30.27)

The mandalas of the lords of the [four] quarters consist of six levels; there should be five for the crown princes; those of the vassals consist of four levels, and that of the city governors is likewise recommended. (30.28)
For illustrious Vaiśyas and Śūdras, as well as for commanders of armies, [houses] of three stories, two stories, or one story are recommended; these are favored by all gods and men.
In this regard:
"That which was stated for the twice-born and others in such numbers—all that is desired for the gods, as well as what was spoken by the lord of the twice-born for kings. (30.30)

"Parāśara has declared that what was spoken by a Vaiśya applies to Śūdras, and everything spoken by one of the twice-born applies to those of lower status; there should be nothing spoken for the low that exceeds [the rules for] the high. (30–31)
In the Kali age, it is traditionally taught that no celestial mansion (vimāna) exceeding one hundred cubits in height should be constructed;
for if it were higher than that, it would be afflicted by the distresses of great winds and other calamities.
The inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) shall be [measured] from half of its own diameter as specified without distinction;
the width of the gabled hall (kūṭaśālā) shall be one-ninth of the width of the temple structure (vimāna).

The length is twice the width in both the even and odd compartments; in the cage-like vestibule (*pañjarālindaka*), which is equal [in size], there should be a wall (*bhitti*) of half of a half-part. (30–34)
Or else, there may be thirty-five porticos, with the remainder consisting of the main body of the house and so forth.
This concludes the section on the division of the floor.
The temple structure is traditionally known to be twofold: the *kāya* (the body) and the *anukāya* (the secondary body). 30–35.
The base, the pillar, the wall, the pitcher, the small pillars, the pot, the beam, and the jayantas follow in this order. (30–36)
The *anumārga* is the body (*kāya*), and it is then called the *anukāya*.
The *uttara*, *vājana*, *śreṇī*, *balīka*, and *karṇapatrikā* [are its parts]. (30–37)
The joints, door-leaves, bolts, and coverings; the water-jars, creepers, and arches, together with the fist-seals and the eight auspicious symbols (30–38).

The lotus-stalks (mṛṇālikā), the staffs (daṇḍikā), the non-prihāras, the nostrils (nāsikā), the bands (paṭṭikā), the eaves (valabhī), the binding altars (bandhavedikā), and the lattices (jālakāni). || 30-39 ||

Likewise, there are the *karṇakūṭas*, the *kūṭas*, the *nīḍakoṣṭhas*, and so forth; as well as the upper coverings, the arrangements, the lime, the clods of earth, the bricks, and other such materials. (30–40)
For names that follow the body are indeed common;
those appropriate to the region are indeed minor and small palaces.
The [temple style] is considered to be threefold: Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara.
That which is square or elongated is declared to be Nāgara.
A temple made of stone is prescribed as being hexagonal or octagonal, or equally square, or even oblong; or it may be quadrangular from the neck downwards. (30–43)
Above the throat, it is eight-sided and is also known to be liquefied;
it may be circular, oval, or even two-sided or circular. (30–44)
That which is below the neck is four-cornered, and that which is above it is circular;
this is the vimāna known as vesara, and these three are said to be tripled [in their proportions].
The *nāgara* style is *sāttvika*, the *drāviḍa* is remembered as *rājasa*, and the *vesara* is *tāmasa*; these three have Brahmā and the other deities as their presiding divinities. (30.46)
That [scripture] is traditionally said to belong to three ages, to have three colors, and to consist of three principles (tattvas) respectively.
The region of Nāgara is traditionally defined as that which lies between the Himavat and the Vindhya mountains.
The land appropriate for a Drāvila is called Drāviḍa, and not otherwise;
the land situated between the Agastya and Vindhya mountains is considered Vesarabhūmi. (30.48)
Some maintain that all [these qualities] exist in all places;
however, in this context, it is intended that the commonality consists in the construction of the floor. (30.49)
A single-story [temple] is prescribed with three, five, seven, or nine cubits;
furthermore, a two-story [temple] should have a number of cubits equal to eleven or seventeen. (30–50)
One should construct [the temple] with three stories using fifteen [parts], and indeed seventeen;
from that point upward, one should increase by five cubits for each story.
One should calculate the measurement of the twelve levels of the abodes according to the rules;
for small and great celestial palaces (vimānas), the height is twice the width.
In the small and medium [temples], the height is two-sevenths less than double [the width];
the height of the smallest inferior [temple] shall be half a part less than that.
In Vyāsa, there should be a pedestal (pīṭha) in the central square surrounded by eight squares;
outside of that, the inner sanctum (garbhagṛha) should be formed by a row of eight squares.
Outside of that row of squares is the wall, and the door is located within one square.
This divine temple is said to have a single wall and a single floor.
In the same way, within the eighty-one-square layout of the palace's extent,
the inner sanctum (garbhamandira) together with its pedestal (sapīṭha) shall be located in the central nine-square section.
Outside of that, one should fashion the wall and the door by means of a row of compartments;
outside of that, one should fashion the central channel all around by means of a row.
Outside that, one should join the wall of the palace in a row and the door;
the door should be placed in either the eastern or western wall at the distance of one square from each end.
In this manner, small pavilions should be understood according to one's preference;
one may construct them as single-storied or up to two stories high, according to one's capacity.
The height here should be twice the width of these [elements].
When the height is divided into eight parts, the base (adhiṣṭhāna) shall consist of one part. (30.60)
The height of the pillar is two parts, while the entablature (prastara) is one part;
the neck (kaṇṭha) is one part, the spire (śikhara) is two parts, and likewise the pinnacle (sthūpī) is one part.
In this manner, one should assemble the single-storied and two-storied *dhāma* structures;
therein, the height of the base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is divided into three parts, and [the proportions] are established according to those parts.
One should construct the *jagatī* with one part, and likewise the *kumuda* with one part;
then, in the remaining portion consisting of four parts, one should construct the *paṭṭikā* with one part.
There may be an interval of one part, while the remaining two parts constitute the *pratimukha*;
this shall be the foundation for small and insignificant celestial palaces (*vimāna*). (30.64)
The foundation for palaces belonging to those of the primary caste and other castes, as appropriate, is described as being provided with a pedestal (sopapīṭha). || 30-65 ||
*Masūraka*, *adhiṣṭhāna*, *vastu*, *ādhāra*, *kuṭṭima*, *tala*, and *ādyāṅga*—these are synonymous terms. (30.66)
That which is always occupied by a temple with its own constituent parts,
being firmly constructed from stone and other materials, is designated as the *adhiṣṭhāna* (the foundation).

Having first firmly constructed the foundation on the site according to the previously mentioned method, and having performed the deposition of the embryo (garbhanyāsa), one should then install the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha).
If there should be an upapīṭha for those [structures] that have a lower base (adhiṣṭhāna), it is for the sake of height, for the sake of beauty, and especially for the sake of protection. || 30-69 ||
The Vedībhadra, Prātibhadra, and Subhadra are considered to be of three types;
the upapīṭha is one-twelfth of the height, and the upānaha is two parts out of twelve.
The lotus-projection shall be half a part, and the neck shall be five parts;
above that, the *kampa* shall be half a part, the lotus one part, and the *vājana* one part. (30.71)

With the remaining portion, there is an upward tremor; thus the *upapīṭhaka* (subsidiary pedestal) has eight limbs, or it may be fashioned with six limbs, excluding the lotuses above and below. (30.72)
This is declared to be the auspicious altar (vedībhadraka), suitable for all types of mansions, and it is of two kinds:
[constructed] with twenty-two, twenty-four, or eleven parts, and with twelve, ten, or nine parts.
One should add two degrees, one degree, and a portion of a degree of Rāma;
that [result] up to the end of the birth [sign] is in the exaltation when divided by thirty-nine parts. (30.74)
The *pāduka*, the *paṅkaja*, the *kampa*, the *kaṇṭha*, and the higher *ambuja*, as well as the *kapota*, *āliṅga*, *kānta*, and so forth, are said to be the *prativājana*. (30.75)
This [pedestal] is called Prātibhadra; it is endowed with all ornaments. In the portion of the base, its height consists of two parts, and from those arises the birth-lotus.
Half [of the height] is for the neck (gala), half for the lotus (padma), and two parts for the fillet (vājana).
Half is for the lotus again, and likewise for the tremor (kampa); the neck is eight [parts], and the upper part is one part.
With half [of the height] comes the lotus, while the *gopāna* (eaves) and the *kampa* (moulding) above it consist of three [parts each];
this is indeed called by the name Subhadraka, an *upapīṭhaka* (subsidiary pedestal).
It should be adorned with lions, elephants, sea-monsters, serpents, spirits, leaves, and so forth; it should have fish-muzzes on each face, and its head should be mounted by a child. (30.79)
In this regard, Maya says:

"The pedestal (pīṭha) consists of three, two, or one measure, being respectively twice the height of the occupied base (adhiṣṭhāna), or equal to it, or one and a half, or one and a quarter, or five parts, or two parts, or equal to the fire (three parts)."

That [pedestal] should be symmetrical with its various parts, well-proportioned, and constructed with excellent materials; furthermore, one should place beneath it a *tūpapīṭha* that is firm and appropriately suited to all the [deity’s] abodes.

Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, concerning the procedure for the secondary pedestal (upapīṭha) and the classification of vimānas by caste and so forth, in the Kriyāpāda of the latter section of the *Siddhāntasāra*, the *Śrīmadīśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*. 30.
